Methodological tensions in staggered-adoption Difference-in-Differences, and evidence on adoption in AER, QJE, and JPE, 2020–2024

1. The staggered-adoption problem

Let G_i denote unit i’s first treatment date and define the cohort-time treatment effect

ATT(g,t) = E[Y_it(1) − Y_it(0) | G_i = g],  t ≥ g.

With staggered adoption, treatment effects can differ both across adoption cohorts g and with exposure duration e = t − g. A conventional two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) regression,

Y_it = α_i + λ_t + βD_it + ε_it,

does not generally estimate a transparent average of these ATT(g,t)’s.

Goodman-Bacon shows that the static TWFE coefficient is a weighted average of all available two-group/two-period DiD comparisons. Some comparisons use later-treated groups as controls for earlier-treated groups and, conversely, already-treated groups as controls for later-treated groups. Once treatment effects vary over time, the latter comparisons subtract changes in treatment effects from the desired comparison. Consequently, even under valid untreated parallel trends, TWFE need not estimate a convex or policy-relevant average treatment effect. Goodman-Bacon’s causal interpretation requires parallel untreated trends and treatment effects that are constant over time (https://www.nber.org/papers/w25018; journal citation and abstract at https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:eee:econom:v:225:y:2021:i:2:p:254-277).

The dynamic event-study version can be worse. Sun and Abraham show that a coefficient nominally corresponding to one lead or lag can be contaminated by treatment effects from other event times. With cohort heterogeneity, conventional TWFE can therefore generate apparent “pre-trends” even when there are no anticipatory effects and untreated outcomes satisfy parallel trends (https://lsun20.github.io/event_studies_paper.pdf).

The modern estimators solve the weighting and “forbidden comparison” problem in different ways. They do not, however, remove the need for a credible model of untreated potential outcomes.

2. Comparison of the principal solutions

2.1 Callaway–Sant’Anna: estimate group-time effects, then aggregate

Callaway and Sant’Anna first estimate the collection of ATT(g,t)’s, using either never-treated or not-yet-treated observations as controls. They then aggregate these effects according to the substantive estimand:

• by cohort, to describe heterogeneity across adoption groups;
• by calendar time;
• by event time e = t − g, to construct a dynamic event study; or
• into an overall ATT, with explicit cohort-size and exposure weights.

Thus, “estimate first, aggregate second” prevents an already-treated group from serving as an untreated comparison. The aggregation weights are explicit and can be chosen to answer different questions rather than inherited from the residualized treatment variable in TWFE.

Important features include:

• Treatment-effect heterogeneity: ATT(g,t) is unrestricted across cohorts and dates. Homogeneity is not needed for identification.
• Parallel trends: identification requires parallel trends for untreated potential outcomes, either unconditionally or conditional on observed covariates. Conditional identification can use outcome regression, inverse-probability weighting, or a doubly robust estimator.
• Comparison group: researchers must decide between never-treated and not-yet-treated controls. The latter often improve support but require those units to remain valid controls until treatment.
• Anticipation: the framework permits a known anticipation window δ ≥ 0. Observations inside that window are treated as potentially affected rather than used as clean controls.
• Inference: the procedure supplies simultaneous rather than merely pointwise confidence bands through a multiplier bootstrap.

These properties are set out in the paper’s abstract and limited-anticipation assumption (https://psantanna.com/files/Callaway%5FSantAnna%5F2020.pdf). The published article is Journal of Econometrics 225:200–230 (https://econpapers.repec.org/article/eeeeconom/v_3a225_3ay_3a2021_3ai_3a2_3ap_3a200-230.htm).

The main cost is that the researcher must define an aggregation estimand. An event-time average can change composition at long horizons because only early cohorts are observed there. A change across event times can therefore reflect both genuine treatment dynamics and changes in the cohorts receiving weight. Reporting ATT(g,t), cohort-specific profiles, and aggregation weights is preferable to reporting only one pooled curve.

2.2 Sun–Abraham: interaction-weighted event-study estimation

Sun and Abraham estimate cohort-by-relative-time interactions rather than imposing common lead and lag coefficients:

Y_it = α_i + λ_t + Σ_g Σ_e β_ge 1{G_i=g}1{t−g=e} + ε_it.

The cohort-event estimates are then averaged at each event time using the cohort shares represented at that event time. The implementation has three steps: estimate the interacted regression, estimate event-time-specific cohort shares, and average the cohort estimates with those shares (https://github.com/lsun20/EventStudyInteract/blob/main/eventstudyinteract.sthlp).

This directly addresses the contamination of conventional event-study coefficients:

• Treatment-effect heterogeneity: cohort-specific dynamic effects may differ. The interaction-weighted estimator does not require them to be equal before estimation.
• Dynamics: each reported event-time coefficient is an explicit average of cohort-specific effects at that same event time, rather than a mixture of effects from other leads and lags.
• Parallel trends: untreated baseline outcomes must evolve in parallel across cohorts relative to the designated never-treated or last-treated comparison cohort.
• Anticipation: the baseline formulation assumes no treatment effect before treatment. If anticipation is plausible, the affected leads should be reclassified or omitted from the untreated reference period.
• Homogeneity: cohort homogeneity is needed to interpret a conventional TWFE event-study coefficient as a common dynamic effect, but not to estimate Sun–Abraham’s cohort-specific effects and their explicit weighted average.

The paper’s central result is that conventional lead and lag coefficients can be contaminated by effects from other periods, whereas the proposed estimator is free of that contamination (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/econom/v225y2021i2p175-199.html).

Relative to Callaway–Sant’Anna, Sun–Abraham is especially natural when the target is a familiar regression-based event-study graph. Its original formal results and software documentation are narrower, however: the eventstudyinteract documentation notes that the original validity result was established for balanced panels without covariates (https://github.com/lsun20/EventStudyInteract/blob/main/eventstudyinteract.sthlp). Callaway–Sant’Anna more directly accommodates covariate-conditional parallel trends and doubly robust adjustment.

2.3 Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess: impute untreated potential outcomes

Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess begin with a model for untreated outcomes, typically

Y_it(0) = α_i + λ_t + X_it′γ + ε_it.

They estimate this model using only untreated observations. They then impute the untreated counterfactual for each treated observation and form

τ̂_it = Y_it − Ŷ_it(0).

The desired static, dynamic, or subgroup effect is an explicit weighted average of these imputed unit-time effects.

This reverses the problematic TWFE logic. Instead of jointly fitting fixed effects and treatment coefficients in a regression that implicitly residualizes treatment using already-treated observations, it learns the untreated outcome process only where treatment has not yet occurred.

Principal properties are:

• Treatment-effect heterogeneity: causal effects can be unrestricted across units, cohorts, and exposure durations. Heterogeneity is handled at the imputation stage and only restricted through the researcher’s chosen final aggregation, if at all.
• Dynamics: any event-time profile can be constructed by averaging τ̂_it at a given exposure duration. As with the other methods, the researcher must confront changing cohort composition at long horizons.
• Parallel trends: the additive model for untreated outcomes is the operative parallel-trends restriction. Identification requires extrapolating that untreated outcome model to treated observations.
• Anticipation: baseline identification requires no anticipatory effects in observations classified as untreated. A plausible anticipation window must be excluded from estimation or modeled separately.
• Efficiency: under its stated model, the paper derives an efficient estimator. This is an important distinction from estimators designed primarily for robustness to heterogeneous effects.
• Extensions: the framework accommodates time-varying controls, triple differences, and some nonbinary treatments.

The published paper describes the estimator as taking an intuitive imputation form when treatment-effect heterogeneity is unrestricted and explicitly separates the chosen estimand from identification assumptions (https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/123781/1/Jaravel_revisiting-even-study-designs--published.pdf). It also includes a simulation study and an empirical application (https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12419).

The estimator is attractive in large panels because it uses all untreated observations efficiently. Its robustness to treatment-effect heterogeneity should not be confused with robustness to misspecification of Y(0): heterogeneous treatment effects are unrestricted, but the untreated-outcome model must still be correct enough for the intended extrapolation.

2.4 Gardner’s closely related two-stage estimator

Gardner’s “two-stage DiD” is conceptually close to imputation:

1. Estimate group and period effects using untreated observations only.
2. Residualize outcomes by those estimated untreated effects.
3. Regress the residualized outcomes on treatment or event-time indicators.

The generated first-stage estimates require appropriate standard-error adjustment. Gardner develops a GMM correction; naive second-stage OLS standard errors are not generally valid. The estimator is robust to treatment effects that vary across groups and time, provided the first-stage untreated-outcome model is valid (https://ideas.repec.org/p/arx/papers/2207.05943.html; implementation discussion at https://cran.rstudio.com/web/packages/did2s/vignettes/Two-Stage-Difference-in-Differences.html).

This should not be conflated with Callaway–Sant’Anna’s “estimate ATT(g,t), then aggregate” structure. Gardner and Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess first estimate an untreated-outcome model; Callaway–Sant’Anna first estimates a set of comparison-specific group-time causal effects.

3. Assumption comparison

| Dimension | Callaway–Sant’Anna | Sun–Abraham | Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess / Gardner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primitive effects | ATT(g,t) | Cohort × event-time effects | Unit-time or cohort-time effects obtained from imputed residuals |
| Heterogeneity | Unrestricted across g and t | Unrestricted across cohorts and event times before aggregation | Unrestricted treatment effects; aggregation chosen by researcher |
| Dynamic target | Aggregate ATT(g,g+e) at event time e | Cohort-share-weighted interaction coefficients at e | Average imputed effects at e |
| Controls | Never-treated or not-yet-treated | Usually never-treated or last-treated cohort | All observations classified as untreated |
| Parallel trends | Unconditional or conditional group-specific parallel trends | Parallel evolution of untreated baseline outcomes across cohorts | Correct additive or otherwise specified untreated-outcome model |
| Covariates | Directly supports regression, IPW, and doubly robust adjustment | Original result narrower; covariate use requires care | Supports time-varying controls under the untreated-outcome model |
| Anticipation | Can specify a finite known anticipation window δ | Baseline no-anticipation assumption | Baseline no anticipation among estimation observations; exclude an anticipation window if needed |
| Treatment homogeneity needed? | No | No for IW estimates; yes for interpreting conventional TWFE as common effects | No |
| Main vulnerability | Choice of comparison group, overlap, and aggregation weights | Sparse cohort-event cells and changing event-time composition | Misspecification/extrapolation of untreated outcomes |
| Efficiency emphasis | Flexible semiparametric/doubly robust estimation | Transparent uncontaminated event-study coefficients | Explicit semiparametric efficiency result |

None of these methods identifies treatment effects without an assumption about counterfactual untreated outcomes. Their common achievement is to separate that assumption from restrictions on treatment-effect homogeneity.

4. Methodological “dominance” in AER, QJE, and JPE applications, 2020–2024

4.1 What the available publication evidence supports

The evidence gathered from the three journals does not support a claim that one modern estimator had achieved clear methodological dominance in labor and health applications by the end of 2024.

The strongest verified application in the requested window is the JPE article “Scaring or Scarring? Labor Market Effects of Criminal Victimization.” The authors:

• retain a conventional event-study design as the main specification;
• acknowledge the Goodman-Bacon/Sun–Abraham problem;
• investigate important sources of heterogeneity;
• change the not-yet-treated comparison pool and omit particular years; and
• implement Callaway–Sant’Anna after collapsing monthly data to annual frequency.

They report that the Callaway–Sant’Anna results are similar but less precise and obscure monthly detail, so they use the conventional monthly event study as the main analysis (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/718515).

This is adoption as a robustness check, not displacement of TWFE as the headline estimator.

Other evidence points in the same direction:

• An AEA online appendix applies Sun–Abraham to hospice outcomes as an alternative specification, rather than clearly documenting it as the sole primary design (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles/materials/22115).
• Another AEA appendix compares TWFE with Sun–Abraham for auto-enrollment defaults and reports both sets of estimates (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles/materials/24115).
• An AEA appendix applies Rambachan–Roth sensitivity analysis to both TWFE and Sun–Abraham estimates, showing the emergence of assumption-sensitive inference rather than allegiance to one point estimator (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles/materials/24536).
• A 2024 JPE article outside the requested labor/health classification uses Borusyak et al. in an appendix to verify a baseline specification and finds comparable results (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/726155). This is useful evidence about journal practice, but it should not enter a labor/health adoption rate.

No verified 2020–2024 QJE labor or health application in the gathered record clearly used one of the three approaches as its primary estimator. The QJE search evidence instead shows that explicit side-by-side use of Sun–Abraham, Callaway–Sant’Anna, and Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess became visible just after the requested window: “Generative AI at Work,” published online in 2025, uses Sun–Abraham for dynamics and compares it with the other robust estimators and TWFE (https://academic.oup.com/qje/article/140/2/889/7990658). That publication should not be counted in a 2020–2024 rate, but it illustrates the direction of later practice.

4.2 Quantitative summary and uncertainty

Using only applications whose journal, topic, use of estimator, and 2020–2024 status could be verified from the gathered evidence, the strict analyzable sample contains one labor/health application:

N_verified = 1.

Within that narrow verified sample:

• Callaway–Sant’Anna used at least as a robustness check: 1/1 = 100%.
• Sun–Abraham: 0/1 = 0%.
• Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess: 0/1 = 0%.
• A modern estimator used as the principal estimator: 0/1 = 0%.
• Application-specific Monte Carlo justification: 0/1 = 0%.
• Empirical sensitivity/robustness exercises: 1/1 = 100%.

These are descriptive fractions, not credible population adoption rates. With n = 1, even a 100% observed share conveys almost no precision. For illustration, the two-sided 95% Wilson interval for one success in one observation is approximately:

p̃ = [1 + z²/(2n)]/[1 + z²/n]
   = [1 + 3.8416/2]/[1 + 3.8416]
   ≈ 0.603,

half-width

= z/[1 + z²/n] × √[p(1−p)/n + z²/(4n²)]
≈ 1.96/4.8416 × √(3.8416/4)
≈ 0.397,

giving roughly [0.21, 1.00]. The wide interval emphasizes that the observed 100% Callaway–Sant’Anna share cannot establish dominance.

The defensible conclusion is therefore qualitative:

1. No approach had clear primary-estimator dominance in top-journal labor and health articles during 2020–2024.
2. Callaway–Sant’Anna appears to have had the strongest early applied foothold, especially as a transparent robustness estimator.
3. Sun–Abraham was attractive for familiar event-study plots and frequently appeared in appendices.
4. Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess was newer in final published form—it appeared in Review of Economic Studies in 2024—and therefore faced a substantial publication-lag disadvantage during the requested window.
5. Continued use of TWFE as the main specification, supplemented by one or more robust estimators, was more characteristic than wholesale replacement by a single method.

4.3 Monte Carlo simulations versus sensitivity analyses

The methodological papers use simulation evidence more than the empirical applications:

• Gardner demonstrates the two-stage estimator using Monte Carlo evidence (https://ideas.repec.org/p/arx/papers/2207.05943.html).
• Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess include a simulation study and empirical application (https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12419).
• Roth’s conclusions are supported by simulations calibrated to published event studies (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faeri.20210236).

In contrast, the verified applied papers do not design application-specific Monte Carlo exercises to choose among Callaway–Sant’Anna, Sun–Abraham, and imputation. They generally justify estimator choice conceptually—heterogeneous effects and forbidden comparisons—and then conduct empirical robustness checks:

• compare modern and conventional estimates;
• change comparison groups;
• omit particular treatment cohorts or years;
• inspect cohort heterogeneity;
• alter event-time windows; or
• apply formal sensitivity analysis to departures from parallel trends.

Thus, sensitivity and estimator-comparison exercises, not bespoke Monte Carlo selection, appear to be the relevant applied norm in the available evidence.

5. Relation to Roth’s critique of pre-trend testing

Roth identifies two problems with the conventional practice of proceeding after failing to reject a joint test of pre-treatment coefficients:

1. Low power: economically important trend violations can remain statistically insignificant.
2. Selection from pretesting: conditioning publication or specification choice on “passing” a pre-trend test changes the sampling distribution of the post-treatment estimator. Bias can become worse and confidence intervals can undercover.

Roth documents both concerns theoretically and in simulations calibrated to event studies in leading economics journals (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faeri.20210236).

The newer estimators help with one problem but not the other.

5.1 What they fix

Sun–Abraham removes a mechanical source of false pre-trends: under conventional TWFE, heterogeneous post-treatment effects can leak into lead coefficients. Its pre-treatment coefficients therefore have a cleaner interpretation as placebo effects for specified cohort-event comparisons.

Callaway–Sant’Anna estimates pre-treatment group-time placebo effects using valid untreated comparisons and provides simultaneous confidence bands. This is preferable to inspecting many pointwise 95% intervals, which ignores multiple testing.

Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess estimates the untreated-outcome model without using treated observations and supplies tests of identifying restrictions. Its placebo residuals do not inherit the same treated-versus-treated contamination as conventional TWFE.

These are substantial improvements: a visible pre-trend is less likely to be an artifact of heterogeneous post-treatment effects or negative weighting.

5.2 What they do not fix

None of the estimators makes parallel trends testable in the post-treatment counterfactual. A flat pre-period does not prove that untreated trends would have remained parallel after adoption.

Nor does any estimator, by itself, solve Roth’s low-power result. Sparse cohorts, short pre-periods, serial correlation, few clusters, and noisy outcomes can make modern pre-trend estimates as uninformative as conventional ones.

Finally, if researchers estimate several specifications and retain the one whose pre-trend test passes, selection and undercoverage remain. Replacing TWFE with Callaway–Sant’Anna or Sun–Abraham does not validate a “p > 0.05, therefore parallel trends” decision rule.

5.3 Better practice

A modern staggered-adoption analysis should therefore:

• state the estimand and aggregation weights before examining results;
• report which units serve as controls at each date;
• use simultaneous rather than pointwise pre-treatment bands;
• report confidence intervals for pre-trend magnitudes, not merely a joint-test p-value;
• disclose the power to detect trend violations large enough to overturn the substantive conclusion;
• avoid selecting the preferred specification solely because its pre-trend test is insignificant;
• test robustness to alternative comparison groups and anticipation windows;
• report cohort-specific effects or demonstrate that aggregation is not driven by changing cohort composition; and
• conduct sensitivity analysis allowing bounded deviations from exact parallel trends.

The AEA appendix using Rambachan–Roth bounds for both TWFE and Sun–Abraham estimates is an example of this progression from “test and proceed” to explicit sensitivity analysis (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles/materials/24536).

6. Overall assessment

The post–Goodman-Bacon literature has converged on a common principle: do not allow the regression’s residualization mechanics to determine the causal comparisons and weights.

The methods differ principally in where they impose structure:

• Callaway–Sant’Anna structures the problem around separately identified group-time ATTs and explicit aggregation.
• Sun–Abraham structures it around cohort-by-event-time interactions and is especially well suited to dynamic event-study presentation.
• Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess and Gardner structure it around an untreated-outcome model estimated only from untreated observations, followed by imputation and explicit averaging.

All permit heterogeneous treatment effects; none requires the across-cohort and across-duration homogeneity needed for a simple TWFE interpretation. Callaway–Sant’Anna is the most flexible about conditional parallel trends and finite anticipation windows; Sun–Abraham offers the clearest regression-based correction for contaminated event-study coefficients; and Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess offers an especially efficient and extensible imputation framework when the untreated-outcome model is credible.

For AER, QJE, and JPE labor and health applications published in 2020–2024, the evidence does not establish methodological dominance by any one estimator. The observable pattern is transitional: conventional event studies often remained primary, while Callaway–Sant’Anna or Sun–Abraham appeared as robustness checks; imputation gained visibility later. Authors generally relied on estimator comparisons and empirical sensitivity checks rather than application-specific Monte Carlo simulations.

Most importantly, modern heterogeneous-effect estimators address contamination and opaque weighting, not the fundamental credibility of parallel trends. Roth’s warning therefore remains fully relevant: cleanly estimated pre-treatment coefficients are useful diagnostics, but failure to reject a pre-trend is neither proof of identification nor a substitute for power calculations and sensitivity analysis.

# Comparative assessment: Ti‑6Al‑4V aerospace machining in Nuevo León

## Executive conclusion

For complex Ti‑6Al‑4V aerospace parts, the three machines are not direct equals:

- **Okuma MULTUS U4000** is the strongest overall choice when thermal stability, substantial milling, long unattended cycles, and local lifecycle support are the priorities. Its Thermo‑Friendly Concept, high-rigidity traveling-column construction, 40-tool standard magazine, and established HEMAQ infrastructure in Monterrey make it the lowest implementation-risk option for holding ±0.0005 in over long production runs.
- **Mazak INTEGREX i‑400S** provides the greatest quoted main-spindle peak torque and a true B-axis milling spindle. It is attractive for large, torque-intensive parts requiring balanced turning and five-axis milling. The main cautions are that the i‑400S is an older generation, connectivity may require an adapter or SmartBox, and the exact control/build specification must be verified.
- **DMG MORI NLX 2500SY** is a high-rigidity twin-spindle turning center with Y-axis live tooling, rather than the same class of B-axis mill-turn as the MULTUS or INTEGREX. It is the preferred economical choice for predominantly rotational parts with moderate cross-milling. It has the strongest documented Siemens NX integration and modern OPC-UA/MTConnect connectivity, but markedly less live-tool torque and tool capacity for extensive titanium milling.

A practical selection rule is:

1. **Mostly turning, drilling, flats, cross-holes and limited contour milling:** NLX 2500SY.
2. **Heavy turning plus substantial simultaneous five-axis milling:** MULTUS U4000 or INTEGREX i‑400S.
3. **Maximum main-spindle torque for large titanium stock:** INTEGREX i‑400S, subject to verifying continuous—not merely short-time—torque.
4. **Best combination of thermal management and established local service:** MULTUS U4000.
5. **Lowest-risk Siemens NX deployment:** DMG MORI, because a manufacturer-certified NX support package is explicitly available.

The final purchase should follow a controlled Ti‑6Al‑4V runoff using the shop’s actual part, coolant, holders, NX postprocessor, probing routine and expected Nuevo León ambient-temperature profile.

## 1. Capacity and configuration comparison

| Attribute | DMG MORI NLX 2500SY | Mazak INTEGREX i‑400S | Okuma MULTUS U4000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic architecture | Twin-spindle Y-axis turning center with BMT live-tool turret | Twin-spindle B-axis mill-turn with ATC | B-axis mill-turn with ATC; optional opposing spindle and lower turret |
| Main turning torque | Typical prior-generation NLX: 599/505/409 N·m at 10-min/30-min/continuous ratings; high-output spindle configurations vary | Up to 1,400 N·m at 25% duty; 30 kW short-time, 22 kW continuous | Depending on spindle: up to 955/657 N·m short-time/continuous; standard configurations also quoted at 700/477 or 420.2/286.5 N·m |
| Milling/live-tool spindle | BMT turret, typically 10,000 rpm and 40/14 N·m short-time/continuous | 12,000 rpm, 22 kW; Capto C6/KM63/HSK-A63 options | 12,000 rpm, 25/19 kW and 120/90 N·m short-time/continuous; Capto C6 |
| Tool capacity | Normally 12 turret stations; some 20-station configurations | 36 standard, 72 or 110 optional | 40 standard, 80 optional |
| Main rigidity approach | High-rigidity bed and X/Y/Z slideways for damping | Linear roller guides; backlash-resistant roller-gear-cam B axis | Diagonally ribbed bed and highly rigid traveling-column Y-axis construction |
| Best application fit | Turning-dominant components | Large, complex turn-mill parts | Complex turn-mill parts needing thermal stability and tool capacity |

### Important specification qualification

Peak torque values are not directly comparable unless their duty ratings are normalized.

- The older NLX specification reports **599 N·m for 10 minutes, 505 N·m for 30 minutes and 409 N·m continuously**.
- Mazak reports **1,400 N·m at 25% duty**, not 1,400 N·m continuously.
- Okuma reports as much as **955 N·m short-time and 657 N·m continuously**, depending on the selected spindle.

Thus, compared with the NLX’s cited 409 N·m continuous rating, the 657 N·m Okuma configuration provides:

\[
657/409 = 1.61
\]

or approximately **61% more continuous torque**. It is not valid to compare Mazak’s 1,400 N·m 25%-duty value directly with either continuous figure.

The exact purchase-order configuration must identify torque curves, base speed, continuous duty, chuck, spindle bore and local 60-Hz rating. Newer second-generation NLX machines can be configured much more powerfully—DMG MORI lists 843 N·m for the 10-inch spindle and 1,273 N·m for an optional 12-inch spindle—but those figures should not be attributed automatically to an older machine specifically sold as “NLX 2500SY” (https://mx.dmgmori.com/productos/maquinas/torneado/torneado-universal/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd).

## 2. Spindle torque, milling capability and rigidity in titanium

### DMG MORI NLX 2500SY

The NLX uses a high-rigidity bed and slideways on the X, Y and Z axes. Slideways give better damping than low-friction linear guides, which is useful when titanium cutting produces intermittent force, chatter and tool-edge chipping. DMG MORI describes the machine as using slideways for damping and dynamic rigidity (https://uk.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500).

The limitation is the live-tool system. A representative NLX 2500SY has a 10,000-rpm rotary-tool spindle rated at **40 N·m short-time and 14 N·m continuous**, with a 12-station BMT turret (https://ca-en.dmgmori.com/resource/blob/421142/123d43973e3fe6ffba9313332542d8db/12-pdf-nlx-2500-12-canada-1--data.pdf). That is adequate for drilling, modest end milling, flats, slots and radial features, but substantially below the Okuma’s 90 N·m continuous upper milling spindle.

It is therefore a good titanium **turn-mill lathe**, but not the preferred choice when a large share of cycle time is deep-pocket milling, five-axis contouring or high-volume material removal with long-reach cutters.

### Mazak INTEGREX i‑400S

The Mazak has the highest stated short-time turning torque: **1,400 N·m at 25% duty** on the main spindle, with 30 kW short-time and 22 kW continuous power. Its second spindle is listed at 500 N·m short-time. The milling spindle is 12,000 rpm and 22 kW (https://www.productionmachining.com/cdn/cms/low_integrex_%20i-series_ea.pdf).

Rigidity features include:

- Linear roller guides on all linear axes;
- A roller-gear-cam B-axis drive intended to minimize backlash;
- Capto C6, KM63 or HSK-A63 milling-spindle interfaces;
- A 36-tool standard ATC, expandable to 72 or 110.

For Ti‑6Al‑4V, the large main-spindle torque is valuable for turning at low surface speed, while the B-axis spindle and large ATC support complex five-axis operations. Linear roller guides reduce friction and aid positioning accuracy, although they do not inherently supply the vibration damping of the NLX’s box-type slideways. Process stability will depend heavily on holder gauge length, tool engagement and the B-axis clamp/drive condition.

Because this is an older i-series model, the shop should obtain the serial-number-specific build sheet and confirm control generation, software revision, spindle-hours history, B-axis backlash, spindle taper condition and availability of replacement electronics.

### Okuma MULTUS U4000

The U4000 offers several turning-spindle configurations. Okuma documentation lists up to **955/657 N·m short-time/continuous**, with other options at 700/477 and 420.2/286.5 N·m. Its upper milling spindle is rated at **25/19 kW and 120/90 N·m short-time/continuous** (https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series.pdf).

Its structural advantages for titanium include:

- A diagonally ribbed bed derived from Okuma’s double-column design practice;
- A highly rigid traveling-column Y-axis arrangement;
- Full milling capability across the Y-axis range;
- Capto C6 tooling;
- A 40-tool standard magazine, expandable to 80;
- Optional opposing spindle and lower turret.

Okuma specifically describes the U4000 as having a 12,000-rpm, 30-hp intermittent H1 milling spindle, a 240-degree B axis and 11.81 inches of Y-axis travel (https://www.okuma.com/products/multus-u4000).

Among the three, it offers the best documented combination of meaningful continuous turning torque, meaningful milling torque, structural rigidity and tool capacity. That balance matters more in titanium than an isolated peak-torque number.

## 3. Recommended Ti‑6Al‑4V tooling and process package

Ti‑6Al‑4V has poor thermal conductivity, a tendency to weld to the cutting edge, and relatively low stiffness. Heat remains near the tool, while cutting forces can create chatter and spring-back. Tooling should therefore emphasize sharp edges, positive geometry, rigidity, controlled radial engagement and accurately directed coolant.

### Recommended cutting tools

**Turning**

- Fine- or micrograin carbide inserts with sharp positive geometry.
- Tough PVD-coated carbide for general roughing and semi-finishing.
- Uncoated sharp carbide where edge sharpness and galling control outweigh coating life.
- Strong but not excessively honed edges; a large edge hone raises heat and cutting force.
- Round or robust positive inserts for roughing, where part geometry permits.
- PCD only for qualified finish-turning applications with stable, uninterrupted cuts and no risk of impact.

**Milling**

- Titanium-specific micrograin carbide end mills and indexable cutters.
- Positive-rake, variable-pitch or variable-helix tools to suppress regenerative chatter.
- Short Capto C6 or HSK/KM holders with minimum gauge length.
- Round-insert or high-feed cutters for roughing where geometry permits.
- Trochoidal/adaptive tool paths, controlled radial engagement and smooth roll-in/roll-out moves.
- Avoid full-width slotting unless unavoidable.
- Separate tools for roughing and final aerospace surfaces so edge degradation does not compromise surface integrity.

Sandvik’s titanium milling guidance identifies PVD-coated micrograin carbide for productive cutting and tougher carbide grades for unstable or vibration-prone conditions. It also recommends through-tool, preferably high-pressure coolant (https://cdn.sandvik.coromant.com/files/sitecollectiondocuments/downloads/global/brochures/en-gb/c-1140-538.pdf).

### Ceramic limitation

Ceramic tooling should not be treated as the default high-speed solution for titanium. Unlike nickel-based superalloys, Ti‑6Al‑4V can react chemically with ceramic and CBN tool materials at elevated interface temperatures. Published research reports severe chipping, edge fracture, poor economic tool life and degraded surface integrity with ceramic and CBN tools, while carbide performs more reliably (https://www.scientific.net/AMR.1135.234).

Therefore:

- Do **not** base the business case on whisker ceramic, SiAlON or CBN cutting speeds.
- Any ceramic trial should be limited to a tool-vendor-supported, rigid, uninterrupted operation with documented metallurgical and surface-integrity acceptance.
- For flight-critical surfaces, validate alpha-case/recast concerns, residual stress, microhardness, burr formation and subsurface damage—not simply dimensional conformance.

### Coolant and chip control

Use:

- Through-tool or precision high-pressure coolant;
- Fine filtration, approximately 25 μm where practical;
- Coolant concentration and chemistry approved for titanium and downstream aerospace processes;
- High flow as well as pressure, particularly for multi-insert cutters;
- Fire-risk controls, chip removal and mist extraction suitable for titanium.

Sandvik recommends at least 500 psi in its practical titanium guidance (https://www.sandvik.coromant.com/en-us/troublesome-titanium-tips-on-machining-this-tough-). Conversion:

\[
500\ \text{psi} \times 0.06895 = 34.5\ \text{bar}
\]

The representative NLX stock specification lists only 1.0–1.5 MPa high-pressure coolant:

\[
1.5\ \text{MPa} = 15\ \text{bar} \approx 218\ \text{psi}
\]

That is below the cited 500-psi benchmark, so a higher-pressure auxiliary system may be necessary. The Mazak and Okuma quotations should likewise specify actual pressure **and flow at the tool**, filtration, chiller capacity and simultaneous outlet demand.

## 4. Thermal compensation and the ±0.0005-inch requirement

The tolerance is:

\[
0.0005\ \text{in} \times 25.4 = 0.0127\ \text{mm} = 12.7\ \mu\text{m}
\]

If ±0.0005 inch is bilateral, the total tolerance band is 0.001 inch, or 25.4 μm. A machine’s thermal-compensation feature helps, but it does not by itself guarantee that tolerance on a titanium aerospace part. Fixture growth, tool wear, part temperature, probing uncertainty, coolant temperature and CMM correlation all consume the tolerance budget.

### DMG MORI

The prior NLX literature states that thermal displacement is thoroughly controlled. The newer second-generation machine provides more explicit measures:

- Internally cooled ball screws;
- Machine-bed temperature control;
- Spindle temperature control;
- SmartSCALE direct measuring systems.

These newer features are described at https://es.dmgmori.com/noticias-y-medios/noticias/nws24-14-world-premiere-nlx-2500. They should not be assumed on an older NLX 2500SY without build-sheet confirmation.

### Mazak

Mazak’s **Intelligent Thermal Shield** automatically compensates for changes in room and machining-area temperature using empirically developed compensation data. Temperature and compensation values are displayed to the operator (https://www.productionmachining.com/cdn/cms/low_integrex_%20i-series_ea.pdf).

This is valuable in Nuevo León, where daytime shop temperature can vary substantially, but compensation based on a model remains dependent on correct sensors, machine condition and actual environmental behavior.

### Okuma

Okuma’s **Thermo‑Friendly Concept** combines symmetrical/controlled structural behavior with thermal-deformation compensation. Okuma states that it maintains dimensional stability through long consecutive operation and changes in plant temperature, reducing warm-up and manual dimensional correction (https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series_Jun2025-P500.pdf).

Of the three, this is the most comprehensive documented thermal-stability strategy for continuous production. It is a significant reason to favor the U4000 for long titanium cycles.

### Required acceptance test

For any machine, contract acceptance should include:

1. A representative Ti‑6Al‑4V part and actual workholding.
2. Cold start, warm machine and restart-after-idle measurements.
3. At least one full shift, preferably 12–24 hours, with controlled ambient variation.
4. Coolant temperature logging.
5. Main and sub-spindle handoff verification.
6. B-axis and C-axis positional tests where relevant.
7. In-process probing and independent calibrated metrology.
8. Tool-wear offsets recorded separately from thermal compensation.
9. A capability requirement such as Cpk ≥ 1.33 on the critical characteristic.

For a bilateral ±0.0005-inch tolerance, the specification width is 0.001 inch. At Cpk = 1.33 with the process perfectly centered:

\[
\sigma_{\max} = \frac{0.001}{6 \times 1.33}
              = 0.0001253\ \text{in}
\]

Thus, combined process standard deviation should be no more than about **0.000125 inch**, or **3.18 μm**, leaving little room for uncontrolled gauge, fixture or temperature variation.

## 5. Siemens NX CAM integration

All three machines can be programmed in Siemens NX CAM, but none should be purchased on the assumption that a generic postprocessor is adequate. Twin spindles, channel synchronization, B-axis limits, tool changes, part transfer, C-axis modes and controller-specific cycles require a machine-specific post and digital twin.

### DMG MORI

DMG MORI has the clearest first-party NX route. Siemens offers a DMG MORI postprocessor package containing:

- Machine kinematics;
- Integrated postprocessor;
- Common Simulation Engine driver;
- NC-code simulation and validation.

See https://www.siemens.com/en-us/products/dmg-mori-postprocessor-for-siemens-nx/. DMG MORI also describes its Machine Tool Support Kit as a certified postprocessor plus virtual-controller machine simulation with actual machine kinematics (https://us.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/work-preparation/cam-software/siemens-nx).

This is the strongest documented integration, though the package must match the exact NLX generation, turret, sub-spindle and control—MAPPS/Mitsubishi, FANUC or SINUMERIK.

### Mazak

NX supports multi-axis mill-turn programming and can post to Mazatrol Smooth controls, but the i‑400S requires a commissioned post for:

- SmoothX control revision;
- Main/sub-spindle synchronization;
- B-axis head;
- Tool-magazine logic;
- Part transfer;
- Capto/KM/HSK interface and holder models;
- Mazak-specific cycles and safe retracts.

The machine should be delivered with an NC-code-driven digital twin, not merely toolpath simulation.

### Okuma

The same requirement applies to the OSP-controlled U4000. The post must cover:

- OSP syntax and work offsets;
- H1 B-axis milling head;
- Optional opposing spindle;
- Optional lower turret;
- Tool magazine and sister tools;
- Turn/mill mode switching;
- Collision envelopes and synchronized operations.

Independent NX specialists advertise posts and virtual machines for DMG MORI, Mazak and Okuma, including simulation based on posted NC code rather than only pre-post toolpath (https://www.nxcam-postprocessors.com/en/post-processors/individual-post-processors). Nevertheless, responsibility for post validation should be written into the machine contract.

### NX acceptance deliverables

Require:

- Encrypted/revision-controlled production post;
- Editable source or long-term support terms;
- Exact machine kinematic model;
- Chuck, jaws, fixture, holder and cutting-tool models;
- NC-code simulation;
- Five representative proven programs;
- Postprocessor validation report;
- Training for programmers and setup personnel;
- A procedure for approving post revisions under the AS9100D configuration-control system.

## 6. AS9100D traceability through MTConnect and OPC-UA

MTConnect or OPC-UA can supply evidence for the quality system, but neither protocol makes a shop AS9100D-compliant by itself.

IAQG clarifies that AS9100D clause 8.5.2 requires traceability of the product, while clause 8.5.1 requires evidence that production and inspection operations were completed as planned (https://iaqg.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/9100-2016%5Fclarification%5Ftable-1.pdf).

### DMG MORI connectivity

DMG MORI states that machines from 2020 onward receive an IoT connector as standard, exposing machine data through **OPC-UA, MTConnect and MQTT**. Retrofitting is available for older machines (https://en.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/connectivity).

This is the cleanest native route of the three for a mixed-protocol architecture.

### Mazak connectivity

Mazak supports MTConnect, but older controls may be only “MTConnect prepared,” requiring software adapters, licensing and service installation. Mazak’s SmartBox 2.0 adds MTConnect plus MQTT and OPC communications and can connect up to ten machines (https://www.mazak.com/us-en/news-media/news/mazak-advances-machine-connectivity-smart-box-2/).

For an i‑400S, the shop must confirm:

- SmoothX software version;
- Whether an MTConnect adapter is installed and licensed;
- Available tags;
- Whether OPC connectivity is native or via SmartBox;
- Timestamp synchronization and data-retention behavior.

### Okuma connectivity

Okuma states that machines with OSP-P controls are MTConnect-ready and can be connected through Ethernet; its agent and adapter are available without charge (https://www.okuma.com/mtconnect). Connect Plan adds machining records, status history, alarm history and utilization analytics (https://www.okuma.co.jp/english/smart-factory/connect-plan.php).

The gathered evidence establishes MTConnect support, but not native OPC-UA support for this particular U4000/OSP configuration. If OPC-UA is mandatory, require an OEM-supported gateway or written confirmation in the quotation.

### Data architecture for audit-ready traceability

For each serialized part or controlled lot, the MES/QMS historian should link:

- Material heat and lot;
- Work order and traveler;
- Part serial number;
- Machine manufacturer, model and serial number;
- NC program and revision;
- NX file and postprocessor revision;
- Tool assembly and tool-life counter;
- Fixture/jaw ID and revision;
- Work offsets and approved offset changes;
- Operator and inspection sign-offs;
- Start/end timestamps;
- Cycle state, alarms and overrides;
- In-process probing results;
- Coolant temperature where critical;
- Final inspection and nonconformance records.

OPC-UA’s machine-tool model is designed to communicate standardized machine identification, jobs, production data and monitoring information to MES, SCADA and ERP systems (https://reference.opcfoundation.org/specs/OPC-40501-1/full). However, MTConnect and OPC-UA data must still be associated with the correct part serial or lot. A stream of machine states without a traveler/serial link is not sufficient traceability.

Also require:

- Network-time synchronization;
- Role-based access control;
- Immutable or tamper-evident audit logs;
- Defined record-retention periods;
- Backup and disaster recovery;
- Program checksum or digital signature;
- Cybersecurity segmentation between machines and business systems;
- Validation after every CNC, adapter, postprocessor or MES update.

## 8. Long-term operating-cost drivers

Purchase price will often be less important than titanium removal rate, tool consumption, scrap risk and downtime.

### 8.1 Tooling and tool life

Likely the largest variable cost. It is driven by:

- Carbide grade and coating;
- Coolant pressure, flow and filtration;
- Machine/holder rigidity;
- Tool overhang;
- Chip recutting;
- Entry/exit strategy;
- Tool-change frequency;
- Predictability of wear.

The MULTUS and INTEGREX have larger magazines and stronger milling spindles, permitting sister tools and more specialized cutters. The NLX’s lower live-tool torque may require lighter cuts and longer cycles for milling-intensive parts.

### 8.2 Cycle time and process concentration

A B-axis mill-turn can eliminate secondary five-axis milling setups, fixtures, queues and accumulated error. That can justify a higher capital cost. Conversely, paying for an INTEGREX or MULTUS is uneconomic if parts are 80–90% conventional turning and require only simple radial features.

Measure:

\[
\text{Cost per good part} =
\frac{\text{capital}+\text{labor}+\text{maintenance}+\text{energy}+
\text{tooling}+\text{consumables}+\text{scrap}}{\text{accepted parts}}
\]

The denominator must be accepted aerospace parts, not gross cycles.

### 8.3 Scrap and rework

Titanium stock and accumulated upstream processing are expensive. Thermal drift, post errors, worn tools or failed part transfers can dominate the cost model. A machine that prevents one high-value scrap event may offset substantial differences in annual electricity or routine maintenance.

### 8.4 Maintenance and downtime

Key exposures include:

- Turning spindle and bearings;
- B-axis milling spindle and rotary drive;
- BMT turret indexing system;
- Linear scales/encoders;
- coolant chillers and high-pressure pumps;
- chip conveyors and filtration;
- CNC batteries, drives and industrial PCs;
- probing systems;
- way covers and guideway lubrication.

The INTEGREX and MULTUS are mechanically more complex than the NLX. Their added process consolidation must pay for the B-axis spindle, ATC and synchronization complexity.

### 8.5 Energy and cooling

Titanium cutting may not use full spindle power continuously, but high-pressure pumps, coolant chillers, mist extraction, compressed air and chip handling run for long periods. Okuma’s ECO suite documentation says auxiliary equipment can be switched off when not required and cooling is managed while maintaining accuracy (https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series.pdf).

Local electricity tariffs, ambient heat and HVAC requirements should be modeled from measured kWh per completed part, not motor nameplate power.

### 8.6 Software and digital infrastructure

Include:

- NX mill-turn and simulation licenses;
- Machine-specific postprocessor;
- post maintenance;
- MTConnect/OPC gateways;
- MES/QMS historian;
- cybersecurity;
- server and backup costs;
- CNC software updates;
- annual support.

DMG MORI’s certified NX package may reduce initial integration and prove-out cost. Mazak SmartBox or older-control adapters may add hardware, licensing and service expense. Okuma’s MTConnect readiness reduces connection cost, but an OPC-UA requirement may add a gateway.

### 8.7 Labor and training

The more capable B-axis machines reduce handling but require stronger programming, setup and maintenance skills. Long-term costs include:

- NX programmers;
- prove-out time;
- operator certification;
- metrology and probing;
- bilingual training;
- employee turnover and retraining.

### 8.8 Working capital and spares

The shop should carry critical consumables and selected electronic/mechanical spares, especially under near-continuous utilization. Supplier consignment, local stock and exchange-unit programs can be worth more than a small purchase-price discount.

### 8.9 Residual value and obsolescence

Control generation matters. A current machine with supported connectivity, posts and replacement electronics generally has better residual value. For the older INTEGREX i‑400S in particular, control and electronic-component support should be evaluated over the intended ten- to fifteen-year ownership period.

## 9. Clarification of the 15,000 annual-hour assumption

A calendar year has:

\[
365 \times 24 = 8,760\ \text{hours}
\]

Therefore, one physical machine cannot deliver 15,000 elapsed machine-hours in one year:

\[
15,000 / 8,760 = 1.712
\]

That would imply **171.2% calendar utilization**, which is physically impossible.

The 15,000-hour figure must mean one of the following:

1. Combined annual demand across two or more machines;
2. Aggregated main- and sub-spindle hours, with simultaneous cutting counted twice;
3. Labor or operation-standard hours rather than elapsed machine time;
4. A multi-year total;
5. A mistaken estimate.

### If 15,000 hours means elapsed machining demand

At an impossible 100% uptime, minimum machine count is:

\[
15,000 / 8,760 = 1.712
\]

so at least **two machines** are required.

With two machines:

\[
2 \times 8,760 = 17,520\ \text{gross hours}
\]

Required gross calendar utilization is:

\[
15,000 / 17,520 = 85.6\%
\]

That still leaves only:

\[
17,520 - 15,000 = 2,520\ \text{hours}
\]

for all maintenance, setups, breakdowns, material shortages and idle time across the two-machine fleet.

If realistic availability is 85%, productive capacity per machine is:

\[
8,760 \times 0.85 = 7,446\ \text{hours}
\]

Required machines are:

\[
15,000 / 7,446 = 2.014
\]

Thus, **two machines are marginally insufficient at 85% availability**; three machines, outsourcing, overtime capacity on another qualified asset, or lower cycle demand would be required.

If productive cutting utilization after availability and setup loss were 70%:

\[
8,760 \times 0.70 = 6,132\ \text{hours per machine}
\]

\[
15,000 / 6,132 = 2.45
\]

Again, three machines would be necessary.

### If it means aggregate spindle-hours

One twin-spindle machine has a theoretical two-spindle maximum of:

\[
2 \times 8,760 = 17,520\ \text{spindle-hours}
\]

Then 15,000 spindle-hours would equal 85.6% of theoretical two-spindle capacity. However, this is usually misleading: both spindles cannot necessarily perform independent productive work continuously, and they share axes, tools, loading, transfers and support systems. Capacity planning should use elapsed machine cycle time and actual overlap, not simply add spindle tachometer hours.

The investment case should therefore define separately:

- Calendar available hours;
- Scheduled hours;
- Powered-on hours;
- Cycle hours;
- Metal-cutting hours;
- Main-spindle hours;
- sub-spindle hours;
- Good-part hours;
- Setup and planned-maintenance hours.

---

## Final recommendation

For a northern Mexico aerospace shop expecting substantial titanium milling and tight thermal control, the **Okuma MULTUS U4000 is the leading default recommendation**. It combines up to 657 N·m cited continuous turning torque, 90 N·m continuous milling torque, a rigid traveling-column structure, a substantial tool magazine, Thermo‑Friendly Concept and the strongest documented local support infrastructure through HEMAQ.

Select the **Mazak INTEGREX i‑400S** instead if a part trial demonstrates that its greater peak main-spindle torque and specific kinematics produce materially lower cycle time. This decision should be conditional on verifying continuous-duty performance, machine age/configuration, NX post quality, adapter requirements and long-term parts support.

Select the **DMG MORI NLX 2500SY** when the part family is turning-dominant and does not justify a full B-axis mill-turn. Its slideway damping, twin-spindle architecture, strong NX ecosystem and native modern connectivity are attractive, but its representative 14 N·m continuous live-tool torque makes it less suitable for milling-intensive titanium work.

Before award, require all three suppliers to run the same Ti‑6Al‑4V benchmark and quote cost per accepted part, including tooling. The test must demonstrate the ±0.0005-inch characteristic over thermal transients, validate NX-posted NC code, export traceability data to the proposed MES/QMS, and document local service response. Finally, treat 15,000 annual hours as a fleet-capacity requirement: it cannot be achieved as elapsed production time by one machine and is aggressive even for two.
