final.content:
# ERP Interface Design for Manufacturing Supervisors Moving from AS/400

## Executive findings

For production-floor supervisors aged roughly 45–60 who have limited experience outside a legacy AS/400 system, the available evidence supports a **hybrid interface**:

- Keep a small, stable set of primary tasks and status indicators persistently visible.
- Use progressive disclosure for exceptions, detailed inventory dimensions, material adjustments, scheduling, routing, costing, and other occasional functions.
- Preserve advanced-function discoverability through clearly labeled secondary actions, search, and a consistent “More actions” location—not icon-only or deeply nested menus.
- Provide a separate exception-oriented supervisor workspace rather than placing every KPI and transaction on the landing page.

SAP S/4HANA, Oracle NetSuite, and Microsoft Dynamics 365 all provide role-based presentation, but implement it differently:

- **SAP S/4HANA/Fiori:** strongest emphasis on role-specific app catalogs, spaces, pages, and task-focused apps. This can produce effective progressive disclosure, but mixed Fiori and legacy SAP GUI/Web Dynpro applications can reduce consistency.
- **Oracle NetSuite:** retains persistent module navigation and record forms, overlaid with role-based “centers,” dashboards, custom forms, and permissions. It offers strong discoverability but can expose substantial form and dashboard complexity unless aggressively configured.
- **Microsoft Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management:** offers the clearest documented shop-floor pattern: configurable, touch-optimized role views with “My jobs,” “Active jobs,” and selectively exposed toolbar actions, while broader supervisor workspaces surface exceptions.

There is **no credible, head-to-head published study found here** reporting task-completion percentages or training hours for these three products on identical inventory and work-order tasks among 45–60-year-old production supervisors. Vendor documentation establishes interface capabilities, and case studies report operational improvements, but generally do not isolate navigation design as the cause. Therefore, claims that one product intrinsically produces a particular completion-rate or training-time advantage would be unsupported.

---

## 1. Progressive disclosure versus persistent navigation

### Progressive disclosure

Progressive disclosure initially presents only information and actions needed for the current task, revealing secondary functions in details panels, dialogs, additional tabs, or secondary toolbars.

Likely benefits for the target workforce include:

- Smaller visual search space.
- Fewer opportunities to select an irrelevant action.
- Lower working-memory demand during unfamiliar workflows.
- Easier role-specific training.
- Reduced risk that a supervisor changes planning, costing, or inventory-control data unintentionally.

Its principal risk is **poor discoverability**. A supervisor who occasionally needs to adjust consumption, inspect a BOM component, change a schedule, or examine batch inventory may not remember where a hidden function resides.

### Persistent navigation

Persistent navigation keeps modules, task categories, or common actions visible throughout the application.

Likely benefits include:

- Stable orientation and easier recovery from navigation errors.
- Better discovery of occasional functions.
- Greater transfer for AS/400 users accustomed to fixed menu structures and known option paths.
- Less dependence on remembering which contextual menu contains an action.

Its costs are:

- More choices competing for attention.
- Larger visual search space.
- Greater likelihood of selecting the wrong transaction or data scope.
- Longer initial training when the interface exposes the full ERP information architecture.
- Dashboard crowding, especially when several roles are combined.

### Evidence relevant to age and experience

A controlled study of feature-rich mobile interfaces examined whether visually reducing the feature-search space improves navigation by older adults. Its premise and findings support reducing visible alternatives to improve navigation efficiency and accuracy, while still making features retrievable on demand (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3613904.3642796).

An earlier experiment comparing hyperlink and non-hyperlink navigation found overall effectiveness advantages for hyperlinks, but older users experienced more menu disorientation from hyperlinks than younger users (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1240624.1240676). This cautions against assuming that numerous shortcuts and cross-links always improve performance.

These studies are not ERP trials, and their “older adult” samples do not exactly match working supervisors aged 45–60. They are nevertheless directionally relevant because the key moderator is likely not chronological age alone, but the combination of:

- Low familiarity with modern graphical conventions.
- Reduced confidence during a high-consequence transition.
- Reliance on procedural memory formed around a stable legacy interface.
- A need to divide attention between the system and shop-floor operations.

The design implication is not “hide everything.” It is to **reduce the primary search space while maintaining stable, labeled paths to advanced functions**.

---

## 2. Product comparison

## 2.1 SAP S/4HANA and SAP Fiori

### Navigation model

SAP describes business roles as a fundamental Fiori UX concept: roles represent the work a person performs, and SAP-delivered role templates can be copied and refined for actual organizational responsibilities. Roles are connected to catalogs, spaces, pages, application visibility, and authorization (https://learning.sap.com/courses/exploring-the-authorization-concept-for-sap-fiori-on-sap-s-4hana/creating-business-roles-for-sap-fiori-content).

This is essentially app-level progressive disclosure:

1. The role determines which app catalog is available.
2. Spaces and pages organize the selected applications.
3. A task-focused app exposes the relevant workflow.
4. Record details and advanced actions are reached within the app.

SAP also allows legacy transactions—SAP GUI for HTML or Web Dynpro—to be included in Fiori catalogs and launched from tiles. That protects functional coverage but can create abrupt shifts in interaction style. SAP’s inventory training example specifically shows an inventory role catalog containing Fiori services plus a legacy Web Dynpro Physical Inventory Analysis application (same source).

### Inventory management

SAP’s documented inventory role pattern can expose inventory applications such as **Material Documents Overview** through a dedicated inventory-management catalog. This keeps inventory functions separate from unrelated finance or administration functions while allowing a supervisor to drill from summaries into material-document details (https://learning.sap.com/courses/exploring-the-authorization-concept-for-sap-fiori-on-sap-s-4hana/creating-business-roles-for-sap-fiori-content).

The role/catalog approach is advantageous when a supervisor’s main inventory tasks are narrowly defined—for example:

- Review stock or material movements.
- Investigate shortages.
- Post or inspect goods movements.
- Perform or review physical-inventory activity.

The risk is under-provisioning. If an occasional but legitimate exception function is omitted from the role or page, the user may not be able to find—or even access—it without changing roles or requesting authorization.

### Production/work-order creation

SAP’s production-order documentation describes **Create Production Order** and **Manage Production Orders** as rich applications. A production order may expose material, operation, status, planned and actual costs, component and operation overviews, release, availability checks, capacity planning, technical close, goods movements, cost analysis, and confirmation details (https://learning.sap.com/courses/explaining-scenarios-in-production-accounting/detailing-a-production-order).

That breadth makes progressive disclosure particularly important. The preferred supervisor flow is:

1. Present the required order type, material, plant, quantity, and schedule first.
2. Default routing, BOM, scheduling profile, and release behavior where the business process permits.
3. Show validation and material-availability issues before submission.
4. Place capacity, cost analysis, detailed operation maintenance, and technical closing behind clearly labeled detail areas or secondary actions.
5. Return the user to a filtered “my plant/my area” order list after creation.

### Expected effect

Fiori’s role design should reduce initial search and training burden relative to exposing the full SAP application estate. However, that is a reasoned design expectation, not a documented product-specific completion-rate result. Benefits will depend heavily on:

- How narrowly roles are configured.
- Whether spaces and pages match real plant responsibilities.
- How many legacy applications remain.
- Whether users with multiple responsibilities receive one coherent combined page or several roles they must switch among.

---

## 2.2 Oracle NetSuite

### Navigation model

NetSuite uses role-based **centers**. Each center contains persistent tabbed pages and links relevant to the assigned role. Each page can contain a real-time dashboard composed of portlets. Users can personalize dashboards, and administrators can publish standardized dashboards to groups (https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/chapter_N131898.html).

Users with multiple roles can switch roles, causing the interface to refresh to the corresponding center. Administrators can create:

- Custom centers.
- Custom tabs and links.
- Custom roles.
- Published dashboards.
- Role-specific permissions and transaction forms.

This is a more persistent-navigation-oriented model than a highly reduced task shell. It supports discoverability, but administrators must control the number of tabs, links, portlets, reminders, searches, and fields.

### Inventory management

NetSuite’s WMS permissions can be assigned selectively to custom roles. Inventory-processing permissions cover inventory search, creation, transfer, cycle counts, replenishment, bin transfers, and assembly picking/building for work orders. Oracle explicitly advises omitting permissions for tasks a role does not perform—for example, not assigning Work Order permission if work orders are outside that role (https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/section_156520480478.html).

For supervisors, an effective center would persistently display only:

- Inventory exceptions or shortages.
- Counts awaiting review.
- Work orders needing material.
- A direct inventory search.
- Primary create or release actions.

Detailed item dimensions, replenishment settings, bin/status maintenance, and administrative searches should remain accessible through record details or a labeled secondary inventory tab.

### Work-order creation

NetSuite’s standard work-order path is persistently navigable as:

**Transactions → Manufacturing → Enter Work Orders**

The form can include customer, assembly, BOM and revision, phantom subassemblies, WIP, routing, automatic lag calculation, quantity, order status, scheduling method, supply-required date, start/end dates, subsidiary, department, class, location, component lines, allocation, commitment, priority, relationships, sales-team data, communications, tasks, phone calls, files, and notes (https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/article_161538823664.html).

This is comprehensive, but potentially cognitively expensive. The documentation notes that field order and availability can differ by custom form, providing the mechanism needed to simplify it.

For the target users, create a dedicated supervisor work-order form that:

- Shows assembly, quantity, location, required date, and release status first.
- Defaults subsidiary, department, class, location, BOM revision, and normal scheduling method.
- Displays components as read-only unless adjustment is part of the supervisor’s job.
- Hides CRM relationships, sales teams, communications, and outsourcing fields when irrelevant.
- Reveals WIP, routing, phantom-subassembly, lag, and manual date override options only under an “Advanced production settings” section.
- Blocks or warns on irreversible choices. Oracle notes, for example, that after an assembly build is associated with a work order, certain assembly and quantity changes become constrained (same source).

### Expected effect

NetSuite’s persistent tabs and role center may feel more predictable to an AS/400 user than a collection of loosely related application tiles. Conversely, the standard work-order record can present too much information. NetSuite will therefore benefit more from **custom forms and published role dashboards** than from simply assigning a standard manufacturing role.

---

## 2.3 Microsoft Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management

### Navigation model

Dynamics 365 provides general module navigation and broad management workspaces, but also a purpose-built **Production Floor Execution** interface. Microsoft describes it as touch-optimized, visually contrasted for shop-floor accessibility, and organized around filtered job views (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/production-floor-execution-use).

Administrators can create separate configurations for different work cells or roles. Each configuration can control:

- Which tabs appear.
- Whether the main view is Active jobs, All jobs, My jobs, or My machine.
- Whether job details appear.
- Which actions are on the primary toolbar.
- Which actions are on the secondary toolbar.
- The order of tabs and actions.

Microsoft gives the concrete example of displaying a job-instructions button in one work cell but omitting it in another where instructions are unnecessary (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/production-floor-execution-tabs).

This is the strongest documented example among the three products of deliberate progressive disclosure at the production-floor interface.

### Inventory and material use

Production Floor Execution supports material consumption and inventory accuracy during job execution. Workers can:

- Register batch or serial numbers.
- Scan tracked components.
- Report good and scrap quantities.
- Adjust actual material consumption.
- Reserve specific material batches or serials.
- Keep inventory current when actual consumption differs from the plan.

The **Adjust material** action can be placed in a primary toolbar, secondary toolbar, or shown in the progress/scrap dialog after a quantity is entered (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/production-floor-execution-use).

That placement choice directly illustrates the design tradeoff:

- Put it on the primary toolbar if adjustment is frequent and time-critical.
- Put it in the report-progress dialog if it is normally associated with completion.
- Put it on the secondary toolbar if it is legitimate but occasional.

For supervisors, the broader Production Floor Management workspace can surface material exceptions as tiles. Selecting an exception tile drills into the affected BOM/formula lines and release-to-warehouse action, rather than showing all material detail continuously (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/improved-visibility-into-material-exceptions).

### Production/work-order workflow

The floor interface is primarily for executing jobs against production orders rather than full production-order creation. Workers select a job, choose **Start job**, confirm quantity, and later use **Report progress** or **Report scrap**. The interface separates:

- **My jobs:** assigned work.
- **Active jobs:** work already started by the signed-in worker.
- **All jobs:** all matching unfinished jobs.
- **My machine:** machine state, counters, maintenance, and downtime.

The initial list can still contain many columns—order, operation, product, requested, started, completed, scrap, remaining, and unit—so configurations should prioritize the columns and view appropriate for a supervisor’s role.

Production-order creation and planning remain in the richer Supply Chain Management client. Therefore, a supervisor who both executes and creates orders needs a deliberate bridge: a persistent “Create production order” or “Manage production orders” action in the supervisor workspace, but not the full planning module on every floor screen.

### Expected effect

Dynamics’ separation of execution, exception management, and full planning is well aligned with the target population. The risk is fragmentation: if a user must move unpredictably among the floor interface, general client, mobile warehouse application, and Power Apps, training and context-switching costs can negate the benefits.

---

## 3. Comparative workflow assessment

| Dimension | SAP S/4HANA/Fiori | Oracle NetSuite | Dynamics 365 SCM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary navigation pattern | Role-based app launchpad, spaces/pages, task apps | Role center with persistent tabs, links, and dashboard portlets | General navigation plus role/configuration-specific workspaces and floor interface |
| Inventory workflow | Role catalog and focused inventory apps; possible legacy-app mix | Persistent inventory links, searches, dashboards, role permissions | Exception tiles, inventory inquiries, scanning, and contextual material adjustment |
| Work-order creation | Dedicated Create/Manage Production Order apps with extensive downstream detail | Large configurable transaction form reached through persistent menu | Full creation in main client; floor UI focuses on job start, progress, scrap, and material use |
| Progressive-disclosure capability | High if roles/pages/apps are carefully configured | Moderate to high through custom forms, roles, and dashboards; standard forms may remain dense | High in Production Floor Execution through configurable tabs, details, and toolbars |
| Occasional advanced functions | App finder, detail pages, related apps, legacy transactions | Stable module paths, custom tabs, record subtabs | Secondary toolbar, dialogs, details view, or bridge to full client |
| Main risk | Role/catalog sprawl and inconsistent legacy screens | Dashboard and form overload | Fragmentation between streamlined workspace and full client |
| Best fit for target supervisors | Curated plant-supervisor page plus direct task apps | Published supervisor center plus reduced custom forms | Configured floor UI plus exception-focused supervisor workspace |

---

## 4. Evidence on cognitive load during ERP transitions

ERP transition load is not caused by the visual interface alone. Users must simultaneously learn:

1. New labels and navigation.
2. New transaction sequences.
3. Changed responsibilities and approvals.
4. New relationships among inventory, production, purchasing, quality, and finance.
5. New error consequences because integrated records immediately affect other functions.

A comparative study of younger and older SAP users describes perceived ERP complexity as reducing the ability to perform tasks and increasing perceived workload. It also argues that perceived usefulness can reduce workload by helping users handle demands more effectively (https://aisel.aisnet.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1092&context=wi2015). This means simplification should not remove information users need to understand or trust the process: a sparse interface that conceals status or consequences can itself create stress.

A study of 128 ERP users across two organizations found that the pace of ERP functionality and interface change significantly affected work overload, work-life conflict, and role ambiguity; work overload and role ambiguity were strong predictors of ERP-induced exhaustion (https://exa.ai/library/publication/njlkbvfxhk3). Although this is not specific to one of the three modern products, it supports:

- Stabilizing navigation during rollout.
- Avoiding frequent layout changes immediately after go-live.
- Announcing and training changes before they appear.
- Keeping labels and button locations consistent across sites.

Post-implementation SAP training research distinguishes three learning outcomes:

- **Skill-based:** ability to operate the tool.
- **Cognitive:** understanding how to use the system to solve business problems.
- **Metacognitive:** confidence in one’s ability to use it.

It warns that narrow procedural training does not reliably transfer to real-world problem solving and recommends continuous, collaborative, cross-functional learning rather than one-time instruction (https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2012/38996/38996.pdf).

A quasi-experiment involving two groups of approximately 35 learners over five weeks found that teaching ERP workflow concepts as an advance organizer improved the accuracy and retention of users’ ERP mental models compared with conventional procedure-oriented training (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/761849.761864). The sample consisted of students rather than production supervisors, so the exact effect size cannot be transferred, but the instructional principle is relevant: explain why inventory, production, and downstream transactions are linked before teaching clicks.

### Implications for AS/400 migration

AS/400 experts are not true novices. They possess strong domain and procedural knowledge but may have a rigid system-specific mental model. Training should explicitly map old concepts to new ones:

| Legacy concept | New-system training question |
|---|---|
| Menu option or command code | Which role page, center tab, workspace, or search replaces it? |
| Function-key confirmation | Which button posts, saves, releases, or merely closes? |
| Fixed screen sequence | Which steps are now automated or conditionally skipped? |
| Plant/item defaults | Which values are inherited from role, device, location, BOM, or item master? |
| Error code | Where is validation displayed, and how is the error corrected? |
| Batch job/report | Is the result now real-time, scheduled, or dashboard-based? |

This mapping reduces extraneous cognitive load while preserving useful legacy knowledge.

---

## 5. What successful migrations measure

Training attendance and login counts are inadequate measures of competency. A useful measurement framework should establish a legacy baseline, test in a representative sandbox, and continue through stabilization after go-live.

Change-management practice commonly separates:

- **Speed of adoption:** how quickly people begin using the new process.
- **Ultimate utilization:** how many intended users actually use it.
- **Proficiency:** how correctly and effectively users perform after adoption (https://www.prosci.com/blog/governing-erp-benefits-beyond-go-live).

## 5.1 User proficiency

Measure proficiency by role and workflow, not with a generic system quiz.

Recommended observed tasks:

- Find inventory for an item at the correct plant, warehouse, location, batch, and status.
- Identify a shortage or material exception.
- Create a normal work order using defaults.
- Create an exception order that requires an advanced setting.
- Release or start an order/job.
- Report good quantity, scrap, and material variance.
- Correct a deliberately introduced validation error.
- Explain the downstream inventory impact.

Useful proficiency score:

\[
\text{Proficiency} =
0.40(\text{accuracy})+
0.25(\text{independent completion})+
0.20(\text{time score})+
0.15(\text{exception-handling score})
\]

Each component can be normalized to 0–100. The heavier weights on accuracy and independence reflect manufacturing risk.

A user should be considered competent only after completing both routine and exception scenarios, for example:

- At least 95% critical-field accuracy.
- 100% completion of safety, quality, and traceability steps.
- No trainer intervention in two consecutive sessions.
- Median completion time within an agreed range of experienced users.
- Successful retest after 7–14 days to measure retention.

## 5.2 Task completion

Report both:

\[
\text{Unassisted completion rate}
=
\frac{\text{tasks completed correctly without help}}
{\text{tasks attempted}}
\times 100
\]

and:

\[
\text{Assisted completion rate}
=
\frac{\text{tasks completed correctly with or without help}}
{\text{tasks attempted}}
\times 100
\]

The difference between the two rates is important. A high assisted rate with a low unassisted rate indicates that the workflow is technically usable but not yet learned or discoverable.

Segment results by:

- Age band.
- Prior graphical-software experience.
- Plant and shift.
- Role.
- Workflow.
- Routine versus exception task.
- Interface variant.

Do not use age as a proxy for ability; use it to check whether a design disproportionately burdens a group.

## 5.3 Error reduction

Separate errors by severity:

- **Navigation error:** wrong page, tab, role, or action.
- **Input error:** incorrect quantity, date, plant, location, status, or order type.
- **Process error:** skipped release, missing confirmation, incorrect posting sequence.
- **Inventory error:** incorrect batch, serial, bin, status, or material consumption.
- **Recovery failure:** inability to identify and correct an error.
- **Downstream error:** rework in planning, purchasing, warehouse, quality, or finance.

Calculate:

\[
\text{Error rate per 100 transactions}
=
\frac{\text{validated user-caused errors}}
{\text{transactions}}
\times 100
\]

\[
\text{Error reduction}
=
\frac{\text{baseline error rate}-\text{new error rate}}
{\text{baseline error rate}}
\times 100
\]

Example: if legacy or pilot performance is 8.0 errors per 100 work orders and the stabilized role-based interface produces 3.0:

\[
\frac{8.0-3.0}{8.0}\times100=62.5\%
\]

Also measure correction time and business impact. Ten harmless navigation errors are not equivalent to one incorrect batch posting.

## 5.4 Time-to-competency

Define the starting point and threshold explicitly:

\[
\text{Time-to-competency}
=
\text{date/time proficiency threshold is first sustained}
-
\text{start of role training}
\]

Report:

- Formal training hours.
- Practice hours.
- Calendar days to competency.
- Number of production transactions to competency.
- Median and 75th-percentile time-to-competency.
- Time to routine-task competency separately from exception competency.

A sustained threshold is preferable to a one-time test—for example, meeting target accuracy and speed for five consecutive shifts or two consecutive weekly observations.

## 5.5 Cognitive-load and confidence measures

Pair operational telemetry with short user measures:

- Single Ease Question after each task.
- NASA Task Load Index or a short mental-effort scale after a workflow.
- Confidence rating before and after training.
- Number of hesitations, backtracks, opened-and-abandoned pages, help requests, and role switches.
- Search use and unsuccessful search terms.
- Support tickets per 100 users.
- Supervisor or “floor walker” interventions per shift.

This distinguishes three different problems:

- A slow but accurate user may need practice.
- A fast but error-prone user may need stronger validation.
- A user with excessive backtracking may be facing poor information architecture.

---

## 6. Quantitative implementation evidence and its limits

Available customer cases show that cloud manufacturing systems can improve operational performance, but generally do not attribute improvements specifically to progressive disclosure or persistent navigation.

### Oracle ecosystem example

Litoplas, using Oracle Fusion Cloud SCM rather than NetSuite, reported:

- Inventory reliability increasing from 57% to 96%.
- Inventory accuracy increasing from 96% to 99.9%.
- Preparation and staging time decreasing 20%.
- Picking and packing transaction time being cut in half.
- Production increasing 40% (https://www.oracle.com/customers/litoplas/).

Quantitative interpretation:

- Inventory reliability gain:

\[
96\%-57\%=39\text{ percentage points}
\]

Relative improvement:

\[
\frac{96-57}{57}\times100=68.4\%
\]

- Inventory accuracy gain:

\[
99.9\%-96\%=3.9\text{ percentage points}
\]

Remaining inaccuracy fell from 4.0% to 0.1%:

\[
\frac{4.0-0.1}{4.0}\times100=97.5\%
\]

This is strong operational evidence, but it is **not NetSuite-specific and not a controlled UI comparison**.

### SAP example

Jabil reported that visibility into open sales orders by facility improved from more than an hour to seconds after moving to SAP S/4HANA Cloud, along with real-time material visibility and inventory-management efficiency (https://news.sap.com/2023/06/jabil-transforms-innovates-sap-s-4hana-cloud/). The case does not report supervisor training hours, completion rates, or user-error reductions.

Kiara Health reportedly completed a greenfield S/4HANA implementation in four months with no business disruption, using best-practice templates and tightly controlled scope (https://news.sap.com/africa/2021/04/pharma-plant-digitally-transforms-with-sap-s-4hana-in-just-4-months/). This demonstrates migration speed, not individual time-to-competency.

### Microsoft example

A documented AS/400-to-Dynamics 365 manufacturing case claims a 40% reduction in manual production-entry tasks, automated production-order planning, and real-time order and stock status (https://uliseswebfiles.blob.core.windows.net/static-files/web/ulises-case-study-manufacturing.pdf). Because this is an implementation-partner case rather than an independent controlled study, the figure should be treated as directional.

Microsoft customer stories report broader gains in visibility, standardization, and automation. Walki, for example, replaced fragmented and manual supply-chain processes and reported a 25% reduction in month-end close time alongside better inventory and cost visibility (https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/25076-walki-group-oy-dynamics-365-supply-chain-management). Again, the result cannot be assigned specifically to its navigation design.

### Overall evidentiary conclusion

The evidence is strongest for:

- Role-based configuration as an established capability.
- Reduced search space and stable task-focused interfaces as sound usability principles.
- Continuous, conceptual, and collaborative training as a means of improving ERP understanding.
- Operational benefits from cloud ERP integration and automation.

The evidence is weak for:

- Exact product-by-product training-time comparisons.
- Exact task-completion advantages caused by progressive disclosure.
- Age-specific completion or error rates among 45–60-year-old manufacturing supervisors.
- Causal claims that dashboards alone improve proficiency.

These gaps should be filled through preproduction testing with the actual workforce rather than vendor assumptions.

---

## 7. Role-based views versus comprehensive dashboards

### Role-based views are better for primary-task efficiency

A simplified role view is preferable when:

- The user performs a small set of high-frequency actions.
- Transactions carry inventory, quality, or financial consequences.
- The user is transitioning from a stable legacy workflow.
- The shop-floor environment creates interruption and divided attention.
- Different work cells require different actions.
- Training time is constrained.

Dynamics’ configurable primary and secondary toolbars demonstrate the appropriate mechanism. SAP’s role catalogs and pages provide an equivalent app-level approach. NetSuite can achieve it through custom roles, centers, published dashboards, and forms.

### Comprehensive dashboards are useful for supervision—but only when exception-oriented

Supervisors differ from operators because they must maintain situational awareness across jobs, materials, machines, and exceptions. A dashboard therefore remains valuable if it answers:

- What requires action now?
- Which orders are late, blocked, short, or over-consuming?
- Where is inventory below requirement?
- Which jobs have unusual scrap or downtime?
- What has changed since the last review?

A dashboard should not attempt to expose every transaction, KPI, and reporting link. That turns monitoring into visual search. NetSuite’s portlet model is especially susceptible to gradual dashboard accumulation; SAP pages can similarly accumulate excessive tiles; Dynamics workspaces can accumulate tiles, lists, and Power BI content.

### Recommended synthesis

Use a three-layer model:

**Layer 1: Persistent task rail**

Always visible:

- My work/orders.
- Inventory lookup.
- Create work order.
- Report or review production.
- Exceptions.
- Help.

**Layer 2: Role dashboard**

A limited set of actionable items:

- Material shortages.
- Orders blocked or due today.
- Scrap or consumption variance.
- Inventory/count discrepancies.
- Downtime or maintenance requests.
- Approvals awaiting action.

Each indicator must drill directly to the filtered records requiring action.

**Layer 3: Progressive advanced functions**

Available through labeled details or “More actions”:

- Alternative routing.
- WIP and scheduling controls.
- Batch/serial reservations.
- Manual material-consumption adjustment.
- Cost analysis.
- Capacity and planning detail.
- Technical close or reversal.
- Cross-plant and cross-company views.

This retains primary efficiency without making the occasional advanced function effectively invisible.

---

## 8. Recommended validation study before rollout

Run a within-site usability pilot comparing two realistic prototypes:

- **Variant A:** simplified role view with progressive advanced actions.
- **Variant B:** comprehensive dashboard with persistent module navigation.

Use representative supervisors, including users from each shift and a range of prior software experience. Test at minimum:

1. Find available inventory.
2. Investigate a batch/location discrepancy.
3. Create a normal work order.
4. Create an order requiring an advanced scheduling or routing option.
5. Handle a material shortage.
6. Report or correct material consumption.
7. Recover from an incorrect entry.

Measure:

- Unassisted completion.
- Correct completion.
- Median time.
- Errors per task.
- Backtracks and abandoned pages.
- Assistance requests.
- Cognitive-load rating.
- Seven- or fourteen-day retention.
- Time needed to locate an occasional advanced function.

A design should not be selected solely because routine tasks are faster. A suitable decision rule would weight:

- 40% routine-task accuracy and speed.
- 25% exception-task success.
- 20% error recovery.
- 15% cognitive load and confidence.

The preferred design is likely to be the role-based variant, but only if advanced-function success remains acceptable. If advanced tasks are difficult to find, improve labels, search, and stable secondary navigation rather than returning all controls to the main screen.

---

## Conclusion

For mid-sized manufacturers migrating from AS/400, neither an extremely sparse interface nor a comprehensive dashboard is sufficient. The best-supported design is a **role-based, exception-oriented hybrid**:

- Persistent navigation for a small number of core tasks.
- Progressive disclosure inside inventory and work-order workflows.
- A concise supervisor dashboard focused on actionable exceptions.
- Stable and explicitly labeled access to advanced functions.
- Defaulting and automation of plant, BOM, routing, location, and scheduling values where safe.
- Continuous, workflow-conceptual training reinforced with realistic cross-functional scenarios.
- Measurement of independent completion, errors, retention, cognitive load, and sustained time-to-competency.

Among the documented products, Dynamics 365 provides the most explicit configurable shop-floor progressive-disclosure model; SAP Fiori provides the strongest app- and role-centered architecture; and NetSuite provides the most persistent role-center and record-navigation model, but requires careful dashboard and form reduction. Actual outcomes will depend more on role design, process standardization, defaults, training, and post-go-live measurement than on the ERP brand alone.

# Gift Economies from Kula to Code, Likes, and Tokens: A Comparative Literature Review

## Executive summary

Anthropological theories of the gift do not describe a non-economic realm opposed cleanly to markets. They show how transfers create relationships, obligations, identities, status, and political power. Four interventions define the classical debate:

- **Bronisław Malinowski’s Trobriand ethnography** established that kula valuables circulate according to ceremonial rules distinct from, but intertwined with, utilitarian barter. Exchange is embedded in kinship, rank, magic, travel, and reputation rather than reducible to profit.
- **Marcel Mauss** generalized such cases into a theory of the gift as a “total social phenomenon.” Gifts appear voluntary but carry obligations to give, receive, and return; objects retain something of persons and groups, so circulation reproduces society.
- **Marshall Sahlins** converted reciprocity into a continuum—generalized, balanced, and negative—whose form varies with social distance. His framework explains why generosity, equivalent exchange, and opportunistic appropriation coexist.
- **Feminist anthropologists** demonstrated that canonical accounts privileged prestigious, publicly visible male transactions while obscuring women’s productive, reproductive, domestic, ceremonial, and affective labor. Annette Weiner restored Trobriand women’s wealth and theorized “keeping-while-giving”; Gayle Rubin exposed the patriarchal implications of treating women themselves as exchanged gifts; Marilyn Strathern challenged both Western individualism and simple feminist-economic translations of Melanesian relations.

Open-source software, social-media attention, and cryptocurrency governance confirm the classics’ central insight that exchange constructs social relations. But they undermine a binary opposition between gift and commodity. Code may be freely given yet commercially appropriated; likes may enact recognition while simultaneously producing proprietary data; governance tokens turn membership and collective authority into transferable, priced assets. Contemporary exchange is therefore best understood as **hybrid and infrastructurally mediated**: gift-like relations generate commodities, while markets and technical protocols organize who may give, receive, reciprocate, govern, and capture value.

## 1. Conceptual orientation: gift and commodity as ideal types

A gift is not simply an object transferred without money. In the anthropological tradition, its distinguishing feature is the relationship it creates or expresses. A commodity transaction ideally alienates an object from its seller through an impersonal, commensurable price; a gift ideally remains attached to giver and recipient through memory, identity, obligation, or reputation. Neither form exists in complete purity.

Three analytical dimensions are especially useful:

1. **Alienability:** Does the transfer terminate the previous owner’s claims, or does an enduring attachment remain?
2. **Commensuration and temporality:** Is an equivalent price fixed at the moment of exchange, or is return delayed, uncertain, and qualitatively different?
3. **Social consequence:** Does exchange primarily settle an account, or create an ongoing relationship, debt, identity, or hierarchy?

The classical literature already complicates the binary. Kula operates alongside barter; Maussian gifts are simultaneously generous and interested; Sahlins locates multiple reciprocities within the same society. Contemporary digital systems intensify this interpenetration because a single action can be a gift to one party and a commodity-producing input for another.

## 2. Malinowski: kula as ceremonial circulation

### 2.1 Ethnographic contribution

In *Argonauts of the Western Pacific* (1922), Malinowski described the kula network linking island communities in the Massim region around the Trobriand Islands. Two classes of shell valuables circulated in opposite directions: red shell necklaces, **soulava**, and white shell armbands, **mwali**. Participants maintained partnerships across islands, received one category, and subsequently reciprocated with the other. The valuables were not ordinarily retained permanently; renown came from acquiring distinguished objects and passing them onward.

Malinowski carefully distinguished kula from ordinary barter. Kula voyages were accompanied by practical trade, but ceremonial valuables were governed by different rules and meanings. The system could not be explained by immediate utility, supply and demand, or profit and loss. It was connected to rank, mythology, magic, canoe construction, seafaring, political alliance, aesthetic valuation, and personal fame (full primary text: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/55822/55822-h/55822-h.htm).

This was also a methodological intervention. Long-term fieldwork and participant observation allowed Malinowski to show that apparently “economic” conduct was embedded in a wider institutional complex. The kula refuted the image of a universal “primitive economic man” driven solely by material maximization.

### 2.2 Reciprocity and status

Kula return was neither an instantaneous swap nor a permanently free donation. An opening gift created an expectation of a later counter-gift. Equivalence was socially judged rather than established by a posted price, and timing was delayed. Generosity enhanced prestige; stinginess or failure to return damaged reputation and partnership. The system thus transformed valuables into vehicles of biography and status.

Kula also showed that circulation can matter more than consumption. The value of a famous shell object partly derived from its history and former holders. In modern terms, its provenance was social rather than merely technical.

### 2.3 Limits

Malinowski’s account centered highly visible male voyages and partnerships. That focus helped make kula paradigmatic, but it also encouraged later theorists to identify “the economy” with prestigious male circulation. Women’s production, mortuary distributions, reproductive work, and control of other forms of wealth received much less analytical prominence. This omission became central to feminist revisions.

## 3. Mauss: obligation and the “total social phenomenon”

### 3.1 The three obligations

Mauss’s *Essai sur le don*, first published in 1923–24, compared Polynesian, Melanesian, Northwest Coast, and archaic legal materials. Its central paradox is that gifts are represented as voluntary, spontaneous, and disinterested but are in practice obligatory and interested. Mauss decomposed gift exchange into obligations:

- to **give**, demonstrating generosity, standing, and willingness to enter relations;
- to **receive**, acknowledging the giver and accepting social connection;
- to **return**, preserving honor and preventing subordination.

The essay’s primary question is what “force” in the thing given compels repayment. Mauss’s answer invokes both indigenous ideas—most famously the Māori **hau**—and a broader sociological principle: gifts are not entirely separable from their donors. The exchange of things is simultaneously an exchange of persons, moral claims, and group identities. A modern annotated translation and its contents are available from HAU Books (https://haubooks.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Marcel-Mauss-The-Gift-Expanded-Edition-Selected-Annotated-and-Translated-by-Jane-Guyer.pdf).

### 3.2 Total prestations

For Mauss, gift systems are “total social phenomena” because religious, legal, moral, economic, political, aesthetic, and kinship institutions operate together. The potlatch, for example, joins generosity to rivalry, destruction, credit, honor, and hierarchy. Gifts produce solidarity, but they can also humiliate recipients or place them in debt. Reciprocity is therefore not synonymous with equality.

Mauss moves beyond Malinowski in scale and ambition. Malinowski reconstructs one regional institution ethnographically; Mauss extracts a comparative theory of social integration and moral obligation. Yet Mauss relies substantially on ethnographies such as Malinowski’s rather than equivalent direct fieldwork.

### 3.3 Gift and commodity in Mauss

Mauss did not posit a timeless, innocent gift economy diametrically opposed to corrupt commerce. His examples include interest, competition, credit, valuables resembling money, and strategic self-interest. What distinguishes the gift is not absence of calculation but the incomplete separation of persons and things.

His concluding political argument was also normative. Modern societies should preserve mutuality, social insurance, and generosity against the reduction of all relations to market contract. But the essay’s own evidence warns against romanticization: obligatory gifts can bind, rank, and dominate.

## 4. Sahlins: reciprocity as a structured continuum

In “On the Sociology of Primitive Exchange,” collected in *Stone Age Economics* (1972), Marshall Sahlins systematized reciprocity according to expected return and social distance. The text explicitly adopts a substantivist anthropology of economics rather than assuming that orthodox microeconomic models are universally adequate (https://files.libcom.org/files/Sahlins%20-%20Stone%20Age%20Economics.pdf).

### 4.1 Generalized reciprocity

Generalized reciprocity is assistance without a stipulated equivalent or deadline: feeding children, helping close kin, or sharing where need outweighs precise accounting. A return may be expected in a diffuse moral sense, but not as a matching payment.

This is closest to the common-language notion of generosity, although it still takes place within durable relations and expectations. It need not be altruism detached from sociality.

### 4.2 Balanced reciprocity

Balanced reciprocity expects a recognizable return within a socially appropriate period. Ceremonial exchange, many gifts between peers, and direct exchange fall in this middle range. Kula is principally balanced reciprocity: return is delayed and relational, but failure to reciprocate has consequences.

### 4.3 Negative reciprocity

Negative reciprocity seeks to obtain something for less than one gives—or, at the limit, for nothing. Bargaining, opportunism, theft, and exploitative appropriation occupy this pole. Sahlins’s key proposition is that reciprocity varies with social distance: generalized reciprocity tends to prevail among close relations, balanced reciprocity among more distant partners, and negative reciprocity at the social periphery.

### 4.4 Contribution and qualification

Sahlins clarifies that “reciprocity” is not a single norm. His continuum integrates solidarity and exploitation into one field and helps analyze digital systems in which cooperative sharing among peers coexists with extraction by remote firms.

Its limitation is that social distance alone cannot explain gendered power, institutional ownership, colonial conditions, or platform control. A wife’s unpaid care, for example, may occur at minimal social distance but remain unequal. Likewise, a platform can be socially intimate in interface design while legally and economically distant from users.

## 5. Feminist anthropology: recovering labor, power, and gender

### 5.1 Annette Weiner and the reanalysis of the Trobriands

Annette Weiner’s return to the Trobriand Islands produced a decisive reappraisal. *Women of Value, Men of Renown* (1976) examined internal exchanges of women’s and men’s wealth, annual yam distributions, land and kinship, and women’s mortuary distributions—domains largely marginalized in Malinowski’s kula-centered account. An HRAF summary emphasizes that Malinowski gave women’s roles little coverage, whereas Weiner documented women’s wealth and its importance in life-cycle and mortuary exchange (https://ehrafworldcultures.yale.edu/cultures/ol06/documents/025).

Women produced and distributed banana-leaf bundles and fiber skirts in mortuary ceremonies. These activities were not peripheral domestic tasks: they reproduced matrilineal identity, relationships with the dead, rank, and collective continuity. Men’s public renown consequently depended on a broader reproductive and ceremonial economy in which women were central.

In *Inalienable Possessions* (1992), Weiner shifted exchange theory from reciprocity alone to the paradox of **“keeping-while-giving.”** Some possessions should not be permanently alienated; if circulated, they should ultimately return, while others authenticate identity, ancestry, and rank precisely through retention. The University of California Press summary notes that Weiner treats reciprocity as the surface of deeper strategies for preserving identity and power, and links women’s control of cloth wealth to rank and hierarchy (https://www.ucpress.edu/books/inalienable-possessions/paper).

This revises both Malinowski and Mauss. Circulation is not the whole story: control over what remains outside exchange can be more powerful than giving. Nor does every gift dissolve the distinction between person and possession in the same way. Gender determines whose property, labor, and ritual authority become visible.

### 5.2 Gayle Rubin: women as gifts

Gayle Rubin’s 1975 “The Traffic in Women” subjected structuralist kinship theory to feminist critique. Drawing on Lévi-Strauss’s extension of Mauss, Rubin observed that marriage systems often treat women as the gifts through which men establish alliances. The central problem is therefore not simply that women give less prestigious objects; women may be positioned as objects of exchange rather than autonomous exchanging subjects.

Rubin named the broader organization of sexuality, kinship, and gender the **sex/gender system**. Her intervention reveals an unexamined asymmetry in theories that celebrate exchange as the foundation of society: fraternity among male exchangers can be built through control over women’s sexuality and labor. The essay is available here: https://philpapers.org/archive/RUBtti.pdf.

Rubin does not imply that all marriages are literal commodity sales. Rather, she shows that the grammar of gift exchange can naturalize gender hierarchy. Reciprocity among some actors may presuppose the restricted agency of others.

### 5.3 Marilyn Strathern: gender, dividuality, and the danger of imported categories

Marilyn Strathern’s *The Gender of the Gift* (1988) criticizes unexamined assumptions in both Western anthropology and some feminist theory. The University of California Press describes the book as a sustained reconsideration of Melanesian social life and of Western categories used in cross-cultural comparison (https://www.ucpress.edu/books/the-gender-of-the-gift/paper).

Strathern argues that Western concepts of the bounded individual, property, labor, society, production, and exploitation cannot simply be projected onto Melanesian relations. Melanesian persons may be understood as relational or “partible”: composed through the contributions of others and rendered in exchange. Gifts do not merely travel between pre-existing individuals; they make relations and persons perceptible.

Her account nevertheless foregrounds a gendered problem. In highland pig exchanges, wives’ work raising pigs can be incorporated into transactions through which husbands acquire public names and prestige. Men appear as transactors, while women’s productive contributions may be subsumed into the gift. Yet Strathern resists treating this automatically as wage-like appropriation, because the Western assumption that an individual naturally owns and alienates “his or her labor” may itself misdescribe local personhood.

This produces a productive tension with feminist political economy:

- A materialist reading asks who works, who is recognized, and who accumulates prestige.
- Strathern asks whether “work,” “ownership,” and “exploitation” already encode Western commodity assumptions.
- A satisfactory analysis must retain both cautions: avoid romanticizing relational personhood, but also avoid imposing individualist categories as universal.

### 5.4 Gendered labor beyond Melanesia

Feminist research broadens the object of exchange from prestigious valuables to the labor that makes exchange possible: cultivation, cooking, care, childbirth, kin maintenance, emotional support, ritual preparation, hospitality, and reputation management. Such labor is often naturalized as love or duty and therefore excluded from economic accounting.

A modern review of female cooperation notes that women’s collective activity spans childcare, food production, markets, political and ceremonial institutions, and exchange networks, much of which has been overlooked by models emphasizing male bonding and hunting (https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rstb/article/378/1868/20210425/42666/Female-cooperation-evolutionary-cross-cultural-and).

The core feminist lesson is thus not merely “add women.” It is that visibility and valuation are political:

- Public exchange may rest on hidden production.
- Reciprocity within intimate relations can legitimate unequal burdens.
- Gifts of care can be morally compulsory.
- Prestige may accrue to the person who presents an object rather than those whose labor produced it.
- Categories such as “voluntary,” “domestic,” and “non-economic” can conceal coercion.

## 6. Comparative synthesis of the classical models

| Question | Malinowski | Mauss | Sahlins | Feminist revisions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary object | Regional kula network | Comparative institution of gifting | Types of reciprocity | Gendered production, reproduction, personhood, and power |
| Main mechanism | Ceremonial circulation and partnership | Obligations to give, receive, and return | Expected return varies with social distance | Visibility, control, embodiment, reproductive labor, and unequal agency |
| View of calculation | Not reducible to utility or profit | Interest and generosity coexist | Ranges from diffuse aid to self-interested appropriation | Calculation is shaped by gender and by whose labor is counted |
| Relation of object to person | Valuables carry histories and prestige | Gift retains something of giver/group | Depends on reciprocity type | Some possessions remain inalienable; persons may be constituted through others’ labor |
| Principal blind spot | Male-centered public exchange | Tendency toward broad generalization and masculine exchange subjects | Limited account of gender and institutional power | Risk, in some versions, of importing Western categories too directly |
| Contemporary utility | Networks, reputation, circulation | Obligation, relational debt, “free” offers | Differentiates sharing, equivalence, and extraction | Reveals invisible labor and unequal capture of prestige/value |

Together, the literature rejects four simplifications:

1. Gifts are not necessarily free.
2. Commodities are not necessarily socially disembedded.
3. Reciprocity is not necessarily equal.
4. What appears to be exchange among visible actors may depend on invisible contributors.

## 7. Open-source software: generalized sharing, reputation, and corporate capture

### 7.1 Why open source resembles a gift economy

Free and open-source software (FOSS) is freely inspectable, modifiable, and redistributable under licenses. Contributors may give code, documentation, bug reports, testing, moderation, or support to a pool used by strangers. Direct repayment by each user is ordinarily impossible and unnecessary. This resembles **generalized reciprocity**: contributors benefit from a collectively maintained body of code without matching each use to an equivalent return.

It also resembles kula and Maussian exchange:

- Contributions display competence and generate reputation.
- Project membership and trust develop through repeated giving.
- Acceptance of code recognizes the contributor.
- Licenses can impose obligations on downstream users, particularly where modifications must remain shareable.
- Code retains provenance through commit histories and attribution, much as a valuable’s biography matters in ceremonial circulation.

Christopher Kelty notes that “gift economy” became a common explanation for FOSS, usually emphasizing a commons of code, reputation, belonging, and norms. But he also warns that this folk model often lacks engagement with Malinowski, Mauss, and later anthropology (https://kelty.org/or/papers/unpublishable/Kelty-Gifts-Dec-2006-Revised.pdf). FOSS is not a closed nonmonetary sphere: contributors, firms, foundations, users, and markets overlap.

### 7.2 Where FOSS departs from the classical gift

Digital code is largely non-rival: giving a copy does not deprive the giver of use. This changes the material basis of reciprocity. A kula necklace cannot be held simultaneously by every participant; an open-source library can be copied globally at near-zero marginal cost. Return therefore often takes indirect forms—improvements, reputation, employment, learning, compatibility, or ideological satisfaction.

Not all giving requires return. Research on digital gifts argues that web pages, posts, advice, and some software contributions are made available without enforceable reciprocal obligation and arise from multiple motivations (https://eldervass.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Elder-Vass-2015d-Moral-Economy-of-Digital-Gifts-IJSQ-PPV.pdf). This challenges overly strong readings of Mauss in which every gift necessarily creates a determinate counter-debt.

At the same time, licenses function as impersonalized reciprocity rules. Instead of a personally remembered debt, the legal-technical infrastructure may require attribution, preservation of freedoms, or source disclosure. Obligation moves from dyadic morality into standardized governance.

### 7.3 Commodity entanglement

Open source is also an industrial input. Firms sell hosting, integration, cloud services, hardware, support, and proprietary complements built around freely circulating code. Paid employees and volunteers collaborate on the same repositories. A 2020 Linux Foundation/Harvard survey reported that **48.7%** of respondents were paid by an employer to contribute to FOSS (https://www.linuxfoundation.org/hubfs/2020FOSSContributorSurveyReport_121020.pdf?hsLang=en).

Quantitatively:

- Paid by employer: 48.7%
- Not paid by employer: 100% − 48.7% = **51.3%**
- Difference: 51.3 − 48.7 = **2.6 percentage points**

Thus the sampled field was almost evenly split, not a pure volunteer gift economy. The figure is survey-based and should not be treated as a measure of all global contribution hours.

FOSS consequently reinforces Mauss more than a gift/commodity dichotomy: apparently free contributions are interested in heterogeneous ways and become embedded in institutions of employment, prestige, and profit. It also confirms Sahlins’s coexistence of reciprocities. Peer collaboration may be generalized or balanced, while a corporation that incorporates volunteer labor without proportionate return may be interpreted as negative reciprocity.

### 7.4 Gendered and invisible labor

FOSS reproduces the classical bias toward prestigious visible transfers. Code commits are analogous to public ceremonial valuables, while moderation, documentation, mentoring, conflict resolution, accessibility, and community maintenance may remain less visible.

A recent survey of 142 OSS contributors estimated that respondents regarded roughly **two in three tasks** as invisible and **50.1%** of their work as uncompensated (https://arxiv.org/html/2401.06889). These estimates are self-reports from a small, nonrepresentative sample and therefore indicate a pattern rather than a population total.

The 2017 GitHub Open Source Survey found:

- 95% of respondents were men;
- 3% women;
- 1% non-binary;
- women reporting unwelcome language/content: 25%, versus 15% of men;
- stereotyping: 12% of women, versus 2% of men.

Derived comparisons:

- Women’s reported exposure to unwelcome content was 25/15 = **1.67 times** men’s rate.
- Women’s reported stereotyping was 12/2 = **6 times** men’s rate.
- The reported interest-to-intention gap was also gendered: 68% of women said they were very interested in future contributions, but only 45% said they were very likely to contribute, a **23-point gap**; for men, 73% versus 61%, a **12-point gap**.

The survey included approximately 5,500 randomly sampled GitHub participants plus more than 500 respondents from other communities, but nonresponse and platform coverage limit generalization (https://opensourcesurvey.org/2017/; methodology: https://github.blog/2017-06-02-announcing-an-open-data-set-on-the-open-source-community/).

These findings strongly support the feminist critique: a rhetoric of voluntary community contribution can obscure unequal access to free time, safety, recognition, and technical authority. As with Trobriand and highland exchange, the person publicly credited with the prestigious object may depend upon less visible relational labor.

## 8. Social-media attention: gifts converted into metrics and commodities

### 8.1 Likes, mentions, and recognition

Likes, shares, comments, follows, and mentions are small transfers of attention. They can express approval, care, affiliation, condolence, or acknowledgment. They often invite return: friends reciprocally like posts; creators thank followers; users exchange visibility. This resembles Mauss’s obligations to give, receive, and return, but with reciprocity accelerated and quantified.

Sahlins’s continuum also applies:

- **Generalized:** attention among friends or support communities without close accounting.
- **Balanced:** reciprocal following, commenting, and “engagement” expected within a recognizable period.
- **Negative:** spam, manipulation, engagement bait, harassment, or extraction of users’ attention and data without a proportionate return.

A study of the “digital gift” argues that Facebook likes and Twitter mentions circulate mutual recognition, while the surrounding “Like economy” entangles gift relations with markets (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0263276415619474).

### 8.2 Metrification changes the gift

Classical gifts are often deliberately resistant to exact equivalence. Social media converts attention into counts: followers, views, likes, shares, and engagement rates. Gerlitz and Helmond show that Like buttons transform affective responses into comparable metrics, enable data flows among platforms and websites, and operate as tracking infrastructure (https://www.annehelmond.nl/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Gerlitz-Helmond-2013-LikeEconomy.pdf).

This produces a distinctive hybrid:

1. User A gives recognition to User B.
2. The platform records the act as behavioral data.
3. The metric ranks content and profiles.
4. Advertisers and creators use the metric as evidence of audience value.
5. The platform monetizes prediction, targeting, and access to attention.

The same click is therefore:
- a relational gift to another user;
- unpaid labor producing a metric;
- raw material for a proprietary data commodity;
- a signal in algorithmic governance.

This differs from kula because the infrastructure owner can copy, aggregate, and sell information about every transfer while controlling visibility. The platform is not merely another exchange partner; it defines the rules, records the transaction, and appropriates the meta-value generated by circulation.

### 8.3 “Accumulation by gift”

Digital firms frequently offer “free” services in exchange for participation, data, content, and social enrollment. A study of “accumulation by gift” argues that this benign framing masks structural asymmetry: gift-like enrollment permits private appropriation of personal data and obscures its value (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2053951719897092).

This reinforces Mauss in one sense: “free” offerings create obligations and dependencies. But it reverses his interpersonal model. The platform’s return is standardized service, while users’ gifts—content, data, attention, network effects—are aggregated into corporate capital. The parties do not possess equal knowledge or bargaining power, and there may be no meaningful opportunity to refuse individual transfers while remaining socially connected.

### 8.4 Feminist analysis of attention labor

Social-media production involves affective and reproductive work: maintaining relationships, cultivating intimacy, moderating communities, presenting an attractive self, and absorbing hostility. Feminist scholarship argues that digital-media theories have often neglected the legacy of unpaid “women’s work” and the indirect relation between affective labor and capitalist value (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1527476413487607).

The comparison with Weiner and Strathern is direct. Visible posts and influencer reputations are sustained by hidden labor, while platforms capture value from relational activity. Gender, race, class, and sexuality affect whose self-presentation is expected, whose care labor is normalized, and who bears harassment and moderation burdens. Social media thus reinforces classical gift theory’s insight into recognition while vindicating feminist warnings that the language of generosity and community can disguise unequal work.

## 9. Cryptocurrency and DAO governance: tokenizing reciprocity and authority

### 9.1 Blockchain as social ledger

Cryptocurrencies use shared ledgers to record transfers, provenance, and ownership. Anthropological comparisons with Yapese stone money emphasize that both systems depend on a continuous, socially recognized history of transactions, although stone valuables were not simply modern currency (https://anthrosource.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sea2.12154).

This resembles kula insofar as value depends on circulation, collectively known history, and network recognition. Yet cryptocurrency usually makes assets highly alienable, divisible, transferable, and priceable. It converts provenance into an automated record while often stripping away the durable personal relationship between giver and receiver.

### 9.2 DAOs as commons governance

Decentralized autonomous organizations use tokens, smart contracts, forums, and proposals to coordinate collective resources. In principle, they resemble gift or commons institutions:

- open-source developers contribute code;
- members provide liquidity, labor, ideas, and moderation;
- token distributions or “airdrops” reward early participation;
- treasuries fund public goods;
- protocol rules encode expectations of contribution and return.

Some projects explicitly use blockchain for commoning. Research on the Ğ1/Duniter currency describes a community-governed monetary commons with self-organization, bundles of rights, and a universal dividend (https://revuesim.org/index.php/sim/article/view/1131). Work on commons-oriented DAOs similarly proposes governance structures combining technology, community rules, and Ostrom-style collective-action principles (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/blockchain/articles/10.3389/fbloc.2023.1287249/full).

These arrangements strengthen Sahlins’s and Mauss’s relevance. Tokens can institutionalize generalized reciprocity across strangers, reward contributions after a delay, and materialize membership in a collective project.

### 9.3 Governance tokens collapse political membership into property

Most token-voting systems allocate votes in proportion to transferable assets: one token, one weighted unit of influence. This is neither a classical gift nor democratic “one person, one vote.” It fuses commodity ownership, investment, and political authority.

The result challenges the gift/commodity distinction in several ways:

- An airdrop can be a gift that creates loyalty, participation, and an expectation of future labor.
- The recipient may immediately sell it as a commodity.
- A governance contribution may raise token price, producing a financial return.
- Reputation and authority become partially transferable through token purchase.
- The collective’s constitutional rules become objects of speculation.

Mauss’s obligations are formalized and financialized. “Give” may mean stake capital or provide liquidity; “receive” means accept protocol risk and rules; “return” is delivered through tokens, fees, voting power, or appreciation. The diffuse social debt of the gift becomes a programmable and tradable claim.

### 9.4 Plutocracy and concentration

The democratic promise is limited by unequal token ownership and low participation. An empirical study of 21 DAOs found highly concentrated voting rights, hidden monetary costs of on-chain governance, and substantial pointless governance activity (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2302.12125). Another analysis of Aave, Compound, Lido, and Uniswap found that in many votes the minimal coalition able to determine the result was around **three addresses** (https://arxiv.org/html/2407.10945v1).

The latter statistic does not mean three human beings necessarily control every DAO: one address may represent an exchange, delegate, multisignature wallet, or organization, and coalition size varies by proposal. Nonetheless, it demonstrates the difference between nominally open participation and effective power.

The design dilemma is structural. Research in *Management Science* concludes that token-weighted voting alone cannot simultaneously resist both Sybil attacks—one actor creating many identities—and plutocracy—wealthy actors controlling the vote (https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.2023.01536). Tokens make influence costly to fake, but they also make authority purchasable.

This resembles competitive gifting and potlatch, where those with the greatest capacity to give can acquire rank and subordinate others. It also resembles Weiner’s argument that power lies in controlling assets that authenticate collective identity. But unlike many classical gifts, governance tokens are designed for liquid markets; “keeping-while-giving” becomes staking or delegation while retaining an economic claim.

### 9.5 Gender and invisible governance labor

DAO research has concentrated more on token distribution than on gendered maintenance. Yet the feminist framework identifies an immediate research agenda: distinguish compensated, token-visible contributions from moderation, onboarding, conflict management, documentation, community care, and reputational work. If governance rewards capital provision and code more readily than care and maintenance, it reproduces the same hierarchy found in male-centered ceremonial exchange and open-source communities.

A ledger can make transfers transparent without making all labor visible. “On-chain transparency” is therefore not social transparency. It records what protocol designers choose to count.
