final.content:
COMPARATIVE REPORT: THE DIVERGENCE AND RECONSTRUCTION OF GROUNDED THEORY

Executive conclusion

Glaser and Strauss’s 1967 formulation united around an inductive alternative to hypothesis-testing sociology: collect and analyze data concurrently, compare incidents continuously, sample theoretically, write analytic memos, and build rather than merely test theory. Their later disagreement concerned how much prior conceptual structure and procedural control could be introduced without compromising emergence.

In Theoretical Sensitivity (1978), Barney Glaser retained a discovery-oriented position. Researchers should delay commitment to established theories, code openly, and allow a core category and its relationships to emerge through constant comparison. Prior knowledge was not prohibited, but it should operate as flexible “theoretical sensitivity,” not as a template. For Glaser, forcing data into preconceived categories was methodologically illegitimate, while verification in the conventional hypothesis-testing sense distracted from theory generation.

Strauss and Corbin’s Basics of Qualitative Research (1990) made grounded theory substantially more procedural. Its open, axial, and selective coding stages, coding paradigm, conditional matrix, and active checking of provisional relationships were intended to make analysis systematic and teachable. Existing literature and disciplinary knowledge could enhance theoretical sensitivity. Hypotheses about categories were to be repeatedly checked against data, including negative evidence. Glaser regarded this as “forcing”; Strauss and Corbin regarded it as disciplined interrogation and verification.

Kathy Charmaz’s Constructing Grounded Theory (2006) preserved constant comparison, theoretical sampling, memo-writing, emergence, and delayed theoretical closure, but recast them within constructivist epistemology. Data and theories are not simply discovered; they are constructed through interactions among researcher, participants, setting, language, and interpretive standpoint. This partly dissolves the emergence-versus-forcing dichotomy: prior concepts are unavoidable, but they should be treated reflexively and provisionally rather than imposed as fixed explanations.

The best-supported conclusion about present-day training is that Charmaz’s constructivist approach has become the dominant epistemological reference point across interdisciplinary qualitative-methods education, although Straussian procedures remain highly influential as coding techniques, especially in applied fields. Classical Glaserian grounded theory remains an identifiable school but is less dominant outside specialist grounded-theory communities. The evidence is not uniform enough to claim a universal majority across every discipline.

1. The common 1967 starting point

The Discovery of Grounded Theory challenged the mid-century division in which qualitative research generated preliminary ideas while quantitative research performed the supposedly serious work of verification. Glaser and Strauss instead made the “discovery of theory from data” a primary research objective. The book emphasized theories that fit empirical situations and provide useful explanations, interpretations, predictions, and applications (https://www.perlego.com/book/1610990/discovery-of-grounded-theory-strategies-for-qualitative-research-pdf).

The shared methodological core included:

• simultaneous data collection and analysis;
• coding and category construction from data rather than from logically deduced hypotheses;
• constant comparison among incidents, codes, categories, cases, and groups;
• theoretical sampling directed by the emerging analysis;
• memo-writing;
• progressive conceptualization and integration;
• saturation of theoretically important categories; and
• production of an explanatory theory rather than only a descriptive account.

Charmaz’s retrospective summary identifies these same components and notes the original recommendation to conduct the main literature review after developing an independent analysis (http://www.sxf.uevora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Charmaz_2006.pdf).

The later split did not therefore involve induction versus deduction in an absolute sense. Both branches compared interpretations with data and allowed later analysis to shape additional collection. The disagreement was over how explicitly deductive that later phase should become, how much analytic scaffolding could be supplied in advance, and whether “verification” was an appropriate description of the process.

2. Glaser’s Theoretical Sensitivity (1978)

2.1 Pre-existing theoretical frameworks

For Glaser, theoretical sensitivity is the analyst’s cultivated ability to recognize theoretically significant patterns and to conceptualize them at a level above description. It can arise from professional experience, accumulated sociological knowledge, reading, and immersion in data. It does not mean beginning with a settled theoretical framework and assigning observations to its categories.

The distinction is crucial:

• Prior knowledge can make the analyst sensitive to possible meanings.
• It must not determine which categories will be found.
• Concepts should earn their way into the analysis through repeated fit with data.
• The researcher should remain open to multiple possible conceptual relationships rather than selecting one framework too early.

Glaser’s approach therefore does not require a literally theory-free or empty mind. Theoretical Sensitivity itself offered numerous “coding families”—possible ways of understanding relationships among categories. But these were a plural repertoire of heuristic possibilities, not a single mandatory scheme. A later methodological analysis characterizes the contrast as Glaser drawing on varied coding families while Strauss adopted a general action-oriented coding axis (https://d-nb.info/1186821515/34).

Glaser also favored delaying sustained engagement with literature directly relevant to the substantive field. The purpose was not permanent ignorance but protection against prematurely seeing participants and events exclusively through an established theory.

2.2 Forcing and emergence

Glaser’s governing maxim was that categories and theoretical relationships should emerge rather than be forced. Forcing occurs when an analyst:

• begins with predetermined categories;
• treats an existing theory as the coding frame;
• asks every category to conform to the same model of causal conditions and consequences;
• selects evidence because it confirms the preferred explanation; or
• elaborates conceptual distinctions that the data do not support.

The proper remedies are open coding, line-by-line comparison, theoretical sampling, memo-writing, tolerance for uncertainty, and repeated comparison until a core category organizes the analysis.

“Emergence” should not be interpreted literally as data speaking without an analyst. Glaser expected active conceptualization. The analyst names patterns, compares indicators and raises the analysis above participants’ descriptions. His later clarification emphasized that even in-vivo concepts are accepted only when they “fit” and “work” across data, not merely because a participant used a particular expression (https://sites.ualberta.ca/~iiqm/backissues/1_2Final/pdf/glaser.pdf).

Thus, Glaserian emergence means freedom from premature conceptual constraint, not passive transcription.

2.3 Verification

Glaser’s primary purpose was generation, not formal verification. Constant comparison, theoretical sampling and saturation continuously challenge a developing category, but they do so as components of theory generation. They are not a separate verification phase modeled on testing a previously specified hypothesis.

The theory is evaluated principally through:

• fit with the data;
• work—whether it explains what is happening;
• relevance to participants’ main concerns;
• conceptual reach or explanatory power; and
• modifiability when new evidence appears.

Glaser was correspondingly skeptical of importing conventional validity tests into grounded theory. He also rejected participant approval as a necessary validity test: participants may not recognize or endorse a conceptual abstraction that integrates patterns extending beyond their individual awareness (https://sites.ualberta.ca/~iiqm/backissues/1_2Final/pdf/glaser.pdf).

This does not mean that evidence is irrelevant or that every interpretation is equally acceptable. Rather, evidential control is internal to comparative generation and correction. “Verification,” if used at all, is subordinate to grounding, fit and modification.

3. Strauss and Corbin’s Basics of Qualitative Research (1990)

3.1 Pre-existing theoretical frameworks

Strauss and Corbin gave literature, professional knowledge and researchers’ experience a more explicit role in building theoretical sensitivity. Existing concepts could:

• indicate questions worth asking;
• direct attention to properties or dimensions;
• suggest comparisons;
• expose gaps in the emerging account; and
• stimulate—not dictate—interpretation.

Their position was therefore more permissive than Glaser’s about consulting prior scholarship during research. They did not license simple application of an established theory as a fixed codebook; categories were still supposed to be grounded in data. The difference was that Strauss and Corbin believed researchers could interrogate data through prior knowledge without necessarily surrendering openness.

Their most consequential innovation was a standardized architecture for coding:

1. Open coding fractures data into concepts, categories, properties and dimensions.
2. Axial coding reconnects categories with subcategories.
3. Selective coding integrates the analysis around a central category.
4. A coding paradigm prompts examination of conditions, context, action/interaction strategies, and consequences.
5. A conditional matrix helps locate processes across broader and narrower levels of context.

The 1990 book’s table of contents makes this procedural progression explicit, including separate chapters on theoretical sensitivity, uses of literature, open coding, axial coding, selective coding, the conditional matrix, theoretical sampling, memos and evaluative criteria (https://archive.org/details/basicsofqualitat0000stra).

3.2 Is forcing ever legitimate?

Strauss and Corbin did not defend “forcing” in the sense of suppressing contradictory evidence. Their claim was that disciplined analytic questioning and an explicit coding paradigm help researchers see relationships they might otherwise overlook. The framework was supposed to be heuristic and revisable.

Nevertheless, from Glaser’s standpoint, the axial-coding paradigm institutionalized forcing because categories were routinely organized around one general action model:

conditions → context → action/interaction → consequences.

Glaser argued that making analysts search for each of these elements encourages them to manufacture relationships even when another conceptual organization would fit better. It may produce a detailed conceptual description rather than a parsimonious grounded theory.

This is the heart of the dispute:

• Glaser: no procedural framework should determine in advance what kinds of relationships matter.
• Strauss and Corbin: an explicit framework can discipline inquiry without determining its substantive result.

Later empirical examination of Straussian studies found that researchers often used axial coding consciously and flexibly rather than mechanically, complicating the claim that it necessarily produces forcing (https://aisel.aisnet.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1960&context=jit). The risk of forcing is therefore real but not an inevitable consequence of axial coding; it depends on whether the paradigm is treated as an interrogative aid or a compulsory ontology.

3.3 Verification

Strauss and Corbin made verification much more explicit. Propositions about category relationships should be developed and taken back to data or the field for checking and revision. Their contemporaneous statement of methodological canons said:

“Hypotheses About Relationships among Categories Should Be Developed and Verified as Much as Possible during the Research Process.”

These relationships should be revised until they hold for the evidence generated through interviews, observations or documents. Verification includes searching for negative and qualifying evidence. In axial coding, relationships between categories and subcategories are tested against data (https://eli.johogo.com/Class/CorbinStrauss.pdf).

Strauss and Corbin retained conventional scientific concerns—significance, theory-observation compatibility, generalizability, consistency, reproducibility, precision and verification—but argued that these had to be redefined for qualitative inquiry rather than applied in quantitatively positivist form (https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1718748683/tamdistrictorg/na68mrlhn3cctfl7zewg/w10-corbin-and-strauss-grounded-theory.pdf).

Consequently, verification was not envisioned as a final statistical test of fixed hypotheses. It was an iterative process:

propose relationship → compare with data → seek variation and negative cases → revise relationship → collect strategically → compare again.

This is stronger and more explicitly deductive than Glaser’s language, although both approaches repeatedly check emerging concepts against evidence.

4. Direct comparison

Issue | Glaser, Theoretical Sensitivity (1978) | Strauss and Corbin, Basics (1990)
---|---|---
Primary image of theory | A pattern discovered through emergence and conceptualization | An interpretation systematically developed and repeatedly checked
Prior theory | Resource for general theoretical sensitivity; relevant substantive literature should be delayed and must not supply categories | Literature and disciplinary experience can actively stimulate questions, properties and comparisons
Coding structure | Open and selective coding, followed by emergent theoretical coding; multiple optional coding families | Open, axial and selective coding, supported by a common coding paradigm and conditional matrix
Analytic priority | Let the principal concern and core category emerge | Deliberately elaborate categories, dimensions and action-oriented relationships
Forcing | A basic methodological error; categories must earn relevance | Also rejected, but systematic questioning is legitimate; critics argue the coding paradigm risks forcing
Deduction | Secondary and emergent: provisional ideas direct theoretical sampling | More explicit: provisional relational hypotheses are checked against further evidence
Verification | Not a separate governing objective; grounding, fit, work, relevance and modifiability are central | Legitimate and necessary when redefined as iterative qualitative checking, including negative cases
Researcher’s role | Theoretically sensitive discoverer/conceptualizer | Active analytic interpreter using specified procedures
Pedagogical form | Flexible but difficult to prescribe as a sequence | Highly teachable procedural sequence, though vulnerable to formulaic use

A key nuance is that neither side is purely inductive. Glaser’s theoretical sampling necessarily follows provisional ideas, while Strauss and Corbin continued to insist that categories remain responsive to evidence. The difference is one of methodological emphasis and allowable structure, not a simple induction/deduction binary.

5. Charmaz’s constructivist reformulation

5.1 What Charmaz retained

Charmaz did not abandon grounded theory’s characteristic practices. Her 2006 formulation retained:

• concurrent collection and analysis;
• initial and focused coding;
• constant comparison;
• memo-writing;
• theoretical sampling;
• saturation or sufficiently developed categories;
• attention to social processes; and
• construction of an interpretive theoretical account.

Her summary still defines grounded-theory coding as constructing codes and categories from data rather than from preconceived, logically deduced hypotheses (http://www.sxf.uevora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Charmaz_2006.pdf).

She therefore sided with Glaser against treating Strauss and Corbin’s coding paradigm as a mandatory template. Her procedures were framed as flexible guidelines rather than prescriptive rules.

5.2 Resolving preconception versus theoretical sensitivity

Charmaz rejected the possibility of a completely neutral observer discovering categories already contained within data. Researchers inevitably enter inquiry with language, disciplinary assumptions, social positions, experiences and interests. Participants likewise construct meanings within particular historical and social circumstances.

The solution is not to eliminate prior understanding—an impossible objective—but to make it visible and revisable:

• use prior concepts as sensitizing rather than definitive concepts;
• compare them with participants’ meanings and actions;
• examine where they fail;
• remain open to unexpected categories;
• write reflexive memos about analytic decisions and standpoint; and
• delay theoretical closure even if relevant literature cannot realistically be ignored.

This reframes Glaser’s “theoretical sensitivity.” Sensitivity is neither a blank mind nor a license to apply theory. It is an explicitly reflexive engagement among prior knowledge, field experience and emerging interpretation.

5.3 Resolving emergence versus forcing

Constructivist grounded theory treats emergence as interactional rather than naturalistic. Categories do not simply reside in raw data waiting to be discovered. They are constructed through:

• what participants say and do;
• what researchers ask and observe;
• the relationship between participant and researcher;
• the conditions under which accounts are produced;
• coding choices and language; and
• the researcher’s theoretical rendering.

This position preserves the ethical force of the anti-forcing principle—researchers should not make evidence conform to settled theories—while abandoning the stronger objectivist image that theory passively emerges from data.

Charmaz’s later account explicitly says that constructivist grounded theory uses the original methodological strategies but shifts their epistemological foundations, treats data as co-constructed, and increases methodological self-consciousness (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1609406917719350).

5.4 Resolving generation versus verification

Charmaz replaced both positivist verification and unqualified discovery with interpretive evaluation. Her framework asks whether an analysis is:

• credible—supported by sufficient, systematic and well-analyzed evidence;
• original—offering new categories, relationships or conceptual insight;
• resonant—making sense of participants’ experiences and broader social processes; and
• useful—contributing to understanding, practice, policy or further inquiry.

This is not verification as proof of a correspondence between theory and an independent objective reality. Nor is it the claim that participant agreement alone validates a theory. It is an assessment of interpretive adequacy, grounding, reflexivity, explanatory reach and practical significance.

Charmaz also inherited older criteria such as fit, usefulness, conceptual density, durability, modifiability and explanatory power (http://www.sxf.uevora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Charmaz_2006.pdf). A 2020 review confirms that grounded-theory quality criteria vary by version and traces the original tradition’s criteria to credibility, applicability, fit and systematic comparison (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14780887.2020.1780357).

5.5 The epistemological shift

Charmaz’s intervention was more than a procedural compromise. It shifted grounded theory:

• from objectivist discovery to interpretive construction;
• from the detached analyst to a situated, reflexive researcher;
• from data as unmediated facts to data as produced through interaction;
• from a single discoverable explanatory reality to partial, situated and revisable interpretations; and
• toward explicit consideration of power, inequality, voice, silence and research relationships.

This distinguishes Charmaz even from Strauss and Corbin. Although their pragmatist and symbolic-interactionist orientation contained constructivist tendencies, their 1990 procedures retained the language of verification and systematic scientific canons. Charmaz made the epistemological break explicit.

6. The paradigm wars of the 1990s–2000s

The grounded-theory dispute mirrored a broader conflict over ontology, epistemology, validity and authority in social research.

Guba and Lincoln’s influential 1994 typology distinguished positivism, postpositivism, critical theory and constructivism, arguing that methodological choices are secondary to a paradigm’s assumptions about reality and knowledge. They openly identified with constructivism (https://ethnographyworkshop.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/guba-lincoln-1994-competing-paradigms-in-qualitative-research-handbook-of-qualitative-research.pdf).

One periodization divides the disputes into:

• 1970–1990: postpositivist and constructivist challenges to positivism;
• 1990–2005: conflict among postpositivist, constructivist and critical paradigms;
• after 2005: renewed conflict among evidence-based movements and mixed-methods, interpretive and critical traditions (https://us.sagepub.com/sites/default/files/upm-binaries/51015_ch_1.pdf).

Against this background:

• Glaser defended methodological autonomy from hypothesis-testing positivism but retained realist/discovery language.
• Strauss and Corbin tried to make qualitative theory development procedurally explicit, systematic and verifiable, partly answering demands for rigor.
• Charmaz aligned grounded theory with the interpretive and constructivist turn, emphasizing situated knowledge and reflexivity.
• Later critical and postmodern adaptations extended this shift by foregrounding discourse, power, inequality and excluded viewpoints.

The debate also concerned institutional legitimacy. Strauss and Corbin’s stepwise procedures made grounded theory easier to teach, audit and defend before committees expecting methodological transparency. Charmaz offered a way to retain such rigor without treating procedure as neutral or equating validity with positivist verification.

By the 2000s, the field had largely moved from searching for one correct qualitative paradigm to recognizing a family of grounded-theory methodologies. The remaining requirement is methodological coherence: researchers should identify which version they use and align their epistemology, coding practices, claims and quality criteria accordingly.

7. Which position dominates contemporary training?

7.1 Available 2020–2024 evidence

The evidence gathered here supports a qualified rather than absolute conclusion.

First, a 2021 review examined 210 grounded-theory studies across 15 highly ranked education journals over 18 years. It found that Straussian approaches were most frequent overall, but Charmaz’s constructivist approach had increased over the latest decade. Only 29.5% of the studies actually delineated a grounded theory (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/16094069211052203).

Quantitative conversion:

210 × 0.295 = 61.95

Thus, approximately 62 of 210 studies produced or clearly delineated a grounded theory, leaving approximately:

210 − 62 = 148 studies,

or 70.5%, that did not. This suggests that what is commonly taught or cited as “grounded theory” is often used as a coding technique rather than as the complete methodology advocated by any of the three traditions.

Second, a 2023 review of three high-profile library and information science journals—Journal of Documentation, Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, and Library & Information Science Research—reported that the Charmazian constructivist version was the most popular identified approach (https://distantreader.org/stacks/journals-ojs/aliseacp/aliseacp-1297.pdf).

Third, prominent methodology discussions in the period continue to use Charmaz as a central reference. The 2020 article on quality in grounded theory was co-authored by Charmaz and organizes quality around version-sensitive criteria rather than one universal verification standard (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14780887.2020.1780357). Contemporary instructional literature also identifies Charmaz’s approach as the most important “second-generation” grounded theory, while noting continuing conflicts among versions (https://us.sagepub.com/sites/default/files/upm-assets/59193_book_item_59193.pdf).

7.2 Interpretation

Taken together, these patterns indicate a divided form of dominance:

• Epistemological and general qualitative-methods dominance: Charmaz.
• Procedural coding influence: Strauss and Corbin.
• Specialist classical-grounded-theory continuity: Glaser.

Charmaz’s Constructing Grounded Theory appears to be the leading cross-disciplinary training reference where programs emphasize reflexivity, positionality, co-construction and interpretive epistemology. Strauss and Corbin remain extremely influential because open/axial/selective coding provides a clear teachable sequence. Many students consequently use a hybrid: constructivist language and Charmaz citations combined with Straussian coding terminology.

Glaser’s position remains influential in dedicated classic-grounded-theory networks and among researchers committed to emergence, core categories and delayed literature review. But it is less consistent with the reflexive, interpretive orientation now common in broader qualitative-methods curricula.

7.3 Limits of the dominance claim

The requested conclusion cannot be treated as a comprehensive census of all 2020–2024 syllabi or citations. The available evidence includes recent journal reviews and contemporary methodological publications, but no single global citation database count restricted to “major methodology journals” for every year from 2020 through 2024.

Further qualifications are necessary:

• The education review found Straussian dominance over its full 18-year window, not necessarily in 2020–2024 alone.
• Disciplinary differences are substantial: education, nursing, information systems, management and information science do not use the variants identically.
• Citations do not always reveal actual practice. Researchers may cite Charmaz while using Strauss and Corbin’s coding sequence, or cite the original 1967 text while conducting generic thematic analysis.
• Book editions complicate citation comparisons: contemporary authors often cite Charmaz’s 2014 second edition or later editions of Corbin and Strauss rather than the specific 2006 and 1990 editions.
• Major journals show widespread methodological mixing and incomplete reporting.

The defensible conclusion is therefore not that constructivism has eliminated its rivals. Rather, Charmaz’s constructivist framing currently supplies the field’s most influential general epistemological vocabulary, while Straussian proceduralism remains embedded in training and applied coding practice.

8. Overall assessment

The evolution of grounded theory can be understood as successive answers to three questions.

First: How can researchers use prior knowledge without predetermining results?

• Glaser: cultivate theoretical sensitivity but delay substantive theoretical commitment.
• Strauss and Corbin: use literature, experience and a coding paradigm to interrogate data systematically.
• Charmaz: acknowledge that prior knowledge is unavoidable, then subject it to reflexive and comparative scrutiny.

Second: When does analytic structure become forcing?

• Glaser: when a framework determines categories or relationships before they earn relevance in data.
• Strauss and Corbin: structure is legitimate when it operates as a revisable heuristic and its relationships are checked against evidence.
• Charmaz: all analysis is constructed, but forcing can be minimized through flexibility, reflexivity, close comparison and attention to participants’ meanings and power relations.

Third: What counts as verification?

• Glaser: fit, work, relevance and modifiability developed through constant comparison; no separate positivist verification stage.
• Strauss and Corbin: iterative checking and revision of relational hypotheses, including searches for negative evidence.
• Charmaz: credibility, originality, resonance and usefulness, grounded in transparent and reflexive interpretive practice.

Charmaz’s major achievement was to show that methodological rigor need not depend either on Glaser’s discovery rhetoric or on a quasi-verificationist coding apparatus. Her reformulation retained the systematic discipline that made grounded theory distinctive while relocating its claims within a constructivist account of knowledge. The cost is that grounded theory no longer promises discovery in a strong realist sense; its products become situated constructions rather than theories simply extracted from data.

Contemporary qualitative training largely accepts that epistemological shift. Yet the day-to-day mechanics of coding still bear Strauss and Corbin’s imprint, and Glaser’s warning remains pertinent: procedural clarity can become a substitute for genuine emergence, especially when researchers mechanically label text without theoretical sampling, constant comparison or theory construction.

final.content:
# WISC-V versus NEPSY-II in the assessment of ADHD and working-memory deficits in children aged 8–12

## Executive conclusion

Neither the WISC-V nor the NEPSY-II can diagnose ADHD. ADHD is a behavioral-developmental diagnosis requiring evidence of persistent symptoms and impairment across settings, exclusion of alternative explanations, and integration of parent, teacher, child, and clinical information. Neuropsychological tests can characterize associated cognitive weaknesses but have inadequate sensitivity and specificity as stand-alone diagnostic instruments.

For detecting **working-memory weakness specifically**, the current evidence favors the **WISC-V Working Memory Index (WMI), supplemented where appropriate by the Auditory Working Memory Index (AWMI)**, over the NEPSY-II:

* WISC-V provides a co-normed, explicitly defined working-memory composite combining auditory-verbal Digit Span and visual Picture Span. AWMI permits more focused auditory assessment.
* NEPSY-II has no global working-memory index. Word List Interference assesses verbal working memory, while Response Set, Auditory Attention, and some other tasks place mixed demands on working memory, attention, inhibition, and set shifting. These tasks may reveal executive-control problems, but they cannot isolate working memory as cleanly.
* ADHD working-memory effects are heterogeneous and often modest on standard Wechsler tasks. WISC-V WMI weakness therefore supports formulation and intervention planning but is not a diagnostic marker.
* No adequately powered, independent, head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy study was located that administered both complete WISC-V and NEPSY-II working-memory measures to 8–12-year-olds and reported sensitivity, specificity, ROC area, and likelihood ratios. Consequently, it is not scientifically defensible to claim that either battery has demonstrated superior numerical sensitivity.

NEPSY-II has greater **breadth and task diversity** for examining attention and executive control. It may be more clinically informative when the question is whether apparent memory failure arises from sustained attention, response inhibition, interference, or set-shifting difficulty. That breadth should not be confused with higher sensitivity to working-memory deficits or superior ecological validity.

The ecological-validity evidence does **not** establish that NEPSY-II is more ecologically valid than WISC-V. Both are highly structured, one-to-one, performance-based assessments. Both sample what a child can do under optimized conditions rather than reliably predicting how the child independently manages competing demands in an ordinary classroom or home. NEPSY-II tasks may have greater surface resemblance to selected real-world demands, but resemblance—“verisimilitude”—is not the same as demonstrated prediction of everyday functioning—“veridicality.” Informant ratings, structured observations, academic data, and, where available, naturalistic or virtual-reality tasks remain necessary.

---

## 1. Scope and search method

### 1.1 Review question

The review addressed four linked questions:

1. Can WISC-V or NEPSY-II diagnose ADHD in children aged 8–12?
2. Which instrument is more sensitive to working-memory deficits?
3. What do pediatric-neuropsychology reviews conclude about NEPSY-II’s ecological validity relative to WISC?
4. What are the principal theories, influential studies, methodological limitations, conflicts, and research gaps?

Evidence specific to ages 8–12 and current editions was prioritized. Older WISC and first-edition NEPSY studies were retained only where they establish theoretical or historical foundations or where current-edition evidence was unavailable.

### 1.2 Sources and search coverage

Searches used combinations of:

* `ADHD`, `attention-deficit`, `hyperactivity`;
* `WISC-V`, `WISC`, `NEPSY-II`, `NEPSY`;
* `working memory`, `executive function`, `attention`, `inhibition`;
* `sensitivity`, `specificity`, `diagnostic validity`, `ROC`;
* `ecological validity`, `everyday functioning`, `BRIEF`;
* `child`, `pediatric`, `8–12`, `school age`;
* `systematic review`, `meta-analysis`, and `neuropsychologist`.

The evidence base included literature indexed or retrieved through PubMed/PMC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, publisher platforms, and test-publisher technical documentation. Particular weight was given to systematic reviews that themselves searched major bibliographic databases. For example:

* Wilson’s WISC-V/WAIS-IV meta-analysis searched PsycINFO, Embase, and MEDLINE, screened 306 records, and included 18 data sources (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11110614/).
* The 2024 *Pediatrics* diagnostic-tools review synthesized 231 studies, including 74 studies of neuropsychological tests (https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/153/4/e2024065854/196923/Tools-for-the-Diagnosis-of-ADHD-in-Children-and).
* The 2023 continuous-performance-test review searched MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, and PubMed through January 2023 and applied QUADAS-2 (https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(23)00171-5/abstract).
* A recent systematic review of 30 years of ADHD/WISC research searched Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and MEDLINE through September 2024, identifying 27 WISC-III/IV studies and 6,486 participants; it is relevant historically but does not directly establish WISC-V diagnostic accuracy (https://dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=10575541).

Because no complete export of every database result, duplicate-removal log, or dual-review screening record was available for the present report, this should be treated as a **structured comprehensive evidence review, not as a new PRISMA-compliant systematic review**. Publication-grade claims should be checked against the final full texts and test manuals before submission.

### 1.3 Evidentiary hierarchy

Highest weight was assigned to:

1. systematic reviews and meta-analyses;
2. independent psychometric or diagnostic-accuracy studies;
3. independent pediatric-neuropsychologist reviews;
4. normative and special-group manual studies;
5. uncontrolled clinical series and case studies.

Manufacturer studies are useful for standardization, reliability, and initial validity, but they are not equivalent to independent diagnostic validation.

---

## 2. What the instruments measure

### 2.1 WISC-V

WISC-V is principally an individually administered measure of intellectual and cognitive abilities for ages 6:0–16:11. It yields five primary indices:

* Verbal Comprehension;
* Visual Spatial;
* Fluid Reasoning;
* Working Memory;
* Processing Speed.

The WMI is based primarily on:

* **Digit Span**, an auditory-verbal task incorporating forward, backward, and sequencing demands;
* **Picture Span**, a visual working-memory task.

The ancillary AWMI provides a more auditory-verbal emphasis, drawing on Digit Span and Letter–Number Sequencing. The Cognitive Proficiency Index combines working-memory and processing-speed information. Pearson’s summary confirms the WMI, AWMI, and related index structure (https://www.pearson.com/content/dam/one-dot-com/one-dot-com/global/Files/efficacy-and-research/reports/WISC-V-Research-Report-v5.pdf).

The WISC-V therefore provides comparatively reliable, co-normed estimates of working-memory performance, but those estimates are not process-pure. Digit Span and Picture Span also depend on attention, encoding strategy, language or visual processing, motivation, and test-taking behavior.

### 2.2 NEPSY-II

NEPSY-II is a flexible developmental-neuropsychological battery for ages 3–16, consisting of 32 subtests and four delayed tasks across six theoretically defined domains:

* Attention and Executive Functioning;
* Language;
* Memory and Learning;
* Social Perception;
* Sensorimotor;
* Visuospatial Processing.

The manual expressly states that its domains are “theoretically, not statistically, derived,” that subtests within a domain may correlate weakly, and that domain composites are not reported. Interpretation is intended principally at the subtest and process-score level (https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf).

For children aged 8–12, the most relevant tasks include:

* **Word List Interference**: verbal working memory, repetition, ordered recall, and resistance to interference;
* **Auditory Attention**: selective and sustained auditory attention;
* **Response Set**: maintenance and shifting of a complex response set, with inhibition of a previously learned response;
* **Inhibition**: naming, inhibition, and switching under time pressure;
* **Animal Sorting**: concept formation and set shifting;
* **Memory for Designs**: immediate and delayed spatial memory;
* **List Memory**: learning and delayed verbal recall.

Only Word List Interference is explicitly described as a verbal working-memory measure. Response Set places working-memory demands on the child but is deliberately multicomponential. Thus, “NEPSY-II working memory” is not a single psychometric construct comparable to WISC-V WMI.

---

## 3. ADHD diagnosis: what neuropsychological tests can and cannot do

The 2024 *Pediatrics* systematic review included 231 studies of ADHD diagnostic tools. Seventy-four used neuropsychological tests:

\[
74/231 = 0.320 \approx 32.0\%
\]

Reported neuropsychological-test sensitivities ranged from 22% to 100%, specificities from 22% to 100%, and AUCs from 0.59 to 0.93. The apparently perfect results came from unreplicated, study-specific composites; performance deteriorated when ADHD was distinguished from clinically referred children rather than unusually healthy controls (https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/153/4/e2024065854/196923/Tools-for-the-Diagnosis-of-ADHD-in-Children-and).

Even continuous-performance tests, designed more directly around sustained attention and response control, provide only modest discrimination. Across 19 studies, pooled estimates were:

| CPT metric | Sensitivity | Specificity |
|---|---:|---:|
| Total/ADHD score | 0.75, 95% CI 0.66–0.82 | 0.71, 0.62–0.78 |
| Omissions/inattention | 0.63, 0.49–0.75 | 0.74, 0.65–0.81 |
| Commissions/impulsivity | 0.59, 0.38–0.77 | 0.66, 0.50–0.78 |

The authors concluded that CPTs should be used only within a comprehensive diagnostic process (https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(23)00171-5/abstract). Since neither WISC-V nor NEPSY-II is primarily an ADHD diagnostic test, expectations of diagnostic accuracy should be lower still unless a rigorously validated composite is developed.

Clinical interpretation must distinguish:

* **diagnostic sensitivity**: proportion of children with ADHD correctly identified;
* **sensitivity to a cognitive deficit**: ability to detect working-memory weakness when it is actually present;
* **group sensitivity**: statistically lower average performance among ADHD groups;
* **clinical utility**: usefulness for case formulation, intervention, or differential diagnosis.

Many publications use “sensitive” in the third or fourth sense without reporting diagnostic sensitivity. A significant mean difference or Cohen’s \(d\) is not a sensitivity coefficient.

---

## 4. Working memory in ADHD: foundational evidence

### 4.1 Seminal meta-analysis

Martinussen et al.’s meta-analysis included 26 studies published from 1997 through 2003 and classified working-memory tasks by modality and by storage versus storage-plus-manipulation. Reported ADHD-control effect sizes were:

| Working-memory component | Effect size | 95% CI |
|---|---:|---:|
| Spatial storage | 0.85 | 0.62–1.08 |
| Spatial central executive | 1.06 | 0.72–1.39 |
| Verbal storage | 0.47 | 0.36–0.59 |
| Verbal central executive | 0.43 | 0.24–0.62 |

The deficits remained after considering language/learning comorbidity and general intellectual ability (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15782085/).

The modality difference is substantial:

\[
\frac{1.06}{0.43}=2.47
\]

Thus, the reported spatial central-executive effect was approximately 2.5 times the verbal central-executive effect. Likewise:

\[
\frac{0.85}{0.47}=1.81
\]

The spatial-storage effect was approximately 1.8 times the verbal-storage effect.

This matters because WISC-V WMI samples both visual and auditory working memory, whereas the clearest NEPSY-II working-memory task, Word List Interference, is verbal. It gives WISC-V a theoretical coverage advantage. It does not prove greater clinical sensitivity, because Picture Span is not identical to the spatial central-executive paradigms that generated the largest meta-analytic effects.

### 4.2 Broader neurocognitive meta-review

A review of 34 ADHD neurocognitive meta-analyses extracted 253 standardized mean differences; 244 favored controls:

\[
244/253=0.964 \approx 96.4\%
\]

The unweighted mean working-memory effect was \(d=0.54\). Other domains with comparable effects included response inhibition, reaction-time variability, intelligence/achievement, and planning/organization (https://academic.oup.com/acn/article/33/2/143/3926568).

A group effect of \(d=0.54\) is meaningful but leaves extensive overlap between distributions. Under an equal-variance normal approximation, the proportion of overlap is:

\[
2\Phi(-d/2)=2\Phi(-0.27)\approx 0.787
\]

or approximately **79% overlap**. This calculation illustrates why working-memory weakness cannot function as a diagnostic signature: many children with ADHD perform normally, and many children without ADHD—especially those with learning, language, anxiety, sleep, or other neurodevelopmental problems—perform poorly.

---

## 5. Evidence for WISC-V

### 5.1 Meta-analysis of current Wechsler editions

Wilson’s meta-analysis searched PsycINFO, Embase, and MEDLINE, screened 306 sources, and synthesized 18 data sources with 1,842 neurodivergent participants. The child evidence included 856 WISC-V assessments, of whom 226 had ADHD:

\[
226/856=0.264 \approx 26.4\%
\]

Children and adults with ADHD generally performed within age-expected ranges, with only slightly reduced working-memory scores. The review concluded that Wechsler profiles are not sufficiently sensitive or specific for diagnosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11110614/).

Methodological strengths included:

* explicit eligibility criteria;
* duplicate-data handling;
* multilevel random-effects models;
* risk-of-bias assessment;
* correction for multiple comparisons;
* sensitivity analyses for heterogeneity and publication bias;
* second-rater coding of 25% of data with reported complete agreement.

Limitations included:

* only 226 children with ADHD;
* age range 6–16 rather than a separate 8–12 analysis;
* few studies reporting subtest-level data;
* predominantly White and male samples;
* inconsistent documentation of medication and comorbidity;
* cross-sectional designs;
* aggregation across referral and national contexts.

### 5.2 Clinical-profile studies

A 2021 study compared 62 children with ADHD plus specific learning disorder, 35 with learning disorder alone, and 62 controls. The ADHD-plus-learning-disorder group had lower WMI, PSI, FSIQ, AWMI, and CPI than controls. However, impairment was broad rather than ADHD-specific, and the design could not separate ADHD from learning-disorder effects (https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/17/9948).

This study supports WISC-V’s utility for describing strengths and weaknesses but provides weak evidence for ADHD diagnosis because:

* the ADHD group was necessarily comorbid;
* no ADHD-only group was included;
* diagnostic sensitivity and specificity were not reported;
* multiple indices were reduced, weakening specificity.

A 2024 measurement-invariance study compared 91 children and adolescents with ADHD with 91 demographically matched controls. Configural and metric invariance were supported, but full scalar invariance was not; partial scalar invariance required freeing intercepts for Digit Span, Picture Span, Coding, Symbol Search, Vocabulary, and the working-memory and processing-speed factors. Reliability was better for general intelligence than for narrow indices. These findings caution against treating WMI group differences as if the scale operated identically in ADHD and control groups.

A 2025 psychometric study of 250 students with ADHD and 250 normative students reported diagnostic validity for processing speed but not for working memory (https://brieflands.com/journals/ijpbs/articles/153741). This conclusion conflicts with profile studies, but the paper warrants substantial caution: purposeful clinical sampling, uncertain diagnostic verification, use of a “confidence interval” or sensitivity-coefficient approach rather than conventional ROC analysis, and apparent inaccuracies in its description of WISC-V development reduce confidence in its diagnostic claims.

An online 2026 study of 241 recently diagnosed children and adolescents reported lower WMI and PSI and lower Cognitive Proficiency than General Ability, but concluded that discrepancies were neither sensitive nor specific enough to serve as diagnostic markers (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0). This is consistent with the broader synthesis: group-level weakness does not yield individual-level diagnosis.

### 5.3 Manufacturer validity evidence

Pearson’s WISC-V supplement included ADHD special groups of approximately 46–47 children, mean age around 11 years, who completed parent-rated BASC-2 and Brown ADD measures. Pearson describes these studies as evidence concerning construct and ecological validity (https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/wisc-v/wisc-v-tech-manual-supplement.pdf).

The supplement is useful but limited by:

* small samples;
* reliance on concurrent parent ratings;
* multiple correlations;
* restricted score ranges within clinical groups;
* absence of independent replication;
* absence of classroom observation or prospective functional outcomes;
* manufacturer authorship.

Correlations with rating scales establish, at most, concurrent association. They do not establish that WISC-V performance predicts everyday working-memory failures.

### 5.4 Overall WISC-V judgment

WISC-V is well suited to answering:

* Is working-memory performance low relative to age peers?
* Is it low relative to the child’s reasoning abilities?
* Is the weakness primarily auditory, visual, or both?
* Could cognitive proficiency contribute to academic inefficiency?

It is poorly suited to answering:

* Does this child have ADHD?
* Are observed everyday attention failures caused by a working-memory deficit?
* Will the child function adequately in an unstructured classroom because WMI was average?

---

## 6. Evidence for NEPSY-II

### 6.1 Independent pediatric-neuropsychologist review

Brooks, Sherman, and Strauss—pediatric neuropsychologists affiliated with Alberta Children’s Hospital/University of Calgary and the University of Victoria—published a detailed independent review of NEPSY-II covering its 32 subtests, reliability, validity, strengths, and limitations (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09297040903146966).

The review recognized NEPSY-II as an unusually broad and flexible pediatric battery but emphasized that validity varies across scores and constructs rather than residing in the battery as a unitary property. The clinical attraction is hypothesis-driven subtest selection and process analysis. The corresponding risk is fragmented interpretation, multiple comparisons, and over-attribution of a low score to one latent ability.

A second independent test review by Davis and Matthews appeared in the *Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment* (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0734282909346716). Available summaries indicate generally adequate-to-high reliability and useful discriminative information but also note complexity, training demands, and a shortage of independent validation studies.

### 6.2 ADHD special-group evidence

The NEPSY-II standardization program included ten clinical groups, including ADHD. Manual-derived effect sizes summarized in the Brooks review suggest small-to-moderate ADHD-control differences on several attention/executive scores; examples include approximately \(d=0.54\) for an Auditory Attention combined score and \(d=0.73\) for Response Set total correct. These are not pure working-memory effects and do not supply cut-score sensitivity or specificity.

Interpretation is constrained because:

* standardization clinical groups were relatively small;
* several scores were examined;
* medication status and comorbidity may not have been fully controlled;
* healthy normative controls inflate apparent discrimination relative to clinically referred comparison groups;
* the evidence is partly manufacturer-generated;
* no validated multivariate ADHD classification rule emerged.

A clinical comparison of 36 children/adolescents with ADHD and 36 with specific learning disorder reported poorer NEPSY-II inhibition, cognitive flexibility, short-term verbal memory, and verbal working memory in ADHD. However, the broad age range of 5–15, small samples, group IQ differences, and lack of healthy controls limit inference.

A 2025 study of 48 children aged 8–15 divided among ADHD, anxiety, and comorbid ADHD-plus-anxiety groups found no significant group differences in working memory or attention. NEPSY-II inhibition time differentiated groups more clearly: anxiety-only participants were more efficient than ADHD and comorbid participants (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12191324/). The study illustrates both the potential relevance of inhibition and the weakness of working-memory performance for differential diagnosis. Its small three-group sample and absence of a neurotypical group preclude stable diagnostic estimates.

### 6.3 Structural validity

A recent confirmatory-factor analysis examined 23 NEPSY-II scores from 600 children aged 7–12 in the normative sample. The best model included a general factor and four first-order factors, but most general-factor loadings were below .50:

* range: .21–.69;
* mean: .44.

Domain-specific effects were still smaller, while subtest-specific effects were strong. The authors concluded that results support careful subtest-level rather than composite-level interpretation (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09297049.2024.2357376).

This study is directly age-relevant and methodologically strong because of its \(N=600\), balanced sex composition, and explicit comparison of alternative factor models. Its principal limitation is that it used normative rather than ADHD data. It informs construct interpretation, not diagnostic accuracy.

### 6.4 Overall NEPSY-II judgment

NEPSY-II is particularly useful when the examiner needs to determine whether poor performance emerges under:

* interference;
* increased rule complexity;
* inhibition requirements;
* set shifting;
* prolonged auditory attention;
* learning and delayed recall;
* spatial versus verbal memory conditions.

It is less satisfactory for producing a single, reliable estimate of “working-memory capacity.” Low Response Set or Word List Interference performance should not be treated as interchangeable with a low WISC-V WMI.

---

## 7. Which test has better sensitivity for working-memory deficits?

### 7.1 Direct answer

**For a psychometrically explicit estimate of working-memory weakness, WISC-V is preferable. For qualitative analysis of how attention, inhibition, shifting, and interference disrupt memory performance, NEPSY-II is complementary rather than superior.**

This is a construct-coverage and measurement judgment, not a demonstrated head-to-head difference in diagnostic sensitivity.

### 7.2 Comparative matrix

| Criterion | WISC-V | NEPSY-II | Best-supported conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Explicit working-memory composite | WMI; optional AWMI | None | WISC-V advantage |
| Auditory-verbal working memory | Digit Span; Letter–Number Sequencing in AWMI | Word List Interference; mixed demands in Response Set | WISC-V better standardized; NEPSY-II offers interference analysis |
| Visual working memory | Picture Span | Memory for Designs, but primarily framed as spatial memory rather than a WM index | WISC-V closer to a cross-modal WM composite |
| Executive-control demands | Limited within WMI | Extensive: Response Set, Inhibition, Animal Sorting | NEPSY-II advantage for process differentiation |
| Reliability through aggregation | Composite scores reduce task-specific error | Subtest interpretation emphasized | WISC-V advantage for trait estimation |
| ADHD diagnostic specificity | Poor | Poor/insufficiently established | Neither |
| Published sensitivity/specificity for WM deficit | Not adequately established | Not adequately established | No winner empirically |
| Ecological validity | Limited | Limited | No established NEPSY-II superiority |
| Utility for intervention planning | Cognitive profile and academic accommodation | Neuropsychological process analysis | Complementary |

### 7.3 Why WISC-V may still miss ADHD-related working-memory problems

An average WMI does not rule out ADHD-related working-memory dysfunction because:

1. the one-to-one setting minimizes distraction;
2. tasks are brief and externally structured;
3. the examiner supplies goals, pacing, and prompts;
4. motivation and novelty can temporarily normalize performance;
5. ADHD is cognitively heterogeneous;
6. laboratory working memory and everyday goal management are not identical constructs;
7. standard WMI tasks may under-sample the spatial central-executive processes showing the largest ADHD effects in meta-analysis.

Thus, WISC-V has the better measure of working-memory performance under standardized conditions, but neither WISC-V nor NEPSY-II is necessarily highly sensitive to everyday working-memory failure.

---

## 8. Ecological validity

### 8.1 Conceptual distinctions

Ecological validity has at least two relevant meanings:

* **Verisimilitude:** how closely the test resembles an everyday activity.
* **Veridicality:** how well test performance predicts actual behavior or outcomes in daily life.

A task can look realistic yet fail to predict classroom functioning. Conversely, an abstract task can have ecological validity if it robustly predicts meaningful outcomes.

### 8.2 Pediatric-neuropsychology reviews

Olson, Jacobson, and Van Oot’s pediatric review noted that neuropsychologists are increasingly expected to predict everyday functioning, yet most ecological-validity knowledge comes from adult populations and the child evidence is comparatively underdeveloped (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21622965.2012.686330).

Chaytor and Schmitter-Edgecombe’s influential review of everyday cognitive prediction is repeatedly cited in the pediatric literature as documenting limited or variable ecological validity for traditional neuropsychological measures. Spooner and Pachana similarly argued for greater methodological attention to ecological validity.

The strongest cross-method synthesis is Toplak, West, and Stanovich’s practitioner review. Across 20 studies—13 child and seven adult samples—only 68 of 286 correlations between performance tests and executive-function ratings were significant:

\[
68/286=0.238 \approx 23.8\%
\]

The median correlation was \(r=.19\), corresponding to:

\[
r^2=.19^2=.0361
\]

Thus, the methods shared only about **3.6% variance** at the median. The authors proposed that performance tests measure the efficiency of cognitive abilities under structured conditions, whereas ratings measure success in goal pursuit over time in ordinary environments (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23057693/).

This is not merely evidence that one method is “better.” It supports a two-level framework:

* tests assess optimal or constrained performance;
* ratings and observations assess typical deployment of abilities.

Both can be valid while measuring different levels of functioning.

### 8.3 NEPSY-II versus WISC-V

No high-quality pediatric-neuropsychologist review was located that directly demonstrated superior ecological validity for NEPSY-II over WISC-V using matched predictive criteria.

NEPSY-II may appear more ecological because:

* Response Set requires maintaining and changing rules;
* Inhibition introduces speeded conflict;
* Word List Interference approximates competing-memory demands;
* Route Finding and Clocks have familiar content;
* multiple error types permit qualitative behavioral analysis.

Nevertheless, these remain examiner-led, decontextualized, short-duration tasks. The child does not independently choose the goal, organize materials over long periods, resist naturally occurring distraction, or manage emotional and motivational consequences. NEPSY-II therefore offers broader executive sampling, not established ecological superiority.

WISC-V’s manufacturer supplement describes correlations with parent behavior ratings as evidence relevant to ecological validity, but the ADHD samples were small and the criteria were concurrent questionnaires rather than independent naturalistic outcomes (https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/wisc-v/wisc-v-tech-manual-supplement.pdf). The same caution applies when NEPSY-II scores are correlated with executive ratings.

A study of 141 preterm and 77 term preschool children found that performance-based intelligence and executive tests, including NEPSY-II, were not consistently associated with parent- or teacher-reported everyday executive functioning. Although younger than the target age and not an ADHD study, it reinforces the cross-method problem.

Emerging naturalistic methods may improve prediction. A 2024 virtual-reality study included 76 participants aged 9–17, 40 with ADHD and 36 neurotypical controls. The ADHD group made more errors, commissions, new actions, and forgotten actions; forgetting was associated with lower everyday independence, \(r=-.281\). The result is preliminary but illustrates the type of outcome-linked assessment missing from both standard batteries (https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9067/11/8/986).

### 8.4 Ecological-validity conclusion

The defensible synthesis is:

1. NEPSY-II has broader executive-task content than WISC-V.
2. Some NEPSY-II tasks possess greater face validity or verisimilitude.
3. Neither battery has strong evidence of veridicality for everyday ADHD impairment.
4. There is no sufficient evidence that NEPSY-II is globally more ecologically valid than WISC-V.
5. Parent and teacher ratings, direct observation, school records, and functional tasks are not optional substitutes for missing test data; they assess different and clinically essential levels of behavior.

---

## 9. Theoretical frameworks

### 9.1 Inhibitory-control model

Barkley’s influential model conceptualized behavioral inhibition as a foundational deficit disrupting working memory, self-regulation, internalization of speech, and behavioral synthesis. NEPSY-II Inhibition and Response Set map more visibly onto this framework than WISC-V WMI.

Evidence conflicts with a universal-inhibition model, however. Not every child with ADHD has an inhibition deficit, and meta-analytic effects occur across several domains rather than one core process.

### 9.2 Multicomponent working-memory model

The Martinussen meta-analysis classified performance by verbal versus spatial modality and storage versus central-executive manipulation. Its larger spatial effects support a multicomponent account rather than a unitary “short-term memory” deficit. WISC-V’s auditory and visual working-memory subtests align better with this framework than a single NEPSY-II verbal interference task.

### 9.3 Executive-function unity and diversity

NEPSY-II embodies a broad, theoretically organized model encompassing attention, inhibition, shifting, planning, fluency, and monitoring. The recent factor analysis supports multidimensionality but also shows strong task-specific variance and weak domain-specific effects. That pattern accords with “task impurity”: every executive task recruits multiple basic and executive processes.

### 9.4 Optimal performance versus goal management

Toplak and colleagues’ framework distinguishes cognitive efficiency under structured conditions from success in independent goal pursuit. This model explains why a child can obtain average WISC-V or NEPSY-II scores but show severe classroom disorganization, forgotten instructions, incomplete assignments, and dependence on adult prompts.

### 9.5 Multiple-pathway and dimensional accounts

The broad distribution of ADHD effects across working memory, inhibition, reaction-time variability, vigilance, and planning supports heterogeneous or multiple-pathway models. It also favors dimensional analysis of symptom severity and functional impairment over attempts to locate a universal cognitive profile.

---

## 10. Methodological appraisal and conflicting evidence

### 10.1 Why findings conflict

The literature alternately reports clear working-memory weakness, small average differences, or no significant group differences. The discrepancies are attributable to:

* different ADHD diagnostic criteria and verification procedures;
* varying proportions of inattentive and combined presentations;
* medication continuation versus washout;
* learning, language, anxiety, autism, sleep, and mood comorbidity;
* exclusion of low-IQ participants;
* age ranges much broader than 8–12;
* healthy versus clinical comparison groups;
* verbal versus spatial task composition;
* storage versus manipulation requirements;
* use of index means rather than process scores;
* small clinical samples and low statistical power;
* multiple-testing and selective-reporting risk;
* failure to report diagnostic thresholds or ROC analyses;
* cultural and linguistic differences in norms.

### 10.2 Group differences versus diagnostic classification

A statistically significant mean difference does not establish useful classification. With a moderate effect such as \(d=.54\), the approximate distributional overlap is 79%. Even a well-replicated group effect will generate many false negatives and false positives at the individual level.

Diagnostic studies should report:

* sensitivity and specificity at prespecified cutoffs;
* ROC AUC;
* positive and negative likelihood ratios;
* predictive values at realistic ADHD prevalence;
* calibration;
* external validation in clinically referred samples.

Most WISC-V and NEPSY-II studies do not.

### 10.3 Incremental validity

The clinically relevant question is not whether a test differentiates ADHD from exceptionally healthy controls. It is whether it improves decisions after parent and teacher symptom ratings, developmental history, interview, observation, and academic assessment are already available.

Neither battery has convincing evidence of substantial incremental diagnostic validity over those sources. Their principal value is explanatory and prescriptive: identifying cognitive and learning needs, examining differential diagnoses, and guiding accommodations.

### 10.4 Test-age and edition problems

Older WISC-III/IV and NEPSY-I findings remain influential but cannot automatically be transferred to WISC-V and NEPSY-II. WISC-V changed factor structure and added Picture Span; NEPSY-II removed domain composites and changed several attention/executive tasks. Edition-specific validation is required.

---

## 11. Citation and influence analysis

Formal citation counts could not be verified from a single citation index and therefore should not be invented. Influence was instead judged by recurrence across systematic reviews, test manuals, and subsequent theoretical or methodological papers.

The most influential works in this evidence network are:

1. **Barkley (1997), inhibition/self-regulation theory** — foundational for conceptualizing ADHD as executive dysregulation and repeatedly cited in assessment literature.
2. **Martinussen et al. (2005)** — seminal modality-by-process working-memory meta-analysis; still central to claims that spatial working memory may be more impaired than verbal working memory (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15782085/).
3. **Chaytor and Schmitter-Edgecombe (2003)** — foundational review of neuropsychological tests and everyday cognitive skills.
4. **Toplak, West, and Stanovich (2013)** — highly influential synthesis demonstrating weak performance-test/rating correspondence and proposing efficiency versus goal-pursuit constructs (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23057693/).
5. **Brooks, Sherman, and Strauss (2010)** — principal independent pediatric-neuropsychology review of NEPSY-II (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09297040903146966).
6. **Wilson (2024 issue; online 2023)** — current-edition Wechsler meta-analysis showing only slight ADHD working-memory reduction and inadequate diagnostic specificity (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11110614/).
7. **2024 *Pediatrics* systematic review** — broad state-of-the-art evaluation of ADHD diagnostic tools, emphasizing heterogeneous and generally low-strength neuropsychological evidence (https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/153/4/e2024065854/196923/Tools-for-the-Diagnosis-of-ADHD-in-Children-and).
8. **Recent NEPSY-II structural analysis** — important current evidence that subtest-specific variance is substantial and domain interpretation requires caution (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09297049.2024.2357376).

A publication should describe these works as conceptually or methodologically influential, not attach numerical citation rankings without a documented Web of Science, Scopus, or Google Scholar search date and deduplication method.

---

## 12. Clinical implications for an 8–12-year-old

### 12.1 Recommended assessment sequence

1. **Establish the diagnostic phenotype**
   * development and medical history;
   * parent and teacher DSM-based ratings;
   * impairment in at least two settings;
   * onset and persistence;
   * interview and behavioral observation;
   * review of sleep, anxiety, mood, trauma, hearing/vision, medication, and learning history.

2. **Assess academic and language factors**
   * reading, written language, mathematics;
   * receptive and expressive language where indicated;
   * school attendance, instruction, and response to intervention.

3. **Use WISC-V when the question concerns overall cognitive profile**
   * WMI and AWMI for working-memory estimation;
   * WMI–reasoning discrepancies only as descriptive, not diagnostic;
   * inspect Digit Span process scores and Picture Span rather than relying only on WMI;
   * consider PSI and CPI, while avoiding an “ADHD profile” inference.

4. **Add selected NEPSY-II subtests when process differentiation is needed**
   * Word List Interference for verbal working memory under interference;
   * Auditory Attention/Response Set for increasing attention and set-maintenance demands;
   * Inhibition for speeded inhibition and switching;
   * Memory for Designs or List Memory where encoding versus retention is in question.

5. **Measure everyday executive functioning separately**
   * parent and teacher executive-function ratings;
   * direct classroom observation where possible;
   * work samples, assignment completion, multistep-instruction performance;
   * functional or naturalistic tasks.

### 12.2 Interpretation principles

* Do not infer ADHD from a low WMI, low Response Set, or a WMI/PSI profile.
* Do not exclude ADHD because WMI and NEPSY-II attention scores are average.
* A low WMI is not specific to ADHD; consider learning, language, anxiety, sleep, depression, intellectual functioning, and effort.
* A poor Response Set score may reflect attention, working memory, inhibition, language comprehension, or shifting.
* Multiple low NEPSY-II subtests require correction for base rates and consideration of the number of scores inspected.
* Medication status, time of day, fatigue, and behavioral observations should be reported.
* The report should separate test-based capacity from everyday performance.

---

## 13. Research gaps and priorities

### 13.1 Direct comparative diagnostic study

The most important missing study is a preregistered, independent comparison of WISC-V and NEPSY-II in 8–12-year-olds, including:

* ADHD-only, ADHD-plus-learning-disorder, anxiety, autism, learning-disorder-only, and neurotypical groups;
* blinded, consensus DSM diagnosis independent of test scores;
* medication status standardized or modeled;
* complete WISC-V WMI/AWMI and prespecified NEPSY-II working-memory/executive measures;
* ROC curves, sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, and calibration;
* external replication.

### 13.2 Define the reference standard for “working-memory deficit”

Sensitivity cannot be estimated without an independent criterion. Future studies should prespecify whether deficit means:

* a latent working-memory factor derived from multiple tasks;
* ecologically observed multistep-instruction failure;
* academic impact;
* rating-scale elevation;
* a threshold on an independent experimental battery.

Using one test as the criterion for validating the other creates circularity.

### 13.3 Ecological prediction

Studies should prospectively test whether WISC-V and NEPSY-II predict:

* classroom task completion;
* following multistep directions;
* homework independence;
* prospective memory;
* academic growth;
* treatment or accommodation response.

Models should compare WISC-V, NEPSY-II, ratings, observation, and naturalistic tasks and report incremental \(R^2\), cross-validated prediction, and calibration.

### 13.4 Heterogeneity

Research should stratify or model:

* inattentive versus hyperactive-impulsive symptom dimensions;
* sex and gender;
* socioeconomic and linguistic background;
* comorbidity;
* sleep;
* medication;
* symptom severity;
* age within the 8–12 developmental period.

Girls, racial and linguistic minorities, and children outside high-income English-speaking settings remain underrepresented.

### 13.5 Psychometric modernization

Needed advances include:

* item-level and process-level modeling;
* latent-variable separation of attention, storage, manipulation, and inhibition;
* measurement-invariance testing in ADHD and comorbid groups;
* normative base rates for multiple low scores;
* repeated measurement to estimate intraindividual variability;
* computational modeling of response time and error patterns;
* open data, preregistration, and independent validation.

### 13.6 Current norms and test revision

NEPSY-II was published in 2007 and WISC-V in 2014. Secular changes, educational technology, and demographic shifts strengthen the case for updated norms and direct evaluation of cultural-linguistic fairness.

---

## 14. Final synthesis

The evidence supports three distinct conclusions.

First, **neither WISC-V nor NEPSY-II should be used to diagnose ADHD**. Their scores lack the required individual-level sensitivity and specificity, and the controlled testing environment incompletely represents real-world impairment.

Second, **WISC-V is the better-supported instrument for quantifying working-memory weakness**, because it provides an explicit, co-normed, cross-modal WMI and optional AWMI. The conclusion is about measurement architecture and available evidence—not proven superiority in a direct diagnostic-accuracy trial. ADHD-related WMI reductions are generally small to moderate and insufficiently specific.

Third, **NEPSY-II is valuable as a complementary process-oriented battery**, particularly for investigating whether apparent memory difficulty worsens with interference, rule switching, inhibition, or sustained attention. Its broader executive content does not establish better ecological validity. * behavioral-developmental ADHD assessment as the diagnostic foundation;
* WISC-V for general cognitive and working-memory profiling when clinically indicated;
* targeted NEPSY-II subtests for hypothesis-driven process analysis;
* academic, language, rating-scale, observational, and functional evidence for real-world interpretation.

Any stronger claim—particularly that NEPSY-II is more ecologically valid or that one battery has empirically superior sensitivity for ADHD working-memory deficits—currently exceeds the evidence.
