final.content:
# DSM-5 and ICD-11 Autism Diagnosis: Sensory Processing, Evidence, Guidance, Safety, and Coding

## Executive summary

DSM-5 and ICD-11 are closely aligned in defining autism through two required domains: (1) social-communication/social-interaction differences and (2) restricted, repetitive, or inflexible behavior, interests, or activities. Both recognize atypical sensory responses within the second domain, but they operationalize them differently:

- **DSM-5 gives sensory processing a discrete, countable position:** hyper-/hyporeactivity or unusual sensory interest is one of four restricted/repetitive behavior criteria, and any two of the four are required. Sensory differences can therefore supply **one-half of the restricted/repetitive-behavior threshold**, but cannot establish autism without another restricted/repetitive feature and all three social-communication criteria.
- **ICD-11 treats sensory differences as one possible manifestation** within a broader, clinically judged range of restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns. It does not impose DSM-5’s “two of four” algorithm, so the exact numerical weight of sensory evidence is not specified.
- Neither manual permits a diagnosis based on sensory processing differences alone. Both require developmental onset, core social-communication differences, and meaningful functional impairment.
- Direct head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy evidence comparing final DSM-5 and final ICD-11 autism requirements is extremely limited. Available research mainly compares DSM-5 with DSM-IV/ICD-10, evaluates ICD-11 clinical utility across mental disorders generally, or compares the manuals descriptively. Claims that one is demonstrably more sensitive or specific than the other are therefore premature.
- WHO promotes national implementation of ICD-11; NICE permits either ICD-11 or DSM-5; APA and the American Academy of Pediatrics continue to anchor US diagnosis in DSM-5/DSM-5-TR while claims are coded in ICD-10-CM.
- None of the three reviewed advocacy organizations formally declares DSM-5 or ICD-11 categorically “more neurodiversity-affirming.” Their materials more strongly favor inclusive, non-stigmatizing language, recognition of sensory experience, and needs-based support than a particular manual.

---

## A. Side-by-side criteria

| Issue | DSM-5 (2013) | ICD-11 (adopted 2019; effective 2022) | Practical comparison |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Core social-communication criteria** | Requires persistent deficits across multiple contexts in **all three** areas: (1) social-emotional reciprocity; (2) nonverbal communicative behaviors; and (3) developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships. DSM-5-TR later inserted “all” to clarify that this was already DSM-5’s intended threshold. In addition, at least two of four restricted/repetitive behavior criteria are required. APA clarification: https://www.psychiatry.org/File%20Library/Psychiatrists/Practice/DSM/DSM-5-TR/APA-DSM5TR-AutismSpectrumDisorder.pdf; criteria reproduced by CDC: https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html | Requires persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication, outside the expected range for age and intellectual development, plus persistent restricted, repetitive, and inflexible behavior/interests/activities. ICD-11 provides illustrative manifestations rather than DSM-style mandatory subcriterion counts. WHO CDDR: https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content | Both require both broad domains. DSM-5 is more explicitly algorithmic and potentially more restrictive because all three social-communication subcriteria and two restricted/repetitive criteria must be documented. ICD-11 relies more heavily on clinician judgment about a sufficient “range” of manifestations. |
| **Sensory-processing mention and weighting** | Criterion B4 is “hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment,” including pain/temperature indifference, adverse responses to sounds or textures, smelling/touching objects, and visual fascination with lights or movement. It is **one of four B criteria**; at least two B criteria are needed. Thus sensory differences can count as one required feature but are neither mandatory nor sufficient. https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html | Atypical sensory responses—persistent hypersensitivity, hyposensitivity, or unusual interest in sensory stimuli—are included as possible manifestations of the restricted/repetitive/inflexible domain. ICD-11 does not assign them a separate numbered criterion or a fixed “one of four” value. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/; WHO CDDR: https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content | DSM-5 makes sensory evidence more visible and auditable but gives it a fixed maximum contribution: **1 of the 2 required B features**. ICD-11 allows more contextual weighting but less inter-rater transparency. In neither system can sensory symptoms compensate for absent core social-communication differences. |
| **Severity/specifiers** | Clinician assigns separate support-need levels for each core domain: Level 1, “requiring support”; Level 2, “requiring substantial support”; or Level 3, “requiring very substantial support.” Also specify intellectual impairment, language impairment, associated medical/genetic/environmental condition, another neurodevelopmental/mental/behavioral condition, and catatonia. Autism Speaks summary: https://www.autismspeaks.org/blog/expert-qa-dsm-5-and-asd | No direct equivalent of DSM-5’s three support-level scale. ICD-11 subcategories primarily combine presence/absence of disorder of intellectual development with degree of functional-language impairment: mild/no impairment, impaired functional language, or complete/almost complete absence of functional language. Base category and codes are described at https://www.icd11-code.com/6a02/ and in WHO’s CDDR above. | DSM-5 severity is framed around current support needs in each domain, although support ratings may change by setting and available accommodation. ICD-11 emphasizes intellectual development and functional language, which is useful for coding but does not by itself capture sensory burden, adaptive functioning, masking, or total support need. Neither has a sensory-severity specifier. |
| **Age/onset** | Symptoms must be present in the **early developmental period**, but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed capacity or may be masked by learned strategies later in life. Current or historical evidence can count. https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5 | Onset must occur during the developmental period, typically early childhood, but features may become fully apparent only later when social demands exceed capacity. https://www.icd11-code.com/6a02/ | Substantively very similar. Neither requires diagnosis by a fixed age, and both permit adult diagnosis when developmental evidence supports lifelong features. |
| **Functional-impairment threshold** | Symptoms must cause **clinically significant impairment** in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning and must not be better explained by intellectual disability/global developmental delay. https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5 | Deficits must be sufficiently severe to cause impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational, or other important areas. Features are usually pervasive but may vary by context. https://www.icd11-code.com/6a02/ | Both require impairment rather than neurodivergent traits alone. ICD-11 explicitly names family and educational functioning and foregrounds contextual variation. In either system, clinicians should assess the effort and accommodations needed to maintain apparently adequate performance, rather than equating masking with absence of impairment. |

### Sensory-weighting illustration

Under DSM-5:

- Required restricted/repetitive threshold = **2 of 4 criteria**.
- If sensory criterion B4 is present, its formal contribution is:

\[
1 \div 2 = 50\%
\]

of the minimum B-domain count.

This does **not** mean sensory features constitute 50% of the whole autism diagnosis: all three social-communication criteria, developmental onset, functional impairment, and exclusionary considerations still apply.

Under ICD-11, no equivalent percentage can be calculated because the manual does not prescribe a fixed number of sensory versus nonsensory manifestations.

---

## B. Evidence synthesis

### Central evidence finding

No identified peer-reviewed study directly estimated sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, or negative predictive value for **final DSM-5 versus final ICD-11 autism criteria in the same representative sample against an independent reference standard**. The closest literature is indirect: DSM-5 versus DSM-IV/ICD-10 studies, broad ICD-11 utility research, and structured textual comparisons.

GRADE ratings below are report-level judgments for the specific question “How accurately or usefully does DSM-5 perform versus ICD-11 for autism?” They consider risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and publication bias. Because no randomized design is appropriate for diagnostic classification, observational diagnostic studies can still provide useful evidence, but indirect retrospective reclassification warrants downgrading.

| Source | Design and sample | Main findings and statistics | Applicability and GRADE |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Kulage et al., “How Will DSM-5 Affect Autism Diagnosis? A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-analysis” (2014)** | Systematic review/meta-analysis. **418 records identified; 14 studies included.** It primarily compared proposed/final DSM-5 classification with DSM-IV-TR-era diagnoses, not ICD-11. | Individual studies reported reductions in ASD classification of **7.3%–68.4%**. Pooled decrease in ASD diagnosis was **31% (95% CI 20%–44%; p=0.006)**. Thus the implied retained proportion is approximately \(100\%-31\%=69\%\). Pooled decreases were **22% (16%–29%; p<0.001)** for autistic disorder and **70% (55%–82%; p=0.01)** for PDD-NOS. The estimated 70% decrease for Asperger’s disorder was not statistically significant because of wide uncertainty: **70% (26%–94%; p=0.38)**. Search result/source: https://www.academia.edu/30116704/How_Will_DSM_5_Affect_Autism_Diagnosis_A_Systematic_Literature_Review_and_Meta_analysis | Demonstrates risk of DSM-5 under-classification relative to older criteria, especially PDD-NOS, but cannot establish DSM-5 versus ICD-11 performance. Heterogeneous samples and retrospective criterion mapping add bias. **GRADE: Low** for DSM-5 threshold effects; **Very low** for DSM-5-versus-ICD-11 inference because of severe indirectness. |
| **Wilson et al., “Comparison of ICD-10R, DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5 in an Adult Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Clinic” (2013)** | Primary retrospective/clinical reclassification study; **n=150 intellectually able adults** assessed in a specialist clinic. It compared DSM-5 with ICD-10 research criteria and DSM-IV-TR, not ICD-11. | Of adults diagnosed with ASD under ICD-10R, **56%** met DSM-5 ASD criteria; a further **19%** met draft DSM-5 social communication disorder criteria. Of those with DSM-IV-TR autistic disorder/Asperger syndrome, **78%** met DSM-5 ASD criteria. Relaxing the number of required criteria or counting uncertain items increased sensitivity without materially sacrificing specificity, although the retrieved source did not provide the full numerical sensitivity/specificity table. https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/ | Clinically important adult evidence, particularly for people without intellectual disability. However, specialist-clinic selection, retrospective mapping, uncertain criteria, and use of ICD-10R rather than ICD-11 limit applicability. **GRADE: Low** for DSM-5 versus ICD-10R; **Very low** for extrapolation to ICD-11. |
| **First et al., “An organization- and category-level comparison of diagnostic requirements for mental disorders in ICD-11 and DSM-5” (2021)** | Structured expert/textual comparison, not a patient diagnostic-accuracy study. Compared ICD-11 CDDR essential features with DSM-5 criteria for **103 diagnostic entities**. | Across all diagnoses, **20/103 (19.4%)** had major differences, **42/103 (40.8%)** minor definitional differences, **10/103 (9.7%)** minor differences attributable to greater DSM-5 specification, and **31/103 (30.1%)** were essentially identical. Check: \(20+42+10+31=103\), and percentages total \(19.4+40.8+9.7+30.1=100.0\%\). https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825 | Useful for conceptual harmonization, including how DSM’s algorithms differ from ICD’s flexible guidelines, but supplies no autism-specific patient sensitivity/specificity estimate. **GRADE: Very low** for comparative diagnostic accuracy; **Low-to-moderate** for descriptive/manual-level comparison. |
| **“Clinical Utility of ICD-11 Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements …: A Systematic Review” (2025)** | Systematic review of case-controlled field studies, ecological implementation studies, and qualitative/mixed-method research; **19 included studies** across mental disorders rather than autism alone. | Positive clinical-utility findings were reported by **78.95%** of studies. Numerically, \(15/19 \times 100=78.95\%\), implying approximately four studies did not provide an overall positive result. Negative findings or implementation obstacles appeared mainly in qualitative/mixed studies. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/00332941251335596 | Meets the systematic-review requirement but is highly indirect for autism and does not establish superiority to DSM-5. Heterogeneous outcomes and designs make pooling difficult. **GRADE: Very low** for the autism-specific DSM-5-versus-ICD-11 question. |
| **“Autism spectrum disorder in ICD-11—a critical reflection of its possible impact on clinical practice and research” (2024)** | Peer-reviewed critical perspective; no patient sample. | Argues that ICD-11 permits more combinations and uses broader, sometimes subjective concepts, potentially improving accommodation of diversity but possibly reducing specificity and increasing false-positive diagnosis. These are reasoned hypotheses, not observed false-positive rates. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/ | Valuable for identifying testable safety concerns, but it cannot quantify accuracy or establish causal effects. **GRADE: Very low** for diagnostic effects. |

### Interpretation

1. **The strongest quantitative concern is under-inclusion under DSM-5 relative to older systems**, particularly for people formerly classified as PDD-NOS or for intellectually able adults. That does not prove ICD-11 is more sensitive, because ICD-11 is not simply ICD-10 with updated terminology.
2. **ICD-11 may be more flexible**, but greater flexibility can theoretically improve sensitivity while reducing reproducibility or specificity. Current evidence does not quantify that tradeoff for autism.
3. **Sensory weighting has not been isolated experimentally.** No identified study reported how many people qualified under DSM-5 specifically because sensory criterion B4 supplied the second restricted/repetitive feature, or whether ICD-11’s nonnumeric sensory formulation changed case ascertainment.
4. Overall certainty that either manual has superior diagnostic accuracy is **very low**.

---

## C. Clinical-guideline and professional positions

### World Health Organization

- WHO is the owner and implementing authority for ICD-11. The World Health Assembly adopted it in 2019; it formally came into effect on **1 January 2022**. WHO encourages prompt adoption but permits countries to continue ICD-10 as long as necessary during transition: https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/icd-11-implementation.
- WHO’s 2024 Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements are intended to support accurate, reliable diagnosis internationally: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240077263.
- For sensory processing, WHO includes hyper-/hyporeactivity and unusual sensory interests within the restricted/repetitive/inflexible domain, but does not make sensory differences independently sufficient or assign a numeric weight.
- Position: **adopt ICD-11 as the global classification framework**, with nationally managed transition. This is not a claim that sensory features should outweigh social-communication evidence.

### American Psychiatric Association

- APA continues to present DSM-5-TR as the US clinical diagnostic manual. It describes DSM and ICD as **companion publications**: DSM supplies diagnostic criteria and explanatory text, while ICD codes support reimbursement and morbidity/mortality reporting: https://www.psychiatry.org/psychiatrists/practice/dsm/frequently-asked-questions.
- APA has not replaced DSM criteria with ICD-11 criteria for US practice. DSM-5-TR remains compatible with the HIPAA-approved ICD-10-CM system.
- APA explicitly retains sensory hyper-/hyporeactivity or sensory interest as one of four restricted/repetitive manifestations and clarifies that **all three** social-communication subcriteria are required: https://www.psychiatry.org/File%20Library/Psychiatrists/Practice/DSM/DSM-5-TR/APA-DSM5TR-AutismSpectrumDisorder.pdf.
- Position: **continued DSM-5-TR diagnosis in US psychiatric practice, harmonized where possible with ICD**, rather than immediate clinical adoption of ICD-11 diagnostic requirements.

### American Academy of Pediatrics

- The AAP’s 2020 clinical report reflects DSM-5 and describes autism through the two DSM domains. It recommends developmental surveillance, autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months, comprehensive evaluation, and evidence-based, shared decision-making: https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/145/1/e20193447/36917/Identification-Evaluation-and-Management-of.
- Current AAP diagnostic resources call for a **DSM-5-TR-focused interview** covering social communication and restricted/repetitive behavior: https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/autism/autism-diagnosis-in-primary-care/.
- AAP notes that sensory symptoms occur in autism, ADHD, anxiety, and other neurodevelopmental conditions; in DSM-5 they count within restricted/repetitive behavior: https://publications.aap.org/toolkits/book/338/chapter/5732478/Sensory-Symptoms-of-Autism-Spectrum-Disorder.
- Position: **DSM-5/DSM-5-TR remains the clinical anchor in US pediatrics.** Sensory differences are diagnostically relevant but nonspecific and should be assessed alongside social communication, development, hearing/vision, adaptive function, and differential diagnoses. AAP has not issued a recommendation to replace DSM-5-TR with ICD-11.

### NICE

- NICE explicitly recommends using information from all sources and clinical judgment to diagnose autism under **ICD-11 or DSM-5**, rather than relying on one autism-specific instrument: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/CG128/chapter/recommendations.
- NICE asks diagnostic teams to consider sensory sensitivities when constructing the person’s profile, together with communication, motor, adaptive, mental-health, physical-health, and participation needs.
- Its recognition guidance includes over- or under-reaction to textures, sounds, smells, food taste/texture, and other sensory input: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Appendix-Features-suggesting-possible-autism.
- Position: **either ICD-11 or DSM-5 is acceptable**, with multidisciplinary, context-sensitive assessment. Sensory differences are important clues and support-planning targets, not stand-alone diagnostic proof.

---

## D. Autism advocacy-organization positions and neurodiversity

No reviewed organization makes a formal evidence-based declaration that one manual is categorically “more neurodiversity-affirming.” The more defensible synthesis is that different features of each manual align—or conflict—with neurodiversity principles in different ways.

### 1. Autistic Self Advocacy Network

ASAN’s detailed policy work concerned the draft DSM-5 rather than final ICD-11. It regarded several DSM-5 changes as improvements:

- unifying former autism-spectrum subtypes;
- recognizing the broad spectrum;
- including sensory issues in domain B, described as a “significant step forward.”

Source: https://autisticadvocacy.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/06/ASAN_DSM-5_2_final.pdf.

However, ASAN opposed the highly restrictive requirement to meet all three social-communication criteria, warning that it could make diagnosis more difficult for adults, women and girls, racial/ethnic minorities, and other underrepresented groups: https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/05/asan-talking-points-for-public-comment-on-dsm-5-autism-spectrum-disorder-criteria/.

**Synthesis:** ASAN’s position supports DSM-5’s unified spectrum and explicit sensory inclusion but criticizes restrictive thresholds and service-loss risk. Because ASAN did not provide an equivalent final ICD-11 appraisal in the retrieved evidence, it cannot fairly be said to rank ICD-11 over DSM-5. A flexible ICD-11 formulation may appear more inclusive, but attributing that preference to ASAN would be unsupported.

### 2. National Autistic Society

The National Autistic Society accepts diagnosis under either DSM-5 or ICD-11 and explicitly translates deficit-oriented terminology into more affirming language:

- communication and social-interaction “differences”;
- repetitive behavior as potentially self-soothing or self-regulating;
- restricted interests as focused or dedicated interests;
- sensory differences as part of autistic experience.

It notes that many autistic people do not consider autism a disease or disorder, even though clinical manuals use that language: https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment.

Its sensory guidance correctly explains that sensory differences are one of four DSM-style restricted/repetitive examples, that two are required, and that sensory differences are not themselves mandatory: https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/about-autism/sensory-processing.

It describes autism as a “lifelong neurodivergence and disability” and states that neurodiversity regards autism as natural human variation: https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/what-is-autism.

**Synthesis:** NAS does not identify a winning manual. Its own language is more neurodiversity-affirming than either manual’s deficit/disorder framing. It treats both manuals as necessary clinical systems that should be interpreted through lived experience, strengths, context, sensory access, and support needs.

### 3. Autism Speaks

Autism Speaks primarily explains and endorses practical use of DSM-5 in the United States. It highlights:

- the unified spectrum;
- addition of sensory symptoms;
- two required restricted/repetitive manifestations;
- separate support levels for each domain.

Sources: https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5 and https://www.autismspeaks.org/blog/expert-qa-dsm-5-and-asd.

Its symptom description also frames stimming as potentially regulating emotion and recognizes alternative communication methods, alongside sensory over-/undersensitivity: https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-symptoms.

**Synthesis:** Autism Speaks’ available materials favor DSM-5 operationally, but do not directly compare it with ICD-11 or call it more neurodiversity-affirming. Its recognition of sensory regulation and multiple communication modes is affirming, while the underlying DSM deficit and severity terminology remains medicalized.

### Cross-organization conclusion

A neurodiversity-affirming framework would favor:

1. recognition of sensory experience and self-regulation;
2. identity-respecting language;
3. accommodation rather than normalization as the default goal;
4. support based on individual needs rather than a diagnostic label or global severity score;
5. inclusion of masked, culturally diverse, female, adult, and nonspeaking presentations.

DSM-5’s explicit sensory criterion and unified spectrum advance items 1 and 4, but its rigid social-communication count can threaten inclusion. ICD-11’s contextual flexibility may better accommodate varied presentations, but its lack of an explicit counting rule can reduce transparency and consistency. On present advocacy evidence, **neither manual is clearly endorsed as the more neurodiversity-affirming one**.

---

## E. Diagnostic-safety risks

### 1. Underdiagnosis under DSM-5’s fixed threshold

The principal documented risk is that people meeting older autism criteria may not meet DSM-5:

- Meta-analysis estimated a **31% pooled reduction** in ASD classification relative to DSM-IV-era criteria.
- In one adult specialist clinic, only **56%** of ICD-10R-diagnosed adults met DSM-5 ASD criteria.
- People formerly diagnosed with PDD-NOS showed the largest pooled reduction, approximately **70%**.

Potential consequences include delayed recognition, reassignment to social communication disorder, and loss of eligibility where services or insurance require an autism diagnosis. Risk may be greater for adults, people without intellectual disability, people who mask, women and girls, and culturally underrepresented populations.

These results predate final ICD-11 comparison and should not be interpreted as proving that ICD-11 would diagnose every excluded individual.

### 2. Possible overdiagnosis or inconsistent diagnosis under ICD-11

ICD-11’s broader, example-based language may allow clinicians to recognize presentations that do not fit DSM’s fixed algorithm. The corresponding risk is greater clinician-to-clinician variation and possible false positives where:

- sensory sensitivity is common but caused by anxiety, trauma, ADHD, migraine, hearing/vision conditions, obsessive-compulsive phenomena, or another neurodevelopmental condition;
- social difficulties are inferred from internal experience without adequate developmental corroboration;
- “restricted/inflexible” patterns are interpreted too broadly.

The 2024 critical reflection argues that ICD-11’s flexibility could reduce specificity and increase false-positive diagnosis, but it supplies no measured false-positive rate: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/. This is therefore a **plausible safety concern, not demonstrated comparative harm**.

### 3. Sensory-focused presentations

A person with marked sound, texture, pain, food, light, movement, or interoceptive differences may be harmed in either direction:

- **False negative:** clinicians discount sensory history because social behavior appears superficially typical or masked.
- **False positive:** clinicians over-attribute nonspecific sensory differences to autism without the required social-developmental pattern.
- **Misclassification:** sensory distress is labeled defiance, anxiety, behavioral noncompliance, an eating disorder, or personality pathology without assessing autism—or, conversely, all sensory distress is attributed to autism and medical causes are missed.
- **Under-documentation:** ICD-11’s lack of a numbered sensory criterion may make sensory needs less visible in templated assessments.
- **Checkbox distortion:** DSM-5’s explicit B4 criterion may make documentation easier, but can encourage binary “present/absent” coding without describing modality, severity, context, avoidance, seeking, pain, or functional consequences.

Best practice is to document sensory modality, hyper- versus hyporesponsivity, sensory seeking, developmental history, frequency, context, coping strategies, accommodations, and functional effects. Hearing, vision, pain, feeding, sleep, neurologic, trauma-related, anxiety, and ADHD differentials should be evaluated where indicated.

### 4. Inappropriate interventions

No retrieved comparative study showed that DSM-5 versus ICD-11 itself causes a particular inappropriate intervention. The main pathway is indirect:

\[
\text{criterion interpretation} \rightarrow \text{diagnosis/coding} \rightarrow \text{service eligibility} \rightarrow \text{intervention}
\]

Risks include:

- denial of useful accommodations after a false-negative diagnosis;
- sensory exposure or compliance-focused treatment that ignores pain or overload;
- unnecessary autism-specific treatment after a false positive;
- treatment of stimming or sensory self-regulation solely because it appears atypical, rather than because it is harmful;
- failure to address medical conditions when sensory behavior is assumed to be “just autism.”

NICE and AAP guidance mitigate these risks by requiring multisource clinical judgment, differential diagnosis, functional profiling, and shared decision-making rather than diagnosis from a sensory checklist alone.

### 5. Severity and service-allocation risk

DSM-5 support levels can be mistaken for stable global measures, although a person may have different needs by domain and setting. ICD-11 language/intellectual-development subcategories can similarly understate sensory, adaptive, executive-function, or mental-health needs. Neither system’s coding shorthand should replace an individualized support assessment.

---

## F. Reimbursement and coding

### United States

- US clinicians generally use **DSM-5-TR to determine the psychiatric diagnosis**, but claims must use the HIPAA-approved **ICD-10-CM** code set.
- APA states that ICD-10-CM has been the official US coding system since 1 October 2015 and is the only permissible diagnostic coding system for US clinical claims: https://www.psychiatry.org/File%20Library/Psychiatrists/Practice/DSM/DSM-5-TR/APA-DSM5TR-Coding.pdf.
- DSM-5/DSM-5-TR autism spectrum disorder generally maps to **ICD-10-CM F84.0, Autistic disorder**. The wording is less contemporary than DSM-5’s “autism spectrum disorder,” but F84.0 is the standard billable mapping.
- A DSM diagnosis does not itself guarantee coverage. Payers may require documentation of medical necessity, functional impairment, standardized assessment, provider qualifications, prior authorization, age limits, or state-specific autism mandates.
- **ICD-11 is not currently the HIPAA-mandated US morbidity/billing code set.** The National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics is studying implementation, governance, mapping, costs, and whether a US clinical modification or linearization is needed: https://ncvhs.hhs.gov/subcommittees-work-groups/icd-11-workgroup/.
- Therefore, using ICD-11 diagnostic concepts in a US evaluation does not presently replace ICD-10-CM F84.0 on claims and does not automatically expand or restrict insurance coverage.

### European Union and wider Europe

- There is no single EU-wide payer or uniform implementation date. Member states control clinical coding, reimbursement, disability eligibility, and service rules.
- ICD-11 became internationally effective in 2022, but WHO permits continued ICD-10 use during national transition: https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/icd-11-implementation.
- Many European systems continue to use national ICD-10 modifications or translations for reimbursement while preparing ICD-11. Transition must account for diagnosis-related groups, tariffs, risk adjustment, registries, and historical data.
- Where implemented, ICD-11 codes autism under **6A02** with subcategories based primarily on intellectual development and functional-language impairment, for example 6A02.0 through 6A02.5: https://www.icd11-code.com/6a02/.
- Adoption of ICD-11 terminology does not by itself mandate payment. National payer rules must be amended to recognize ICD-11 codes and map them to benefits, tariffs, and eligibility pathways. During transition, dual coding or crosswalks may be necessary.
- Consequently, a person may clinically meet ICD-11 autism requirements while reimbursement still depends on an ICD-10 code or national administrative definition.

---

## Overall conclusions

1. **Sensory processing is diagnostically relevant but not independently diagnostic in either manual.**
2. **DSM-5 weights sensory differences more explicitly:** they are one of four numbered restricted/repetitive criteria and can provide one of the two required features.
3. **ICD-11 weights sensory evidence more flexibly but less transparently:** sensory responses are possible manifestations in a clinically judged domain without a numerical quota.
4. Both systems require social-communication differences, developmental onset, and meaningful impairment.
5. Existing evidence raises a credible concern that DSM-5’s algorithm may exclude some people recognized under older criteria, especially certain adults and former PDD-NOS presentations. Evidence that ICD-11 causes overdiagnosis remains theoretical rather than quantified.
6. WHO supports ICD-11 implementation; NICE permits either system; APA and AAP continue to center DSM-5/DSM-5-TR in US clinical diagnosis.
7. No reviewed advocacy organization establishes that one manual is categorically more neurodiversity-affirming. Explicit sensory recognition, inclusive thresholds, respectful language, and needs-based support matter more than the label of the manual.
8. In the United States, reimbursement remains tied to ICD-10-CM—usually F84.0—not ICD-11. Across Europe, ICD-11 adoption and payer effects are national and uneven.
9. The major research need is a prospective, blinded, multisite study applying DSM-5 and ICD-11 independently to the same diverse child and adult cohort, reporting inter-rater reliability, sensitivity, specificity, service consequences, and the incremental diagnostic contribution of sensory evidence.

final.content:
Farm-management and traceability platform assessment for a 5,000-member coffee cooperative

Date: 12 October 2026

Executive conclusion

The cooperative should not select Olam AtSource or FLOCERT Fairtrace as its primary farm-management platform.

• AtSource is a buyer-led sustainability and assurance program restricted to ofi/Olam supply chains, not a generally licensable cooperative system. It is appropriate only if the cooperative has a firm ofi/Olam purchasing relationship and the buyer pays for implementation. Its traceability is normally only to farmer-group level, although Olam’s underlying Farmer Information System can collect farm GPS data and bag-level transactions.

• Fairtrace is FLOCERT’s online platform for reporting and verifying Fairtrade transactions. It is necessary for relevant Fairtrade-certified trade relationships, but it does not replace farmer registration, field surveys, offline procurement, plot mapping, inventory, or an internal management system.

The strongest primary-platform candidates are:

1. SourceTrace DATAGREEN — best functional fit where farmers have basic phones and connectivity is weak. It supports field-agent smartphones, older Java phones and POS-type devices, offline/low-bandwidth operation, GPS, certification workflows, traceability and back-end integration. Confirm its current product roadmap, language coverage, polygon/GIS capabilities and support capacity before contracting.

2. Farmforce Origin — strongest documented all-round option for a cooperative-led first-mile system: offline Android field collection, GPS polygons, certification surveys, farmer records and bag-level traceability. Spanish and Indonesian are listed; Amharic/Oromo and local Indonesian languages would require confirmation or localization. Public prices are unreliable, so a binding 5,000-farmer quotation is essential.

3. Koltiva KoltiTrace — strongest alternative for polygon mapping, deforestation/EUDR risk management, and implementation support, particularly in Indonesia and Colombia. It offers offline plot mapping, transaction and farm-management applications, certification-preparation services and field support. Pricing is custom and smartphone dependence is greater than with SourceTrace.

Recommended procurement decision: run a competitive pilot between SourceTrace and either Farmforce or Koltiva. Use the same 300–500 farms across the three countries, including steep coffee plots and week-long offline scenarios. Select on measured data quality and five-year total cost, not on vendor demonstrations. Continue using Fairtrace and Fairtrade Plot Insights as certification interfaces; require the selected system to export data to them rather than trying to replace them.

1. What the cooperative actually needs

The solution must cover two different layers:

A. Cooperative operating system

This should manage:

• Members, households and plots
• GPS points and boundary polygons
• Internal inspections and corrective actions
• Farmer training and farm-management plans
• Coffee deliveries, weights, quality, payments and premiums
• Lot aggregation, warehouse movements and sales
• Traceability from farmer/plot through export lot
• Certification evidence and buyer exports
• Offline field work and synchronization

B. Certification portals

These remain authoritative for their respective schemes:

• Fairtrace records and verifies Fairtrade transactions, including volume, price and premium.
• Fairtrade Plot Insights receives plot geodata and performs deforestation-risk analysis.
• Rainforest Alliance’s Certification Platform receives farm data and geolocation files, runs geographic risk assessments, supports self-assessments and manages the audit workflow.

No evaluated commercial product eliminates the need to submit data to those scheme-owned systems.

2. Comparative scorecard

Scores use a five-point scale: 5 = very strong; 1 = poor or unsuitable. “Basic-phone usability” distinguishes direct use by farmers from an agent-assisted system in which farmers need no smartphone.

| Solution | Basic-phone/low-tech fit | Mountain plot mapping | RA/Fairtrade readiness | Languages for the three countries | Offline operation | Budget transparency/affordability | Overall role |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| SourceTrace DATAGREEN | 5 | 4, subject to polygon test | 4 | 3, verify exact languages | 5 | 3, quote required | Leading primary-platform candidate |
| Farmforce Origin | 3 | 4 | 4 | 4 for Spanish/Indonesian; gap in Ethiopia | 5 | 2, quote required | Leading primary-platform candidate |
| Koltiva KoltiTrace | 3 | 5 | 5 | 4, but verify Amharic/Oromo and farmer app | 5 for field mapping | 2, custom pricing | Leading compliance-focused candidate |
| AtSource/OFIS | 3 through agents and SMS | 3–4 | 3 | 3, exact current languages unclear | 3, not fully documented publicly | 1, not an open standalone product | Use only within an Olam/ofi supply chain |
| FLOCERT Fairtrace | 1 | 1 itself; Plot Insights handles uploaded geodata | 5 for Fairtrade only; 1 for RA | 3 for administrators | 1 | 5 for eligible certified organizations, but not an FMIS | Mandatory companion for Fairtrade, not primary system |
| Fairfood Trace/Connect, if “FairTrace” meant Fairfood | 5 via collector and NFC card | 1–2 | 2 | 3, translations supported | 5 | 2, quote required | Low-tech transaction add-on, not full agronomy/certification system |

The scores reflect publicly documented capabilities, not hands-on testing. No vendor reviewed publishes credible field accuracy results for steep, tree-covered coffee terrain.

3. Detailed comparison

3.1 SourceTrace DATAGREEN

Usability and basic phones

SourceTrace is the clearest fit for heterogeneous devices. Its DATAGREEN Remote system supports “regular Java enabled phones,” smartphones, tablets, POS-like devices, computers and laptops. It was designed for low bandwidth or operation without a permanent connection. It can also connect to receipt printers, smart-card readers, digital scales and barcode/QR scanners (https://sourcetrace.com/the-platform/).

This does not mean every farmer should enter agronomic data personally. A better design is:

• Cooperative enumerators use Android smartphones for surveys and GPS mapping.
• Buying agents use phones or POS devices for deliveries, weighing and receipts.
• Farmers receive paper receipts, SMS messages or smart-card/QR identification.
• Cooperative staff use the web dashboard and certification modules.

That accommodates farmers who have only voice/SMS phones or no personal phone.

GPS and mountainous terrain

The platform supports built-in phone GPS and geographic maps. Independent descriptions also report geolocation and offline field capture. However, the public evidence does not establish:

• Whether its current mobile product captures full plot polygons, rather than only points
• Whether it stores horizontal-accuracy values for every vertex
• Whether it supports offline basemaps
• Whether it can pause, resume and repair boundary walks
• Its measured error under coffee canopy or on steep slopes

These must be demonstrated in the pilot. Do not accept “GPS enabled” as proof of certification-grade polygons.

Certification and buyer integration

SourceTrace offers farmer profiling, traceability, certification and supply-chain modules. Earlier documentation describes an Android certification application for field assessments against Fair Trade and Organic requirements. Its back-end adapter supports web services, XML, databases, files and batch or real-time integration, which is useful for exporting to buyer and certification systems (https://sourcetrace.com/the-platform/).

The cooperative should require current, configurable checklists for:

• Rainforest Alliance farm and group requirements
• Fairtrade coffee and small-producer-organization requirements
• Internal inspections and corrective actions
• Premium and payment records
• EUDR-aligned plot and lot exports

Language and offline operation

The evidence supports offline and low-bandwidth operation strongly. Exact current support for Spanish, Bahasa Indonesia, Amharic, Oromo and country-specific terminology was not publicly verified. Localization must therefore be a contractual deliverable, including forms, validation messages, training materials and administrator screens.

Cost

SourceTrace does not disclose a usable price. A GSMA profile says pricing includes one-time onboarding plus a monthly subscription based on registered farmers; in some deployments it is based on acreage or commodity ecosystems. Consequently, the cooperative must obtain a five-year fixed quotation.

Verdict

Best candidate when basic-phone inclusion, offline operation and flexible hardware matter most. It should proceed to pilot, but only after checking the vendor’s current support organization and modern polygon/export capabilities.

3.2 Farmforce Origin

Usability and basic phones

Farmforce’s normal operating model is an Android mobile application for field staff plus a web system for managers. It is not a feature-phone farmer application. Farmers can nevertheless participate without owning smartphones because enumerators and buying-station personnel collect the data.

Farmforce says its solutions are built to work offline and is piloting a farmer-facing application designed around low literacy and gamification (https://farmforce.com/products/farmer-app/). Because that farmer app was described as a pilot, it should not be treated as a production requirement unless the vendor contractually confirms availability in all three countries.

GPS and mountainous terrain

Farmforce registers farmers and maps their fields as GPS polygons. It can import existing shapefiles or let field staff map locations using the mobile application. Each farmer and field receives a unique identifier. Its Origin system links farmer records, family information and mapped fields with subsequent field and supply-chain activities (https://farmforce.com/products/information-management-system-ims/).

This is a stronger documented mapping workflow than AtSource or Fairtrace, but public materials still provide no measured accuracy for mountain coffee. The pilot must test polygon closure, overlap detection, area calculations and GNSS accuracy logging.

Certification and traceability

Farmforce offers bag-level traceability: uniquely coded bags can be linked to a farmer’s field and remain identifiable as they are aggregated into lots and containers. Certification surveys and audit requirements can be loaded into the mobile application, while farmer certification IDs can be stored in profiles (https://farmforce.com/products/information-management-system-ims/).

This is well aligned with:

• Fairtrade’s requirement to monitor individual members’ sales against estimated production
• Audit evidence for premiums, training and internal inspections
• Buyer requests for plot-to-lot traceability
• Rainforest Alliance and EUDR geolocation records

However, evidence of a direct live API to Fairtrace, Fairtrade Plot Insights or Rainforest Alliance was not found. Require GeoJSON, KML, shapefile and CSV exports plus documented APIs.

Language and offline operation

A third-party software listing reports Chinese, English, French, Hindi, Indonesian, Portuguese, Serbian, Spanish, Thai, Turkish and Vietnamese. Spanish and Indonesian therefore appear available. Amharic and Oromo are not listed. The same sources and implementation descriptions report offline mobile collection.

Cost

Farmforce’s official public pages do not disclose enterprise pricing. Third-party listings report inconsistent figures, including NOK 330 per year and US$1,950 per user per year, which plainly cannot both describe the same 5,000-farmer deployment. One third-party estimate puts implementation at NOK 55,000–220,000.

If that implementation estimate were applicable, the one-time cost per enrolled farmer would be:

• Low case: NOK 55,000 ÷ 5,000 = NOK 11 per farmer
• High case: NOK 220,000 ÷ 5,000 = NOK 44 per farmer

These figures exclude subscriptions, devices, connectivity, mapping labor, support, labels, printers, scales and certification costs. They are not reliable enough for selection and should only be used to identify the need for a binding quotation.

Verdict

A strong, relatively mature all-round option. It should be shortlisted, especially if bag-level traceability and configurable certification workflows receive high weighting. Ethiopian localization and total cost are the principal uncertainties.

3.3 Koltiva KoltiTrace

Usability and basic phones

Koltiva uses different applications for different actors:

• FarmXtension for agronomists and field teams
• FarmGate for transactions
• FarmCloud for farmers
• KoltiTrace MIS for management and traceability

The farmer-facing approach is smartphone-oriented. It is therefore less suitable than SourceTrace for direct use by farmers with basic phones, but field agents can operate the system on farmers’ behalf. The cooperative should request SMS or paper-receipt workflows for non-smartphone members.

GPS and mountainous terrain

Koltiva explicitly supports offline plot mapping and collection of GPS points or polygons. It recommends polygons for more accurate deforestation-risk assessment and future regulatory compliance. Its field services can walk plot boundaries, verify land legality and support producer registration (https://www.koltiva.com/eudrcompliance).

This makes it the strongest compliance-mapping proposition on paper. Nevertheless, “high precision” is not a quantified accuracy guarantee. The same field acceptance tests should apply.

Certification and buyer integration

Koltiva combines geolocation, supply-chain mapping, deforestation screening, transaction traceability and compliance reporting. It advertises API-first ERP integration, including SAP, and optional use of risk layers from sources such as the Joint Research Centre and Global Forest Watch (https://www.koltiva.com/eudrcompliance).

Its services explicitly include producer preparation for Rainforest Alliance and support for Rainforest Alliance, Fairtrade and other standards. Koltiva also offers training, documentation, audit preparation and field verification. This is valuable if the cooperative lacks enough internal inspectors.

Language and geographic fit

Koltiva originated in Indonesia and has a substantial Indonesian implementation base. It has also digitally validated coffee producers in Colombia and other Latin American countries. Those are material advantages for two of the cooperative’s three countries. Public evidence was insufficient to confirm Ethiopian language support or a comparable Ethiopian coffee deployment.

Cost

Koltiva does not publish prices. Available descriptions characterize its model as customized enterprise pricing based on farmer count, geography, modules, integrations and field services. The cooperative should separate the quote into:

• Software license
• Initial configuration and localization
• Mapping service
• Training and certification support
• API/integration work
• Support and hosting
• Per-transaction charges
• Renewal and data-export fees

Verdict

Best candidate if the priority is EUDR/deforestation compliance plus field implementation support, especially in Indonesia and Colombia. It may be more expensive than a software-only option and needs an Ethiopia proof of capability.

3.4 Olam AtSource and OFIS

What AtSource is

AtSource is a sustainability, traceability and assurance offering created by Olam. It provides buyers with sustainability metrics, environmental footprints, risk assessments and third-party verification. AtSourceV and AtSource+ trace product back to a farmer group or estate, rather than necessarily to an individual plot. AtSource+ adds granular data, primary-data environmental footprints and annual third-party audits (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html).

Most importantly, AtSource is “open to ofi and Olam Group product supply chains.” It is not described as a general SaaS platform that an independent cooperative can simply license (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html).

Underlying farmer system

Olam’s underlying Farmer Information System, OFIS, is more operationally relevant. It provides:

• An Android application designed for remote areas
• Farmer surveys and GPS points
• Multilingual data collection
• Training records
• Purchases, input distribution and finance
• Farmer development plans
• SMS messages to farmers
• Cooperative internal-management functions
• Bag coding and farm-to-fork traceability

Olam reported nine languages and operation in 21 countries in 2017. The OFIS brochure describes GPS points and farm maps but does not clearly document modern polygon accuracy or fully offline synchronization (https://www.olamgroup.com/content/dam/olamgroup/files/uploads/2017/07/New-OFIS-Brochure-1.pdf).

Certification integration

AtSource is an independent Olam assurance framework, not Rainforest Alliance or Fairtrade certification. Its sustainability assessment and chain-of-custody records may support buyers, but they do not substitute for certification audits or scheme portals.

Cost and strategic risk

No public per-farmer price is available because AtSource is embedded in Olam/ofi sourcing relationships. The larger issue is commercial dependence: data access, continued use and buyer choice may become tied to an Olam supply chain.

Verdict

Consider AtSource only if:

• ofi/Olam is or will be a committed buyer;
• it funds or substantially subsidizes onboarding and field work;
• the cooperative retains ownership and export rights over member, plot and transaction data;
• the contract permits data portability to other buyers and certifiers; and
• traceability reaches the plot and delivery level required by the cooperative.

Otherwise, it is unsuitable as the cooperative’s independent core platform.

3.5 FLOCERT Fairtrace

Fairtrace is often misunderstood. It is FLOCERT’s online collaboration and assurance platform for Fairtrade-certified companies. One party reports a Fairtrade transaction and its counterpart verifies it through a “virtual handshake.” Relevant traders report Fairtrade sales and direct producer purchases quarterly and include price and premium information when acting as a payer or conveyor (https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf).

For producer organizations, reporting obligations are more limited; they generally verify transactions reported by customers. Access is for FLOCERT-certified customers.

Strengths

• Authoritative Fairtrade volume, price and premium reporting
• Direct fit with FLOCERT audits
• Counterparty verification
• No need to procure a duplicate platform for the same reporting function

Limitations

• Browser-based online workflow
• Not designed for direct farmer use
• No field-agent offline workflow
• No native farm boundary collection
• No general agronomy, inventory or internal-inspection system
• No Rainforest Alliance certification function

Fairtrade Plot Insights fills part of the geodata gap. It is free for certified coffee and cocoa small-producer organizations, accepts point and polygon files, performs validation and deforestation-risk analysis, and is available in English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian and Vietnamese. It can share EUDR-compatible GeoJSON with trade partners and is being linked with Fairtrace contracts (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf).

Verdict

Retain Fairtrace and Plot Insights as Fairtrade destination systems. Do not score Fairtrace as an alternative to SourceTrace, Farmforce or Koltiva because it addresses a different part of the workflow.

3.6 If “FairTrace” refers to Fairfood Trace rather than FLOCERT Fairtrace

Fairfood’s Trace/Connect is a separate product. Its collector application works without internet, and each farmer can validate transactions using an NFC farmer card without owning a smartphone. The open-source project description says it:

• Is used by collectors rather than farmers
• Minimizes data entry
• Works offline and synchronizes later
• Supports translations
• Does not require farmers to have a phone, internet connection or email
• Records registration, deliveries, payments and evidence

See https://fairfood.org/connect/ and https://github.com/Fairfood/trace-app.

This is excellent low-tech transaction design, but the evidence does not show a complete farm-management, GPS-polygon, agronomic inspection or Rainforest Alliance solution. It is best viewed as a transaction/transparency component, not the cooperative’s full platform.

4. GPS mapping requirements for mountain coffee

Mountain terrain, dense coffee canopy, shade trees, narrow plots and deep valleys can degrade ordinary phone-GNSS performance through satellite obstruction and reflected signals. None of the vendors publishes enough evidence to guarantee a particular accuracy under these conditions.

Certification file precision must not be confused with field accuracy. Fairtrade requires coordinates with at least six decimal digits. Six decimal degrees represent roughly 0.11 metres of latitude resolution:

111,000 metres per degree × 0.000001 degree = 0.111 metres.

That is only the resolution of the stored coordinate. A phone can output six decimal places while its real position is several metres or more from the true boundary.

The selected system should therefore meet the following contractual requirements:

• Record a GPS point and polygon for every production plot, even where certification presently permits only a point.
• Store latitude, longitude, timestamp, device ID and reported horizontal accuracy.
• Warn or block collection when reported accuracy exceeds the cooperative’s threshold.
• Allow the mapper to wait for accuracy to stabilize.
• Support pause/resume and later repair of boundary walks.
• Detect self-crossing polygons, sharp spikes, duplicate points and implausible areas.
• Flag overlaps among members’ plots.
• Work with downloaded offline basemaps.
• Export WGS 84 GeoJSON, KML and shapefiles.
• Preserve stable farmer and plot IDs through updates.
• Permit connection to higher-quality external Bluetooth GNSS receivers for difficult or disputed plots.
• Retain original tracks and an audit history rather than overwriting them.

Pilot acceptance tests should include at least:

1. Repeated mapping of the same 30 plots by two enumerators.
2. Ten plots in each country, including steep slopes and heavy canopy.
3. Comparison of calculated area and boundary position between repetitions.
4. Tests with the phone in airplane mode.
5. A seven-day offline period followed by synchronization.
6. Upload of the results into both Fairtrade Plot Insights and the current Rainforest Alliance platform.
7. Rejection and correction of intentionally invalid or overlapping polygons.

5. Certification requirements that the platform must satisfy

Fairtrade

From 1 January 2027, the Fairtrade coffee standard requires geolocation for 100% of members’ coffee plots: at least a GPS point for plots below four hectares and a polygon for plots over four hectares. The cooperative must also prioritize polygons in high-deforestation-risk areas. Fairtrade separately requires a system monitoring individual members’ production and sales to detect sales beyond estimated production (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/standards/small-scale-producer/coffee/Coffee_SPO_EN.pdf).

Plot Insights requires:

• Unique farmer and plot IDs
• Plot area
• Coordinates with at least six decimals for points
• WGS 84
• Valid non-self-crossing polygons
• No major plot overlaps
• Polygons for plots of four hectares or more
• Annual updates

It accepts KML, GeoJSON and shapefiles for polygons and additional spreadsheet formats for points. The selected platform should generate these files directly rather than requiring manual GIS reformatting.

Rainforest Alliance

Rainforest Alliance requires certificate holders to submit geolocation data for farm units in points and polygons and operates its own Certification Platform for:

• Farm data and geolocation uploads
• Geographic risk assessments
• Self-assessments and indicator reporting
• Audit preparation and corrective actions
• Traceability and claims

The management annex says certificate holders are responsible for providing geolocation for all farm units. The current RACP documentation is at https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/management-annex-v12 and https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/introduction-to-rainforest-alliance-online-systems.

The commercial platform should therefore maintain a reusable “master farmer and plot registry” and export scheme-specific versions. It should not create separate, inconsistent farmer databases for each certification.

6. Language requirements

A single national language is insufficient in all three countries. The tender should require:

• Colombia: Spanish throughout, with configurable local terminology.
• Ethiopia: Amharic plus at least Oromo for major coffee areas; additional local-language forms should be configurable.
• Indonesia: Bahasa Indonesia, with configurable local-language prompts where needed.
• Administrator interfaces: English plus the relevant national language.
• Audio, icon or assisted workflows for low-literacy users.
• Translation of validation errors, not only form labels.
• Unicode support for Ethiopian scripts.
• Local-language training manuals and help-desk support.

Current evidence:

• Farmforce publicly lists Spanish and Indonesian, but not Amharic or Oromo.
• Fairtrade Plot Insights supports Spanish and Indonesian but not Amharic.
• SourceTrace supports multilingual/customized deployments, but the exact language list must be verified.
• AtSource/OFIS reported nine languages in 2017 without establishing that all required languages are currently available.
• Koltiva has strong Indonesian and Latin American operational fit, but Ethiopian localization remains unverified.

Language configuration should be demonstrated with real field forms during the pilot, not promised for a later release.

7. Cost analysis and procurement model

Reliable per-farmer prices are not publicly disclosed for the leading commercial products. Any exact ranking by cost would therefore be misleading.

Known position

| Platform | Public cost evidence | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| AtSource | No independent cooperative price | Usually embedded in Olam/ofi sourcing; commercial dependence matters more than nominal license |
| FLOCERT Fairtrace | Available to eligible certified organizations | Certification and staff costs remain; it is not a substitute for FMIS spending |
| Fairtrade Plot Insights | Free for certified coffee/cocoa SPOs | Valuable destination tool but mapping labor and source-system costs remain |
| SourceTrace | Onboarding plus subscription commonly based on farmers, acreage or commodity ecosystem | Requires detailed quote |
| Farmforce | Conflicting third-party prices; official enterprise cost not public | Ignore headline directory price; request binding quote |
| Koltiva | Custom enterprise pricing | Separate software from field services and certification support |
| Fairfood Trace | No usable public cooperative price found | Request quote if considered as an add-on |

Required cost formula

For each vendor, calculate:

Annualized five-year cost per farmer

= [implementation + localization + integration + devices + mapping + training + five years of licenses/support/hosting/transaction fees] ÷ 5 years ÷ 5,000 farmers.

Illustrative comparison—not a vendor-price estimate:

If a proposal includes:

• US$75,000 implementation and localization
• US$50,000 devices and mapping equipment
• US$40,000 annual software, hosting and support

then five-year cost is:

US$75,000 + US$50,000 + (5 × US$40,000)
= US$325,000.

Annualized cost per farmer:

US$325,000 ÷ 5 ÷ 5,000
= US$13 per farmer per year.

Every vendor should be evaluated using this same formula. The cooperative should also calculate marginal cost for adding another 1,000 farmers and for replacing damaged phones.

The request for proposal should explicitly price:

• 5,000 farmers and all their plots—not merely 5,000 database records
• At least three country environments
• All field-agent and administrator accounts
• Offline mobile applications
• Required languages
• Initial data migration
• Polygon collection and correction
• Certification form configuration
• Fairtrace, Plot Insights and Rainforest Alliance exports
• API access
• Labels, printers and barcode/QR equipment
• Hosting, backups and security
• Local support and service levels
• Major version upgrades
• Full data export on termination
• Five-year price escalation ceiling

Avoid per-transaction pricing unless capped. High-volume coffee deliveries can make an apparently cheap system expensive during harvest.

8. Recommended selection process

Phase 1: written qualification

Invite SourceTrace, Farmforce and Koltiva. Invite AtSource only through a formal ofi/Olam purchasing proposal. Require each bidder to answer “available now,” “requires configuration,” or “not available” for every requirement.

Phase 2: paid pilot

Pilot 300–500 farmers, approximately divided as follows:

• Colombia: 100–170
• Ethiopia: 100–170
• Indonesia: 100–170

At 450 farmers, a balanced allocation would be 150 per country, representing:

450 ÷ 5,000 = 9% of cooperative members.

That is large enough to expose language, connectivity, mapping and synchronization problems while limiting implementation risk.

Phase 3: weighted decision

Recommended weighting:

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---:|
| Offline/basic-phone inclusion and field usability | 20% |
| GPS polygon quality and data validation | 20% |
| Certification and buyer-data compatibility | 20% |
| Five-year total cost per farmer | 20% |
| Languages, training and local support | 10% |
| Data ownership, security, API and exit rights | 10% |
| Total | 100% |

Minimum pass conditions should override total score:

• Full offline data entry for at least seven days
• Successful synchronization without duplicates
• Successful Fairtrade and Rainforest Alliance geodata uploads
• Spanish, Bahasa Indonesia and agreed Ethiopian-language forms
• Complete data export without vendor assistance
• Contractual cooperative ownership of farmer and plot data
• No restriction on selling coffee to competing buyers

9. Final recommendation

Preferred strategy

1. Shortlist SourceTrace, Farmforce and Koltiva.
2. Make SourceTrace the initial reference candidate because of its basic-phone and low-bandwidth architecture.
3. Pilot Farmforce if the cooperative prioritizes mature farmer/field records and bag-level traceability.
4. Pilot Koltiva instead of, or alongside, Farmforce if EUDR/deforestation screening and outsourced field implementation are the highest priorities.
5. Use Fairtrace and Plot Insights as Fairtrade companion systems.
6. Use the Rainforest Alliance Certification Platform as the destination for Rainforest Alliance certification data.
7. Consider AtSource only as a buyer-funded channel, never as the cooperative’s only copy of its data.

Likely choice by strategic priority

• Lowest-connectivity and basic-phone priority: SourceTrace.
• Strongest balanced first-mile and bag traceability: Farmforce.
• Strongest compliance mapping and field-service package: Koltiva.
• Lowest incremental Fairtrade reporting cost: Fairtrace plus free Plot Insights—but only as companions to a core system.
• Guaranteed ofi/Olam buyer relationship with buyer-funded deployment: AtSource/OFIS may be worthwhile, subject to data portability.
• NFC-card transaction verification without farmer smartphones: Fairfood Connect may be a useful add-on.

No final award should be made until the vendors complete the same mountain-GPS, offline synchronization, language and certification-export tests and provide a five-year, all-inclusive cost per farmer.
