final.content:
UCC Analysis: Navy Widgets Delivered Instead of Charcoal Gray

Executive conclusion

Buyer did not rightfully reject the widgets. Although an exact charcoal-gray requirement could make navy widgets nonconforming under the UCC’s perfect-tender rule, Buyer lost the right to reject by:

1. failing to notify Vendor within the contractual 10-day inspection period;
2. waiting 56 days after delivery;
3. installing and operating all 1,000 widgets;
4. praising their performance without mentioning color; and
5. painting 600 widgets, an unequivocal exercise of ownership and substantial alteration.

Buyer therefore accepted the goods under UCC § 2-606 and must pay the contract price under § 2-607. Revocation of acceptance is also unlikely because the color was readily observable, the functional value was not impaired, Buyer substantially changed 60% of the goods, and Vendor promptly offered replacement.

At most, Buyer may have a claim for proven damages attributable to the color deviation, assuming its May 10 notice preserved that remedy despite the 10-day clause. Buyer is not entitled simply to impose a 40% refund while retaining and continuing to use the widgets. If conformity is required, Vendor’s prompt two-week replacement offer is the appropriate cure, particularly for the 400 unpainted widgets.

I. Governing UCC rules

A. Perfect tender

For a single-delivery sale, UCC § 2-601 provides that if the goods or tender “fail in any respect to conform to the contract,” the buyer may reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept commercial units and reject the remainder. This is the perfect-tender rule.  
https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-601

Ramirez v. Autosport confirms that even minor defects can initially support rejection: the seller must tender goods conforming precisely to the contract. But Ramirez also emphasizes that seller-cure provisions mitigate the rule’s harshness.  
https://law.justia.com/cases/new-jersey/supreme-court/1982/88-n-j-277-0.html

“Substantial performance” therefore is not itself a complete answer to a timely pre-acceptance rejection. Functional compliance does not automatically erase an express color specification. Substantiality becomes more important in determining:

- whether trade usage qualifies the color requirement;
- whether the buyer accepted the goods;
- whether acceptance may be revoked;
- whether cure is reasonable; and
- the amount of any damages.

B. Timely rejection and contractual inspection period

Under UCC § 2-602(1), rejection must occur within a reasonable time after delivery or tender and is ineffective unless the buyer seasonably notifies the seller.  
https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-602

The parties may contractually establish a period for actions that the UCC otherwise requires within a reasonable time, provided the agreed period is not “manifestly unreasonable.” UCC § 1-302(b).  
https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/1/1-302

Here, the contract requires notice within 10 days. That period is likely enforceable because color is an immediately visible characteristic that does not require operational testing. UCC § 2-513 gives a buyer a reasonable opportunity to inspect goods before acceptance.  
https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-513

C. Acceptance through conduct

Under UCC § 2-606, acceptance occurs when the buyer:

- signifies after inspection that the goods conform or will be retained despite nonconformity;
- fails to make an effective rejection after a reasonable opportunity to inspect; or
- performs an act inconsistent with the seller’s ownership.

Acceptance of part of a commercial unit constitutes acceptance of that entire unit.  
https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-606

Installation of equipment has been treated as conduct inconsistent with the seller’s ownership. See United States ex rel. Fram Corp. v. Crawford, holding that installation of supplied equipment constituted acceptance under § 2-606(1)(c).  
https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/443/611/246326/

D. Revocation after acceptance

Once goods have been accepted, rejection is no longer available. UCC § 2-607(2) expressly provides that acceptance precludes rejection.  
https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607

A buyer may instead revoke acceptance under UCC § 2-608 only if:

1. the nonconformity substantially impairs the value of the goods to that buyer;
2. the buyer accepted on the reasonable assumption that the defect would be cured but it was not cured, or accepted without discovering a defect that was difficult to discover or concealed by seller assurances;
3. revocation occurs within a reasonable time after discovery or when discovery should have occurred; and
4. revocation occurs before a substantial change in the goods’ condition not caused by their defects.

https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-608

E. Seller’s right to cure

Under UCC § 2-508:

- if the contract time has not expired, a seller may seasonably notify the buyer and make a conforming tender within that time; and
- even after the original time has expired, a seller that reasonably believed the goods would be acceptable, with or without an allowance, may seasonably notify the buyer and receive a further reasonable time to substitute conforming goods.

https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-508

T.W. Oil, Inc. v. Consolidated Edison holds that a seller acting in good faith may cure after the original delivery deadline if it reasonably expected the original tender to be acceptable and seasonably offers substitute performance.  
https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/court-of-appeals/1982/57-n-y-2d-574-0.html

II. Was navy instead of charcoal a nonconformity?

A. Buyer’s strongest argument

The purchase order specified a color reference number. If that reference unambiguously required charcoal gray, delivery in navy did not literally conform. Section 2-601’s “fail in any respect” language means Buyer initially could have rejected based on color even though the widgets met every functional specification.

The absence of an express “shade variance” rejection clause does not necessarily eliminate the contractual color requirement. Nor does excellent load capacity and durability make an express color specification irrelevant.

The architect’s later confirmation supports Buyer’s position that color had genuine commercial importance: navy reportedly created contrast problems in the showroom. This makes the complaint more than purely fabricated dissatisfaction.

B. Vendor’s stronger interpretive argument

The purchase order emphasized load capacity and durability, and the widgets satisfied all functional requirements. Industry practice also treats minor color variations as acceptable for functional components.

Under UCC § 1-303, a usage of trade may give particular meaning to contract terms and may supplement or qualify them. Express terms and usage should be construed consistently where reasonable, although an irreconcilable express term controls over trade usage.  
https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/1/1-303

Accordingly:

- If “navy” is merely a commercially acceptable shade deviation within the industry tolerance surrounding the stated reference, the widgets may be conforming as the trade understands that term.
- If navy is materially outside the color reference rather than a minor shade variance, the express reference controls and the goods were technically nonconforming.

The facts do not include objective color measurements, an approved physical sample, or the tolerance attached to the reference number. There is therefore some uncertainty about initial conformity. Nevertheless, the more likely litigation assumption is that navy versus charcoal constitutes at least a technical color nonconformity. That does not make Buyer’s later rejection effective.

III. Buyer’s attempted rejection was untimely

Delivery occurred March 15, 2024. Buyer first notified Vendor on May 10, 2024.

Elapsed time:

- March 16–31: 16 days
- April: 30 days
- May 1–10: 10 days
- Total: 16 + 30 + 10 = 56 days

Thus, notice came eight weeks after delivery. Compared with the contractual 10-day period, Buyer was 46 days late.

Color could have been determined immediately by ordinary visual inspection. Unlike a latent durability or load-capacity problem, no eight-week operational trial was necessary. The architect’s later analysis may have clarified the design consequences, but it did not make the navy color itself difficult to discover.

Because the 10-day period is likely reasonable for a visible color issue, Buyer’s May 10 rejection was ineffective under §§ 1-302 and 2-602. Even without the clause, 56 days of use before raising an obvious color discrepancy would probably exceed a reasonable rejection period.

IV. Buyer accepted the widgets

Multiple independent acceptance factors apply.

A. Failure to reject after inspection opportunity

Buyer had a reasonable opportunity to inspect color upon delivery and did not reject within 10 days. That alone supports acceptance under § 2-606(1)(b).

B. Installation and operation

Buyer installed and operated all 1,000 widgets for eight weeks. Installation and sustained commercial use are inconsistent with Vendor’s continuing ownership and therefore constitute acceptance under § 2-606(1)(c).

This was not limited testing reasonably necessary to inspect functionality. Buyer placed the entire shipment into service and continued using it while demanding a large price reduction.

C. Painting 600 widgets

Buyer painted 600 of the 1,000 widgets black:

600 ÷ 1,000 = 0.60 = 60%

Only 400 widgets, or 40%, remained unpainted.

Painting custom goods a different color is a particularly clear exercise of dominion inconsistent with Vendor’s ownership. It also materially changes their condition and complicates or eliminates Vendor’s ability to resell or replace them as originally delivered.

D. Buyer’s communications

Buyer’s March emails praised performance and omitted any color objection. Performance praise alone may not expressly waive every specification, but it reinforces the objective conclusion that Buyer was treating the shipment as accepted. The silence is especially significant because color was visible and the contract established a 10-day notice period.

E. No valid partial rejection

Buyer did not segregate or timely reject any commercial units. It installed and used all units and altered 600. Section 2-601(c) could have permitted acceptance of some commercial units and rejection of others, but Buyer did not exercise that option seasonably.

V. Revocation of acceptance is not available

Because Buyer accepted the widgets, its May 10 communication can only plausibly be treated as an attempted revocation or notice of breach—not an original rejection. Revocation is unlikely for four reasons.

A. Substantial impairment is doubtful

The widgets met all load-capacity, durability, and functional requirements. Industry practice considers minor color variations acceptable for functional components. Buyer’s continued operation of all widgets further suggests that their principal value was not substantially impaired.

The architect’s statement provides some evidence of Buyer-specific aesthetic impairment. Section 2-608 asks whether the nonconformity substantially impairs value “to him,” so a documented showroom design problem is legally relevant even if the widgets remain functional.

Even so, the surrounding facts weaken substantial impairment:

- Buyer used every widget for eight weeks.
- Buyer solved the alleged showroom mismatch for 600 units by painting them black.
- Buyer wants to keep all widgets operating.
- Buyer seeks a 40% refund rather than return or replacement.
- The purchase order emphasized performance criteria rather than showroom aesthetics.
- There was no special rejection clause for shade variance.

On balance, Buyer has shown inconvenience and an aesthetic mismatch, but probably not substantial impairment sufficient for revocation of the entire shipment.

B. The nonconformity was readily discoverable

Section 2-608(1)(b) protects a buyer who accepted without discovering a defect because discovery was difficult or because of seller assurances. Navy rather than charcoal was visible immediately. Nothing indicates concealment or any Vendor assurance that delayed inspection.

The architect’s later conclusion concerns the consequence of the visible color, not a latent defect in the goods.

C. Buyer did not accept on an assumption of cure

Buyer gave Vendor no color notice before May 10. It therefore could not have accepted in March on a reasonable assumption that Vendor would cure a disclosed color issue. Moreover, once notified, Vendor immediately did offer cure.

D. Buyer substantially changed the goods

Section 2-608(2) requires revocation before a substantial change in condition not caused by the goods’ own defects. Painting 600 widgets black is a substantial buyer-caused alteration. That independently defeats revocation as to those widgets and materially undermines attempted revocation of the shipment as a whole.

VI. Vendor’s replacement offer is a valid and reasonable cure

Even assuming Buyer had made a proper rejection, Vendor has a strong cure right under § 2-508(2). Vendor had reasonable grounds to believe the tender would be acceptable because:

- all emphasized functional specifications were satisfied;
- trade practice tolerates minor shade variations in functional components;
- the contract had no express rejection provision for shade variance;
- Buyer installed and used every unit;
- Buyer praised performance; and
- Buyer did not mention color during the inspection period.

Vendor offered replacement immediately after receiving notice, with a two-week lead time. On these facts, two weeks appears reasonable, absent evidence that the showroom faced an immovable deadline or that replacement would create extraordinary disruption.

T.W. Oil supports allowing cure where the seller acted in good faith and reasonably expected the tender to be accepted. Vendor’s immediate response is materially stronger than refusing to address the discrepancy.

Strictly speaking, because Buyer had already accepted the widgets, § 2-508’s rejection-based cure mechanism is not the sole governing rule. Nevertheless, the replacement offer remains important because it:

- supplies the requested conforming performance;
- undermines any assertion that the problem is incurable;
- limits recoverable consequential loss;
- supports Vendor’s good faith;
- provides a commercially reasonable resolution; and
- makes Buyer’s insistence on a 40% windfall less defensible.

Buyer should at minimum permit cure for the 400 unpainted widgets if it insists on exact charcoal-gray conformity. Replacement of the 600 painted units may require Buyer to restore or tender them in an acceptable condition or bear consequences attributable to its alterations.

VII. Buyer cannot unilaterally demand a 40% refund

Acceptance requires Buyer to pay at the contract rate. UCC § 2-607(1). Acceptance precludes rejection but does not automatically eliminate every damages remedy. If Buyer gave legally sufficient notice of breach, it may recover proven losses caused by nonconformity.  
https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607

Under UCC § 2-714, damages for accepted nonconforming goods are ordinarily:

- the loss resulting in the ordinary course from the breach; or
- for breach of warranty, the difference at acceptance between the value of the goods received and the value they would have had as warranted.

Incidental or consequential damages may be available in an appropriate case.  
https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-714

Nothing in the stated facts establishes that navy widgets were worth 40% less than charcoal widgets. Indeed, Buyer’s continued full use, complete functional conformity, accepted trade tolerance, and ability to repaint suggest a much smaller loss.

A defensible damages claim would require evidence such as:

- reasonable repainting costs for the 400 unpainted widgets;
- documented labor or installation costs necessarily caused by replacement;
- measurable diminution in value;
- proven showroom redesign costs; or
- foreseeable lost sales directly caused by the contrast issue.

Costs Buyer voluntarily incurred painting 600 widgets black may be recoverable only if they were reasonable, foreseeable mitigation of an actual breach and if timely notice requirements were satisfied. Painting before notifying Vendor and before giving Vendor an opportunity to replace the goods weakens that claim.

The 10-day clause may also bar all remedies for an obvious defect if it clearly applies to breach notices and not merely to rejection. At minimum, § 2-607(3)(a) requires notice within a reasonable time after Buyer discovered or should have discovered the breach. Because Buyer should have noticed the color at delivery, Vendor has a substantial argument that the 56-day delay bars or limits even damages.

VIII. Factor-by-factor conclusion

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| Conforming goods | Functionally conforming; likely a technical color nonconformity unless trade tolerance qualifies the color reference |
| Perfect tender | Would have allowed prompt rejection for a genuine color deviation |
| Substantial performance | Does not erase a timely perfect-tender objection, but strongly weighs against revocation and a large refund |
| Use after inspection | Installation and eight weeks of operation constitute acceptance |
| Alteration | Painting 600 units, or 60%, is inconsistent with Vendor’s ownership and prevents revocation as to those units |
| Timeliness | Notice after 56 days was 46 days beyond the contractual period and was not seasonable |
| Buyer communications | Performance praise and silence concerning visible color support acceptance |
| Aesthetic impairment | Architect’s statement supports some Buyer-specific harm but likely not substantial impairment of the whole shipment |
| Trade usage | Supports Vendor’s reasonable belief that the shade would be accepted and may qualify the color term |
| Cure | Immediate replacement with a two-week lead time is likely reasonable |
| Requested 40% refund | Unsupported without proof of corresponding diminished value or actual damages |

Final determination

Buyer did not rightfully reject. The perfect-tender rule could have supported rejection during the agreed inspection period if navy materially departed from the charcoal-gray color reference, but Buyer did not preserve that remedy. Its delay, installation, continuous operation, favorable communications, and alteration of 60% of the shipment constitute acceptance.

Buyer must therefore retain and pay for the widgets, subject only to any timely and provable claim for damages arising from the color discrepancy. Revocation is unavailable because the color was obvious, functional value remained intact, Vendor offered prompt cure, and Buyer substantially altered the goods.

The commercially and legally appropriate outcome is acceptance subject to Vendor’s reasonable cure—most plausibly replacement of the 400 unpainted widgets and a negotiated solution for the 600 Buyer painted—not a unilateral 40% refund while Buyer keeps all 1,000 widgets in use.

final.content:
RESPONDEAT SUPERIOR AND SUMMARY-JUDGMENT ANALYSIS

Executive conclusion

The better conclusion is that Daniel Rocha was an employee acting within the scope of employment when the collision occurred. The company therefore should not receive summary judgment disclaiming vicarious liability. If the stated facts are undisputed and supported by admissible evidence, the sedan driver has a strong basis for partial summary judgment establishing that Rocha’s actionable driving negligence, if proven, is attributable to the company.

Three facts are decisive:

1. Rocha was a delivery driver operating in the middle of his workday and intending to resume scheduled deliveries immediately.
2. A supervisor expressly texted Rocha to pick up lunch for two warehouse coworkers, making the trip an assigned or at least supervisor-authorized dual-purpose errand rather than a purely personal lunch trip.
3. The employer’s policy permitting “team support errands” had become effective May 1, 2024—44 days before the June 14 collision—and the company later reimbursed the detour’s mileage.

The four-block deviation and Rocha’s personal interest in lunch do not transform the trip into a substantial “frolic.” The cellphone glance is evidence of negligence in performing the trip, not evidence that he abandoned the employer’s business. Company rules against personal detours likewise do not control because the evidence supports a finding that this was not merely personal; moreover, an employee’s prohibited or negligent manner of carrying out an assigned task ordinarily remains within scope.

Because no jurisdiction is specified and “Route 7” could refer to roads in numerous states, this report applies the mainstream Restatement and common-law approach. Exact wording and burden-shifting rules may vary by jurisdiction.

I. Governing law

A. Basic rule and employee status

Under Restatement (Third) of Agency § 7.07:

- An employer is vicariously liable for a tort committed by an employee acting within the scope of employment.
- An employee acts within scope when performing assigned work or engaging in a course of conduct subject to the employer’s control.
- Conduct is outside scope when it occurs in an independent course of conduct not intended to serve any employer purpose.
- An “employee” is an agent whose principal controls or has the right to control the manner and means of performance.  
  (Restatement excerpt: https://opencasebook.org/casebooks/16481-selected-excerpts-of-restatement-of-agency-third-professor-randle-pollard/as-printable-html/)

The familiar Restatement (Second) formulation asks whether the conduct:

1. was of the kind the employee was employed to perform;
2. occurred substantially within authorized time and space limits; and
3. was actuated, at least in part, by a purpose to serve the employer.

Conduct outside those limits or “too little actuated” by an employer-serving purpose falls outside scope. Relevant incidental-conduct factors include the time, place and purpose of the conduct; its similarity to authorized work; whether the employer could expect it; the instrumentality used; and the extent of departure from the authorized method. (Restatement §§ 228–229 excerpt: https://opencasebook.org/casebooks/9130-torts/as-printable-html/7/)

An employer need not receive the sole or predominant benefit. A trip serving both an employee’s personal interest and an employer interest can fall within the “dual purpose” rule. The New Jersey Supreme Court, for example, describes the exception as covering an employee who simultaneously serves an employer interest and a personal interest. Carter v. Reynolds, https://law.justia.com/cases/new-jersey/supreme-court/2003/a-104-01-opn.html.

B. Summary-judgment standard

Under the federal formulation, summary judgment is proper only when “there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact” and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title28/html/USCODE-2024-title28-app-federalru-dup1-rule56.htm.

Scope of employment is ordinarily a fact question. It becomes a question of law when the material facts are undisputed and permit no conflicting reasonable inference. Perez v. Van Groningen & Sons, Inc., 41 Cal. 3d 962, 968 (1986), https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/perez-v-van-groningen-sons-inc-30781.

Thus, there are three possible summary-judgment outcomes:

- summary judgment for the employer if only an independent personal frolic can reasonably be inferred;
- denial of both sides’ motions if competing reasonable inferences remain; or
- partial summary judgment for the plaintiff if the undisputed evidence establishes scope as a matter of law.

II. Application

A. Rocha’s employee status is effectively undisputed

Rocha is identified as the company’s “delivery driver,” had an assigned route and delivery schedule, and was subject to company policies regulating detours. A supervisor could direct him by text to perform an errand. Those facts establish both actual control and the right to control:

- the company selected the work—deliveries and, according to the text, the lunch pickup;
- it controlled route-related behavior through its detour policy;
- it monitored or established a delivery schedule;
- a supervisor exercised operational authority over Rocha; and
- it reimbursed mileage connected with the trip.

This is not the typical independent-contractor problem. On the supplied record, no reasonable factfinder could classify Rocha as an independent contractor merely because he left his usual route. Employee status should be established on summary judgment.

B. The lunch pickup was assigned or authorized work

The supervisor’s text told Rocha to pick up lunch for the two warehouse coworkers. That is direct evidence of an assigned task. Under Restatement § 7.07, performing “work assigned by the employer” is within scope unless the employee embarked on an independent course of conduct not intended to serve any employer purpose.

This trip was not independent in that sense. Rocha was responding to a supervisor’s direction and transporting items for coworkers. The fact that the coworkers had requested sandwiches earlier that morning reinforces that the supervisor’s message concerned an actual workplace need rather than Rocha inventing a personal side trip.

The deleted approving email is therefore corroborative rather than indispensable. Metadata confirming that the email existed does not, by itself, prove every word of its contents, but testimony, the supervisor’s text, recipient records, or other secondary evidence may establish those contents. Federal Rule of Evidence 1004 permits other evidence of a writing’s contents when the original has been lost or destroyed, subject to the rule’s bad-faith limitation. https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre/rule_1004.

If the email was deleted after a preservation duty arose, separate spoliation issues could follow. But metadata showing mere existence, without evidence of when, why, or by whom it was deleted, is insufficient by itself to require a dispositive adverse inference. More importantly, the surviving supervisor text independently supports authorization.

C. The temporal and geographic deviation was minor

The collision occurred during the workday, while Rocha was on schedule and planning to continue deliveries immediately after lunch. The lunch stop was four blocks off the assigned route.

No block length is provided, so exact distance cannot be calculated. Even using a rough urban range of approximately 1/16 to 1/8 mile per block, four blocks would represent only about:

- 4 × 1/16 mile = 0.25 mile; to
- 4 × 1/8 mile = 0.50 mile.

That estimate is illustrative only; actual block dimensions may differ. Qualitatively, however, a four-block deviation is small and bears little resemblance to an extended personal journey.

The trip also occurred between active work assignments rather than during a commute to or from work. Rocha remained on schedule and intended to resume deliveries immediately, supporting continuous employment rather than an abandonment followed by a later reentry.

A recent analogous decision reversed summary judgment for an employer where an employee, after work-related midday errands and a personal hamburger stop, was returning to a scheduled business meeting. The court held that whether the employee remained within scope presented a fact question and rejected reliance on the going-and-coming rule because the workday was already underway. Kulzer v. Way, 379 So. 3d 568 (Fla. 5th DCA 2024), opinion PDF: https://cases.justia.com/florida/fifth-district-court-of-appeal/2024-5d23-0750.pdf?ts=1706890235.

Rocha’s case is stronger for the plaintiff than Kulzer because his supervisor affirmatively directed the lunch pickup.

D. The errand materially benefited the employer

The employer-benefit factor does not require a direct sale, delivery, or immediate monetary gain. Here, the trip supported two warehouse employees by bringing them lunch, potentially allowing them to remain at the warehouse and minimizing work interruption. It also carried out a supervisor’s workplace-management decision.

The company itself characterized this category as a “team support errand.” That characterization is evidence that such errands serve organizational needs, employee coordination, or productivity. The policy became effective May 1, 2024, while the collision occurred June 14, 2024:

- May 1 to June 1: 31 elapsed days;
- June 1 to June 14: 13 additional days;
- total elapsed time: 44 days.

Thus, the policy was not adopted after the collision, even though the reimbursement occurred afterward. The retroactive mileage payment is a post-accident act, so it should not alone decide historical scope or operate automatically as a legal admission. Nevertheless, it corroborates the supervisor’s instruction and the company’s position that the trip fit an existing policy.

The closest factual authority is Wilson v. Joma, Inc., 537 A.2d 187 (Del. 1988). There, an employee left during lunch to obtain sandwiches for himself and coworkers. Most coworkers ordinarily remained at the business so customers would not be inconvenienced. Although the practice was informal and mileage was not reimbursed, the Delaware Supreme Court reversed summary judgment for the employer because material factual disputes existed over the trip’s dual purpose and benefit to the business. https://openjurist.org/537/a2d/187/wilson-v-joma-inc-1956917.

Rocha presents substantially stronger evidence of employer purpose than Wilson:

- a supervisor expressly directed the pickup;
- an email reportedly approved it;
- a written policy covered “team support errands”;
- the company reimbursed mileage; and
- the deviation was only four blocks.

By contrast, cases finding no scope during lunch generally involve trips undertaken solely for the employee’s own meal, without a supervisor’s direction or employer benefit. Matheson v. Braden, for example, affirmed summary judgment where the employee drove home for the purely personal purpose of lunch. https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ga-court-of-appeals/1573561.html. Rocha’s trip was not purely personal.

E. The personal-detour prohibition does not eliminate scope

The company will emphasize that its general policy prohibited personal detours. That argument is weak for two independent reasons.

First, this detour was not exclusively personal. It was undertaken after a supervisor directed Rocha to obtain lunches for warehouse coworkers and while a policy expressly allowed “team support errands.” The more specific supervisor instruction and team-support policy reasonably distinguish this errand from prohibited personal stops.

Second, violating a company rule does not automatically take an employee outside scope. In Perez, the employee violated a rule against carrying passengers while operating the employer’s tractor. The California Supreme Court held scope established as a matter of law because he was still performing the assigned tractor work. The court explained that authorization of the precise negligent act is unnecessary and that an employer cannot avoid respondeat-superior liability merely by ordering employees to act carefully. https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/perez-v-van-groningen-sons-inc-30781.

The relevant question is not whether every detail of the trip complied with policy; it is whether Rocha had abandoned the employer’s affairs for an independent personal venture. The supervisor’s instruction, coworker purpose, effective team-support policy, reimbursement, continuing schedule, and immediate intent to resume deliveries collectively foreclose—or at minimum create a strong factual dispute against—such a finding.

F. Rocha’s cellphone glance is negligence in performing the errand, not a frolic

Dashcam evidence shows Rocha glanced at his phone two seconds before impact. That conduct is highly relevant to breach, causation, and comparative fault. It does not meaningfully show that he had left the scope of employment.

Employees regularly perform assigned work negligently. Respondeat superior exists precisely because employers may be liable for such negligence even though it is unauthorized. Perez emphasizes that liability can attach when an employee performs the employer’s work in a prohibited or negligent manner. Id.

A two-second glance is transient conduct occurring while Rocha continued driving on the errand. It is not comparable to leaving the route for an unrelated extended activity. Even if the phone use was personal or violated a safety rule, the collision still occurred during the authorized course of driving. The phone use concerns the manner of performance, not the underlying purpose of the journey.

III. Rocha’s underlying negligence and the sedan driver’s injury

Vicarious liability remains derivative: the company is liable only to the extent Rocha committed a tort. The scope ruling does not itself establish every negligence and damages element.

The evidence strongly supports Rocha’s negligence:

- he rear-ended the sedan;
- the sedan’s brake lights functioned properly;
- it braked for fallen lumber, an objectively legitimate roadway hazard; and
- Rocha looked at his phone only two seconds before impact.

The sudden stop is not necessarily a complete defense. A sudden, arbitrary stop can sometimes rebut an inference that the rear driver was negligent. See Eppler v. Tarmac America, Inc., 752 So. 2d 592 (Fla. 2000), https://hallapproved.com/fl/cases/supreme/2000/1860579/. Here, however, the sedan stopped for fallen lumber rather than “for no reason,” its brake lights worked, and Rocha was distracted immediately before impact.

A comparable cellphone case held the emergency doctrine unavailable where a rear driver helped create the emergency by speeding and talking on a cellphone, despite a stopped vehicle ahead. Martinez v. ITF LLC summary: https://exa.ai/library/legal/opinion/c83mypwr7fy.

Nevertheless, the record gives no speeds, following distance, visibility, exact braking interval, or lumber-discovery timing. Those omissions may leave comparative negligence or unavoidable-emergency issues for trial. The fallen lumber could also implicate an unidentified third party. Accordingly:

- negligence appears strongly supported;
- scope of employment is even more clearly supported;
- but complete summary judgment fixing all fault and damages may be premature without traffic-reconstruction facts.

The claimed neck strain is supported by imaging showing soft-tissue injury, which supplies objective evidence of injury. It does not automatically establish that the collision caused all claimed symptoms, the treatment was reasonable, or a particular damages amount. Those remain medical-causation and damages questions unless expert evidence removes all genuine dispute.

IV. Appropriate summary-judgment disposition

A. Employer’s motion

Any company motion for summary judgment on the ground that Rocha was outside the scope of employment should be denied.

At a minimum, the following evidence creates a genuine dispute:

- supervisor’s text directing the lunch pickup;
- metadata confirming an approving email existed;
- the May 1 “team support errands” policy;
- post-collision mileage reimbursement;
- Rocha’s on-schedule status;
- his intent to continue deliveries immediately; and
- the slight four-block deviation.

Wilson establishes that materially weaker evidence concerning a coworker-lunch run was enough to reverse summary judgment for the employer. Rocha’s evidence therefore comfortably defeats an employer motion.

B. Sedan driver’s motion for partial summary judgment

If the supervisor’s text, policy effective date, work status, and route facts are undisputed and admissible, the stronger result is partial summary judgment for the sedan driver on employee status and scope of employment.

No reasonable factfinder could then regard Rocha’s trip as wholly independent of the company:

- he was a controlled delivery employee;
- the supervisor assigned the errand;
- the errand served coworkers and a recognized team-support function;
- it occurred during the workday;
- the geographic deviation was slight;
- he remained on schedule; and
- he was going to resume deliveries immediately.

Like the employee in Perez, Rocha may have performed an assigned activity negligently and contrary to some general rule, but he remained occupied with the company’s business. On this record, the employer-purpose evidence is stronger than the evidence of an independent personal frolic.

If, however, the company presents admissible evidence that the supervisor lacked authority, the text meant something materially different, the May 1 policy was not genuinely in effect, or Rocha had completed the coworker errand and was pursuing a separate personal objective at impact, scope may need to go to a jury. The mere deletion of the approving email is not enough to create such a dispute when the surviving text and other evidence remain uncontradicted.

C. Ultimate liability formulation

The procedurally precise ruling should be:

1. Employee status: established as a matter of law.
2. Scope of employment: likely established as a matter of law on the stated undisputed record; at minimum, sufficiently disputed to defeat summary judgment for the company.
3. Employer benefit: established through the supervisor-directed support of warehouse coworkers and corroborated by the preexisting team-support policy and mileage reimbursement.
4. Rocha’s negligence: strongly indicated by the rear-end impact and two-second phone distraction, but potentially subject to remaining factual questions about speed, following distance, visibility, and the sudden roadway obstruction.
5. Injury and damages: objective soft-tissue evidence supports the claim, but causation, severity, treatment, and amount may remain for trial.

Final determination

The company is vicariously responsible for Rocha’s negligence arising from this collision because Rocha was acting within the scope of employment. The lunch run was, at most, a slight dual-purpose detour—not a substantial personal frolic. The supervisor’s direct instruction and the already-effective “team support errands” policy make the employer nexus particularly strong. Rocha’s cellphone glance and any technical violation of the personal-detour rule concern negligent execution of an employer-connected trip and do not sever respondeat-superior liability.

Accordingly, the court should deny summary judgment to the company and, assuming the stated evidence is undisputed and admissible, grant the sedan driver partial summary judgment that Rocha was acting within the scope of employment. Final judgment against the company should remain contingent on proof—or a separate summary-judgment ruling—that Rocha’s negligence caused compensable injury.

Rocha had received a text message from a supervisor that told Rocha to pick up lunch for the two warehouse coworkers. final.content:
# Memristor-Based Neuromorphic Computing: Physics, Crossbar Engineering, and Benchmark Evidence

## Executive assessment

The controversy has two largely separable questions:

1. **Did HP Labs discover Chua’s 1971 fourth fundamental circuit element?**  
   Not in the strictest interpretation. HP’s titanium-oxide device is unquestionably a useful two-terminal resistive memory whose conductance depends on internal ionic state. It fits the broader 1976 class of *memristive systems*. Whether it realizes Chua’s ideal constitutive relation between charge \(q\) and flux linkage \(\phi\)—and therefore deserves the title “fourth fundamental element”—remains disputed. Vongehr and Meng’s objection is strongest against the historical and ontological claim that the “missing” 1971 element was found, not against the usefulness of resistive-switching devices.

2. **Do memristive devices nevertheless offer a neuromorphic advantage?**  
   Potentially, but primarily through **dense, nonvolatile analog weight storage and in-place matrix–vector multiplication**, not because commercial devices have been proved to embody a unique fundamental law unavailable to CMOS. Device stochasticity, asymmetric updates, drift, limited endurance, sneak current, converters, and control circuitry substantially qualify the ideal density and efficiency claims. Between 2020 and 2024, impressive MNIST and CIFAR-10 hardware results demonstrated viability, but they generally depended on selectors, CMOS periphery, differential encoding, write-and-verify, hardware-aware training, or compensation. They do not establish that memristor *physics itself* supplies intrinsically superior synaptic plasticity.

A source qualification is important: the three named examples are not all documented in “respective IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices” papers. The University of Michigan Ag/a-Si system’s principal array paper is in *Nano Letters*, while Knowm’s original AHaH work appeared in *PLOS ONE* and later technical reports. IEEE TED papers are most directly relevant to the RRAM-selector and variability analysis. Treating all three as TED implementations would conflate separate publication records.

---

## 1. From Chua’s ideal element to HP’s resistive switch

### 1.1 Chua’s 1971 proposition

Circuit theory uses four variables:

- charge \(q\),
- current \(i=dq/dt\),
- flux linkage \(\phi=\int v\,dt\),
- voltage \(v=d\phi/dt\).

The familiar ideal elements supply constitutive relations:

- resistor: \(v=R i\),
- capacitor: \(q=Cv\),
- inductor: \(\phi=Li\).

Chua proposed the remaining direct relation,

\[
d\phi=M(q)\,dq,
\qquad
v=M(q)i,
\]

where the memristance \(M\) depends only on the accumulated charge. A strict ideal memristor is therefore a **state function of charge**, not merely any resistor whose resistance changes with history.

For a periodic voltage or current, an ideal memristor is expected to show a pinched hysteresis loop crossing the origin; the loop normally contracts as frequency rises. But pinched hysteresis by itself is not sufficient to prove the unique \(q\)-to-\(\phi\) constitutive relation: many systems with hidden thermal, ionic, chemical, or structural variables can exhibit similar curves.

### 1.2 What HP demonstrated in 2008

Strukov, Snider, Stewart, and Williams described a nanoscale titanium-oxide structure in which electronic conduction was coupled to motion of charged defects, modeled as a boundary between lower- and higher-resistance regions. Their central claim was that “memristance arises naturally” in nanoscale systems coupling electronic and ionic transport and that this supplied a physical example of the previously missing element (Nature 453, 80–83, DOI 10.1038/nature06932: https://web.archive.org/web/20080505130347/http:/www.nature.com/nature/journal/v453/n7191/full/nature06932.html).

In the simplified HP model, total resistance can be represented schematically as

\[
R(w)=R_{\rm ON}\frac{w}{D}
     +R_{\rm OFF}\left(1-\frac{w}{D}\right),
\]

with the internal boundary \(w\) moved by current. Under assumptions such as linear ionic drift, \(w\) can be related to integrated current and hence to charge.

The paper established three important engineering ideas:

- a two-terminal device can retain an analog conductance state;
- ionic motion can couple state storage directly to electrical operation;
- a passive crosspoint can combine weight storage and multiplication through Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws.

HP’s public announcement went further, saying that the team had “proven the existence” of the fourth fundamental element (https://www.hp.com/hpinfo/newsroom/press/2008/080430a.html). Williams subsequently described memristors as the “functional equivalent of a synapse,” because conductance can represent synaptic strength and can be modified by prior electrical activity (https://spectrum.ieee.org/how-we-found-the-missing-memristor).

Strictly speaking, however, the 2008 *Nature* paper primarily introduced the device model and identification with memristance; the explicit, broad synapse analogy was developed in Williams’s subsequent presentations and neuromorphic proposals. Saying that the *Nature* paper itself fully “established” the synapse analogy slightly overstates its scope.

---

## 2. Vongehr and Meng’s critique and the substantive response

### 2.1 The 2015 critique

Vongehr and Meng argued that “the missing memristor has not been found” (Scientific Reports 5, 11657: https://www.nature.com/articles/srep11657). Their case had four main parts.

#### A. Ideal memristor versus memristive system

The ideal 1971 device has a direct, single-valued \(\phi(q)\) relation. Real resistive memories generally require one or more independent internal variables:

\[
v=R(x,i,t)i,
\qquad
\dot{x}=f(x,i,t),
\]

where \(x\) can describe vacancy concentration, filament geometry, phase fraction, temperature, or interface chemistry. This is the broader “memristive system” formalism introduced by Chua and Kang in 1976, rather than necessarily the ideal 1971 element.

A real device can return to the same accumulated charge with a different filament configuration or resistance because of diffusion, relaxation, temperature, pulse shape, or stochastic atomic motion. If so, resistance is not uniquely determined by \(q\).

#### B. The magnetic-flux objection

Vongehr and Meng read the original symmetry argument physically: the fourth element was proposed alongside a real inductor and therefore should involve the electromagnetic meaning of flux. HP’s titanium-oxide device stores state through material rearrangement and would still operate in a hypothetical nonmagnetic world. On their interpretation, it is therefore a memory resistor, not the physically missing electromagnetic counterpart implied in 1971.

#### C. Resistive switching was not new in 2008

They emphasized that hysteretic thin-film resistance switching and nonvolatile memory predated 2008. What was new was chiefly the reinterpretation and branding of such behavior as the long-sought memristor, together with a particularly influential compact model.

#### D. “Perfect” behavior was not experimentally established

The linear-drift HP model is highly idealized. Real devices exhibit thresholds, nonlinear fields, Joule heating, diffusion, stochastic filament formation, state saturation, relaxation, and device-to-device and cycle-to-cycle variation. Consequently, a fit to a memristive model does not prove the exact constitutive relation required of the ideal element.

Their conclusion was deliberately narrow but important: the 2008 device can be technologically useful while still not being the specific “missing” real element supposedly predicted in 1971.

### 2.2 The HP/Strukov-side response

The defense rests on a different interpretation of circuit variables and on abstraction rather than microscopic mechanism.

1. **Flux linkage in circuit theory is \(\phi(t)=\int v(t)\,dt\); it need not denote magnetic flux in a core.**  
   Under this interpretation, demanding magnetism imports a physical condition not required by the constitutive mathematics.

2. **Fundamental circuit elements are ideal models.**  
   Commercial resistors, capacitors, and inductors also have parasitics, noise, nonlinearities, and hidden physical state. A physical approximation need not reproduce an ideal relation under every voltage, frequency, or environmental condition to instantiate the useful element model.

3. **Coupled ionic and electronic transport can approximate charge-controlled resistance over a restricted operating region.**  
   The fact that more complete device descriptions require additional state variables does not eliminate the utility of the memristor abstraction.

4. **The practical distinction is functional.**  
   The devices are nonvolatile, electrically adjustable two-terminal conductances. For crossbar computation, whether they are called ideal memristors, generalized memristors, RRAM, CBRAM, PCM, or memristive systems does not change the basic multiply–accumulate operation.

Later crossbar work associated with Strukov generally adopted this practical sense. For example, integrated metal-oxide “memristive” crossbars were optimized around forming voltage, switching voltage, endurance, retention, conductance range, and programming current rather than around proof of a unique \(\phi(q)\) law (example paper: https://web.ece.ucsb.edu/%7Estrukov/papers/2015/Nature2015.pdf).

### 2.3 Best resolution of the theoretical dispute

Both sides can be correct under different definitions:

- **Strict historical/theoretical usage:** no commercial resistive memory has convincingly been shown to be an ideal charge-controlled fourth element with resistance uniquely determined by total charge over arbitrary histories.
- **Modern engineering usage:** “memristor” commonly denotes a two-terminal resistive device with an electrically evolving internal state. In that broader sense, commercial Knowm devices and many RRAM, CBRAM, and PCM cells are memristive devices.

Thus, claims that commercial devices have demonstrated the exact fourth fundamental element should be qualified. Claims that they are not useful memristive synapses because they fail that test are also unwarranted.

---

## 3. Crossbar obstacles: sneak paths and variability

For a crossbar driven by row voltages \(V_i\), the ideal current at column \(j\) is

\[
I_j=\sum_i G_{ij}V_i,
\]

which directly computes an analog dot product. Two nonidealities prevent an ideal scaling argument.

### 3.1 Sneak paths

Unselected cells can form alternative conducting routes through floating rows and columns. The sensed current becomes

\[
I_{\rm measured}=I_{\rm target}+I_{\rm sneak},
\]

and \(I_{\rm sneak}\) grows with array size, device conductance, data pattern, and line resistance. In neural inference, IR drop also causes the actual cell voltage to depend on physical location and the simultaneous input pattern.

### 3.2 Device variability

Relevant variations include:

- device-to-device conductance range;
- cycle-to-cycle SET/RESET threshold;
- nonlinear or asymmetric potentiation and depression;
- stochastic filament growth;
- read noise;
- retention drift;
- stuck-at faults and limited endurance.

Differential weights help:

\[
W_{ij}\propto G^+_{ij}-G^-_{ij},
\]

but they double the nominal device count and do not eliminate correlated drift, update nonlinearity, or converter overhead.

---

## 4. Comparison of the three implementations

### 4.1 Knowm AHaH nodes

#### Architecture

Knowm’s Anti-Hebbian and Hebbian, or AHaH, architecture represents one synaptic weight with a **differential pair of incremental memristors**. Multiple selected synapses are coupled to a common node; read and feedback phases produce competing conductance adaptation. The original account describes AHaH nodes as attractor-based adaptive circuits that combine memory and processing and can implement classification, clustering, prediction, control, and optimization (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0085175).

The later kT-RAM proposal places these differential synapses behind a RAM-like addressing structure so that arbitrary selected rows can be temporarily coupled into a node, rather than treating one giant passive crossbar as a permanently all-to-all network (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1406.5633).

#### Sneak-path strategy

Knowm’s key response is architectural:

- use addressable rows/columns and controlled coupling;
- activate only the synapses belonging to a particular AHaH node;
- keep physical arrays comparatively small;
- avoid relying on a large, floating, selectorless array as a literal map of a fully connected layer.

Knowm explicitly acknowledges that selector devices such as 1T1R suppress sneak paths but consume silicon area. Its proposed alternative is to avoid large passive crossbars as the universal topology and use the crossbar primarily as a bank of addressable adaptive elements (https://knowm.org/memristor-crossbars-as-easy-as-raspberry-pi/).

This does not make sneak current disappear. It trades some of the passive crossbar’s theoretical density and one-shot parallelism for controlled access, smaller subarrays, and temporal assembly of nodes.

#### Variability strategy

AHaH computing attempts to **adapt with the physical devices rather than first programming each cell to an exact numerical target**:

- differential pairs cancel part of common-mode variation;
- incremental online updates move weights toward attractor states;
- metastable-switch models represent conductance as the aggregate of many stochastic microscopic transitions;
- continued adaptation can compensate some drift or device mismatch.

Knowm reports bidirectional incremental conductance changes using short, low-voltage pulses below approximately 1 V in its proposed technology (https://arxiv.org/html/1608.04105). Nevertheless, measurements of commercial Knowm devices show probabilistic SET and RESET thresholds and heavy-tailed variability, requiring stochastic rather than deterministic compact models (https://latamt.ieeer9.org/index.php/transactions/article/view/8308).

**Assessment:** AHaH is unusually tolerant of update uncertainty because learning is closed-loop and differential, but it has not demonstrated that variability is harmless at large scale. Its sneak-path solution depends substantially on giving up the idealized giant passive-crossbar operating mode.

---

### 4.2 University of Michigan Ag/a-Si/p-Si system

#### Architecture and measured scale

The Michigan group demonstrated Ag/a-Si/p-Si switches in a \(32\times32\) array. The arithmetic is

\[
32\times32=1{,}024\text{ cells}=1\text{ kb}.
\]

The reported line width was about 120 nm and density about \(2\ {\rm Gbit/cm^2}\). Each crosspoint combined a silver top electrode, amorphous-silicon active layer, and doped polysilicon bottom electrode. The device operates through silver-ion transport and formation or modification of a conductive path. The original paper reported high yield, high ON/OFF ratio, and operation either as rewritable RRAM or write-once memory (https://websites.umich.edu/~wluee/Lu_JoSiCrossbar_NL2009.pdf; abstract: https://pubs.acs.org/nalefd/article/9/2/870/1405741/High-Density-Crossbar-Arrays-Based-on-a-Si).

#### Sneak-path strategy

The asymmetric metal/semiconductor structure provides strongly nonlinear and rectifying behavior, which helps suppress current through improperly biased neighboring cells. Isolation dielectric outside the intended crosspoints also prevents direct top-to-bottom line shorts.

That is materially different from Knowm’s topology-based approach: Michigan sought useful **intrinsic device selectivity** within a dense passive array. However, intrinsic rectification is not equivalent to an ideal selector. At larger dimensions, the residual reverse and half-selected currents still accumulate. The 1-kb demonstration establishes addressability and reproducibility, not unrestricted scaling to very large selectorless arrays.

#### Variability strategy

The Michigan work emphasized fabrication uniformity and large ON/OFF margin rather than algorithmic compensation:

- silicon-compatible bottom electrodes and patterned Ag lines;
- controlled active-layer geometry;
- large resistance separation, making absolute variation less damaging for binary readout;
- measured yield and uniformity across the 1-kb array.

For analog synapses, however, conductive-filament devices remain intrinsically stochastic. A high ON/OFF ratio helps binary memory much more than it guarantees linear, symmetric multilevel updates. Precise neuromorphic weights would still require differential encoding, verify-and-adjust programming, calibration, or hardware-aware training.

**Assessment:** This implementation attacked sneak paths primarily through device asymmetry/nonlinearity and attacked variability through process uniformity and large read margin. It is compelling as dense memory, but its published array result does not by itself demonstrate high-precision analog plasticity.

---

### 4.3 KAIST-associated RRAM/selector approaches

RRAM crossbars commonly insert a nonlinear selector, producing a **1S1R** cell, or an access transistor, producing **1T1R**. Relevant IEEE TED analysis shows that the proper selector depends on whether the array is reading or learning.

#### Sneak-path strategy

A selector remains off under the smaller voltages appearing on unselected or half-selected cells and turns on only when the selected cell receives the full access voltage. This sharply reduces alternative paths.

Analysis of analog 1S1R neuromorphic arrays found:

- a **threshold selector** can improve inference immunity to line-resistance-induced voltage errors because, once on, the selected cell can operate with a more favorable effective current–voltage response;
- an **exponential selector** can better preserve gradual RRAM conductance updates during training;
- the selector optimal for inference is therefore not necessarily optimal for online learning.

The corresponding study summarized this as a preference for different selector characteristics in read and update modes (https://exa.ai/library/publication/sbfbh4nsz1s).

The price is additional voltage, area or process complexity, and possible read disturb. A high selector turn-on voltage may expose the RRAM to enough stress to move its analog state.

#### Variability and read-disturb strategy

A 2020 IEEE TED study statistically measured read-disturb-induced drift in a 2-bit HfO\(_2\) RRAM array, modeled the behavior through filament growth, and proposed a **bipolar read scheme** to cancel or reduce cumulative state displacement. It evaluated the resulting behavior using a VGG-like CIFAR-10 network (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9069908).

This class of approach addresses variability through:

- limiting each cell to a small number of robust conductance levels;
- program-and-verify;
- empirical, state-dependent drift models;
- bipolar or balanced read pulses;
- compensation in weight mapping and neural-network training;
- selectors to isolate half-selected cells.

The general trade-off is important: stronger selection improves sneak-current immunity but may increase access voltage and distort the analog update law. RRAM designs therefore co-optimize selector shape, write pulses, conductance states, wire resistance, and training.

**Assessment:** Compared with AHaH and the Michigan passive array, the RRAM approach uses the most explicit cell-level isolation and calibration. It provides better deterministic control but sacrifices some density and increases peripheral complexity.

---

## 5. Side-by-side engineering comparison

| Implementation | Weight/cell organization | Sneak-path response | Variability response | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Knowm AHaH | Differential memristor pairs, dynamically addressed into adaptive nodes | Small/addressed arrays; controlled coupling; avoids treating a giant passive crossbar as the network | Online attractor learning, differential cancellation, stochastic metastable-switch model | Reduced one-shot parallelism; variability remains substantial; large-scale hardware evidence limited |
| Michigan Ag/a-Si/p-Si | Passive \(32\times32\), 1,024-cell filamentary array | Intrinsic rectification/nonlinearity and physical isolation outside crosspoints | High ON/OFF ratio, process uniformity and binary read margin | Intrinsic selectivity is finite; filament stochasticity complicates precise analog weights |
| RRAM 1S1R/1T1R | Multilevel RRAM plus selector or transistor | Threshold/exponential selector; controlled biasing; sometimes bipolar read | Program-and-verify, low-bit states, drift models, balanced reads, hardware-aware training | Area/process and voltage overhead; selector can distort updates or cause read disturb |

No implementation obtains all four ideal attributes simultaneously: maximum density, unrestricted parallelism, zero sneak current, and precise analog updates.

---

## 6. What the 2020–2024 benchmarks actually show

### 6.1 MNIST results

A 2020 fully hardware-implemented memristor CNN integrated eight arrays of 2,048 cells each:

\[
8\times2{,}048=16{,}384\text{ array cells}.
\]

It achieved **more than 96% MNIST accuracy** and reported energy efficiency more than two orders of magnitude above the compared state-of-the-art GPU. Because “two orders of magnitude” means a factor exceeding roughly \(10^2=100\), this was a substantial system claim. But the result required high-yield arrays and hybrid training specifically designed around device imperfections (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-1942-4).

NeuRRAM, reported in 2022, achieved **99.0% on MNIST** and described its accuracy as comparable to a four-bit quantized software model. Its importance was not merely the number but the co-design of RRAM, circuits, architecture, and algorithms (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04992-8).

A 2024 1-kb self-compliant crossbar study reported:

- **92.36% MNIST** with online LTP/LTD-style training;
- **95.87% MNIST** with offline-trained, quantized multilevel weights;
- about a **1.2 percentage-point** accuracy drop attributed to programming error in its measured VMM demonstration (https://pubs.acs.org/ancac3/article/18/36/25128/233356/Memristive-Architectures-Exploiting-Self).

The fact that offline mapping outperformed device-level online plasticity by

\[
95.87-92.36=3.51\text{ percentage points}
\]

is evidence against assuming that native memristor updating is automatically the better learning mechanism.

### 6.2 CIFAR-10 results

A 2020 PCM experiment mapped a ResNet-32 to a one-million-device prototype. It achieved:

- **93.7% CIFAR-10** immediately after mapping;
- more than **93.5% retained for one day**;
- 361,722 signed synaptic weights, each represented by two PCM cells.

The nominal device use for those weights was therefore

\[
2\times361{,}722=723{,}444\text{ PCM devices}.
\]

The result depended on differential encoding, device-aware training, and compensation through batch-normalization parameters (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-16108-9).

NeuRRAM achieved **85.7% CIFAR-10**, while retaining software-comparable accuracy at four-bit weight precision and supporting several different AI tasks on the same chip (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04992-8).

A separate monolithically integrated RRAM design reported **84.2% CIFAR-10** and up to **78.3 TOPS/W**, using a \(128\times64\) array:

\[
128\times64=8{,}192\text{ crosspoints}.
\]

Its optimization included input splitting, CMOS peripheral circuits, and analysis of multilevel programming rather than reliance on an ideal device alone (https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10138120).

These accuracy figures are not directly rankable: they use different networks, precisions, training assumptions, amounts of measured versus simulated hardware, and definitions of system boundaries. In particular, MNIST is far easier than CIFAR-10, and an inference-only mapped network does not demonstrate online synaptic plasticity.

---

## 7. Do memristors provide better plasticity than CMOS?

### 7.1 Where they have a genuine physical advantage

Memristive devices can provide several synapse-like functions compactly:

- nonvolatile conductance directly represents weight;
- programming pulses can produce potentiation and depression;
- overlapping pre- and postsynaptic pulses can implement an STDP-like timing window;
- volatile and nonvolatile components can mimic short- and long-term memory;
- stochastic switching can be exploited for probabilistic learning;
- crossbar conductance performs multiplication and current summation in place.

A conventional high-precision CMOS synapse may require SRAM or registers plus arithmetic, routing, and update logic. Memristive storage can therefore reduce cell area and, most importantly, data movement.

### 7.2 Why this is not proof of intrinsically superior plasticity

Most demonstrated “plasticity” is engineered through the surrounding pulse circuitry. The same LTP, LTD, STDP, metaplasticity, and homeostatic rules can be implemented in CMOS, often with better repeatability and programmability. CMOS alternatives also avoid filament drift, limited write endurance, destructive read stress, and poorly controlled analog update curves.

Real memristor updates frequently have:

- nonlinear dependence on current state;
- unequal potentiation and depression;
- stochastic thresholds;
- saturation at conductance limits;
- conductance drift after programming;
- cell-to-cell variation.

Consequently, high-performing systems routinely add CMOS drivers, DACs, ADCs, accumulators, selectors, verify circuits, digital calibration, or retraining. The relevant comparison is thus not “one memristor versus tens of transistors,” but **complete hybrid memristor–CMOS system versus complete CMOS compute-in-memory or digital accelerator**, at matched process, model, accuracy, lifetime, and workload.

A 2024 review cautioned that many claimed advantages were inferred from one or a few measured devices while network accuracy was simulated; relatively few studies implemented all ANN operations in full hardware (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-45670-9). That observation explains why spectacular cell-level energy or density does not automatically become a system-level advantage.

---

## 8. Current consensus

The defensible consensus through 2024 is:

1. **Commercial “memristors” are real and useful resistive-memory devices.**  
   Their history-dependent conductance is not in dispute.

2. **They are safely classified as memristive systems.**  
   This terminology covers RRAM, CBRAM, many oxide switches, and PCM without requiring proof that state is uniquely a function of total charge.

3. **Their status as Chua’s exact fourth fundamental element is unresolved and definition-dependent.**  
   Under the strict 1971 constitutive definition, commercial devices have not demonstrated an unambiguous single-valued \(\phi(q)\) relation independent of hidden material variables. Under the broader circuit-theory convention that flux is simply time-integrated voltage and physical elements only approximate ideal models, calling them memristors is accepted engineering usage.

4. **The neuromorphic value does not depend on winning that naming dispute.**  
   Crossbar VMM and nonvolatile analog storage work because of tunable conductance, Kirchhoff summation, and co-location of memory and computation—not because the device has been certified as a fourth fundamental element.

5. **Memristors can yield superior density or energy for particular operations, but superior native plasticity has not been generally proved.**  
   The strongest 2020–2024 results are hybrid accomplishments involving device-aware training and CMOS support. Indeed, the 2024 example in which offline quantized learning exceeded online device learning by 3.51 percentage points illustrates that native conductance dynamics are not automatically the best learning rule.

6. **Crossbar nonidealities determine practical success.**  
   Knowm mitigates them through differential, adaptive, addressable nodes; Michigan used device rectification and large resistance margins; RRAM approaches use selectors, low-bit conductance states, bipolar reads, verification, and compensation. Each solution relinquishes part of the ideal passive-crossbar advantage.

## Final judgment

Williams and the HP team were correct that nanoscale mixed ionic–electronic devices provide a powerful physical substrate for memory and neuromorphic computation. Their 2008 model catalyzed a field and accurately identified the potential of two-terminal adaptive conductances. But the stronger claim that the team definitively found Chua’s unique 1971 fourth fundamental element is not established to the same standard.

Vongehr and Meng correctly exposed the gap between an ideal charge-controlled memristor and real material systems with several hidden, stochastic state variables. Their critique does not invalidate memristive computing; it limits what may be inferred from the term “memristor.”

The benchmark record supports a middle position. Memristive and RRAM hardware can reach useful accuracy—over 96% MNIST in a 2020 full-hardware CNN, 99.0% MNIST and 85.7% CIFAR-10 in 2022 NeuRRAM, and 93.7% CIFAR-10 in device-mapped PCM—but these results arose from hybrid device–circuit–algorithm co-design. The demonstrated advantage is best described as **efficient in-memory analog computation with compact nonvolatile weights**, not as proof that a theoretically fundamental memristor supplies a uniquely superior form of synaptic plasticity.

Compare how three specific crossbar array implementations—Knowm's AHaH nodes, the University of Michigan's Ag/Si memristive system, and RRAM-based approaches from KAIST—address the sneak path problem and device variability issues documented in their respective IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices publications.
