final.content:
RESPONDEAT SUPERIOR ANALYSIS

Conclusion

Assuming the courier negligently caused the June 8, 2024 collision, the company should not receive summary judgment on the pedestrian’s respondeat superior claim. The evidence would permit—and likely strongly support—a finding that the courier was an employee under the common-law control test despite the independent-contractor agreement, personal vehicle, scheduling freedom, and occasional use of his son. The app dictated routes, fixed prices, imposed delivery quotas, threatened account standing over acceptance rates, and automatically suspended couriers who rejected more than two consecutive offers. Those mechanisms constitute substantial practical control over how the delivery work was performed.

Scope of employment and employer benefit are substantially clearer. The accident occurred while the courier was rushing to complete an accepted delivery, during a company-created surge-pricing period, while three deliveries behind quota. He was performing the company’s core delivery service and acting to generate company revenue, not pursuing an independent personal objective. Thus, if employee status is found, scope and benefit would ordinarily be established as a matter of law.

Because the classification evidence is mixed, however, a court applying the traditional multifactor test would most prudently deny both the company’s request for judgment that the courier was an independent contractor and any plaintiff request for a final liability judgment based solely on employee status. It could grant partial summary judgment that the courier was acting within the scope of the delivery assignment and serving the company’s interests, leaving employee status, negligence, causation, and damages for trial. In a jurisdiction giving exceptional weight to actual algorithmic control, the court could instead find employee status for the pedestrian as a matter of law.

This conclusion is necessarily jurisdiction-qualified. Respondeat superior is principally state law, and states differ in their tests and in any statutory treatment of app-based couriers. Cornell’s summary notes expressly that there is no single national respondeat-superior standard (https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/respondeat_superior).

I. Governing law

Respondeat superior ordinarily makes an employer vicariously liable for an employee’s tort committed within the scope of employment. It generally does not apply to a true independent contractor (https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/respondeat_superior).

Under the general common-law test, the central consideration is the hiring party’s right to control the “manner and means” of the work. Other considerations include:

* skill required;
* source of tools and instrumentalities;
* location of work;
* duration of the relationship;
* the principal’s power to assign work;
* the worker’s discretion over when and how long to work;
* method of payment;
* the worker’s role in hiring and paying assistants;
* whether the work forms part of the principal’s regular business;
* employee benefits and tax treatment; and
* the parties’ expressed understanding.

No single factor is dispositive; all incidents of the relationship must be weighed. Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co. v. Darden, 503 U.S. 318, 323–24 (1992), reproduces this framework and rejects any “shorthand formula or magic phrase” (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/503/318).

For scope of employment, Restatement (Third) of Agency § 7.07 provides that an employee acts within scope when performing assigned work or engaging in conduct subject to the employer’s control. Conduct is outside scope when it is an independent course of conduct not intended to serve any employer purpose (https://opencasebook.org/casebooks/16481-selected-excerpts-of-restatement-of-agency-third-professor-randle-pollard/as-printable-html/). A traditional formulation similarly asks whether the conduct was of the kind employed to perform, occurred substantially within authorized time and space, and was motivated at least partly by a purpose to serve the employer. Carter v. Reynolds applies that formulation (https://law.justia.com/cases/new-jersey/supreme-court/2003/a-104-01-opn.html).

At summary judgment, the court does not weigh competing evidence. A genuine dispute exists when a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party; judgment is appropriate only when the evidence is so one-sided that one party must prevail as a matter of law. Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 248–52 (1986) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/477/242).

II. Employee status under the control test

A. Factors supporting employee status

1. Algorithmic control over acceptance of work

The courier nominally could accept or reject orders, but the app automatically suspended anyone who declined more than two consecutive offers. In practical terms, a courier could reject the first and second consecutive offer, but the third consecutive rejection triggered suspension. Automated emails also warned that acceptance rates affected account standing.

That is evidence of a right to discipline or discharge workers for noncompliance, one of the strongest traditional indicators of control. Although the company did not verbally direct the courier, an algorithm can exercise the same practical authority by conditioning continued access to work on accepting assignments.

The formal right to set one’s own schedule therefore does not establish unfettered independence. The courier could decide when to log on, but while logged on he faced meaningful sanctions for refusing assignments. A jury could regard that arrangement as control over the availability, sequence, and volume of work rather than merely control over the final delivery result.

Matter of Vega is particularly persuasive by analogy. The New York Court of Appeals upheld employee status for Postmates couriers even though they decided when to log in and which jobs to accept. Relevant indicators included the platform’s control over assignments, fixed compensation, inability to negotiate fees, and the courier’s integral role in the delivery business (https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2020/2020_02094.htm). Vega concerned unemployment insurance rather than tort liability, so it is not automatically controlling, but it demonstrates that scheduling freedom does not negate employment where the platform retains operational control.

2. App-mandated routes

The platform dictated the route to be followed. Route control reaches the “manner and means” of driving—the very conduct that created the risk to the pedestrian. It is more probative than quality-control rules concerned only with the completed result.

The distinction is important when compared with Black v. Shaffer, an Indiana DoorDash decision affirming summary judgment for the platform. There, the agreement gave the courier control over pickup, delivery, and route selection; she could freely reject opportunities; and DoorDash did not require particular clothing or logos. The driver supplied her equipment and insurance and was paid per delivery (https://public.courts.in.gov/Decisions/api/Document/Opinion?Id=LR7wvSjjR-pLjAwRgxOIfFiQAGbpzBC6_-NGumuVv1LMcbmU1a63Ywnv7QBPetgA0). Here, by contrast, the app mandated routes, constrained rejection through automatic suspension, and reinforced acceptance requirements with account-standing warnings. Those factual differences substantially weaken the company’s reliance on Black.

3. Quotas, surge pricing, and pressure to hurry

At the time of the accident, the courier was three deliveries behind quota and rushing during a surge-pricing period. A delivery quota is evidence that the company controlled expected productivity and timing. Surge pricing and automated warnings supplied additional incentives to accept and complete deliveries quickly.

The company can argue that incentives concern the desired result—prompt delivery—rather than the safe details of driving. But viewed together with mandatory routes and suspension for rejecting offers, the quota permits an inference of continuous operational supervision. The evidence also connects the company’s control directly to the alleged negligent conduct: rushing while driving.

The numerical circumstances reinforce that inference:

* The courier worked 55 hours per week.
* That is 55 ÷ 40 = 1.375, or 137.5% of a conventional 40-hour workweek.
* It is 15 hours above 40, although overtime law is not itself at issue.
* Being three deliveries behind quota supplied a specific performance deficit at the time of the collision.
* The suspension rule made the third consecutive rejection the operative sanction point.

Hours alone do not establish employment because he selected them himself, but 55 hours weekly is consistent with a sustained working relationship rather than sporadic entrepreneurial contracting.

4. No pricing discretion

The courier could not negotiate the price charged to customers or his compensation for particular deliveries. Lack of pricing discretion suggests that he was not operating an independent delivery enterprise offering services at market-negotiated rates. It parallels Vega, where nonnegotiable delivery fees and courier compensation supported employee status.

5. Delivery was the company’s regular business

Food delivery was not peripheral maintenance or an occasional specialized project; it was the service the platform sold to customers. The courier’s work was therefore integral to the company’s ordinary business. Darden identifies whether the work is part of the hiring party’s regular business as an express factor (https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/503/318).

6. Company-branded gear

Company branding suggests integration into the enterprise and creates the public appearance that the courier represents the company. FedEx delivery drivers were held employees under a right-to-control test where, among other things, they wore company uniforms and followed company requirements concerning deliveries. The contractual “independent contractor” label did not conclusively control. Alexander v. FedEx Ground Package System, Inc., 765 F.3d 981 (9th Cir. 2014) (https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/12-17458/12-17458-2014-08-27.html).

The weight of this fact depends on whether the platform required the gear. The stipulated facts say the courier wore branded gear, not expressly that the company mandated it. Voluntary branding carries less weight than a uniform requirement, but it still supports integration and apparent affiliation.

7. Safety onboarding

The onboarding checklist references completion of safety protocols. Required safety instruction can show control over methods, especially where safe vehicle operation is central to the work. Its weight is uncertain because the detailed training records were lost.

B. Factors supporting independent-contractor status

1. Personal vehicle and expenses

The courier supplied his own vehicle and was contractually responsible for liability insurance. Provision of the central instrumentality of work usually favors independent-contractor status. He presumably also bore fuel, maintenance, depreciation, and ordinary operating expenses, although those facts are not expressly stated.

This factor is meaningful but not conclusive. A personal vehicle does not prevent scope-of-employment liability where its use furthers the employer’s business and is contemplated by the work. Carter recognizes exceptions to the ordinary personal-vehicle commuting rule when the vehicle is required for work-related tasks or the trip serves both employer and personal purposes (https://law.justia.com/cases/new-jersey/supreme-court/2003/a-104-01-opn.html). This was not an ordinary commute; the vehicle was actively being used to make the assigned delivery.

2. Schedule autonomy

The courier chose when to work. Under Darden, discretion over when and how long to work favors independent-contractor status. Nevertheless, its weight is reduced by the acceptance-rate rules that constrained the courier after logging in and by his sustained 55-hour workweek.

3. Contractual classification

The agreement denominated the relationship as independent contracting or prohibited employee status. That establishes the parties’ formal expression of intent and favors the company, but it cannot override the practical relationship. Darden requires assessment of all circumstances, not reliance on a contractual phrase. Alexander likewise treated FedEx’s independent-contractor label as nonconclusive.

4. Insurance obligation

Requiring the courier to procure liability insurance shifts a traditional business expense and accident risk to him, favoring contractor status. But contractual risk allocation does not itself determine whether the company retained the right to control his physical performance.

5. Hiring and paying an assistant

The courier occasionally hired his teenage son to help with large orders and paid him directly rather than through the platform. Darden specifically treats the worker’s role in hiring and paying assistants as relevant. This is significant evidence of entrepreneurial discretion.

Its force is limited by its occasional nature and by the possibility that it contravened the platform agreement. If the company prohibited employees or unauthorized helpers, the son’s assistance would be a contractual violation rather than proof that the platform affirmatively granted a right to build an independent delivery business. If the platform knowingly permitted the practice, it would more strongly support contractor status.

6. Payment by delivery

Although the precise compensation arrangement is not fully stated, the references to orders and surge pricing suggest payment by delivery rather than by hour or salary. Job-based payment generally favors independent contracting. The absence of pricing discretion, however, cuts the other way.

C. Overall classification assessment

The evidence is materially stronger for employee status than in an ordinary app-courier case based only on scheduling flexibility and per-delivery payment. Most importantly, the platform controlled three aspects directly related to performance:

1. which assignments the courier could realistically refuse;
2. which routes he had to drive; and
3. the pace expected through quotas, surge incentives, and account warnings.

The right to control need not be exercised by a human supervisor. Automatic suspension and app-mandated routing are practical methods of directing and disciplining performance.

The company nevertheless has substantial contrary evidence: personal vehicle, personal insurance obligation, self-selected hours, contractual classification, probable per-job compensation, and direct hiring and payment of an assistant. Under Darden’s admonition that no factor is decisive, a reasonable jury could weigh those circumstances differently.

Accordingly, the best general-law summary-judgment ruling is:

* deny the company’s motion for summary judgment on the theory that the courier was necessarily an independent contractor;
* likely deny plaintiff’s motion for complete summary judgment on employee status because the instrumentalities, schedule, contract, insurance, and assistant factors create a triable balance;
* permit a jury to decide classification under appropriate control-test instructions.

A court could find employee status as a matter of law if its jurisdiction treats actual control over routes, assignments, discipline, and pricing as outweighing entrepreneurial formalities. Alexander provides an analogous example of delivery drivers being classified as employees at summary judgment even though they could operate multiple routes and hire helpers. But without a specified jurisdiction, treating classification as a jury question is the more defensible prediction.

III. Scope of employment

If the courier is an employee, the collision was within the scope of employment as a matter of law on the supplied facts.

First, he was performing precisely the work assigned: transporting a food order to the customer.

Second, the accident occurred during an active delivery rather than before logging on, after completing work, or during a personal detour. The “going and coming” limitation therefore does not apply.

Third, the conduct occurred within the operational limits imposed through the app’s route and delivery instructions.

Fourth, rushing or driving negligently does not remove conduct from scope merely because the company did not authorize unsafe driving. Negligent vehicle operation is a foreseeable risk characteristic of delivery work. The relevant question is whether he was engaged in assigned delivery activity, not whether the precise negligent manner of driving was permitted.

Fifth, there is no evidence of a “frolic”—an independent personal course of conduct unrelated to the company. The occasional involvement of the courier’s son has no bearing on the particular collision unless the son was involved in this delivery, which the facts do not indicate.

Scope is therefore not a genuine disputed issue. It is far stronger than cases involving an employee’s personal commute or lunch trip. The courier was actively carrying out the delivery when he struck the pedestrian.

IV. Benefit to the employer

The courier’s conduct directly benefited the company in several ways:

* completing the order fulfilled the service sold to the customer;
* completion generated or preserved delivery and platform revenue;
* prompt delivery supported customer satisfaction and repeat platform use;
* working during surge pricing allowed the company to meet elevated demand; and
* attempting to overcome a three-delivery quota deficit furthered the company’s throughput objectives.

The courier presumably also acted for personal compensation, but mixed motivation does not defeat scope. It is enough that he acted at least partly to serve the employer. There is no plausible evidence that the delivery served only a personal purpose.

The benefit element should consequently be resolved for the pedestrian, subject only to any jurisdiction-specific formulation that subsumes benefit within scope rather than treating it separately.

V. Lapsed insurance

The courier’s policy lapsed two weeks before the collision—approximately 14 days. That lapse has several consequences, none of which eliminates respondeat-superior liability:

1. It may constitute breach of the courier’s contract with the platform.
2. It may leave the courier without personal coverage.
3. It may create contractual indemnity or reimbursement issues between the courier and the company, depending on the agreement and state law.
4. It does not transform an employee into an independent contractor.
5. It does not take an otherwise assigned delivery outside the scope of employment.
6. It does not relieve an employer of vicarious liability to an injured third party.

Indeed, if the platform monitored insurance compliance but allowed the courier to remain active after lapse, that could potentially support a separate direct-negligence theory. The facts do not establish whether the company knew or should have known of the lapse, however, and direct negligent hiring, retention, or supervision is analytically distinct from the requested respondeat-superior determination.

VI. Missing training records

The lost training records do not automatically establish either employee status or company negligence. The onboarding checklist is affirmative evidence that safety onboarding was completed, while the missing detailed records prevent either side from establishing the content, quality, or enforcement of those protocols.

If the records were electronically stored, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) would require findings that:

* the information should have been preserved in anticipation or conduct of litigation;
* the company failed to take reasonable preservation steps;
* it cannot be restored or replaced; and
* its loss prejudiced the opposing party.

Curative measures may address prejudice, but an adverse inference that the records were unfavorable generally requires intent to deprive, not merely a routine or negligent migration loss (discussion and text of Rule 37(e): https://judicialstudies.duke.edu/sites/default/files/centers/judicialstudies/judicature/may2017_rule37.pdf).

The present facts show loss during a system migration but do not specify:

* when the migration occurred;
* whether litigation was then reasonably foreseeable;
* whether backup copies exist;
* what preservation steps were taken; or
* whether the company intended to deprive the pedestrian of evidence.

Accordingly, no adverse inference should be imposed on the current record. The loss may justify further discovery and, if preservation duties and prejudice are established, proportionate curative relief. It does not warrant summary judgment by itself.

For classification, the checklist modestly supports employee status if it reflects mandatory training about how to perform deliveries safely. For direct negligence, its evidentiary significance remains unresolved. Respondeat superior itself does not require proof that the company trained the courier negligently; it imputes an employee’s negligence within scope regardless of the employer’s own fault.

VII. Injury, negligence, and damages

A fractured ankle requiring surgery is a legally cognizable physical injury with foreseeable categories of damages, including medical expenses, lost earnings or earning capacity, pain and suffering, rehabilitation, and any permanent impairment. No dollar calculation is possible from the provided facts because there are no medical bills, wage records, impairment ratings, or prognosis.

Vicarious liability also presupposes an underlying tort by the courier. “Collided while rushing” supports an inference of negligent speed, lookout, yielding, or vehicle control, but it does not conclusively establish breach or causation. The parties would still need evidence concerning right of way, speed, traffic controls, pedestrian conduct, and medical causation. Comparative negligence could reduce recovery in many jurisdictions.

Thus, even if employee status, scope, and benefit were all established, a final damages judgment would be premature unless negligence, causation, comparative fault, and damages were undisputed.

VIII. Recommended summary-judgment disposition

The court should enter the following disposition under the general common-law approach:

1. Company’s motion on independent-contractor status: Denied. Mandatory routes, fixed prices, quotas, acceptance-rate discipline, automatic suspension, automated warnings, integration into the delivery business, and branding permit a reasonable jury to find an employment relationship.

2. Pedestrian’s motion on employee status: Ordinarily denied because personal instrumentalities, scheduling choice, insurance responsibility, contractual language, probable per-delivery payment, and direct payment of an assistant supply meaningful contrary evidence. In a jurisdiction emphasizing actual operational control, employee status could instead be entered for the pedestrian as a matter of law.

3. Scope of employment: Partial summary judgment for the pedestrian is appropriate. The courier was actively performing an accepted delivery on the platform’s mandated route; there is no evidence of a personal detour.

4. Benefit to employer: Partial summary judgment for the pedestrian is appropriate. Completion furthered the platform’s core service, revenue, surge-demand response, and quota objectives.

5. Insurance lapse: It does not bar vicarious liability. It concerns coverage, contractual breach, and possible indemnity, not whether the delivery served the company.

6. Missing training records: No automatic adverse inference or summary judgment. The court should first determine preservation duty, reasonable steps, replaceability, prejudice, and—before any adverse inference—intent to deprive.

7. Ultimate liability and damages: Reserved for trial unless the courier’s negligence and causation are separately undisputed.

Overall, the platform faces a substantial vicarious-liability risk. Its strongest defense is the courier’s ownership of the vehicle, contractual status, schedule flexibility, insurance responsibility, and ability to hire his son. Its central weakness is that those formal indicia of independence conflict with powerful evidence of actual algorithmic control over assignments, routes, pricing, productivity, and continued access to work. On this record, the company cannot establish nonliability as a matter of law.

# Feminist Legal Theory Across Legal Traditions: Property, Bodily Autonomy, and Political Power

## Executive summary

Feminist legal theory has not followed a single path from exclusion to equality. It has developed in response to four different configurations of law and power:

1. **Anglo-American critical legal feminism** challenges liberal law’s claim to neutrality. Catharine MacKinnon argues that apparently neutral rules reproduce male dominance, especially in sexuality and violence; Martha Fineman shifts the critique from sex classification to universal vulnerability, dependency, care, and the state’s responsibility for social institutions.

2. **Islamic feminism** distinguishes divine Sharia from fallible, historically produced *fiqh*. Ziba Mir-Hosseini exposes family law as a human juristic construction rather than an immutable divine command, while Amina Wadud rereads the Qur’an through gender, reciprocity, justice, and women’s moral agency. Reform therefore proceeds through reinterpretation, *ijtihad*, constitutional law, and transnational human-rights advocacy—not simply through rejecting religion.

3. **African feminist jurisprudence** addresses legal pluralism: constitutions, statutes, colonial common or civil law, customary law, and sometimes Islamic law coexist. Its central insight is that neither “custom” nor “universal human rights” is neutral. Official customary law was often frozen and patriarchalized through colonial codification, yet abstract individual-rights models can ignore women’s social membership, communal tenure, poverty, and dependence on local institutions. The preferred strategy is often to reconstruct “living” custom while grounding it in substantive equality.

4. **Chinese feminist legal scholarship** navigates a party-state that simultaneously sponsored women’s emancipation, subordinated feminism to socialist development, and now regulates gender in a market economy. State-socialist law attacked arranged marriage and formalized equal family rights, but marketization has exposed women to employment discrimination, unequal housing and rural land allocation, and revived familial norms. Feminists work both within institutions such as the All-China Women’s Federation and through rights-based advocacy, but autonomous organizing remains politically constrained.

Across all four traditions, the key division is not simply religious versus secular or Western versus non-Western. It is between **formal equality** and **substantive power**. Property rights depend on registration, marital and inheritance rules, land institutions, and unpaid care; bodily autonomy depends on who defines consent, sexuality, reproduction, and family authority; political participation depends not only on voting rights but on access to lawmaking, interpretation, religious authority, customary institutions, and the state itself.

---

## 1. Anglo-American critical legal feminism

### From coverture and formal equality to a critique of legal neutrality

Anglo-American feminist law reform initially targeted explicit civil disabilities. English coverture treated a married woman’s legal personality as absorbed into her husband’s. Section 1 of the UK Married Women’s Property Act 1882 made a married woman capable of acquiring, holding, and disposing of property, contracting, and suing as if she were unmarried (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/Vict/45-46/75/enacted?view=plain).

Twentieth-century reform then emphasized equal protection, antidiscrimination, equal pay, and facially gender-neutral family and property rules. Critical legal feminists argued that removing sex classifications did not remove the social hierarchy behind them.

### MacKinnon: from “difference” to dominance

Catharine MacKinnon’s central intervention was to reject the usual equality question—whether women are the same as or different from men. Both alternatives take male experience as the legal norm: women receive equal treatment when they resemble men and “special” treatment when their socially produced difference is recognized.

Her **dominance approach** asks instead whether a rule or institution participates in women’s subordination. Gender is not merely a biological distinction that law happens to regulate; it is a hierarchy constituted through sexuality, coercion, work, representation, and state power. MacKinnon applies this analysis to rape, sexual harassment, pornography, abortion, and sex discrimination in *Toward a Feminist Theory of the State* (https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674896468). Her “Difference and Dominance” formulation describes equality as the antithesis of hierarchy, rather than identical treatment of already unequal groups (https://faculty.gvsu.edu/walhofd/mackinnon.pdf).

This approach transformed sexual harassment from private misconduct into sex discrimination: conduct organized around unequal sexual power could impair women’s employment and citizenship even if conventional law did not recognize a physical injury or explicit discriminatory rule.

### Fineman: vulnerability, dependency, and the family

Martha Fineman extends the critique of the autonomous liberal subject. Formal equality assumes independent individuals who bargain and compete on equal terms. But all people are embodied and vulnerable, while childhood, illness, disability, aging, and care create inevitable dependency. Institutions distribute the resources needed to withstand that vulnerability very unequally.

Fineman’s family-law analysis shows why gender-neutral divorce, custody, and marital-property rules can preserve inequality. A marriage may formally be a partnership of equals, yet women’s lower earnings and disproportionate care work weaken their bargaining position during marriage and after divorce. Her alternative is a **responsive state** that scrutinizes how families, workplaces, markets, welfare systems, and property institutions allocate resilience (https://scholarlycommons.law.emory.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1063&context=faculty-articles). Her dependency analysis also argues that care is socially necessary work whose costs have been disproportionately privatized onto women (https://scholarlycommons.law.emory.edu/faculty-articles/319/).

MacKinnon and Fineman therefore differ in emphasis:

- MacKinnon centers **sexualized dominance and women’s group subordination**.
- Fineman centers **universal vulnerability, dependency, care, and institutional responsibility**.

Both reject the proposition that formally neutral law is necessarily just.

### Rights in practice

**Property.** Women now generally possess independent legal capacity, but substantive outcomes depend on divorce law, title, inheritance, credit, wages, and recognition of care. Separate-property rules may protect independence yet disadvantage a caregiver when major assets are titled to the higher-earning spouse; equal division may also obscure unequal post-divorce earning capacity.

**Bodily autonomy.** Liberal constitutionalism has often located reproductive freedom in privacy or liberty, while dominance feminism asks who controls sexuality and reproduction. The fragility of privacy-based protection became clear in *Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization* (2022), which held that the US Constitution does not confer a right to abortion and returned regulation to legislatures (https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/19-1392_6j37.pdf). Consequently, bodily autonomy now varies sharply by US state. This illustrates MacKinnon’s concern that the public/private distinction can conceal state enforcement of gendered power.

**Political participation.** Formal voting and office-holding rights are broadly equal, but campaign finance, party selection, care burdens, violence and harassment, and unequal economic resources structure who can participate. Anglo-American feminism consequently moved from suffrage to substantive representation and to scrutiny of which experiences count as legally cognizable.

---

## 2. Islamic feminism and the reinterpretation of Sharia

### Sharia is not identical to *fiqh*

Islamic legal feminism emerged partly in response to a false choice between secular feminism and supposedly immutable religious law. Mir-Hosseini’s crucial distinction is:

- **Sharia**: in Muslim belief, the divine path and ethical ideal;
- **Fiqh**: human efforts to understand and derive rules from the Qur’an and Sunna.

Sharia is sacred; *fiqh* is historical, local, plural, and fallible. Treating a patriarchal juristic interpretation as divine conceals the human authority that produced it. Mir-Hosseini therefore argues that gender-unequal family laws can be challenged from within Islamic legal reasoning, especially because marriage and family relations belong to *mu‘amalat*—social transactions open to reason, changing circumstances, and *ijtihad* (https://arabic.musawah.org/sites/default/files/Wanted-ZMH-EN.pdf).

Modern Muslim states often displaced classical jurisprudence in commercial and public law but retained and codified selected *fiqh* rules in personal-status law. Codification gave historically contested opinions the coercive force of a centralized state. The result is frequently a hybrid system rather than simply “traditional Sharia.”

### Marriage, property, and the patriarchal exchange model

Mir-Hosseini reconstructs the classical juristic model of marriage as an exchange organized around:

- the husband’s entitlement to sexual access and the wife’s *tamkin* or obedience;
- the husband’s duty of *nafaqa*, or maintenance;
- payment of *mahr*, or dower;
- greater male access to polygyny and unilateral *talaq*;
- more restricted female routes to divorce.

Importantly, classical Islamic marriage did not automatically merge the spouses’ estates. The wife retained ownership of her dower, prior property, and earnings and was not ordinarily legally obliged to perform unpaid housework. Yet the same system placed matrimonial resources largely under the husband’s control and linked maintenance to obedience. Thus, **formal separate property could coexist with economic and sexual subordination** (https://arabic.musawah.org/sites/default/files/Wanted-ZMH-EN.pdf).

Islamic feminist reform does not merely demand that women become economically identical to men. It challenges the reciprocal bargain—male provision in exchange for female obedience—as inconsistent with contemporary justice, shared responsibility, and women’s full legal agency.

### Wadud: gender-conscious Qur’anic interpretation

Amina Wadud employs Qur’anic sciences but “reads for gender”: she examines whether an interpretation universalizes the patriarchal conventions of its historical setting or moves toward broader principles of justice, dignity, and spiritual equality. Women, in her account, are *khalifa*—moral agents—not derivative beings whose purpose is obedience to men.

Wadud stresses that the Qur’an and Sunna are not rewritten, but all human interpretation and application are open to criticism. An interpretation’s consequences for actual human beings matter. She also links theological interpretation to political and religious participation: because the Qur’an does not reserve moral or ritual authority exclusively to men, male-only leadership is a human institutional construction, not an uncontestable divine rule (https://www.oasiscenter.eu/en/without-women-you-cannot-understand-the-quran).

### Reform within modern states

The 2004 Moroccan Family Code illustrates this hybrid method. Its preamble expressly invokes justice, equality, *ijtihad*, contemporary development, Sharia, and internationally recognized human rights (https://learningpartnership.org/sites/default/files/resources/pdfs/Morocco%20Family%20Code%20%28Moudawan%29%202004%20English.pdf). Reform was therefore framed neither as abandoning Islam nor as mechanically applying classical doctrine.

But outcomes vary enormously among Muslim-majority states. “Islamic law” is not a single legal system: constitutional structures, schools of jurisprudence, legislation, judicial practice, colonial histories, and political regimes differ. Iran, for example, constitutionally guarantees rights subject to “Islamic criteria,” while personal-status rules continue to privilege men in divorce and other family matters; a UN report notes that men may divorce unilaterally while women face demanding evidentiary requirements (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/hrbodies/hrcouncil/sessions-regular/session58/advance-version/a-hrc-58-62-aev-1.pdf).

### Rights in practice

**Property.** Women may possess independent property and dower, but inheritance shares, maintenance rules, marital title, divorce, and access to employment determine effective control. Islamic feminists therefore challenge both discriminatory rules and the assumption that a male breadwinner reliably compensates women for unequal inheritance or family authority.

**Bodily autonomy.** The key contest concerns whether marriage grants a husband control over sex, movement, employment, dress, fertility, or divorce. Islamic feminism replaces obedience and sexual availability with consent, reciprocity, dignity, and shared moral agency.

**Political participation.** Women’s citizenship may be formally recognized while religious interpretation, clerical office, family authority, or eligibility for high office remains gendered. Wadud’s female religious leadership makes interpretive authority itself a field of political participation. Musawah and related movements combine Islamic argument, constitutional equality, lived experience, and CEDAW rather than treating these sources as mutually exclusive.

---

## 3. African feminism, customary law, and human rights

### The problem of legal pluralism

There is no unitary “African legal tradition.” Most African states contain several overlapping normative orders:

- constitutional and statutory law;
- colonial common or civil law;
- customary law, both official and “living”;
- religious law in some jurisdictions;
- regional and international human-rights law.

Women may encounter different rules depending on marriage form, locality, ethnicity, religion, land tenure, or the forum hearing a dispute. Customary law often governs the matters most consequential for women—marriage, divorce, lineage, land, inheritance, widowhood, and traditional authority.

African feminist scholars reject two simplifications. First, patriarchal practices cannot be insulated from criticism merely by calling them culture. Second, customary law should not be treated as an ancient, uniform code. Colonial administrators and male traditional authorities often converted flexible social practices into rigid “official” rules, privileging male lineage and chiefly authority.

Sylvia Tamale consequently criticizes the simple opposition between “culture” and “rights.” Treating culture as fixed and rights as external can restrict African women’s strategies and reinforce the patriarchs who claim exclusive authority to define tradition (https://philpapers.org/rec/TAMTRT). Her broader work emphasizes how statutory law, religion, and reinterpreted custom jointly regulate sexuality, while social movements create forms of sexual citizenship (https://www.ahrlj.up.ac.za/tamale-s).

### Universalism, relativism, and substantive participation

International human rights supply indispensable equality standards, but African feminism questions frameworks that imagine an isolated, property-owning individual detached from kinship, communal land, care, and material scarcity. Conversely, cultural relativism can leave women trapped between submitting to discriminatory community rules and losing the social benefits of community membership.

The alternative is not weaker rights. It is a **contextual, participatory and pluralist universalism**:

- preserve the non-negotiable principles of dignity, equality, and freedom from violence;
- investigate how customary law actually operates rather than relying only on colonial texts;
- give women authority inside customary and traditional institutions;
- consider social and economic conditions needed to exercise a formal right;
- allow custom to evolve under constitutional dialogue rather than either immunizing or abolishing it wholesale.

### Property and “living” customary law

The South African cases show both the promise and limits of constitutional intervention.

In **Bhe**, male primogeniture and statutory “Black law and custom” excluded daughters from intestate inheritance. The Constitutional Court invalidated the discriminatory succession regime. The underlying proceedings showed that Ms Bhe’s daughters could not inherit their deceased father’s estate under the existing rules (https://www.wlce.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/Bhe-constitutional-court-judgment.pdf).

In **Gumede**, the Constitutional Court confronted rules under which women in older customary marriages lacked equal control of family property. It emphasized that customary law exists within a plural constitutional order and noted historical evidence that women had possessed significant rights to arable and household land before later codifications distorted practice (https://www.saflii.org/za/cases/ZACC/2008/23.html).

These decisions demonstrate the distinction between:

- **official customary law**, recorded and enforced through colonial or apartheid institutions; and
- **living customary law**, changing through community practice.

Yet “living law” is not automatically egalitarian: powerful local men may dominate evidence about what community practice is. Women therefore need representation, legal aid, accessible forums, and a voice in defining custom.

### The Maputo Protocol: an African regional synthesis

The 2003 Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Women in Africa—the Maputo Protocol—goes beyond a narrow nondiscrimination model:

- Article 9 requires positive action and increased effective representation in political decision-making.
- Article 14 recognizes sexual and reproductive health, including control over fertility, decisions about whether and when to have children, contraception, and family-planning information.
- Article 21 guarantees widows an equitable inheritance share and women and men equitable shares in parental property (https://africanlii.org/en/akn/aa-au/act/protocol/2003/rights-of-women-in-africa/eng@2003-07-11).

The African Commission’s General Comment No. 6 interprets Article 7(d) to require equitable sharing of joint marital property after separation, divorce, or annulment and emphasizes **substantive**, not merely formal, equality (https://africanlii.org/en/akn/aa-au/doc/general-comment/achpr/2020-03/general-comment-no-6-on-the-protocol-to-the-african-charter-on-human-and-peoples-right-on-the-rights-of-women-in-africa-maputo-protocol-the-right-to-property-during-separation-divorce-or-annulment-of-marriage/eng@2020-03-04/source.pdf).

### Rights in practice

**Property.** Women’s access commonly turns on lineage, marital status, widowhood, communal tenure, land-allocation institutions, and representation in traditional governance. Individual title can empower women but can also facilitate dispossession if registration records only male household heads or if land commercialization dismantles use rights without compensation.

**Bodily autonomy.** The field includes reproductive health, sexual violence, harmful practices, marital authority, and colonial-era regulation of sexuality. The Maputo Protocol supplies unusually explicit regional reproductive guarantees, but enforcement depends on domestic incorporation, health infrastructure, courts, and local authority.

**Political participation.** Constitutions often guarantee equal voting rights, while customary leadership and land institutions may remain male dominated. African feminism therefore treats political participation as extending from parliament to village land boards, traditional courts, family councils, and treaty institutions.

---

## 4. Chinese feminist legal thought between state socialism and marketization

### Socialist transformation and “state feminism”

The PRC’s 1950 Marriage Law attacked arranged and compulsory marriage, male superiority, bigamy, concubinage, child betrothal, and interference with widows’ remarriage. It established free choice, monogamy, equal status in the household, equal rights in family property, mutual inheritance, occupational freedom, and access to divorce (https://www.commonprogram.science/documents/the%20marriage%20law.pdf).

This was both emancipatory and state-building. Women’s liberation was tied to socialist production, modernization, and collective political mobilization. Wang Zheng cautions against portraying Chinese women as merely passive beneficiaries of a patriarchal state. Women working through the All-China Women’s Federation helped construct institutions, mobilize women, and press gender claims inside the party-state. By 1953, the Women’s Federation system had more than 40,000 officials above township and street level, indicating substantial institutional capacity even though “women’s work” remained subordinate to the Party’s central priorities (https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/wangzheng/wp-content/uploads/sites/948/2021/09/2005WangZ_22State-Feminism22.pdf).

The resulting concept of **state feminism** is therefore double-sided:

- the socialist state dismantled important patriarchal legal structures and expanded education, work, and public participation;
- it defined the terms of liberation, treated women partly as productive resources, and restricted autonomous feminist organization.

### Market reform and the return of private inequality

Post-1978 marketization shifted welfare and care costs toward households, exposed women to competitive employment discrimination, commercialized housing, and interacted with patrilocal marriage and son preference. Facial neutrality could therefore produce gendered outcomes.

Urban housing is a major example. A 2011 judicial interpretation was widely understood to strengthen the position of the spouse whose name appeared on the housing deed, even where the other spouse or her family had contributed financially. One reported survey found that more than 80% of marital homes were owned or co-owned by men, while only 30% of marital deeds included the woman’s name (https://dissentmagazine.org/article/womens-rights-at-risk/). These figures are survey-specific rather than a national property census, but they illustrate how title-based neutrality can discount informal contributions and unpaid care.

Rural women face a parallel problem. Collective land rights are formally gender-neutral, but village membership rules and marriage practices can strip “married-out” women of land, compensation, or dividends. Research describes how neutral state policy, progressive statutes, and entrenched local practice have together produced gendered land dispossession (https://brill.com/view/journals/clsr/5/1/article-p33_33.xml).

### Contemporary statutory protection—and its political framework

China’s revised Law on the Protection of Rights and Interests of Women, adopted in 2022, is extensive. It:

- declares gender equality a basic national policy;
- guarantees equal political rights, voting, and eligibility for election;
- requires an “appropriate number” of women representatives and gradual increases;
- protects life, bodily integrity, health, and personal liberty;
- prohibits trafficking and sexual harassment;
- requires the woman’s own consent for fertility operations and special medical treatment;
- recognizes the right to bear children and the freedom not to bear children;
- prohibits employment discrimination based on marriage, pregnancy, or maternity;
- guarantees equal property and inheritance rights.

At the same time, Article 3 explicitly places women’s-rights work under Communist Party leadership, preserving a state-centered rather than autonomously organized model (https://en.spp.gov.cn/2022-10/30/c_948416.htm).

This structure creates a recurring tension: feminist lawyers and scholars can use legislation, litigation, policy consultation, Women’s Federation channels, and public-interest advocacy, but the state retains authority over permissible organization and political agendas.

### Political representation: quantitative assessment

Women held 790 seats in the 14th National People’s Congress elected in 2023, reported as 26.5% (https://data.ipu.org/parliament/CN/CN-LC01/election/CN-LC01-E20230305).

The implied chamber size is:

\[
790 \div 0.265 \approx 2,981
\]

Using the approximately 2,980 filled seats, the verification is:

\[
790 \div 2,980 \times 100 \approx 26.51\%
\]

Thus the published 26.5% is internally consistent. But women remained underrepresented relative to population parity: the gap from 50% was approximately:

\[
50.0 - 26.5 = 23.5 \text{ percentage points}
\]

The UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women also observed that, as of October 2022, no woman sat at China’s highest executive level and recommended quotas or parity measures (https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2023/05/un-womens-rights-committee-publishes-findings-china-germany-iceland-sao-tome).

### Rights in practice

**Property.** Socialist law established formal marital equality, but marketization increased the importance of registered title, earnings, rural collective membership, and family wealth transfers. Women may have equal rights in legislation while losing out through deed registration or village decisions.

**Bodily autonomy.** The 2022 law protects medical consent and freedom to bear or not bear children, but reproductive rights remain embedded in state demographic policy. Bodily autonomy is therefore expressed as a protected interest administered by the state rather than an unlimited sphere beyond state planning.

**Political participation.** Women vote and serve in representative institutions, and the Women’s Federation provides institutional access. Yet “appropriate numbers” are not parity, top leadership remains heavily male, and independent feminist mobilization operates within strict political boundaries.

---

## 5. Comparative findings

| Tradition | Principal feminist critique | Property structure | Bodily-autonomy structure | Political-participation structure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Anglo-American | Neutrality, privacy, and sameness/difference conceal dominance and dependency | Independent legal capacity, but title, marital regimes, wages, and unpaid care shape outcomes | Rights framed through privacy, liberty, equality, consent, and freedom from sexual subordination; US abortion protection is now jurisdictionally fragmented | Formal electoral equality, with continuing structural barriers in parties, resources, care, and harassment |
| Islamic feminism | Patriarchal *fiqh* is incorrectly equated with divine Sharia | Separate female property and dower may coexist with unequal inheritance, male maintenance/control, and asymmetric divorce | Contest between obedience/sexual access and consent, reciprocity, dignity, mobility, and reproductive agency | Citizenship intersects with religious interpretation, family authority, clerical institutions, and state constitutional design |
| African feminist jurisprudence | Both colonialized custom and abstract universalism can silence women | Plural tenure and succession systems; lineage, marriage, widowhood, communal land, and local forums are decisive | Constitutional, customary, religious, and regional norms overlap; Maputo provides strong reproductive guarantees | Participation includes parliament and local customary, land, and judicial institutions; positive action is regionally endorsed |
| Chinese feminist legal thought | State-led emancipation can advance equality while monopolizing feminist agency; market neutrality reproduces inequality | Formal equality confronts deed registration, market wealth, rural membership, and local allocation | Statutory consent and reproductive protections remain embedded in party-state demographic and welfare policy | Institutional participation exists without parity or autonomous political pluralism; women were 26.5% of the NPC in 2023 |

---

## Conclusion

The evolution of feminist legal theory across these traditions reveals four different locations of patriarchal power.

- In Anglo-American law, it lies behind the supposedly neutral liberal subject, the public/private divide, and markets that disregard dependency and care.
- In Muslim family law, it lies in the conversion of historically male *fiqh* into allegedly timeless Sharia and then into centralized state codes.
- In African legal pluralism, it lies both in colonial constructions of customary law and in contemporary control over land, lineage, culture, and local institutions.
- In China, it lies in the interaction of socialist state authority, familial patriarchy, market allocation, and restricted autonomous organization.

Accordingly, women’s rights cannot be measured only by whether a legal text says “equal.” Property requires effective control over land, housing, earnings, inheritance, and the value of care. Bodily autonomy requires consent and freedom from violence, but also the power to challenge marital, religious, customary, medical, and demographic authority. Political participation requires more than the vote: it includes the authority to interpret sacred texts, define custom, shape state policy, control local resources, organize independently, and decide which injuries law recognizes.

The broad convergence is toward **substantive equality**, but the routes remain tradition-specific. The most effective feminist jurisprudence neither treats culture and religion as immutable nor assumes that secular, formally neutral law has already overcome hierarchy.
