final.content:
ClearPoint Neuro: Financial Sustainability and Strategic-Transition Assessment

All dollar amounts are in millions unless otherwise indicated.

Executive conclusion

ClearPoint Neuro remained cash-flow negative through September 2024, but its cash-consumption pattern improved materially. Free cash flow for the first nine months of 2024 was approximately negative $7.72 million, while quarterly operating cash burn declined from $3.84 million in Q1 to $2.67 million in Q2 and $1.20 million in Q3. Revenue grew much faster than cash consumption, and the completed manufacturing transition sharply reduced capital spending.

The balance sheet, however, was strengthened primarily through external capital rather than internally generated cash. ClearPoint raised $16.18 million net in March 2024, then used $10 million to repay its convertible note in August. It ended September with $21.57 million of cash and no debt. That provides a meaningful runway, especially if Q3’s lower burn is sustainable, but the company had not yet demonstrated self-funding operations. Future financing needs depend heavily on continued revenue growth, gross-margin expansion, working-capital discipline, and whether management can approach cash-flow break-even before the existing cash cushion erodes.

Commercially, all three reported revenue categories grew in Q3 2024. Capital equipment and software posted the fastest percentage growth at approximately 133%, but from a very small base. Neurosurgery navigation and therapy grew approximately 49%, while biologics and drug delivery—the largest category—grew approximately 27%. The most strategically important momentum is the shift within biologics from comparatively lower-margin preclinical services toward disposable products used as partners advance through clinical trials. Capital-system placements support that model by expanding the installed base, although equipment sales themselves can be lower-margin, irregular and less economically attractive than the recurring disposable stream they enable.

1. Cash flow, burn rate and financial sustainability

Nine-month free cash flow

ClearPoint reported the following cash flows for the nine months ended September 30, 2024:

- Net cash used in operating activities: $(7.707)
- Net cash used in investing activities: $(0.012)
- Investing activity consisted of $0.012 million of property-and-equipment purchases.

The filing’s cash-flow data are available in ClearPoint’s September 2024 Form 10-Q: https://ir.clearpointneuro.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001285550-24-000121/clpt-20240930.htm

Using operating cash flow plus net investing cash flow:

Free cash flow = operating cash flow + investing cash flow

= $(7.707) + $(0.012)

= $(7.719) million

Under the conventional operating-cash-flow-minus-capital-expenditures definition, the result is identical because the only 2024 investing outflow reported was $0.012 million of capital expenditure:

FCF = $(7.707) − $0.012 = $(7.719) million

Thus, ClearPoint consumed approximately $7.72 million of free cash during the first nine months of 2024.

Quarterly operating cash burn

The nine-month average quarterly operating burn was:

$7.707 million ÷ 3 quarters = $2.569 million per quarter

The cumulative filings also show a marked sequential improvement:

- Q1 2024 operating burn: $3.840 million
- First-half 2024 operating burn: $6.508 million
- Implied Q2 burn: $6.508 − $3.840 = $2.668 million
- Nine-month operating burn: $7.707 million
- Implied Q3 burn: $7.707 − $6.508 = $1.199 million

Therefore:

| Period | Operating cash burn |
|---|---:|
| Q1 2024 | $3.840 million |
| Q2 2024, calculated | $2.668 million |
| Q3 2024, calculated | $1.199 million |
| Nine-month quarterly average | $2.569 million |

Sequential changes were:

- Q2 versus Q1: burn declined by $1.172 million, or 30.5%.
- Q3 versus Q2: burn declined by $1.469 million, or 55.1%.
- Q3 versus Q1: burn declined by $2.641 million, or 68.8%.

The prior-year comparison also improved substantially. Operating cash use was $12.551 million in the first nine months of 2023 versus $7.707 million in 2024:

Improvement = $12.551 − $7.707 = $4.844 million

Percentage reduction = $4.844 ÷ $12.551 = 38.6%

This is a favorable cash-generation pattern: ClearPoint was still consuming cash, but each successive 2024 quarter required less operating funding.

Capital efficiency

Several metrics indicate improving capital efficiency:

1. Nine-month revenue increased from $17.145 million in 2023 to $23.619 million in 2024:

Growth = ($23.619 − $17.145) ÷ $17.145 = 37.8%

2. At the same time, nine-month operating cash burn fell 38.6%.

3. Capital expenditure was only $0.012 million during the first nine months of 2024, compared with $0.696 million in the equivalent 2023 period. This indicates that most of the heavy spending associated with the Carlsbad manufacturing transition had already occurred.

4. The nine-month operating loss narrowed from $17.740 million to $14.142 million even as revenue and commercial activity expanded.

Taken together, revenue growth of almost 38%, lower operating cash use and negligible incremental capital expenditure suggest that ClearPoint was beginning to obtain operating leverage from investments made in prior years.

There are important qualifications. ClearPoint still recorded a $13.528 million nine-month net loss, and $5.204 million of share-based compensation helped bridge the difference between accounting loss and operating cash burn. Moreover, Q3’s operating loss was $5.172 million, slightly worse than $4.897 million in Q3 2023, because R&D and commercial investments continued to rise. Cash efficiency is therefore improving faster than GAAP profitability, but the company had not yet reached a durable earnings or cash-flow inflection.

2. March equity financing, August debt repayment and runway

March 2024 equity offering

In March 2024, ClearPoint sold 2,653,848 shares at a public offering price of $6.50 per share, including exercise of the underwriters’ full option. Net proceeds were approximately $16.2 million after discounts, commissions and expenses: https://ir.clearpointneuro.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001285550-24-000051/clpt-20240331.htm

The nine-month cash-flow statement recorded $16.183 million of net offering proceeds.

August 2024 debt repayment

On August 23, 2024, ClearPoint repaid the full $10 million principal amount, plus interest, of its convertible note held by PTC Therapeutics. The note otherwise would have matured in January 2025. Management emphasized that the repayment eliminated debt without issuing additional conversion shares: https://ir.clearpointneuro.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1118/clearpoint-neuro-announces-early-repayment-of-10-million

The main financing cash flows were:

- Net equity proceeds: +$16.183 million
- Convertible-note repayment: $(10.000) million
- Other equity-related flows, net: approximately $(0.031) million
- Net financing cash inflow: +$6.152 million

The cash bridge was:

Beginning cash                                   $23.140  
Operating cash flow                              (7.707)  
Investing cash flow                              (0.012)  
Financing cash flow                               6.152  
Ending cash                                      $21.573

Although cash declined by only $1.567 million from year-end, that modest decline should not be mistaken for internal cash sustainability. It was the net result of an external equity raise offsetting operating burn and debt repayment. Excluding financing cash flows, operations and investing would have reduced cash by $7.719 million. Including the $10 million debt repayment but excluding the equity offering would have left the company with only roughly $5.4 million before the smaller equity-related cash flows.

The equity raise was therefore strategically important: it enabled ClearPoint both to fund operations and remove the near-term debt maturity. The trade-off was shareholder dilution of roughly 2.65 million shares, while the benefit was a debt-free balance sheet, lower financial risk and avoidance of potential note conversion dilution.

Indicative cash runway

At September 30, 2024, ClearPoint held $21.573 million in cash and cash equivalents.

Using the nine-month average operating burn:

$21.573 ÷ $2.569 = 8.4 quarters, or approximately 2.1 years

Using Q3’s lower operating burn:

$21.573 ÷ $1.199 = 18.0 quarters, or approximately 4.5 years

These are mechanical runway estimates, not forecasts. They exclude future capital spending, working-capital volatility, acquisitions, changes in R&D or commercial investment, and any deterioration or improvement in margins. The large difference between the two estimates demonstrates how sensitive financing needs are to whether Q3’s improvement is repeatable.

A reasonable sustainability assessment is therefore:

- Near-term liquidity appeared adequate at September 2024.
- Eliminating the note reduced refinancing risk and future interest obligations.
- Q3’s $1.2 million operating burn materially improved the probability that existing cash could fund the transition.
- Nevertheless, the company was still dependent on cash reserves and had recently required an equity raise.
- Another financing could become necessary if biologics programs are delayed, service revenue remains volatile, product growth slows, or management continues to increase R&D and commercial spending faster than gross profit.
- Conversely, sustained quarterly burn near Q3 levels, continued margin gains and further disposable-product growth could allow ClearPoint to approach self-funding without another near-term raise.

3. Q3 2024 segment revenue growth

ClearPoint’s Q3 revenue by service line was disclosed in its 10-Q: https://ir.clearpointneuro.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/xbrl_doc_only/11088

Biologics and drug delivery

- Q3 2024 revenue: $4.431 million
- Q3 2023 revenue: $3.487 million
- Increase: $0.944 million

Growth = $0.944 ÷ $3.487 = 27.1%

The category’s composition was:

- Disposable products: $2.062 million versus $0.455 million, up $1.607 million or 353.2%.
- Services and license fees: $2.369 million versus $3.032 million, down $0.663 million or 21.9%.

Thus, headline growth of 27% understates the underlying shift toward products. Partner trial progression drove much higher disposable demand, while fewer preclinical studies reduced service revenue.

Neurosurgery navigation and therapy

- Q3 2024 revenue: $2.860 million
- Q3 2023 revenue: $1.918 million
- Increase: $0.942 million

Growth = $0.942 ÷ $1.918 = 49.1%

The increase reflected new-account activation and rollout of products including SmartFrame OR and PRISM laser-therapy disposables.

Capital equipment and software

- Q3 2024 revenue: $0.831 million
- Q3 2023 revenue: $0.357 million
- Increase: $0.474 million

Growth = $0.474 ÷ $0.357 = 132.8%

Within the category:

- Systems and software products rose from $0.081 million to $0.552 million.
- Related service revenue was comparatively stable, increasing from $0.276 million to $0.279 million.

Summary:

| Revenue category | Q3 2024 | Q3 2023 | Increase | YoY growth |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Biologics and drug delivery | $4.431m | $3.487m | $0.944m | 27.1% |
| Neurosurgery navigation and therapy | $2.860m | $1.918m | $0.942m | 49.1% |
| Capital equipment and software | $0.831m | $0.357m | $0.474m | 132.8% |
| Total | $8.122m | $5.762m | $2.360m | 41.0% |

Capital equipment showed the strongest percentage momentum, but it remained only about 10% of quarterly revenue and benefited from an unusually low prior-year comparison. Biologics was the largest category, accounting for approximately 54.6% of Q3 revenue, and contributed almost as much absolute growth as navigation and therapy. The most economically meaningful momentum was arguably the 353% expansion in biologics disposables because those products can recur as pharmaceutical partners progress through clinical and potentially commercial treatment volumes.

4. Gross-margin changes

Q3 2024 versus Q3 2023

The relevant results were:

- Q3 2024 revenue: $8.122 million
- Q3 2024 gross profit: $4.847 million
- Q3 2023 revenue: $5.762 million
- Q3 2023 gross profit: $3.273 million

Calculated margins:

Q3 2024 gross margin = $4.847 ÷ $8.122 = 59.68%

Q3 2023 gross margin = $3.273 ÷ $5.762 = 56.80%

Change = 59.68% − 56.80% = +2.88 percentage points

Rounded as reported, gross margin increased from 57% to 60%, or approximately three percentage points. The company attributed the improvement primarily to higher volume and lower costs following the 2023 manufacturing-facility transition. Q3 results and that explanation were reported here: https://www.nasdaq.com/press-release/clearpoint-neuro-reports-third-quarter-2024-results-2024-11-07

Six months ended June 30, 2023 versus 2022

The six-month results were:

- First-half 2023 revenue: $11.383 million
- First-half 2023 gross profit: $6.328 million
- First-half 2022 revenue: $10.231 million
- First-half 2022 gross profit: $6.485 million

Source: https://ir.clearpointneuro.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/xbrl_doc_only/10863

Calculated margins:

First-half 2023 gross margin = $6.328 ÷ $11.383 = 55.59%

First-half 2022 gross margin = $6.485 ÷ $10.231 = 63.39%

Change = 55.59% − 63.39% = −7.80 percentage points

Therefore, gross margin fell by approximately 7.8 percentage points in the 2023 six-month period, despite revenue increasing by approximately 11.3%. Gross profit itself declined by $0.157 million.

Management attributed the 2023 compression to two principal factors:

- A greater mix of biologics and drug-delivery preclinical services, which initially had lower margins than product sales.
- Incremental costs related to the transition to the new Carlsbad manufacturing facility.

That explanation is contained in ClearPoint’s Q2 2023 results: https://ir.clearpointneuro.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1094/clearpoint-neuro-reports-second-quarter-2023-results

The subsequent recovery from a roughly 56% first-half 2023 margin to approximately 60% in Q3 2024 suggests that the earlier compression was at least partly transitional rather than a permanent deterioration in unit economics.

5. Strategic interpretation of segment divergence

Biologics and drug delivery: strategic core with changing economics

Biologics and drug delivery is ClearPoint’s largest growth opportunity and represented more than half of Q3 revenue. The company reported relationships with more than 50 biologics and drug-delivery customers at varying stages from preclinical work to late-stage regulatory trials. Its role includes protocol design, preclinical execution, device co-development and supply of products used to deliver therapies directly into the central nervous system.

The Q3 mix shift is particularly important:

- Services declined about 22%.
- Disposable-product revenue increased about 353%.
- Overall biologics revenue still grew 27%.

Preclinical service revenue can be project-driven, labor-intensive and uneven. In contrast, disposable demand linked to active clinical trials—and eventually approved therapies—can be more repeatable and scalable. The 2023 margin compression showed the cost of building the service platform, while Q3 2024 showed the potential payoff as partners moved toward product-consuming stages.

The principal risk is that ClearPoint does not control pharmaceutical partners’ clinical timelines, regulatory approvals or commercial success. Consequently, biologics revenue can remain volatile even if the long-term opportunity is large.

Capital equipment and software: fast growth, but an enabling category

Capital equipment grew 133%, the fastest rate of the three categories, but from only $0.357 million. Such sales are inherently more episodic because system placements depend on hospital budgets, installations and product-launch timing.

Capital equipment’s strategic value is larger than its direct revenue contribution. A new navigation or laser-system placement can:

- Activate a new treatment center.
- Support recurring navigation, therapy and biologics procedures.
- Generate future disposable-product demand.
- Broaden ClearPoint’s presence beyond MRI navigation into operating-room and laser-therapy applications.

The economic distinction is therefore between the placement and the downstream annuity. A strong capital-equipment quarter can establish future procedure capacity but may not immediately maximize gross margin. Management indicated that some equipment components carry little profit and are necessary primarily to enable procedures. The higher-value opportunity lies in increasing utilization and recurring disposable throughput.

What the divergence reveals

The contrast between the two businesses suggests that ClearPoint is evolving toward a platform model:

- Biologics and drug-delivery services establish deep pharmaceutical relationships and embed ClearPoint’s devices into therapy-development programs.
- Capital systems expand the installed clinical infrastructure.
- Navigation, therapy and biologics disposables monetize increasing procedure and trial volumes.
- Software, services and regulatory expertise make the platform harder for partners to replace.

Capital-equipment growth is therefore supportive rather than contradictory to the biologics transition. The equipment segment creates access points, while biologics relationships and recurring disposables provide the potentially larger and more defensible long-term revenue stream.

6. Manufacturing transition, scalability and profitability

ClearPoint leased an approximately 19,462-square-foot Carlsbad facility for office and manufacturing use. The lease began June 1, 2023 and runs through May 31, 2033. The prior Irvine manufacturing lease was terminated effective October 2023. Details are in the company’s filings: https://ir.clearpointneuro.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001285550-24-000121/clpt-20240930.htm

The transition affected results in two stages.

Initial negative effect

During 2023, qualification, clean-room construction, duplicated operations and transition expenses increased cost of revenue. At the same time, ClearPoint was adding lower-margin preclinical services. This combination caused first-half gross margin to fall from 63.4% in 2022 to 55.6% in 2023.

Subsequent scaling benefit

By Q3 2024:

- The transition was substantially complete.
- Capital expenditure had fallen to almost zero.
- Product revenue more than doubled year over year.
- Higher factory throughput spread fixed manufacturing overhead over more units.
- Gross margin recovered to approximately 60%.

This is evidence of manufacturing operating leverage. Once a regulated facility, quality system and trained workforce are in place, incremental production volume can be added at a lower cost per unit, particularly for disposable devices and drug-delivery cannulas.

Future profitability implications

If disposable volume continues to grow, the Carlsbad facility should support:

- Better labor and overhead absorption.
- Larger production runs and purchasing efficiencies.
- Reduced transition-related duplication and disruption.
- A more favorable revenue mix as disposable sales outgrow lower-margin services.
- Higher gross profit available to fund R&D and commercial expansion.

Management indicated on the Q3 earnings call that meaningful scale could support disposable gross margins around 70%, including cannulas, although that is an aspiration rather than reported performance and should not be treated as guidance or a guaranteed outcome. The transcript also noted that capital-system sales can temporarily dilute total margin because some necessary third-party components carry little profit: https://www.roic.ai/quote/CLPT/transcripts/2024-year/3-quarter

The principal scalability constraint is therefore no longer simply physical manufacturing capacity. It is utilization: sufficient clinical procedures, partner trials and product volumes must materialize to absorb the facility’s fixed costs. Regulatory delays, uneven capital placements, or slower pharmaceutical trial enrollment could leave the infrastructure underutilized.

Final assessment

ClearPoint’s September 2024 financial profile was materially stronger than a year earlier but not yet self-sustaining. The company produced negative $7.72 million of nine-month free cash flow, yet sequential operating burn fell to only $1.20 million in Q3. Revenue expanded 41% in the quarter, gross margin improved by roughly three percentage points, and manufacturing capital requirements became minimal.

The March equity raise was essential to this position. Approximately $10 million of the $16.18 million net proceeds was effectively used to retire debt, leaving a net financing cushion of roughly $6.15 million after other financing activity. The result was $21.57 million of cash and no debt, but also additional dilution and continued reliance on external capital.

Strategically, capital equipment posted the fastest reported growth, while navigation and therapy delivered strong recurring-disposable expansion. Biologics and drug delivery remains the most important long-term opportunity because its product revenue is beginning to replace some lower-margin, project-based service revenue. The combination of pharmaceutical development relationships, installed navigation systems and recurring disposables gives ClearPoint a coherent platform strategy.

Financial sustainability will ultimately depend on turning that strategic positioning into repeatable product volume. If the Q3 burn reduction and margin recovery persist, existing liquidity could plausibly bridge the company toward cash-flow break-even. If growth or partner programs slow, the nine-month average burn rate indicates that another equity financing could still be required within roughly two years. The evidence through September 2024 supports improving capital efficiency and scalability, but not yet proven financial independence.

final.content:
PREMIUM RESOURCES LTD. (NOW NEXMETALS MINING CORP.): FINANCIAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CAPITAL-STRUCTURE RISK

All dollar amounts are Canadian dollars unless identified as US dollars. Premium Resources changed its name to NexMetals Mining Corp. in June 2025 and completed a 20-for-1 share consolidation; the June 2025 financial statements restate share and warrant figures on a post-consolidation basis.

Executive conclusion

Premium Resources entered 2025 in a financially stressed position. Shareholders’ equity fell by $13.19 million during 2024, moving from positive equity of $9.75 million to a $3.45 million deficit. The March 2025 equity financing and debt conversion repaired the reported balance sheet and supplied near-term liquidity, but did not eliminate the underlying funding problem: the company remained pre-revenue, used $21.69 million of cash in operations during the first half of 2025, and expressly stated that it did not have sufficient funds for the US$25 million Selebi payment due by January 31, 2026.

The capital structure also contains roughly 10.1 million outstanding warrants against 21.45 million current shares. Full exercise would increase the share count by approximately 47% and leave warrant holders owning about 32% of the enlarged common-share base. Although exercise could provide cash, it is conditional on market prices exceeding exercise prices and would materially dilute existing shareholders.

Near-term committed capital expenditure was only $7,180, but the Selebi contractual milestone due within twelve months was $34.11 million. Together, these amount to approximately $34.115 million—about $7.65 million more than June 2025 cash before funding continuing operations. Across Selebi and Selkirk, the remaining contingent BCL milestone payments total approximately US$74 million, equivalent to about $100.96 million at the June 30, 2025 exchange rate. Consequently, additional financing, renegotiation, a strategic partner, or some combination is necessary to preserve the Botswana assets and keep development work on schedule.

1. Deterioration in shareholders’ equity

The audited balance sheets report:

- December 31, 2023 shareholders’ equity: $9,745,686
- December 31, 2024 shareholders’ deficiency: $(3,447,060)

Source: Premium Resources’ audited 2024 financial statements, consolidated balance sheets and statement of changes in equity: https://nexmetalsmining.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/pnrl_fs_ye-2024.pdf

Calculation:

Change in equity  
= 2024 equity − 2023 equity  
= $(3,447,060) − $9,745,686  
= $(13,192,746)

Percentage deterioration relative to 2023 equity:

$13,192,746 ÷ $9,745,686 × 100  
= 135.37%

Thus, shareholders’ equity deteriorated by $13.19 million, or 135.4% of the opening equity balance. More importantly, it crossed from positive equity into a deficit.

Why the deterioration occurred

The company recorded a 2024 net loss of $42.42 million, compared with $32.38 million in 2023. The loss overwhelmed the equity raised during the year: the statement of changes in equity shows $28.24 million added through private-placement share capital, partially offset by $1.24 million of issuance costs. The company also used $37.60 million of cash in operating activities during 2024 and ended the year with only $6.11 million in cash. These figures are disclosed in the same audited statements: https://nexmetalsmining.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/pnrl_fs_ye-2024.pdf

Refinancing implication

The movement into negative equity signalled urgent refinancing needs rather than ordinary growth financing:

- The company was pre-revenue and had no internally generated operating cash flow.
- Current assets at December 2024 were $7.62 million versus current liabilities of $4.66 million, leaving only a modest current working-capital cushion.
- Total liabilities of $28.40 million exceeded total assets of $24.95 million.
- The auditor highlighted a material uncertainty related to going concern.
- Management stated that the company depended on external financing and would need additional funding to advance Selebi and Selkirk.

The urgency was confirmed by the March 2025 recapitalization: the company raised $46 million in gross equity proceeds and converted $20.88 million of term-loan principal into equity. The transaction materially deleveraged the balance sheet but was a response to—not a resolution of—the recurring funding deficit. Details of the recapitalization are in the company announcement: https://premiumresources.com/investors/news-releases/retransmission-premium-resources-announces-closin-9993/

By June 30, 2025, shareholders’ equity had recovered to $36.56 million, principally because of the private placement and debt conversion. Nevertheless, the company incurred a $30.32 million first-half loss and continued to disclose substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern. The June 2025 statements are available at https://nexmetalsmining.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/q2_2025_report_nexm_fs_mda.pdf

2. Warrant dilution and capital-structure risk

Current common shares

At June 30, 2025, the company had 21,449,318 common shares outstanding on a post-consolidation basis. The 20-for-1 consolidation took effect on June 20, 2025, and the financial statements retroactively adjusted the share and warrant information for comparability: https://nexmetalsmining.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/q2_2025_report_nexm_fs_mda.pdf

Outstanding warrants

Based on the warrant issuances and outstanding balance reported in the June 2025 filing, approximately 10.1 million post-consolidation common shares were issuable upon exercise of outstanding warrants. The major components include:

- warrants carried into 2025, including warrants from the June 2024 financing;
- approximately 3.83 million post-consolidation warrants from the March 2025 private placement; and
- approximately 3.48 million post-consolidation warrants issued in the term-loan debt conversion.

The March 2025 private placement issued 153,333,334 pre-consolidation units, each with one-half warrant, while the debt conversion issued units containing one share and one warrant. The financing terms are described at https://premiumresources.com/investors/news-releases/retransmission-premium-resources-announces-closin-9993/ and reflected on a consolidated basis in the June 2025 filing: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/795800/000149315225011913/form10-q.htm

Potential dilution

Using approximately 10.1 million warrant shares and 21,449,318 currently outstanding shares:

Potential increase over existing shares:

10.1 million ÷ 21.449 million × 100  
≈ 47.1%

Fully diluted shares after warrant exercise:

21.449 million + 10.1 million  
≈ 31.55 million shares

Warrant holders’ share of the enlarged base:

10.1 million ÷ 31.55 million × 100  
≈ 32.0%

Accordingly:

- the share count could rise by approximately 47% relative to the current base; and
- existing shareholders would experience approximately 32% economic dilution, assuming they did not participate and all warrants were exercised.

The exact percentage is modestly sensitive to the precise warrant balance and any exercises, expirations, or amendments after June 30, 2025.

Capital-structure assessment

A potential 47% increase in outstanding shares represents high dilution risk. It indicates that a substantial portion of the company’s financing has been raised through units and debt settlements carrying equity-linked securities rather than through internally generated cash.

Warrant exercise could benefit liquidity because exercise prices would bring additional cash into the company. However, that benefit is uncertain:

- warrants generally will not be exercised unless the market price is above the exercise price;
- exercise timing is controlled by holders rather than the company;
- some warrants do not expire until 2028; and
- relying on warrant proceeds cannot substitute for committed financing needed by a fixed project-payment deadline.

Thus, the warrant overhang creates a trade-off: possible future cash inflow, but potentially severe dilution and continuing pressure on the share price and cost of new equity.

3. Capital expenditures and obligations due within twelve months

Committed capital expenditure

As of June 30, 2025, the company reported committed capital expenditures over the following twelve months of:

$7,180

Source: June 2025 MD&A, “Contractual Obligations and Contingencies”: https://www.sedarplus.ca/csa-party/records/document.html?id=e5d03a696d41a1beb5c8ced8e8e3876694d8d4c53889fe6c4a9e9db2602e5ce4

This very low formally committed amount should not be interpreted as indicating that development is inexpensive. It means that little future spending was contractually locked in at that reporting date. The company still expected substantial discretionary exploration, evaluation, engineering, mine maintenance, and administrative expenditure.

Selebi payment due within twelve months

Under the Selebi asset-purchase agreement, the second installment was:

- US$25,000,000; or
- $34,107,500 using the filing’s June 2025 conversion.

It was payable upon the earlier of regulatory approval of the relevant mining-licence applications and January 31, 2026, the end of the study phase. That deadline fell within seven months of June 30, 2025.

Total identified committed capital expenditure and fixed contractual milestone within twelve months:

$7,180 + $34,107,500  
= $34,114,680

Comparison with liquidity:

June 30, 2025 cash = $26,463,957

Near-term shortfall before operating expenditure:

$34,114,680 − $26,463,957  
= $7,650,723

Therefore, even if every dollar of June 2025 cash were reserved for these commitments, cash was approximately $7.65 million short. In practice the shortfall was larger because cash was also required for payroll, exploration, mine care and maintenance, engineering, drilling, corporate costs, and working capital.

Management explicitly acknowledged that it did not then have sufficient funds to meet the US$25 million Selebi payment and might have to raise additional funding. See the June 2025 financial statements and MD&A: https://nexmetalsmining.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/q2_2025_report_nexm_fs_mda.pdf

4. Total contingent payments to the BCL liquidators

Selebi

The Selebi purchase price was US$56.75 million, payable in three installments:

1. US$1.75 million at closing—already paid.
2. US$25 million upon the earlier of the relevant licence approvals and January 31, 2026.
3. US$30 million upon the earlier of mine commissioning/start of production or the contractual long-stop date tied to licence renewal.

Remaining Selebi contingent milestones:

US$25 million + US$30 million  
= US$55 million

The terms and potential consequence of failing to meet them are summarized in the company’s SEC disclosures: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/795800/000164117225000043/R10.htm

Selkirk

The remaining contingent Selkirk installments are approximately:

- US$11 million associated with completion/delivery of the required feasibility-stage work; and
- US$8 million associated with mine construction/production milestones.

Remaining Selkirk contingent milestones:

US$11 million + US$8 million  
= US$19 million

Combined remaining BCL milestone payments

US$55 million Selebi + US$19 million Selkirk  
= US$74 million

Using the June 30, 2025 exchange rate disclosed in the MD&A of US$1 = C$1.3643:

US$74 million × 1.3643  
= approximately C$100.958 million

These amounts are contingent rather than all being immediately payable. The key distinction is:

- US$25 million, or $34.11 million, had a near-term outside date of January 31, 2026.
- The other US$49 million depends on later feasibility, construction, commissioning, production, or licence-related milestones.

Foreign-exchange movements will change their Canadian-dollar cost.

5. Effect on funding capacity and Botswana development timelines

Liquidity runway

At June 30, 2025, the company had:

- cash of $26.46 million;
- current assets of $29.37 million;
- current liabilities of $5.50 million;
- shareholders’ equity of $36.56 million; and
- no remaining term-loan balance following the debt conversion.

Those figures represent a clear improvement from December 2024. However, first-half 2025 cash used in operations was $21.69 million. A simple historical run-rate calculation gives:

Monthly operating cash use:

$21.686 million ÷ 6  
≈ $3.61 million per month

Cash runway at that rate, before the Selebi payment:

$26.464 million ÷ $3.61 million  
≈ 7.3 months

This is only a rough indicator: expenditure varies with drilling and development activity, and it excludes the US$25 million Selebi installment. Nevertheless, it shows that ordinary operating requirements alone could consume most of the June cash balance around the same period that the Selebi payment became due.

Development-timeline consequences

The financial pressures interact in several ways:

1. Equity erosion raises the cost of capital.  
   The 2024 move into negative equity and the going-concern disclosure weaken bargaining power with lenders and strategic investors. Although the March 2025 recapitalization restored positive book equity, recurring losses continue to erode it.

2. The near-term Selebi payment competes directly with development spending.  
   Cash used to satisfy the $34.11 million payment cannot also fund drilling, feasibility studies, engineering, mine rehabilitation, or Selkirk work. Conversely, spending aggressively on project advancement shortens the time available to finance the milestone.

3. Failure to fund Selebi could jeopardize the core asset.  
   The filings warn that failure to satisfy the post-closing milestones may result in Selebi reverting to the BCL liquidator. The payment therefore has strategic urgency beyond an ordinary debt maturity.

4. Warrant proceeds are not reliable committed funding.  
   Full exercise could raise cash and reduce the external-financing requirement, but only if exercise prices are economically attractive. The company cannot safely plan a fixed January 2026 payment around voluntary exercises.

5. Further equity financing would likely intensify dilution.  
   Existing warrants already imply approximately 32% dilution on a fully exercised basis. A new equity financing to cover the Selebi payment and ongoing work could materially increase that figure, particularly if shares must be issued at a discount.

6. Debt capacity remains constrained.  
   Converting the term loan into equity removed interest and maturity pressure, but a pre-revenue company with recurring losses and asset-payment obligations may face high interest rates, security requirements, restrictive covenants, or limited debt availability.

Overall assessment

Premium Resources/NexMetals had sufficient liquidity in June 2025 to continue near-term Botswana work, but not enough to fund normal operations, the January 2026 Selebi installment, and sustained development of both Selebi and Selkirk without additional capital.

The most probable funding solutions were:

- another equity financing, with additional dilution;
- exercise of in-the-money warrants, if market conditions permitted;
- a strategic investor, joint-venture partner, streaming/royalty transaction, or project-level financing;
- renegotiation or extension of BCL milestone timing; or
- deferral or reduction of discretionary exploration and development programs.

Absent one or more of these measures, the company would face a choice between preserving cash for the Selebi payment and maintaining its planned development pace. Either insufficient payment funding or curtailed technical work could delay studies, licence conversion, construction decisions, and eventual commissioning. Consequently, the combined evidence points to high ongoing refinancing urgency and high capital-structure risk despite the successful March 2025 recapitalization.

Saudi Arabia Industrial Automation Market for Manufacturing, 2015–2025

Executive summary

Saudi Arabia’s manufacturing-automation market expanded materially during 2015–2025, but published estimates differ by more than an order of magnitude because vendors define the market differently. A defensible 2025 range is:

- USD 166.5 million for the narrowly defined “manufacturing automation” market;
- USD 1.01 billion for “smart-factory automation”; and
- Approximately USD 2.20 billion for the broad industrial-automation market, including process automation and related systems.

Using the respective published growth rates to normalize these series suggests indicative 2015 values of approximately USD 94 million, USD 471 million, and USD 816 million. These are modeled back-casts rather than reported historical observations.

Saudi Arabia-specific installed-robot density is not available in the publicly accessible IFR material reviewed. The best transparent equivalent is annual robot imports relative to manufacturing employment: roughly 9.7 imported multipurpose industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers in 2023, increasing to an indicative 24.6–33.7 per 10,000 in 2024 depending on the employment denominator. This is an annual flow metric, not the IFR operational-stock density measure.

Vision 2030 has shifted automation demand from isolated factory projects toward a policy-backed industrial transformation. The most direct measure is the Future Factories Program’s objective to transform 4,000 factories from low-wage, low-skill production toward automation and advanced industrial practices. Other demand drivers include NIDLP’s formal prioritization of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, the National Industrial Strategy’s local-content and industrial-expansion agenda, large automotive and clean-industry investments, and investment-law reforms designed to make foreign and private investment easier.

For named megaproject awards since 2021:

- Siemens Europe is the automation-component partner on the Port of NEOM automated crane package awarded to ZPMC. The overall ZPMC package exceeds SAR 1 billion, or USD 266.7 million, but Siemens’ subcontract value has not been disclosed.
- ABB was appointed in 2021 to provide low-voltage power systems and ABB Ability digital energy/asset management for The Red Sea Project. No contract value was publicly disclosed.
- ABB subsequently announced a Red Sea Global partnership covering more than 1,200 EV chargers at The Red Sea and AMAALA; again, no contract value was disclosed.

The principal sales implication is that vendors should sell factory outcomes—throughput, localization, energy efficiency, uptime and workforce transformation—rather than stand-alone robots.

1. Market size, growth and robotics penetration

1.1 Market-definition problem

“Industrial automation” can include any combination of:

- Industrial robots and collaborative robots;
- Programmable logic controllers, distributed control systems and SCADA;
- Sensors, drives, actuators and machine controls;
- Manufacturing execution systems and industrial software;
- Warehouse and material-handling automation;
- Process instrumentation;
- Digital twins, predictive maintenance and energy-management systems; and
- Engineering, integration and lifecycle services.

Consequently, market estimates are not directly comparable. The following should be treated as three separate market boundaries rather than competing estimates of exactly the same market.

1.2 Market-size estimates

| Market boundary | Published 2025 value | Published growth rate | Indicative 2015 value | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Narrow manufacturing automation | USD 166.5m | 5.89% CAGR, 2026–2033 | USD 94.0m | Likely excludes substantial process automation, components and adjacent infrastructure |
| Smart-factory automation | USD 1,005.1m | 7.89% CAGR, 2026–2034 | USD 470.5m | Broader Industry 4.0/factory-digitization boundary |
| Broad industrial automation | USD 1.99bn in 2024; approximately USD 2.20bn in 2025 | 10.40% CAGR, 2025–2032 | USD 816m | Broadest definition, covering process and discrete automation systems and components |

Sources:

- Grand View Research reports USD 166.5 million of Saudi manufacturing-automation revenue in 2025 and forecasts USD 271.2 million in 2033 at 5.89% CAGR: https://www.grandviewresearch.com/horizon/outlook/manufacturing-automation-market/saudi-arabia
- IMARC reports a USD 1,005.1 million Saudi smart-factory automation market in 2025 and 7.89% CAGR during 2026–2034: https://www.imarcgroup.com/saudi-arabia-smart-factory-automation-market
- Data Bridge reports a USD 1.99 billion Saudi industrial-automation market in 2024 and 10.40% forecast CAGR: https://www.databridgemarketresearch.com/nucleus/saudi-arabia-industrial-automation-market

Quantitative work

A. Narrow manufacturing automation:

2015 estimate = USD 166.5m ÷ (1 + 0.0589)^10  
= USD 166.5m ÷ approximately 1.772  
= approximately USD 94.0m.

B. Smart-factory automation:

2015 estimate = USD 1,005.1m ÷ (1 + 0.0789)^10  
= USD 1,005.1m ÷ approximately 2.136  
= approximately USD 470.5m.

C. Broad industrial automation:

First advance the reported 2024 value by one year:

2025 estimate = USD 1.99bn × 1.104  
= approximately USD 2.197bn.

Then back-cast ten years:

2015 estimate = USD 2.197bn ÷ (1.104)^10  
= USD 2.197bn ÷ approximately 2.69  
= approximately USD 0.816bn.

These calculations assume that the vendors’ forward CAGRs are reasonable proxies for the entire 2015–2025 period. That assumption is uncertain: investment likely accelerated after Vision 2030’s 2016 launch and again after NIDLP’s 2019 launch. Therefore, the calculated 2015 values should be used only for directional sizing.

A practical working estimate for sales planning is approximately USD 1.0 billion for smart-factory automation in 2025. The USD 2.2 billion broad estimate is more appropriate when the addressable portfolio includes process controls, instrumentation, drives, electrification and industrial digital services.

1.3 Robotics penetration

IFR definition

IFR defines robot density as industrial robots in operation per 10,000 persons employed in manufacturing. IFR’s methodological material says World Robotics analyzes manufacturing robot density for more than 40 countries and derives its robot statistics from robot suppliers and national associations: https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Sources___Methods_WR_2024_Industrial_Robots_.pdf

The IFR database-availability chart lists Saudi Arabia as a country code in the industrial-robot installations database: https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Database_-_data_availability_WR_2024.pdf

However, the public IFR summaries reviewed do not publish a Saudi installed-stock or density figure. It would therefore be inappropriate to present a modeled number as an official IFR statistic.

Equivalent annual-flow metric

A transparent proxy can be calculated from robot imports and manufacturing employment:

- Saudi Arabia imported approximately 1,300 multipurpose industrial robots in 2023, according to IndexBox’s customs-based market summary: https://www.indexbox.io/search/industrial-robot-price-saudi-arabia/
- GAStat-derived administrative employment data report 1,341,920 manufacturing workers in Q2 2024: https://gulfmigration.grc.net/saudi-arabia-employed-population-aged-15-and-above-by-nationality-saudi-non-saudi-sex-and-main-group-of-economic-activities-q2-2024/?print=pdf

Annual import intensity:

1,300 ÷ 1,341,920 × 10,000  
= 9.69 imported robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers.

For 2024, IndexBox reports approximately 3,300 Saudi robot imports: https://www.indexbox.io/blog/industrial-robot-gcc-market-overview-2024-1/

Using the same 1,341,920-worker denominator:

3,300 ÷ 1,341,920 × 10,000  
= 24.59 imported robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers.

An alternative Ministry of Industry-based factory employment total is approximately 979,550 workers at the end of 2024. On that denominator:

3,300 ÷ 979,550 × 10,000  
= 33.69 imported robots per 10,000 factory workers.

The underlying factory count was 9,991 operating factories, with SAR 966 billion of cumulative investment: https://www.argaam.com/en/article/articledetail/id/1827405

Interpretation and limitations

- The defensible equivalent penetration measure is therefore approximately 9.7 annual robot imports per 10,000 manufacturing workers in 2023 and approximately 25–34 in 2024.
- The increase from 1,300 to 3,300 units is approximately 154%:

(3,300 ÷ 1,300 − 1) × 100  
= approximately 153.8%.

- Imports are not the same as installations: some units can remain in inventory, be re-exported, go to non-manufacturing applications or replace retired robots.
- A true IFR-style density requires the operational robot stock accumulated over multiple years, adjusted for retirements, divided by manufacturing employment.
- The 1.34 million employment denominator includes the wider manufacturing workforce, while the 979,550 figure covers workers in operating factories under the Ministry’s industrial-factory reporting system. The resulting range should not be interpreted as an official density.
- IFR reported a global manufacturing average of 151 robots per 10,000 workers for 2022 under its then-current methodology: https://ifr.org/img/worldrobotics/Executive_Summary_WR_Industrial_Robots_2023.pdf. Saudi annual import intensity is not directly comparable with this operational-stock measure.

2. How Vision 2030 has driven robotics and automation demand

2.1 NIDLP makes the Fourth Industrial Revolution a formal industrial objective

The National Industrial Development and Logistics Program, launched in 2019 as a Vision Realization Program, aims to turn Saudi Arabia into a leading industrial power and global logistics hub. Its official delivery plan explicitly identifies AI, IoT, 3D printing, robots, and smart factories, mines and grids as Fourth Industrial Revolution technologies expected to increase production, competitiveness and sustainability: https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/5hlpbuuq/2021-2025-national-industrial-development-and-logistics-program-delivery-plan-en.pdf

The plan also identifies:

- Financial enablement;
- Infrastructure development;
- Regulatory reform;
- Localization of advanced technologies;
- Industrial-cluster coordination; and
- Private-sector participation

as mechanisms for implementation.

This matters commercially because robots are no longer treated simply as imported capital equipment. They are positioned as part of a national productivity, localization and industrial-capability agenda.

2.2 Future Factories Program: a direct pipeline of 4,000 factories

The Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources’ Future Factories service states that the program seeks to transform 4,000 factories from dependence on low-wage, low-skilled labor toward operational efficiency, automation and advanced industrial solutions: https://my.gov.sa/en/services/251928

The Ministry’s main digitization track covers:

- Production-line controls;
- Material-handling systems;
- Packaging machines;
- Factory planning and communications;
- Digitization of procedures; and
- Partial cost coverage or provision of qualifying solutions.

Official program description: https://www.mim.gov.sa/en/initiatives-programs/industrial-sector-initiatives/industrial-sector-support-initiative/Future-Factories-Initiative-The-Main-Digitization-Track

Demand effect:

- It creates a named pool of potential factory-transformation accounts.
- It lowers capital barriers for qualifying manufacturers.
- It expands demand beyond large petrochemical and state-owned plants into SMEs.
- It favors phased automation—controls, data acquisition and packaging first, followed by robotics, MES, digital twins and advanced analytics.

Given 9,991 operating factories at the end of 2024, the 4,000-factory objective is equivalent to roughly 40% of the operating-factory base:

4,000 ÷ 9,991 × 100  
= approximately 40.0%.

The populations may not be perfectly identical, but the calculation illustrates the program’s scale.

2.3 National Industrial Strategy and procurement localization

The official National Industrial Strategy states that Saudi Arabia intends to increase local manufacturers’ contribution to:

- Government procurement;
- Capital expenditure of state-owned enterprises; and
- Operating expenditure of state-owned enterprises.

It also prioritizes industries including automotive, pharmaceuticals, food, military manufacturing and machinery/equipment: https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/t0uiiudv/nsd_en.pdf

Demand effect:

Automation suppliers increasingly need to demonstrate local value creation—Saudi assembly, engineering, training, spare-parts availability, technology transfer or partnerships—not only technical performance. Local-content requirements also encourage international manufacturers to build Saudi production capacity, generating automation demand in greenfield plants.

2.4 Investment targets enlarge the manufacturing capital pool

The Ministry of Investment’s National Investment Strategy targets:

- Tripling investment between 2019 and 2030;
- Increasing foreign direct investment from SAR 17 billion in 2019 to SAR 388 billion in 2030; and
- Increasing gross fixed capital formation from 22% to 30% of GDP.

Official source: https://misa.gov.sa/activities/national-investment-strategy/

The SAR 388 billion FDI target is equivalent to approximately USD 103.5 billion at the Saudi riyal’s fixed rate of SAR 3.75 per USD:

SAR 388bn ÷ 3.75  
= USD 103.47bn.

A Ministry investment monitor also cites more than SAR 12 trillion of cumulative investment by 2030: https://eservices.misa.gov.sa/medias/Economic-and-Investment-Monitor-Q3-2025-english-.pdf?attachment=true&context=bWFzdGVyfHJvb3R8NTU2MTQ5OXxhcHBsaWNvbi9wZGZ8aDk5L2gxNC85MTQ4MjU5MzY4OTkwLnBkZnw2ZDhlNjhkZjAxMGQ2MDY2ZjcxMGU2M2Y0ZTIxYmZkNWE5MDcyMjk2Y2Y3MzI1OGI5MDVlOTZlMzU3OWE1Mjg2

SAR 12 trillion is approximately USD 3.2 trillion:

SAR 12tn ÷ 3.75  
= USD 3.2tn.

Not all of this investment is industrial or automation-related, but the targets increase the pool of greenfield factories, logistics assets, utilities and industrial infrastructure that can purchase automation.

2.5 Updated investment regulation

Saudi Arabia redesigned its Investment Law to replace the previous Foreign Investment Law and align regulation with Vision 2030 and the National Investment Strategy. The Ministry of Investment says the updated framework is intended to support GDP growth, economic diversification, investor rights and private-sector participation: https://misa.gov.sa/activities/laws-regulations-copy/

Demand effect:

- A more unified investment framework should reduce entry friction for foreign automation suppliers and manufacturers.
- Stronger investor protections improve the bankability of long-lived industrial projects.
- Foreign manufacturers entering Saudi Arabia become both automation customers and potential local channel or integration partners.

The law’s effect should still be treated as prospective; regulatory reform does not automatically translate into near-term equipment orders.

2.6 Named industrial investments demonstrate the policy-to-demand pathway

NIDLP’s 2023 report cites the PIF–Hyundai joint venture for a highly automated Saudi vehicle plant with investment exceeding SAR 1 billion and planned capacity of 50,000 vehicles annually: https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/2o1mbfnn/nidlp-2023-annual-report-eng.pdf

Conversion:

SAR 1bn ÷ 3.75  
= approximately USD 266.7m.

This is a clear example of how localization policy creates robotics demand: automotive body, paint, assembly, inspection and intralogistics operations generally require high levels of automation.

The same NIDLP report says the Fourth Industrial Revolution ecosystem delivered 75 awareness workshops, 60 technical consultations and 80 product-development services. These activities help build customer knowledge and project pipelines, especially among firms that have not previously deployed advanced automation.

3. Siemens and ABB awards at NEOM and The Red Sea since 2021

3.1 Siemens Europe — Port of NEOM automated crane package

Project/contract

Port of NEOM crane and container-handling equipment package, awarded to Shanghai Zhenhua Heavy Industries Company Limited, with Siemens Europe supplying automation components.

Announcement and scope

NEOM announced in May 2023 that ZPMC had been awarded contracts for:

- Ten ship-to-shore gantry cranes;
- Thirty electric rubber-tyred gantry cranes; and
- Six automated rail-mounted gantry cranes.

NEOM states that the contracts were valued at more than SAR 1 billion and that ZPMC would work with Siemens Europe to deliver the automation components: https://www.neom.com/en-us/newsroom/neom-port-business

Value

Overall ZPMC equipment package:

More than SAR 1bn ÷ 3.75  
= more than USD 266.7m.

Important qualification:

This is not a disclosed Siemens contract value. Siemens is publicly named as the automation-component partner, but neither NEOM nor Siemens disclosed Siemens’ share. The only defensible value is therefore:

- Total associated package: more than USD 266.7 million;
- Siemens-specific estimated value: undisclosed and not reliably estimable from public information.

Subsequent implementation evidence

In 2024, Mevea announced that Siemens was integrating Mevea digital-twin and simulation technology into Port of NEOM crane automation. The technology supports ten automated ship-to-shore cranes and thirty automated electric rubber-tyred gantry cranes: https://www.mevea.com/news-events/news/siemens-integrates-meveas-digital-twin-technology-in-automated-cranes-for-port-of-neom-saudi-arabia/

This confirms an operational Siemens automation role beyond a preliminary memorandum or bid.

Commercial relevance

Although the project is port automation rather than a conventional factory, it is directly connected to Oxagon’s industrial and manufacturing ecosystem. It demonstrates demand for:

- Automated material handling;
- Remote control;
- Digital twins;
- High-availability industrial networks;
- Predictive maintenance; and
- Integrated automation software.

ABB did not disclose a contract value. No reliable award-value estimate can be derived from the number of panels or megawatts because the public scope does not specify:

- ABB contract value: not publicly disclosed;
- Associated Red Sea utilities concession: approximately USD 1.3–1.33 billion, but this is the broader ACWA Power-led utilities project, not ABB’s contract.

The local manufacture of charging pedestals illustrates an important procurement pattern: global technology combined with Saudi local content. This pattern is likely to appear in manufacturing-automation tenders as well.

4. Three practical implications for a manufacturing sales representative

4.1 Target policy-qualified factory cohorts, not the entire market indiscriminately

Priority accounts should be grouped by their fit with Vision 2030 programs:

1. Future Factories candidates among the 4,000 targeted plants;
2. Greenfield automotive, food, pharmaceutical, chemicals, metals and machinery projects identified by the National Industrial Strategy;
3. PIF, state-owned-enterprise and giga-project supply chains;
4. Existing large factories with high energy, labor, quality or downtime costs; and
5. SMEs that can begin with packaging, handling, machine vision or collaborative robots.

The sales representative should ask early:

- Has the factory completed a digital-maturity assessment?
- Is it applying through the Future Factories Program?
- Is funding or cost coverage available?
- Does the project carry local-content targets?
- Is procurement controlled by the factory, a government entity, an EPC contractor or an international OEM?

This prevents time being spent on technically attractive projects that lack an approved funding or procurement route.

4.2 Sell a phased business case tied to measurable outcomes

Saudi customers transitioning from labor-intensive operations may resist a large robot-cell investment unless it is connected to operating economics. The proposal should therefore lead with:

- Output per shift;
- Overall equipment effectiveness;
- Scrap and rework reduction;
- Energy consumed per unit;
- Worker safety;
- Quality traceability;
- Unplanned downtime; and
- Saudi technical-job creation.

A practical phased offer could be:

- Phase 1: production data collection, sensors, networking and controls;
- Phase 2: automated packaging, palletizing, machine vision or intralogistics;
- Phase 3: robot cells, MES and predictive maintenance;
- Phase 4: digital twins, plant-wide optimization and lifecycle services.

This aligns with the Future Factories main digitization track, which treats communications, production-line controls, material handling and packaging as foundations for more advanced automation.

Commercial proposals should include a locally relevant payback model. For example:

Annual benefit  
= labor redeployment savings  
+ avoided downtime  
+ scrap reduction  
+ energy savings  
+ incremental contribution from higher throughput.

Payback period  
= installed project cost ÷ annual net benefit.

The proposal should show conservative, base and upside cases rather than relying on global benchmark savings.

4.3 Build local-content, integration and after-sales capability into the bid

Vision 2030 procurement increasingly rewards local economic value. A foreign sales representative should not approach Saudi manufacturing as an equipment-export market alone.

A competitive bid should address:

- Saudi-based commissioning and service response;
- Local spare-parts inventory;
- Arabic and English operator training;
- Saudi engineer and technician development;
- Cybersecurity and data-hosting requirements;
- Integration with installed PLC, DCS, MES and ERP systems;
- Partnerships with approved Saudi system integrators;
- Local assembly or manufacture where commercially viable; and
- Long-term maintenance and software support.

The Siemens Port of NEOM model—working through ZPMC and a specialist digital-twin provider—and ABB’s locally manufactured EV-charging pedestal model both show that ecosystem partnerships can be more important than direct equipment selling.
