final.content:
# New Zealand construction metalworks / structural-steel fabrication market, 2018–2024

## Executive summary

- The most defensible official definition is ANZSIC06 **C2221, Structural Steel Fabricating**, covering fabricated steel components such as girders, joists, rafters, structural plate and reinforcing mesh. Stats NZ’s classification is documented in its [DataInfo+ entry for C2221](https://datainfoplus.stats.govt.nz/item/nz.govt.stats/ff97cfbd-5ede-42b5-af73-e6dc2ffb2125/1).
- Stats NZ employment in C2221 increased from **4,250 employees in February 2018 to 4,450 in February 2024**, a six-year CAGR of approximately **0.8%**. Employment peaked at 4,600 in 2023 before the 2024 construction downturn.
- No publicly accessible Stats NZ or MBIE table identified in this review publishes annual **C2221 revenue or fabricated tonnage**. Stats NZ’s Annual Enterprise Survey publishes financial data at broader industry levels, while tonnage comes from Steel Construction New Zealand (SCNZ), not government.
- SCNZ consistently described domestic output as approximately **100,000 tonnes a year** from 2018 through 2023. Installed single-shift capacity increased from approximately **120,000 tonnes to 150,000 tonnes in 2023**, indicating substantial spare capacity rather than rapid output growth.
- A transparent revenue estimate cannot be produced from Stats NZ/MBIE evidence alone. A later commercial benchmark—IBISWorld’s January 2026 estimate of **NZ$1.8 billion in 2026** and 2.1% CAGR over 2021–26—would imply about **NZ$1.73 billion in 2024**, but this is retrospective, broader than heavy building-and-bridge fabrication in some respects, and is not an official statistic.
- New Zealand’s ordinary tariff treatment for the principal raw and semi-finished structural-steel headings **HS 7207–7216 is generally Free/0%** under the Customs Working Tariff. Consequently, ordinary customs duty has essentially **no direct impact on local fabricator margins**. Exchange rates, freight, inventory timing, mill concentration, trade remedies and compliance costs are materially more important.
- The market is fragmented and dominated by privately held businesses that do not publish revenue. A genuinely audited “top five by 2023 revenue” is therefore unavailable. Culham Engineering is independently identified as the market leader; D&H Steel has the largest quantified disclosed fabrication range in the evidence reviewed, at **250–400 tonnes per week**, equivalent to **13,000–20,800 tonnes per year** before outsourcing.
- The strongest medium-term opportunity is the infrastructure and seismic-resilience pipeline. The principal near-term risk, as of 2024, was the gap between that long-run pipeline and weak current commercial/infrastructure activity.

---

## 1. Scope and definitions

This report is limited to steel fabricated for:

- building frames, columns, beams, trusses and bracing;
- bridges and transport structures;
- structural plate and associated construction components;
- construction-related reinforcing fabrication where a project source reports only combined steel demand.

It excludes stand-alone steel distribution, roofing, pipes, general machinery, marine fabrication, pressure vessels and industrial maintenance except where a company also competes materially in structural construction.

There is an important boundary issue: ANZSIC C2221 includes some products—particularly reinforcing mesh—that are not normally described as “structural-steel fabrication” by heavy fabricators. Conversely, diversified engineering firms may record structural work under another predominant industry. Stats NZ itself cautions that businesses are classified by predominant activity and company structure can affect where their data are captured in its [Business Performance Benchmarker 2024 metadata](https://datainfoplus.stats.govt.nz/item/nz.govt.stats/234da6a7-c2bf-4274-b654-c53f4bd72983).

---

# 2. Market size and growth, 2018–2024

## 2.1 Official employment series and industry output evidence

| Year | Stats NZ C2221 employee count | YoY change | Structural steel fabricated | Revenue |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2018 | 4,250 | — | ≈100,000 t | Not published at C2221 level |
| 2019 | 4,200 | -1.2% | ≈100,000 t indicative | Not published |
| 2020 | 4,350 | +3.6% | ≈100,000 t indicative; disruption risk from COVID-19 | Not published |
| 2021 | 4,250 | -2.3% | ≈100,000 t indicative | Not published |
| 2022 | 4,450 | +4.7% | ≈100,000 t | Not published |
| 2023 | 4,600 | +3.4% | ≈100,000 t; capacity lifted to ≈150,000 t | Not published |
| 2024 | 4,450 | -3.3% | No new official annual observation identified; ≈100,000 t run-rate is the latest defensible sector benchmark | Not published |

### Sources and interpretation

**Employment.** The employee counts are Stats NZ Business Demography data reproduced by Figure.NZ in its chart [“Employee count in the structural steel fabricating industry in New Zealand”](https://figure.nz/chart/tAQeOoJ0aDCZo3ER-k2pX8VwdLmexeE2c), covering February 2000–2025. Stats NZ describes Business Demography as an annual snapshot of economically significant enterprises; its February 2024 release was published **31 October 2024** ([Stats NZ](https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/new-zealand-business-demography-statistics-at-february-2024)).

These are employee counts, not a labour-force-survey measure. They exclude working proprietors and can be affected by enterprise reclassification.

**Tonnage.**

- SCNZ’s **March 2018** industry update reported that the sector had turned approximately **100,000 tonnes** of plate, hot-rolled and hollow sections into buildings and bridges over the previous 12 months, against estimated capacity of 120,000 tonnes ([SCNZ March 2018](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/SCNZ_Industry-Update_March-2018.pdf)).
- SCNZ’s **September 2018** update repeated approximately 100,000 tonnes of annual output and 120,000 tonnes of capacity ([SCNZ September 2018](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/SCNZ_Industry-Update_September-2018.pdf)).
- The **December 2022** update reported approximately 100,000 tonnes fabricated in the preceding 12 months, 153 fabrication companies, about 5,000 workers and 120,000 tonnes of capacity ([SCNZ December 2022](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/SCNZ-IU-DEC2022_WEB.pdf)).
- The **September 2023** update again reported annual output of approximately 100,000 tonnes but said capacity had risen from 120,000 to **150,000 tonnes** over five years ([SCNZ September 2023](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf)).

The approximately 100,000-tonne entries for 2019–21 and 2024 should therefore be read as an **industry run-rate**, not separately measured annual observations. Neither Stats NZ nor MBIE publishes annual fabricated tonnage.

## 2.2 Growth calculations

### Employment

\[
\text{CAGR}_{2018-24}
=\left(\frac{4,450}{4,250}\right)^{1/6}-1
=0.77\%\text{ p.a.}
\]

Total change:

\[
4,450-4,250=200\text{ employees}
\]

\[
200/4,250=4.7\%
\]

Thus employment expanded modestly over the full period, but fell 3.3% in 2024:

\[
(4,450/4,600)-1=-3.26\%
\]

### Output and utilisation

On SCNZ’s rounded figures:

- 2018 utilisation:

\[
100,000/120,000=83.3\%
\]

- 2023 physical output relative to newly disclosed capacity:

\[
100,000/150,000=66.7\%
\]

SCNZ’s September 2023 forward-workload survey separately reported **41% spare capacity**, which reflects committed forward workload rather than trailing output. Both measures show that investment expanded capacity faster than demand.

### Productivity proxy

Using Stats NZ employee counts and SCNZ’s approximate output:

- 2018:

\[
100,000/4,250=23.5\text{ tonnes per employee}
\]

- 2023:

\[
100,000/4,600=21.7\text{ tonnes per employee}
\]

This is only a rough proxy because SCNZ’s approximately 5,000-worker sector estimate has broader coverage than Stats NZ’s C2221 employee count and because SCNZ tonnage is rounded.

## 2.3 Revenue: what is and is not available

Stats NZ’s Annual Enterprise Survey is the authoritative source for industry financial statistics. Stats NZ describes AES as its most comprehensive financial survey, covering around 500,000 businesses; the **2018 provisional release was published 28 June 2019** ([Stats NZ](https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/annual-enterprise-survey-2018-financial-year-provisional/)), and the **2024 provisional release was published 27 June 2025** ([Stats NZ](https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/annual-enterprise-survey-2024-financial-year-provisional/)).

However, the publicly identified AES table publishes financial performance for broader **C22 Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing**, not a clean annual C2221 revenue series. The Stats NZ benchmarker cannot fill this gap because it:

- reports ratios rather than total industry revenue;
- includes tax-return businesses with turnover between NZ$60,000 and NZ$10 million;
- consequently excludes the largest structural fabricators.

Accordingly, assigning official annual revenue figures to C2221 for 2018–24 would be false precision.

### Retrospective commercial cross-check—not an official 2024 observation

IBISWorld’s report released **12 January 2026** gives a 2026 market size of **NZ$1.8 billion** and a 2021–26 CAGR of **2.1%** ([IBISWorld](https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/industry/structural-steel-fabricating/235/)). Deflating two years:

\[
\text{Implied 2024 revenue}
=\frac{1.8}{1.021^2}
=NZ\$1.727\text{ billion}
\]

This should be treated only as a retrospective commercial estimate. It is not Stats NZ/MBIE data, was not available as of 2024, and may include reinforcing and other products outside a narrow heavy-structural definition.

---

# 3. Leading structural-steel fabricators

## 3.1 Ranking limitations

Most large New Zealand fabricators are privately owned. Ordinary Companies Office annual returns disclose directors and shareholders but generally do **not** disclose income statements. No comparable set of 2023 audited revenue filings was available for the private firms reviewed.

The following is therefore an **evidence-constrained ranking**, using:

1. an independent market-leadership statement where available;
2. disclosed annualised tonnage capacity;
3. workforce and fabrication-facility scale;
4. structural-market positioning.

It is not equivalent to an audited revenue league table.

## 3.2 Indicative top five as of 2023

### 1. Culham Engineering

- **Ownership:** Privately held New Zealand group. Culham says managing director Rob Kirwan and a business partner took full ownership in 2021.
- **Scale evidence:** More than 450 employees and one of New Zealand’s largest fabrication facilities; eight fabrication workshops covering approximately 22,000 m² on a nine-hectare Whangārei site.
- **Ranking basis:** IBISWorld identifies Culham as the company holding the largest share of the New Zealand structural-steel fabrication industry.
- **Relevant sources:** Culham’s [history page](https://culham.co.nz/who-we-are/our-history/) and [company profile](https://culham.co.nz/who-we-are/), originally published **26 June 2015**; [workshop description](https://culham.co.nz/what-we-do/facilities/workshops/), published **13 July 2015**; [IBISWorld report](https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/industry/structural-steel-fabricating/235/), **12 January 2026**.
- **Caveat:** Culham is diversified into heavy engineering, industrial maintenance, coatings, marine and energy work; its total workforce is not exclusively structural construction.

### 2. D&H Steel Construction

- **Ownership:** Privately owned. Public company-profile evidence identifies Michael Sullivan, entities associated with Nigel Harrison, Wayne Carson and Dean Pouwhare among the beneficial interests.
- **Capacity:** **250–400 tonnes per week**, depending on complexity, before outsourcing.
- **Annualised calculation:**

\[
250\times52=13,000\text{ t/year}
\]

\[
400\times52=20,800\text{ t/year}
\]

This equals roughly **13–21%** of the approximately 100,000-tonne national annual output, although actual output need not equal maximum capacity.
- **Relevant sources:** D&H’s [fabrication page](https://www.dhsteel.co.nz/how-we-do-it/fabrication/), published **22 January 2018**; [company history](https://www.dhsteel.co.nz/who-we-are/), **15 January 2018**; and [board/ownership description](https://www.dhsteel.co.nz/who-we-are/key-people/).
- **Caveat:** The 250–400 tonnes/week disclosure is a capability range, not confirmed 2023 production.

### 3. John Jones Steel

- **Ownership:** Privately held. Registry-derived information reports 96% held by Talfourd Trustee No.1 Limited and 4% by Francis John Van Schaijik.
- **Scale evidence:** Three plants—two in Christchurch and one in Timaru—plus approximately 1,000 tonnes of stock held at any time. The Christchurch operation historically included 5,300 m² of workshops and the Timaru facility approximately 4,100 m².
- **Relevant sources:** John Jones Steel’s [company history and plant description](https://jjsteel.nz/about-us); registry-derived [company information](https://www.businesscheck.co.nz/ltd/9429031940740/); and [Kompass facility description](https://www.kompass.com/z/nz/c/john-jones-steel-limited/nz001810/).
- **Caveat:** No reliable 2023 revenue or annual tonnage figure was disclosed. An online estimated revenue figure identified during research was not used because it was neither a Companies Office filing nor an audited account.

### 4. Page & Macrae

- **Ownership:** Page & Macrae Limited is held through Page & Macrae Holdings Limited and ultimate New Zealand holding company IGM Holdings Limited. Registry-derived ownership identifies interests associated with Ian Macrae, Elizabeth Holm, Gloria Macrae and Reanah Reynolds.
- **Scale evidence:** Approximately **180 employees** were reported in a company post dated **31 August 2023**.
- **Relevant sources:** [Page Macrae 2023 company post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7102862403092025344); [CompaniesNZ registry summary](https://www.companiesnz.com/company/178127/page-macrae-limited); and [ownership-network profile](https://oversightsolutions.co.nz/profile/PAGE--MACRAE-LIMITED).
- **Caveat:** Page & Macrae is highly diversified into port equipment, production welding and industrial engineering. Its inclusion is based on fabrication scale, not evidence that it was the fourth-largest pure construction-frame fabricator.

### 5. Red Steel

- **Ownership:** Privately held New Zealand company with management and local investor shareholdings. A registry-derived profile lists Wattyz Enterprises and individual management shareholders.
- **Scale evidence:** 37 employees reported in 2023, with recent multimillion-dollar investment in automated beam and plate processing. Red Steel describes itself as a structural specialist serving industrial, commercial and residential projects across Hawke’s Bay and the North Island.
- **Relevant sources:** Red Steel’s [company website](https://www.redsteel.co.nz/); Moore Markhams’ profile published **27 March 2023** ([Moore Markhams](https://www.markhams.co.nz/news/red-steel-sizing-up-success-at-red-steel/)); registry-derived [ownership record](https://www.businesscheck.co.nz/ltd/9429036239566/).
- **Caveat:** Red Steel is clearly smaller by headcount than the first four. Its fifth-place designation is indicative; the evidence does not exclude another private company of greater 2023 revenue or tonnage.

### Companies not ranked

Steel & Tube had FY2023 group revenue of **NZ$589.1 million** and volume of 146,400 tonnes, but it is principally a distributor and processor rather than a comparable structural-frame fabricator. Its FY2023 infrastructure segment generated NZ$232.8 million ([Steel & Tube FY23 results](https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20%20FY23%20Results%20Presentation%202023.pdf)). Including it would materially overstate its directly comparable fabrication activity.

Likewise, Fletcher Easysteel is primarily a distributor and processor; its own product guide calls it a leading steel distributor ([Easysteel Steel Book](https://www.easysteel.co.nz/web/assets/FBES_01_Book_-_The_Steel_Book_FULL_V13.04.1223_v4B-lowres.pdf)).

---

# 4. Import tariffs on raw structural steel

## 4.1 Relevant HS headings

The main Chapter 72 inputs within the requested range are:

| HS heading | Product relevance to structural fabrication | Ordinary NZ tariff |
|---|---|---:|
| 7207 | Semi-finished products of iron or non-alloy steel | Free / 0% |
| 7208 | Hot-rolled flat products, width ≥600 mm | Free / 0% |
| 7209 | Cold-rolled flat products, width ≥600 mm | Free / 0% |
| 7210 | Flat products clad, plated or coated | Generally Free / 0% |
| 7211 | Flat products, width <600 mm | Free / 0% |
| 7212 | Narrow flat products clad, plated or coated | Generally Free / 0% |
| 7213 | Hot-rolled bars and rods in coils | Free / 0% |
| 7214 | Other bars and rods, including reinforcing bar categories | Free / 0% ordinary duty |
| 7215 | Other bars and rods | Free / 0% |
| 7216 | Angles, shapes and sections—beams, columns, channels and similar profiles | Free / 0% |

Source: New Zealand Customs Service, **Working Tariff Document, Section XV, Chapter 72: Iron and steel** ([Customs tariff schedule](https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/rpfatduk/section-xv.pdf)). Customs explains the machine-readable tariff-rate fields and rate groups in its [Tariff and Concession Data Files readme](https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/y1dmuyec/tariff-and-concession-readme.pdf).

The exact ten-digit tariff item should always be checked because classification depends on width, thickness, alloy content, processing and coating. Preferential free-trade-agreement rates may also apply, but where the normal rate is already Free they do not create an additional tariff saving.

## 4.2 Effective impact on fabricator margins

### Direct ordinary-duty effect

For a shipment with a customs value of NZ$1 million:

\[
\text{Customs duty}=NZ\$1,000,000\times0\%=NZ\$0
\]

Therefore:

- ordinary tariffs neither protect local fabricators from imported raw sections and plate;
- nor impose a direct input-cost penalty on those importing raw steel;
- GST is normally recoverable by GST-registered businesses and should not be treated as a permanent margin cost.

The effective tariff impact on normal raw-steel margins is consequently approximately **zero percentage points**.

### Counterfactual sensitivity

Steel & Tube reported FY2023 infrastructure gross margin of **22.0%** and group gross-margin dollars of NZ$850 per tonne ([FY23 results](https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20%20FY23%20Results%20Presentation%202023.pdf)). Although this is not a pure fabricator benchmark, it illustrates tariff sensitivity.

If a hypothetical 5% tariff applied and tariffed steel represented 50% of contract revenue:

\[
5\%\times50\%=2.5\%\text{ of revenue}
\]

If the cost could not be passed through, a 22% gross margin would fall to:

\[
22.0\%-2.5\%=19.5\%
\]

Relative gross-margin reduction:

\[
2.5/22.0=11.4\%
\]

If virtually all of a distributor’s 78% cost of sales were exposed:

\[
5\%\times78\%=3.9\%\text{ of revenue}
\]

\[
22.0\%-3.9\%=18.1\%
\]

This is a scenario, not New Zealand’s observed ordinary tariff outcome.

### More material border risks

1. **Anti-dumping or countervailing duties:** These are exporter-, country- and product-specific and sit outside the ordinary tariff rate.
2. **Exchange rates and freight:** With no tariff buffer, landed steel prices transmit global mill pricing, NZD movements and shipping costs directly.
3. **Compliance:** Imported structural products must still meet New Zealand standards, traceability and certification requirements. Compliance failures can create rework, delay and warranty costs even where tariff is zero.

Customs data released in response to an OIA request show that HS 7208, 7211 and 7216 imports came from a wide range of countries during 2020–24, but material volumes were concentrated among Australia and Asian suppliers ([NZ Customs OIA dataset, extracted 2 September 2025](https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/yyshc4tn/oia-25-677-iron-and-non-alloy-steel-imports-2020-to-2024.pdf)).

---

# 5. Three major steel-intensive infrastructure projects

## 5.1 Auckland City Rail Link

- **Project:** 3.45 km twin-tunnel urban railway, two new underground stations and major work at Waitematā/Britomart and Maungawhau.
- **Cost:** Approximately NZ$5.5 billion.
- **Reported steel demand:** **29,595 tonnes of steel** across CRL structures.
- **Construction-grade detail:** New Zealand Steel separately reported approximately **25,000 tonnes of locally produced reinforcing steel** over three to four years.
- **Narrow structural-fabrication interpretation:** The 29,595-tonne figure includes reinforcement and is therefore an upper bound for this report’s narrow structural scope. If the 25,000 tonnes of local reinforcement were wholly contained within it, the residual would be:

\[
29,595-25,000=4,595\text{ tonnes}
\]

This 4,595-tonne residual is only a rough indicator—not a verified fabricated structural-steel quantity—because the two sources may use different system boundaries and may include other reinforcement.
- **Timeline as published:** New Zealand Steel’s project announcement stated completion was due in **2024**. That was the published schedule in the source and should not be treated as confirmation of actual completion.
- **Sources:** SESOC conference paper published in **2023**, [“Sustainability in Design and Construction”](https://www.sesoc.org.nz/static/Documents/Conference/2023/SESOC2023-0043-Page-43-98-Page-Ethan-43-98-Page-Ethan.pdf); [New Zealand Steel project announcement](https://www.nzsteel.co.nz/news-and-media/local-steel-for-aucklands-city-rail-link/); [Infrastructure Sustainability Council project description](https://www.iscouncil.org/project/city-rail-link-contract-3-stations-and-tunnels/).

## 5.2 Te Kaha / One New Zealand Stadium, Christchurch

- **Project:** Large covered multi-use stadium and associated civic infrastructure.
- **Steel demand:** Approximately **13,000 tonnes in total**; more than 8,000 tonnes had been installed by September 2024.
- **Timeline:** On track in September 2024 for an **April 2026 opening**.
- **Market significance:**

\[
13,000/100,000=13\%
\]

The project’s total steel requirement is equivalent to roughly 13% of one year’s normal national structural-fabrication output, although procurement and fabrication are spread across several years.
- **Source:** The Press, project update published **19 September 2024**, [“More than half of the steel at Te Kaha installed”](https://www.thepress.co.nz/nz-news/350423579/more-half-steel-te-kaha-installed).

## 5.3 Te Ara Pekapeka / Peacocke transport infrastructure, Hamilton

- **Project:** Major bridge and transport connection supporting the Peacocke growth area.
- **Steel demand:** Reported **3,060 tonnes of structural steel**, including 36 steel girder segments. Approximately 200 tonnes of weathering/Corten steel was fabricated by PFS Engineering.
- **Completion/status:** Reported as a completed project in the **3 September 2024** “by the numbers” update.
- **Market significance:**

\[
3,060/100,000=3.06\%
\]

The project represented approximately 3% of a normal year’s national fabricated structural-steel output.
- **Source:** Waikato Business News, published **3 September 2024**, [“Te Ara Pekapeka—by the numbers”](https://wbn.co.nz/2024/09/03/te-ara-pekapeka-by-the-numbers/).

### Combined order-of-magnitude demand

Using the reported totals:

\[
29,595+13,000+3,060=45,655\text{ tonnes}
\]

This is equivalent to about:

\[
45,655/100,000=45.7\%
\]

of one normal year’s national output. However, this comparison overstates like-for-like structural fabrication because CRL’s figure includes substantial reinforcing steel and all three projects span multiple years.

Using the rough CRL non-reinforcing residual instead:

\[
4,595+13,000+3,060=20,655\text{ tonnes}
\]

or approximately 20.7% of one year’s sector output. The true comparable structural quantity lies between these interpretations.

---

# 6. Strategic risks and opportunities

## 6.1 Risk 1: Zero-tariff import exposure and global landed-cost volatility

**Risk.** Free ordinary tariffs on HS 7207–7216 mean local fabricators receive no tariff protection against raw steel or competing imported products. Margins are exposed to:

- NZD depreciation;
- Asian and Australian mill prices;
- shipping disruption;
- inventory write-downs when global prices fall;
- project bids signed before input-price escalation.

The exposure is demonstrated by the gap between Steel & Tube’s FY2023 and FY2024 performance: FY2024 volume fell 21% and revenue fell 18.7%, from NZ$589.1 million to NZ$479.1 million ([Steel & Tube FY24 results, 26 August 2024](https://steelandtube.co.nz/investor/media/2024/steel-tube-fy24-results-year-ended-30-june-2024)).

**Opportunity/response.** Fabricators can protect margins through escalation clauses, shorter quotation-validity periods, hedging, diversified mill sourcing, common material specifications and higher-value detailing, coating and erection services.

## 6.2 Risk 2: Supply-chain concentration and compliance risk

**Risk.** New Zealand depends heavily on imported plate and sections. Customs’ 2020–24 data for HS 7208, 7211 and 7216 show supply concentrated among a limited number of major origins, especially Australia and Asian mills. A mill outage, shipping interruption or trade-remedy action can therefore delay projects.

Imported fabricated steel also creates certification, traceability and quality risk. SCNZ noted concerns over poor procurement decisions and offshore product quality in its [September 2018 update](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/SCNZ_Industry-Update_September-2018.pdf).

**Opportunity/response.**

- Maintain dual-source approvals and strategic stocks of standard sections.
- Use Steel Fabrication Certification as a differentiator. By September 2023, 65 certified firms represented **92.5% of sector output** ([SCNZ September 2023](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf)).
- Promote local fabrication on schedule certainty, standards compliance, seismic detailing and lower rework risk rather than attempting to compete solely on headline steel price.

## 6.3 Risk 3—and the largest opportunity: pipeline timing versus excess capacity

**Near-term risk.** By September 2023 the sector had expanded capacity to approximately **150,000 tonnes**, while annual output remained about **100,000 tonnes**. That implied roughly 50,000 tonnes of unused physical capacity on the rounded figures. In FY2024, Steel & Tube reported:

- commercial sales down 15%;
- non-residential consents down 15%;
- infrastructure sales down 30% because of project delays and lower government spending.

Source: [Steel & Tube FY24 results presentation](https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20FY24%20Results%20Presentation.pdf), published **August 2024**.

This creates price competition, under-recovery of factory overhead and pressure on less-capitalised firms.

**Long-run opportunity.** The same spare capacity gives New Zealand an ability to absorb a larger infrastructure and resilience programme without immediately resorting to offshore fabrication. Key demand drivers include:

- rail and urban-transit investment;
- bridges and roads;
- seismic strengthening;
- electricity-grid enhancement;
- replacement of assets damaged by severe weather;
- stadiums, hospitals and other complex civic buildings.

The New Zealand Infrastructure Commission’s [Infrastructure Resources Study](https://tewaihanga.govt.nz/media/ayxfshpg/infrastructure-resources-study.pdf) identifies steel as one of four critical physical resources for infrastructure and highlights the importance of transport constraints, supply responsiveness and embodied carbon.

**Required strategic response.**

1. Pursue early contractor involvement and design-assist work so steel solutions are selected before materials become locked in.
2. Expand automated cutting, drilling, welding and digital traceability to improve labour productivity.
3. Use the sector’s spare capacity collaboratively through subcontracting and multi-shift production.
4. Develop lower-carbon procurement propositions, including efficient design, local fabrication, reusable members and auditable embodied-carbon data.
5. Avoid adding further fixed capacity until funded—not merely announced—projects provide sufficient workload visibility.

---

# 7. Overall assessment

As of 2024, New Zealand structural-steel fabrication was a **fragmented, locally capable but cyclically underutilised** market. The clearest observable metrics were approximately **4,450 Stats NZ employees**, about **100,000 tonnes of annual fabricated output**, and approximately **150,000 tonnes of installed annual capacity**.

The market did not lack physical capability. Its central problem was utilisation: capacity investment and employment had outpaced stable tonnage, while the 2024 construction slowdown delayed infrastructure and reduced commercial demand. At the same time, City Rail Link, Te Kaha and Te Ara Pekapeka showed that individual projects can absorb material fractions of annual domestic output.

Ordinary raw-steel tariffs were not a meaningful margin factor because the relevant Chapter 72 rates were generally zero. The economically significant exposures were instead global steel prices, currency, freight, supplier concentration, procurement timing and the risk of competing imported fabrication.

Finally, two requested data points cannot be represented as official statistics without qualification:

- Stats NZ/MBIE do not publish a clean annual C2221 revenue series for 2018–24 in the evidence available.
- Private-company disclosure does not support a verified top-five ranking by 2023 revenue.

Any analysis presenting precise annual market revenue or a definitive private-company revenue league table would therefore rely on paid commercial estimates, confidential company information or unsupported extrapolation rather than publicly verifiable Stats NZ, MBIE or Companies Office evidence.

ARRAY TECHNOLOGIES: SEGMENT PORTFOLIO AND GROSS-MARGIN DIFFERENTIAL

Executive summary

Array Technologies’ segment economics diverged sharply between early 2023 and the nine months ended September 30, 2024:

• In Q1 2023, Array Legacy Operations’ gross margin was 26.2%, only 1.4 percentage points above STI Operations’ 24.7%.
• For the first nine months of 2023, the two segments were effectively at parity: 26.9% for Legacy versus 26.6% for STI, a gap of just 0.3 percentage point.
• For the first nine months of 2024, Legacy’s margin rose to 41.8%, while STI’s fell to 15.1%. The differential consequently widened to 26.7 percentage points.
• STI contributed 28.2% of segment revenue in the first nine months of 2024 but only 12.4% of gross profit. Legacy generated approximately 72% of revenue and 88% of gross profit.

The evidence therefore points to a two-part portfolio. Legacy is the economic engine, benefiting from stronger operational execution, U.S. manufacturing incentives and a differentiated linked-row tracker platform. STI continues to provide strategic value through international reach, local manufacturing and a dual-row product suited to irregular sites, but by 2024 it was materially diluting consolidated margin.

The $162 million STI goodwill impairment recorded in Q3 2024 reinforces that the acquisition had not delivered its originally anticipated economic value on the expected timetable. It does not prove the acquisition was strategically mistaken: STI materially expanded Array’s addressable geography and product set. It does show that Array’s integration priorities should shift from geographic expansion alone toward pricing discipline, product and component standardization, procurement leverage, manufacturing utilization and selective allocation of capital to markets and projects capable of earning acceptable margins.

1. Method and comparability

Gross margin is calculated as:

Gross margin = Segment gross profit ÷ Segment revenue

The analysis uses GAAP segment revenue and gross profit rather than consolidated adjusted gross margin. Dollar figures are in thousands unless stated otherwise.

Later filings recast some 2023 segment gross-profit amounts. For example, the original Q1 2023 filing reported Legacy gross profit of $83.474 million, whereas the Q1 2024 comparative table reports $79.835 million. This report uses the later comparative figures where available because they are the most recently presented segment data. STI’s Q1 2023 gross profit remained $17.705 million. The revised Q1 2023 segment table is available in Array’s 2024 Q1 filing: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000049/R35.htm. The original filing can be reviewed at https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072123000099/R34.htm.

Quarterly Q4 2023 figures are derived by subtracting the nine-month results from full-year 2023 results. Accordingly, Q4 is useful for trend interpretation but is not a separately disclosed quarterly segment table.

2. Gross-margin calculations

A. Quarterly progression

Period             Legacy revenue  Legacy GP  Legacy margin   STI revenue  STI GP   STI margin   Legacy advantage
Q1 2023              $305.204       $79.835      26.2%          $71.569    $17.705     24.7%          1.4 pp
Q2 2023               345.261       102.950      29.8%          162.464     43.452     26.7%          3.1 pp
Q3 2023               244.857        58.233      23.8%          105.581     29.146     27.6%         -3.8 pp
Q4 2023, derived      277.505        76.586      27.6%           64.110      7.643     11.9%         15.7 pp
Q1 2024               114.381        49.086      42.9%           39.022      6.004     15.4%         27.5 pp
Q2 2024               185.160        77.306      41.8%           70.606      8.647     12.2%         29.5 pp
Q3 2024               160.266        65.726      41.0%           71.140     12.589     17.7%         23.3 pp

Illustrative calculations:

• Q1 2023 Legacy margin = $79.835 million ÷ $305.204 million = 26.16%
• Q1 2023 STI margin = $17.705 million ÷ $71.569 million = 24.74%
• Q1 differential = 26.16% − 24.74% = 1.42 percentage points

• Q3 2024 Legacy margin = $65.726 million ÷ $160.266 million = 41.01%
• Q3 2024 STI margin = $12.589 million ÷ $71.140 million = 17.70%
• Q3 differential = 41.01% − 17.70% = 23.31 percentage points

The Q2 2023 and Q2 2024 inputs come from Array’s six-month segment table: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000062/R35.htm. Q3 2024 and comparative Q3 2023 data come from the September 2024 segment table: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R36.htm. Full-year 2023 segment totals used to derive Q4 are reported here: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000011/R28.htm.

B. Cumulative comparison

Period             Legacy revenue  Legacy GP  Legacy margin   STI revenue  STI GP   STI margin   Gap
Q1 2023              $305.204       $79.835      26.2%          $71.569    $17.705     24.7%       1.4 pp
6M 2023                650.465       182.785      28.1%          234.033     61.157     26.1%       2.0 pp
9M 2023                895.322       241.019      26.9%          339.614     90.303     26.6%       0.3 pp
FY 2023              1,172.827       317.605      27.1%          403.724     97.946     24.3%       2.8 pp
Q1 2024                114.381        49.086      42.9%           39.022      6.004     15.4%      27.5 pp
6M 2024                299.541       126.392      42.2%          109.628     14.651     13.4%      28.8 pp
9M 2024                459.807       192.118      41.8%          180.768     27.240     15.1%      26.7 pp

Nine-month 2024 calculations:

• Legacy = $192.118 million ÷ $459.807 million = 41.78%
• STI = $27.240 million ÷ $180.768 million = 15.07%
• Differential = 41.78% − 15.07% = 26.71 percentage points

Year-over-year changes:

• Legacy margin: 41.78% − 26.92% = +14.86 percentage points
• STI margin: 15.07% − 26.59% = −11.52 percentage points
• Expansion in the segment gap: 26.71 − 0.33 = 26.38 percentage points

Thus, almost all of the widening came from opposing movements: a substantial Legacy improvement combined with a substantial STI deterioration.

3. Evolution and persistence of the performance gap

2023: broad economic parity, followed by a late-year warning

During the first three quarters of 2023, the two operations generated similar margins. STI even outperformed Legacy in Q3, at 27.6% versus 23.8%. The nine-month difference was only 0.3 percentage point, indicating that STI was not structurally inferior throughout that period.

The deterioration began visibly in derived Q4 2023, when STI’s margin fell to approximately 11.9% while Legacy remained at 27.6%. Because STI’s quarterly revenue also fell to about $64.1 million, the decline is consistent with a combination of unfavorable project mix, pricing and reduced absorption of operating or supply-chain costs. Array states more generally that gross profit varies with volume, average selling prices, product and geographic mix, commodity costs, logistics, warranty costs and tax incentives.

2024: a sustained, not transitory, divergence

The gap persisted in every reported quarter of 2024:

• Q1: 27.5 points
• Q2: 29.5 points
• Q3: 23.3 points

Legacy remained above 41% in all three quarters. STI remained between 12% and 18%. The modest narrowing in Q3 came from STI’s improvement to 17.7%, not from convergence toward Legacy economics.

The cumulative figures remove some quarter-to-quarter project timing noise. At 9M 2024, Legacy’s 41.8% margin was approximately 2.8 times STI’s 15.1% margin. This duration and scale make it unlikely that the differential was solely the result of one unusually profitable Legacy project or one weak STI shipment.

4. Strategic value and operating efficiency by business unit

Array Legacy Operations

Legacy’s 2024 performance indicates superior gross-level economic efficiency. It generated $192.1 million of gross profit from $459.8 million of revenue in the first nine months, versus STI’s $27.2 million from $180.8 million.

Several competitive and policy advantages help explain the result:

• Array’s flagship DuraTrack design allows one motor to drive multiple rows through articulated driveline joints. The company argues this results in lower assembly and maintenance costs and greater reliability than one-motor-per-row alternatives. Its core U.S. linked-row patent runs to 2030: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072125000023/arry-20241231.htm.
• Array cited operational execution and optimization of U.S. Section 45X benefits for torque tubes and structural fasteners as drivers of 2024 margin performance. Its Q3 release reported consolidated adjusted gross-margin improvement driven by these benefits and execution: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000073/exhibit9912024q3pressrelea.htm.
• Domestic-content demand and U.S. manufacturing incentives strengthen the value proposition for Array’s domestic supply chain and can support both customer economics and supplier cost recovery.
• Legacy’s ability to hold gross margin around 41% despite substantially lower revenue suggests good pricing, procurement and project-selection discipline, although some of that margin resilience is policy-supported rather than purely organic.

Legacy should therefore be viewed as Array’s principal cash and gross-profit engine. Its high margin supports continued investment in DuraTrack, domestic content, automation, resilient-component sourcing and software or service additions that deepen customer switching costs.

STI Operations

STI’s strategic value is different from its current financial efficiency.

Array acquired STI to gain:

• Leadership and manufacturing capability in Spain and Brazil.
• Access to international customers and markets where local content and supply-chain constraints made organic entry difficult.
• A lower-cost dual-row tracker, now branded STI H250, suited to irregular boundaries, fragmented sites and areas with lower wind or snow requirements.
• Greater product breadth alongside DuraTrack and OmniTrack.

At acquisition, Array described STI as having a top-three position in Spain and the number-one position in Brazil, with manufacturing in both countries. The acquisition created design, engineering and manufacturing capacity across three continents: https://ir.arraytechinc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/array-technologies-completes-acquisition-sti-norland. Array’s later product description confirms that STI added a one-motor, two-row tracker designed for irregular and fragmented sites: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072125000023/arry-20241231.htm.

These capabilities expand Array’s addressable market and reduce dependence on the U.S. utility-scale market. They also help the company compete with Nextracker, PV Hardware and GameChange Solar across more site conditions and geographies.

However, STI’s 2024 margins indicate weak conversion of those strategic assets into gross profit. The segment produced 28.2% of 9M 2024 segment revenue but only 12.4% of gross profit:

• STI revenue share = $180.768 million ÷ $640.575 million = 28.22%
• STI gross-profit share = $27.240 million ÷ $219.358 million = 12.42%

This mismatch means STI was materially dilutive to consolidated margin. If the revenue mix remained unchanged but STI earned Legacy’s 41.78% margin, its hypothetical gross profit would be:

$180.768 million × 41.78% = approximately $75.5 million

Actual STI gross profit was $27.2 million, implying an approximately $48.3 million gross-profit shortfall relative to Legacy’s margin rate. This is not a forecast of attainable synergy—products, countries and incentives differ—but it illustrates the economic scale of the portfolio imbalance.

5. Competitive-positioning implications

The contrasting margins suggest that Array is strongest where product differentiation, domestic manufacturing policy and supply-chain execution reinforce one another.

In the U.S.-oriented Legacy business, Array can compete on more than tracker price. Reliability, lower motor count, installation costs, maintenance economics, patent protection, domestic content and 45X-supported production all contribute to customer value and margin resilience. That positioning appears to have enabled Array to preserve strong gross profitability even as 9M Legacy revenue fell 48.6% year over year:

($459.807 million − $895.322 million) ÷ $895.322 million = −48.6%

STI operates in a more internationally exposed portfolio, particularly Brazil and Europe, where currency movements, financing costs, local energy pricing and project delays can exert greater pressure on volumes and pricing. Array specifically cited softness in Brazil and expected both U.S. and international volumes and average selling prices to be lower than in 2023: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000073/exhibit9912024q3pressrelea.htm.

STI’s lower margin does not necessarily mean its tracker technology is uncompetitive. Its 2023 margin parity and Q3 2023 outperformance show that the unit can generate attractive project economics under favorable conditions. Rather, the 2024 data suggest that STI’s competitive position was less defensible economically: international reach and a differentiated site-use case were not enough to offset adverse regional pricing, volume, currency and mix conditions.

The portfolio therefore gives Array wider market coverage but with uneven earnings quality. Legacy supplies economic depth; STI supplies geographic and application breadth.

6. What the differential says about the STI acquisition

The original acquisition case combined strategic expansion with expected financial accretion. Array said the transaction would increase exposure to international markets and be significantly accretive to margins and earnings before synergies. STI had approximately €200 million of 2020 revenue and €43 million of EBITDA, and the announced consideration was approximately €570 million: https://ir.arraytechinc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/array-technologies-acquire-sti-norland.

By September 2024, that financial thesis had come under pressure. Array recorded a $162 million STI goodwill impairment after updating long-term projections and evaluating execution risk. STI goodwill fell from $365.9 million at the start of 2024 to $181.1 million at September 30 after foreign-currency translation and the impairment: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/arry-20240930.htm.

The impairment is important for three reasons:

1. It independently corroborates the margin evidence. Management and its valuation specialist concluded that STI’s expected future cash flows supported a value below its carrying amount.

2. It shows that strategic value did not fully translate into the originally recorded acquisition value. Geographic presence, products and customer relationships remain useful, but their expected financial returns weakened.

3. It raises the required hurdle for future acquisitions. Array should distinguish between buying market access and buying durable economic advantage. International revenue growth alone is insufficient if local pricing, foreign-exchange exposure and project economics produce structurally lower margins.

The acquisition should not be judged solely on STI’s standalone margin. Some acquired technology, customer access or engineering capability may benefit the wider company without appearing in STI gross profit. OmniTrack and cross-portfolio product development, for example, can strengthen Array’s total offering. Nevertheless, the persistent 2024 gap and goodwill impairment show that such benefits had not yet offset STI’s standalone economic underperformance.

7. Integration and portfolio priorities

The margin analysis points to five priorities.

First, transfer Legacy operating discipline without erasing STI’s local strengths.

Array should apply common project-bidding thresholds, contract risk controls, supplier scorecards and gross-margin accountability across both segments. STI’s local customer relationships and manufacturing footprint should be preserved where they confer access, but autonomy should not prevent rigorous portfolio-wide returns management.

Second, accelerate procurement and engineering standardization.

The largest credible operational opportunity is to standardize compatible steel, fasteners, controls and other components across DuraTrack, STI H250 and OmniTrack. Shared specifications and global sourcing can increase purchasing leverage, reduce inventory complexity and improve manufacturing utilization. Product standardization must remain selective because STI’s value partly derives from adaptation to local terrain and construction practices.

Third, manage Brazil as a return problem, not merely a growth market.

The Q3 2024 release identified continuing softness in Brazil. Array should price explicitly for currency, inflation, tariffs and financing volatility; shorten quote-validity periods; use contractual pass-through mechanisms where possible; and avoid low-return volume intended only to protect market share. Local manufacturing is valuable only if its utilization and cost base remain competitive.

Fourth, direct innovation toward whole-project economics.

STI H250’s fit for fragmented sites and OmniTrack’s terrain-following capabilities can reduce grading, permitting and civil-work requirements. Array should sell these products on total installed and lifecycle cost rather than hardware price alone. Demonstrable customer savings provide the clearest path to recovering margin in internationally competitive bids.

Fifth, allocate capital according to risk-adjusted gross-profit contribution.

Legacy merits continued investment because it currently generates substantially more gross profit per dollar of revenue. STI investment should be milestone-based—tied to margin recovery, cash generation, order quality and synergy realization. Divestiture or withdrawal is not compelled by the evidence, but persistent mid-teen margins would justify rationalizing countries, customers or product configurations that fail to cover portfolio-level capital costs.

8. Overall assessment

From Q1 2023 through September 2023, Array’s two segments were economically complementary as well as strategically complementary: margins were close, and STI occasionally outperformed. That balance broke in late 2023 and became pronounced throughout 2024.

By the first nine months of 2024:

• Legacy margin had increased approximately 14.9 points year over year to 41.8%.
• STI margin had declined approximately 11.5 points to 15.1%.
• The cumulative margin differential had widened from 0.3 to 26.7 points.
• STI supplied more than one-quarter of revenue but only about one-eighth of gross profit.

The result is a portfolio with valuable strategic breadth but highly concentrated earnings power. Legacy demonstrates Array’s strongest competitive advantages: differentiated technology, operational execution and alignment with U.S. manufacturing incentives. STI gives Array international reach, local manufacturing and access to project types that Legacy alone might not address, but its 2024 economics reveal weaker pricing power and greater exposure to regional market volatility.

Accordingly, the STI acquisition’s strategic rationale remains credible, but its financial validation is incomplete. The sustained margin differential and impairment indicate that Array’s next stage should prioritize integration quality and economic returns over further footprint expansion. Portfolio optimization depends on converting STI’s geographic and product assets into acceptable gross margins—through disciplined project selection, shared procurement, product standardization and locally appropriate pricing—while continuing to invest in the high-return Legacy platform.

# Protective Collar Delta Ranges

## Executive answer

Sold Call Delta: **0.20 to 0.30** (reason: this is a practical range for retaining meaningful upside while collecting enough premium to subsidize the put. Use approximately 0.20 when keeping the stock/upside participation is the priority; approximately 0.30 when premium income and hedge funding are more important.)

Bought Put Delta: **−0.20 to −0.30**—quoted by magnitude as **20 to 30 delta** (reason: this generally provides meaningful protection without paying for near-the-money insurance. Approximately −0.30 gives a higher floor and responds more strongly to an initial decline; approximately −0.20 is cheaper but leaves a larger deductible.)

Symmetric vs Asymmetric: **Prefer objective-based, usually asymmetric construction rather than mechanically matching deltas. Select the put strike from the maximum loss or protection floor you need, then select the call strike that provides an acceptable amount of upside and/or finances the put.** For a zero-premium collar, equal deltas are neither necessary nor normally sufficient.

A useful default for a 30–90 day collar is:

- Short call: **20–30 delta**
- Long put: **20–30 delta by absolute value**
- Practical starting combination: **short 25–30 delta call and long 20–25 delta put**
- If stronger protection is required: move the put toward **30–40 delta**, accepting either a debit or a closer, higher-delta call.

These are starting ranges, not universal industry standards.

---

## 1. Delta for the sold call

### Recommended range: 0.20–0.30

The choice represents a direct trade-off:

| Call delta | General interpretation | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.15–0.20 | Farther OTM | More upside room; lower approximate probability of expiring ITM | Less premium to fund the put |
| 0.20–0.30 | Balanced collar range | Meaningful premium with some upside retained | Moderate probability of losing the shares/upside |
| 0.30–0.40 | Income/protection emphasis | More premium; can finance a higher-strike put | Lower upside cap and greater assignment exposure |

A 0.30-delta call is commonly interpreted as having approximately a 30% risk-neutral probability of expiring in the money, but this is only a shortcut. Delta’s primary definition is the option’s price sensitivity. Actual assignment probability can differ because of dividends, early exercise, volatility changes, and the difference between risk-neutral and real-world probabilities.

Fidelity emphasizes that covered-call strike selection is subjective: an investor who wants to retain the stock should choose a lower probability of assignment, while an investor willing to sell should choose a higher probability. Fidelity also illustrates an 18-delta OTM call as having approximately an 18% probability of finishing ITM ([Fidelity](https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/investment-products/options/selecting-strike-price-expiration-date); [Fidelity covered-call materials](https://www.fidelity.com/bin-public/060_www_fidelity_com/documents/WritingCoveredCalls_Webinar.pdf)).

### 0.20 versus 0.30

- **Use approximately 0.20** if the stock has substantial expected upside, embedded capital gains, an upcoming catalyst, or a strong preference against assignment.
- **Use approximately 0.30** if the primary objective is financing protection or generating income and the investor would genuinely accept selling at the call strike.
- For a true protective collar, the call strike should also be an acceptable sale price. Delta should not override that requirement.

---

## 2. Delta for the bought put

### Recommended range: −0.20 to −0.30

Put delta should be stated with a negative sign, although traders often say “20-delta put” to mean a delta near −0.20.

| Put delta magnitude | General role | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.10–0.20 | Catastrophe or tail hedge | Relatively inexpensive; preserves more expected return | Large unprotected first loss |
| 0.20–0.30 | Balanced protection | Meaningful response to a decline and a usable floor | Moderate insurance cost |
| 0.30–0.40 | Tight protection | Higher floor and stronger initial hedge | Expensive; may require a closer call |
| Approximately 0.50 | Near-ATM insurance | Very tight protection | High premium and substantially reduced net stock exposure |

A **30-delta put does not mean protection begins 30% below the stock price**. Delta is not percentage distance. It measures option-price sensitivity and is sometimes used as an approximate probability metric. The strike corresponding to −0.30 could be 3%, 8%, or considerably more below spot depending on time to expiration, implied volatility, interest rates, and dividends.

The Options Industry Council notes that stock price, time remaining, and implied volatility all influence delta, and that delta is only sometimes interpreted as approximate probability of expiring ITM ([OIC delta guide](https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/delta)).

### Choosing between −0.20 and −0.30

- **Approximately −0.30:** preferable when capital preservation is the primary goal. It creates a higher floor and the put gains delta more quickly as the stock declines toward the strike.
- **Approximately −0.20:** preferable when the investor is willing to absorb a larger initial drawdown in exchange for lower hedge cost.
- **Approximately −0.10 to −0.15:** appropriate mainly for disaster insurance, not for protecting against ordinary corrections.

The most defensible process is to choose the put from the dollar loss you can tolerate, not from delta alone. If a $100 stock must be protected below $95, the $95 put is the relevant contract regardless of whether its delta happens to be −0.22 or −0.35.

---

## 3. Symmetric versus asymmetric deltas

## Recommendation: asymmetric and objective-based

There is no requirement that the call and put have equal absolute deltas. A collar with a +0.25 call delta and −0.25 put delta is visually “symmetric” in delta terms, but it is not necessarily:

- Equidistant in strike,
- Equal in premium,
- Equal in volatility exposure,
- Zero-cost,
- Or equally likely to touch each strike.

A collar’s initial position delta is approximately:

\[
\Delta_{\text{collar}}
= 1.00-\Delta_{\text{call}}-\lvert\Delta_{\text{put}}\rvert
\]

For example, with a 0.25 short call and −0.20 long put:

\[
1.00-0.25-0.20=0.55
\]

The collar initially retains approximately 55 share-equivalents of directional exposure per 100 shares, all else equal.

### Why zero-cost collars are often asymmetric

Equity options commonly exhibit downside volatility skew: OTM puts may carry higher implied volatility than comparably OTM calls. Consequently, an equal-delta put can cost more than the equal-delta call produces. To establish a zero-premium collar, the investor may need to:

- Sell a higher-delta/closer call;
- Buy a lower-delta/farther put;
- Accept a net debit;
- Use different maturities; or
- Convert the hedge to a put-spread collar by selling a still-lower-strike put.

AQR describes the usual institutional construction as choosing the desired protection first—such as a three-month put struck at 95% of spot—and then selecting the call whose premium most closely matches the put premium. That is a **premium-matched**, not delta-matched, process ([AQR, “Risk and Return of Equity Index Collar Strategies”](https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Journal-Articles/Risk-and-Return.pdf)).

### Practical hierarchy

1. **Set the protection floor:** maximum tolerable loss.
2. **Choose expiration:** how long protection is needed.
3. **Choose the call cap:** minimum acceptable sale price.
4. **Inspect deltas:** verify assignment risk and initial net exposure.
5. **Inspect executable bid/ask prices:** determine actual debit or credit.
6. **Adjust only if necessary:** move the call, put, or maturity to reach the desired budget.

Thus, **sell 0.25–0.30 delta and buy 0.20–0.25 delta** is a reasonable zero-cost starting search, but it is not a guaranteed zero-cost formula.

---

## 4. Percentage distance from the current price

### Fixed percentages are simple but not risk-consistent

“Sell the 10% OTM call and buy the 10% OTM put” is easy to administer, but 10% has very different meanings across stocks and market regimes.

For example:

- On a low-volatility utility stock, a 10% OTM one-month option may have a very small delta.
- On a high-volatility technology or biotechnology stock, it may have substantial delta.
- A 10% move over one month is very different from a 10% move over one year.

Therefore:

- **Use percentage distance when the investment mandate is stated as a specific floor and cap.**
- **Use delta when trying to maintain a more consistent probability/risk profile across volatility regimes.**
- Use both where possible: define an acceptable floor/cap in percentages, then inspect the resulting deltas and premiums.

Allspring specifically argues that delta-based strikes adapt better to changing implied volatility: when volatility rises, a fixed target delta moves farther OTM; when volatility falls, it moves closer to ATM. This helps keep the approximate probability of finishing ITM more stable than a fixed-percentage rule ([Allspring/Cboe](https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/whitepapers/Allspring_options-based-downside-protection.pdf)).

### Institutional fixed-percentage example

The Cboe S&P 500 95-110 Collar Index:

- Holds the S&P 500;
- Buys a **5% OTM quarterly SPX put**;
- Sells a **10% OTM monthly SPX call**.

This is explicitly asymmetric in both strike distance and maturity, and it is not designed as an exact zero-premium collar ([Cboe CLL methodology](https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/newcollardescriptionoct1909.pdf)).

That institutional benchmark demonstrates that “5% down and 10% up” can be a legitimate policy allocation. It does not establish that 10%/10% is optimal.

---

## 5. Example collar

The following is a theoretical illustration, not a live option quote.

### Assumptions

- Stock: **$100**
- Position: **100 shares**
- Expiration: **45 days**
- Interest rate: **4.5%**
- Dividend yield: **1.0%**
- Put implied volatility: **25%**
- Call implied volatility: **22%**
- European Black–Scholes pricing, before commissions and bid/ask spreads

The higher put volatility illustrates a modest downside skew.

### Example Collar

Stock: **$100**

Sell call: **$105 strike, Delta +0.295; approximately $1.383 premium received**

Buy put: **$95 strike, Delta −0.249; approximately $1.361 premium paid**

Net credit/debit:

\[
\$1.383-\$1.361=\$0.022 \text{ credit per share}
\]

\[
\$0.022 \times 100 = \$2.20 \text{ theoretical net credit}
\]

Therefore:

**Net credit: approximately $2.20 per 100-share collar, before spreads, commissions, and fees.**

Initial collar delta:

\[
1.000-0.295-0.249=0.456
\]

The package initially has approximately **+45.6 share-equivalents of delta per 100 shares**.

### Expiration outcomes

Ignoring the small credit:

- **Maximum stock exit value:** $105
- **Minimum stock exit value:** $95
- **Maximum gain from $100:** approximately $5.02 per share, or $502
- **Maximum loss from $100:** approximately $4.98 per share, or $498

The calculations are:

\[
\text{Maximum gain}
=(105-100)+0.022
=\$5.022 \text{ per share}
\]

\[
\text{Maximum loss}
=(100-95)-0.022
=\$4.978 \text{ per share}
\]

This example is nearly symmetric in percentage distance—5% below and 5% above—but not in delta. The call has about 29.5 delta while the put has about 24.9 delta because the assumed call and put volatility inputs, rates, dividends, and strike positions differ.

Actual listed options will rarely produce an exact zero because strikes are discrete and trades execute at bid/ask prices. A “zero-cost” collar generally means approximately zero **initial premium**, not zero economic cost: the investor pays through foregone upside, spreads, taxes, and potentially unfavorable relative option pricing.

---

## 6. Institutional collar structures

Institutional investors generally define collars around portfolio objectives rather than a universal delta pair.

### A. Traditional index collar

Structure:

- Long diversified equities;
- Long index put;
- Short index call;
- Often same or related notional amounts.

Institutions frequently use index options rather than options on every stock because index options provide operational simplicity and broad portfolio hedging. Basis risk remains if the portfolio does not track the index closely.

The Options Industry Council’s pension-fund materials describe the protective collar as purchasing index puts and financing them through short index calls, with the put and call normally sharing an expiration but having different strikes. The structure trades away upside in exchange for a portfolio safety net ([OIC, “ERISA Pension Funds & Listed Options”](https://www.optionseducation.org/getmedia/7f79f663-fef8-4c84-ac81-534cebbee9b7/erisa2001.pdf)).

### B. Premium-matched zero-cost collar

Typical process:

1. Set the put strike from the desired protection floor.
2. Price that put using executable quotes.
3. Find the call strike whose bid approximately pays the put’s ask.

This is the most relevant institutional model for a simple zero-cost collar. It naturally produces asymmetric deltas because the option volatility surface is asymmetric.

### C. Fixed-percentage benchmark collar

Cboe’s 95-110 collar uses:

- Quarterly 5% OTM puts;
- Monthly 10% OTM calls.

Cboe states that there is no unique “best” collar because investors occupy different risk-return comfort zones. Its benchmark was selected to retain a reasonable portion of upside while placing an intermediate risk profile between equities and cash ([Cboe](https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/newcollardescriptionoct1909.pdf)).

### D. Put-spread collar

Many institutional and fund products use:

- Long protective put;
- Short lower-strike put;
- Short upside call.

Selling the lower put reduces the cost but means protection stops below that strike. Cboe’s CLLZ benchmark, for example, buys a monthly 2.5% OTM put, sells a 5% OTM put, and sells an OTM call selected to pay for the put spread ([Cboe methodology](https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/governance/Cboe_Zero-Cost_Put_Spread_Collar_Indices_Methodology.pdf)).

This is often more budget-efficient than continually purchasing an unlimited-protection put, but it protects a defined correction range rather than a catastrophic loss.

### E. Calendar and overlapping collars

More sophisticated programs may use:

- Longer-dated protective puts;
- Shorter-dated calls sold repeatedly;
- Staggered or overlapping expirations;
- Delta-based strikes rather than fixed percentage strikes.

Allspring’s institutional illustration purchases approximately 10% OTM 12-month puts over time, sells four-week 15-delta calls, and also sells four-week 5-delta puts as part of a calendar put-spread collar. It is materially more complex than a simple stock collar, but it illustrates how institutions manage term structure, volatility skew, and roll-date risk rather than requiring equal call and put deltas ([Allspring/Cboe](https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/whitepapers/Allspring_options-based-downside-protection.pdf)).

---

## Final recommendation

For a straightforward collar on 100 shares:

```
Sold Call Delta: 0.20 to 0.30
(reason: balances useful premium against retaining upside; use 0.20 when keeping
the shares is more important and 0.30 when funding protection is more important)

Bought Put Delta: -0.20 to -0.30
(reason: provides a practical balance between hedge cost and protection; use
approximately -0.30 for a higher floor and approximately -0.20 for cheaper tail protection)

Symmetric vs Asymmetric: Prefer asymmetric, objective-based construction.
Choose the put from the required loss floor, then choose the call from the
acceptable upside cap and premium budget. Do not force equal deltas.

Example Collar:
Stock: $100
Sell call: $105 strike, Delta +0.295, premium approximately $1.383
Buy put: $95 strike, Delta -0.249, premium approximately $1.361
Net credit/debit: approximately $0.022 credit per share, or $2.20 per collar
```

For most investors seeking a balanced starting point, search first around a **25–30 delta short call and a 20–25 delta long put**, using the same expiration. Then adjust the strikes based on the actual maximum acceptable loss, acceptable sale price, bid/ask spreads, dividends, tax consequences, and whether assignment is genuinely acceptable.

## Sources

1. Options Industry Council, “Collar—Protective Collar”: https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/collar-protective-collar  
2. Options Industry Council, “Options Delta”: https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/delta  
3. Fidelity, “Selecting a Strike Price and Expiration Date”: https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/investment-products/options/selecting-strike-price-expiration-date  
4. Cboe, S&P 500 95-110 Collar Index methodology: https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/newcollardescriptionoct1909.pdf  
5. AQR, “Risk and Return of Equity Index Collar Strategies”: https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Journal-Articles/Risk-and-Return.pdf  
6. Allspring/Cboe, “Options-Based Downside Protection”: https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/whitepapers/Allspring_options-based-downside-protection.pdf  
7. OIC, “ERISA Pension Funds & Listed Options”: https://www.optionseducation.org/getmedia/7f79f663-fef8-4c84-ac81-534cebbee9b7/erisa2001.pdf
